delayed-routing11 tests

What does late feedback cost a market router?

Hedge/LMSR routing with delayed feedback: regret ≤ ln N/η + ηT/8 + ηD/2 (mean delay inflates horizon by 1+4d̄), 12× regret from ignoring delay against a reactive adversary, delay-tuned rate too cautious on oblivious data, LMSR subsidy ~20× at mean delay 5.

Abstract Code →

Hedge/LMSR routing of modular experts when losses arrive after device-dependent delays: regret ≤ ln N/η + ηT/8 + ηD/2 with D the total outstanding rounds, so mean delay d̄ inflates the horizon by 1+4d̄; ignoring delay costs 12× regret against a reactive adversary at delay 100, the worst-case tuned rate is too cautious on oblivious data, an observable-count adaptive rate recovers most of it, and LMSR subsidy grows about 20× at mean delay 5. Stylised.

balanced-routing10 tests

Is load balancing a congestion price?

Capacity-constrained expert routing as a congestion-priced market: softmax with dual prices, verifier-computable duality-gap certificate from prices alone, sign-update balancing has a ≈2.5/√B sampling floor plus a step-size limit cycle, closed-form two-expert price of balance, Hoeffding load audit.

Abstract Code →

Capacity-constrained expert routing is a softmax with a per-expert price, the Lagrange multiplier of its capacity, and the dual is smooth and concave. Any price vector gives a computable upper bound and, after repair toward the uniform assignment, a feasible lower bound, so a verifier certifies near-optimality from prices alone (gap below 10−4 at the optimum, always above the true suboptimality). Sign-update balancing has a sampling floor of about 2.5/√B in max relative overload that no step size removes, plus a step-proportional limit cycle on a fixed batch (22.6% at γ=0.2, 1.2% at 0.01). Two-expert Gaussian price of balance is closed form with price shift equal to the median gap; a Hoeffding audit of ln(2N/δ)/(2ε2) tokens covered 400 of 400 trials. Synthetic scores only. Stylised.

kelly-markets11 tests

Is risk tolerance the learning rate of a wealth market?

Fractional-Kelly wealth markets as expert routers: risk-tolerance-weighted price, ln(1/s)/λ regret bound, growth-optimal λ*=(π−p)/(q−p), manipulation cost V·χ² vs LMSR b·KL (7.5× stiffer at p=0.99), and a switching-truth trade-off where λ≈0.1–0.2 beats full Kelly 3–7×.

Abstract Code →

When agents bet a fraction λ of wealth Kelly-style, the clearing price is the λ·wealth-weighted mean belief, total wealth is conserved, and λ=1 is exactly the Bayes mixture. Market log-loss exceeds expert i’s by at most ln(1/si)/λi on any sequence (loose on i.i.d. data), the growth-optimal fraction is (π−p)/(q−p), and moving the price against calibrated others costs Vχ²(p0‖p): equal to LMSR b·KL at b=2V for small shifts but 7.5× stiffer at p=0.99. On a truth that switches regimes, full Kelly is wrong about half of every segment (regret about 1630 at T=4000) while λ of 0.1–0.2 cuts it 3–7×. Binary events, static experts. Stylised.

topk-routing6 tests

How should a router pick k distinct experts?

Top-k MoE routing as a capped Hedge market: price min(1, λ w_i) with exact KL projection, regret vs the best fixed k-set held under k ln(N/k)/η+ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it), plain normalisation prices experts above 1 (282/300 rounds, loss understated 3.2×), and systematic sampling gives exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower variance.

Abstract Code →

Sparse mixture-of-experts routing as a capped Hedge market: expert prices are min(1, λ wi) with a single shadow price λ and an exact KL projection. Regret against the best fixed k-set stayed within k ln(N/k)/η + ηTk/2 in every run (41–58% of it, not proved here); plain normalisation prices an expert above 1 in 282 of 300 rounds and understates loss 3.2×; systematic sampling realises exactly k distinct experts with 8–14× lower loss variance. Oblivious losses only.

sleeping-ledger8 tests

How should a router treat modules that are usually asleep?

A self-financed wealth ledger for specialist modules that sleep: total wealth conserved exactly, sleeping wealth frozen (one private ledger per regime), regret ≤ ln(1/π_i)/η + η·n_i in the module's *own* awake time, entry of a module with wealth ε costs incumbents ln(1/(1−ε))/η; matches the regime oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000) where forced-to-report Hedge sits at 0.30 and fixed share is worse.

Abstract Code →

If only awake modules report and each awake module’s wealth is multiplied by 1+η(ℓ̂−ℓi), the ledger is exactly budget balanced, sleeping wealth never moves (each regime keeps a private ledger), and a module’s regret against the market on its awake rounds is at most ln(1/πi)/η + ηni in its own awake time (the exponential variant pays ηT/8 and is not budget balanced). Admitting a module with wealth ε costs each incumbent ln(1/(1−ε))/η in its bound. With recurring regimes the ledger matches the per-round oracle (0.1004 vs 0.1000, regret about 2.7 whatever the number of specialists) while a forced-to-report Hedge sits at the generalist (0.30) and fixed share is worse (0.34–0.36). The bound is loose (measured regret 2.7 against a bound near 103); losses bounded, wake sets exogenous.

sleeping-incentives9 tests

Can a module game a ledger by choosing when to sleep?

When may a module choose to sleep? The ledger pays exactly leave-one-out savings ηW_A(1−p_i)S_i; sleeping *after* seeing losses gains wealth ηp_Bθ(1−θ)/2 (best 1/8) and takes the market in ~130 rounds with the router's loss unchanged; committed *before* serving it is a real saving; the deterring tax ηp_B/2 is a fixed share that halves honest specialists in 6 rounds.

Abstract Code →

Yes, if it declares after seeing its loss. The wealth ledger pays each awake module exactly its leave-one-out saving, ηWA(1−pi)Si, but a module that sleeps whenever its own loss exceeds θ earns ηpBθ(1−θ)/2 per unit wealth against an equal-skill honest rival (best 1/8 at θ=1/2) and takes the market from a 0.1 share in about 130 rounds, while the router’s realised loss stays at 0.5. Declared before the router serves, the same wealth is a real saving that falls from 0.125 to 0.011 as the module’s signal about its own loss gets noisier. A sleeping tax that stops the exploit must be at least ηpB/2, a fixed-share rate that halves an honest specialist asleep 90% of the time in 6 rounds, so commitment, not taxation, is the fix. Two modules, uniform losses, threshold strategies; mean-field predictions 3–8% slow.

decision-markets16 tests

What does it cost to route between models with conditional markets, and what does a stake do to the answer?

Conditional markets that route between models: inverse-propensity Brier is proper even when the router reads the report, exploration costs exactly 1+(K−1)e^{ω²/2τ²} in payment variance (probit: infinite for τ ≤ ω), and a stake gap distorts the reported gap by a closed-form fixed point with second-order harm.

Abstract Code →

Markets that forecast each model’s loss if chosen only ever see the chosen arm. An inverse-propensity Brier payment is exactly proper even when the router reads the report (without the weight a trader shades its forecast, or hides), and its price is exact: E[1/π] = 1+(K−1)eω2/2τ2, so payment variance blows up as the router cools (a probit router has infinite variance for τ ≤ ω; Monte Carlo at τ=0.3 sees 29 against the exact 195). Exploration regret is at most 0.2785τ. Equal owner stakes cancel in the decision, a stake gap shifts the reported gap by a closed-form fixed point, and the loss it causes is second order, ∝(ΔB/k)2. Gaussian, one-shot, stylised.

module-entry6 tests

What share of the mass should a new module get?

Admitting new modules to a Hedge/LMSR router: regret certificates obey a Kraft identity Σ e^{−c_i}=1, so uniform entry 1/(n+1) is the unique minimax rule; prior-optimal shares P_j/S_j cost H(P); the price of entry is exactly ln(1/π)/η independent of the quality gap.

Abstract Code →

When a modular system adds an expert to a Hedge/LMSR router, the regret certificate to every expert is ci/η + ηT/8 with ci = ln(1/πi) + Σj>i ln(1/(1−πj)), and for any share sequence Σi e−ci = 1 (a Kraft identity). So uniform entry π = 1/(n+1) is the unique minimax rule (every ci = ln N, against 4.1–9.7 for constant shares at 4+12 modules), and against a prior on which module will be best the optimal shares are Pj/Sj with expected coefficient equal to the entropy of the prior. The price of entry is exactly ln(1/π)/η for a better arrival and ln(1/(1−π))/η for a worse one, independent of the quality gap; a recency prior cuts simulated regret from 3.11 to 2.70 nats. Known arrival rounds, fixed η. Pure-Python, 6 tests.

06

Prediction-market design

Liquidity, fees, privacy and manipulation in the LMSR markets that aggregate verifier beliefs. Topic page →

anytime-liquidity12 tests

What does not knowing the horizon cost a market maker?

LMSR with time-varying liquidity as anytime Hedge: b_t = c*√t costs exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound, doubling is 1.70× worse, and self-tuning liquidity makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 vs 102 on easy data).

Abstract Code →

An LMSR with liquidity b routes like Hedge with rate 1/b, but the tuned b needs the horizon T. A bt = c√t schedule with c* = 1/(2√ln N) pays exactly √2 over the horizon-aware bound (1.36 rising to 1.41 measured); the doubling trick is 1.70× worse than the continuous schedule against a price-reactive adversary; and self-tuning liquidity bt = Δt−1/ln N makes the subsidy equal the accumulated mixability gap (1.3 against 102 on easy data) with regret at most 2Δ. Regret analysis only. Stylised.

private-markets6 tests

The subsidy cost of privacy in prediction markets

Differentially private LMSR via the binary-tree mechanism: path-wise loss bound, and the accuracy/subsidy cost of privacy.

Abstract Code →

Differentially private LMSR via the binary-tree mechanism: error scales as 1/(bε), tree noise beats per-release noise ~15×, and privacy noise is exploitable so market-maker loss far exceeds b ln 2. Stylised.

market-manipulation9 tests

Who pays for the information in a manipulated market?

Manipulating an LMSR verification market: manipulator loss b·KL(q‖τ) equals the extra informed rent, and manipulation raises accuracy only in a liquidity band (thin: costs 1−2q; deep: neutral).

Abstract Code →

An uninformed manipulator pushing an LMSR verification market from q to τ loses exactly b·KL(q‖τ), which equals to the digit the extra rent it hands to informed traders; the accuracy change is μ[e1(1−q) − e0q − (1−2q)], positive only in a liquidity band (0.107, 0.413 in the baseline): below it nobody enters and manipulation costs 1−2q accuracy, above b = Nc/(H(q)−ln(1/(1−ε))) entry is certain and manipulation is neutral. Matches an executable LMSR Monte Carlo. Stylised.

market-sandwich13 tests

What does a slippage limit give away in a prediction market?

Sandwiching an LMSR verification market: attacker profit is exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost, needs capital ≈ εb/(1−p), dies to a fee ≈ v(1−p)/(2b); pro-rata batching keeps 99% of the extraction, random ordering cuts it 3×.

Abstract Code →

A searcher who buys before and sells after a victim's LMSR trade extracts exactly the victim's slippage tolerance times its fair cost (εC0, error 1.4×10−14 over 216 instances), with a closed-form front-run of about εb/(1−p) shares, so return on capital falls as 1/b. A proportional fee of about v(1−p)/(2b) makes it unprofitable at any tolerance; the victim's optimal tolerance grows only like √log of the stakes; pro-rata batching keeps 0.989–0.999 of the extraction and uniformly random ordering cuts it exactly 3×. Stylised.

order-flow-liquidity10 tests

Who trades decides how liquid a verification market should be

Glosten–Milgrom vs LMSR for a verification market: informed share fixes b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2e-16), peak misspecification regret is scale-free and overconfident b costs 1.5–2.4× more, LMSR subsidy → b* ln 2 is the spread GM charges.

Abstract Code →

A Glosten–Milgrom market maker facing an informed share μ with accuracy q moves its posterior log-odds by exactly 2·atanh(μ(2q−1)) per net buy, so its price path is an LMSR with b* = 1/(2 atanh m) (verified to 2×10−16). A wrong b costs log loss only in a transient whose peak is scale-free in m and 1.8–2.5× worse when overconfident; the LMSR subsidy tends to b* ln 2, exactly the spread the GM maker charges. Stylised.

lmsr-fees8 tests

What does a fee do to a prediction market’s price?

Proportional fees on an LMSR verification market: exact no-trade band [q/(1+f),(q+f)/(1+f)], price lag q/(1+f), dead-market cliff f ≥ 2a−1 (threshold 2 atanh f at ½), exact fee revenue f·b·ln((1−p₀)/(1−p_T)), and a break-even fee that costs +38% Brier error.

Abstract Code →

A proportional fee f on an LMSR verification market gives every trader an exact no-trade band [q/(1+f), (q+f)/(1+f)] of width f/(1+f), so an informed trader leaves the price at q/(1+f). At price ½ a signal of log-likelihood ratio λ moves the price iff f < tanh(λ/2) = 2a−1, above which the market is dead; fee revenue on a monotone path is exactly fb ln((1−p0)/(1−pT)). With ten 0.65-accurate traders, the break-even fee (≈0.11) raises Brier error from 0.115 to about 0.16 and revenue is hump-shaped in f. Naive traders, synthetic signals.

position-rent8 tests

What is a seat in a prediction market worth?

Sequential LMSR seat rents are conditional mutual information: they telescope to the maker's expected loss (≤ b ln 2), fall with position at the Chernoff rate, order only redistributes a fixed total, and entry costs make error fall only ~1/b in the subsidy.

Abstract Code →

In a sequential LMSR verification market the verifier in position k earns in expectation b·I(y; sk | s<k), a conditional mutual information, so seat rents telescope to the maker’s expected loss (at most b ln 2); an explicit cost-function simulation agrees to three decimals. Rents fall with position, the successive ratio approaching e−C (Chernoff information) from below; order only redistributes a fixed total (a 0.9-accurate verifier gets 0.368 of 0.407 first, 0.303 last). With entry cost c, accuracy improves roughly as 1/b: 11 verifiers at b=0.25 (92%), 41 at b=5 (99.6%). Myopic traders, symmetric signals, monotonicity numerical.

market-subspace-descent11 tests

How fast does a prediction market converge when traders only understand part of it?

Convergence of cost-function markets with partially informed traders as randomized subspace descent: maker loss telescopes to ½(e₀'Ae₀−e_T'Ae_T), closed-form slowdown from correlated securities (31→356 rounds at c=0.95, d=5), A-conjugate bundles restore 1−1/d exactly, noisy-belief step size is an SGD step (running mean beats best constant step), LMSR simulation checks the local rates.

Abstract Code →

Traders who each move prices within a subspace of securities make a cost-function market a randomized subspace descent. The market maker’s expected loss telescopes to ½(e0′Ae0 − eT′AeT) whoever trades, so accuracy is bought once. Correlated securities slow single-security traders in closed form (5 securities: 31 rounds to reach 10−3 of the error uncorrelated, 356 at correlation 0.95), while offering A-conjugate bundles restores the exact rate 1−1/d at any correlation. With noisy beliefs the fraction κ a trader moves acts as an SGD step size: floor dκσ2/(2−κ), and a per-security running-mean step beats the best constant step (error 0.26 vs 0.47 at 100 rounds; full steps stay at 5). A simulated 4-outcome LMSR matches the local rate predictions to within 0.01 for two of three bundle designs and is faster than predicted for the third, for a reason not isolated. Quadratic-cost theory with i.i.d. trader arrival and Gaussian belief noise.

cfmm-markets10 tests

What does a constant-product pool concede to informed traders?

Constant-product AMMs as cost-function prediction markets: worst-case loss C0 never attained, informed-trader profit exactly C0(1−n·GM(π)) (ratio to LMSR → ln n, crossover at n=e), polynomial price tails (p=0.999 costs 3.4× LMSR), exact regret identity, no forgiveness gain under regime switches.

Abstract Code →

A Uniswap-style pool with invariant ∏ri = C0n is a cost-function prediction market: its worst-case loss is C0 and is never attained, and a trader who moves the price to belief π earns exactly C0(1 − n·GM(π)) with GM the geometric mean, against C0(1 − H(π)/ln n) for LMSR at equal worst-case loss. Near uniform beliefs the ratio is exactly ln n, so the pool is cheaper than LMSR for two outcomes and dearer from three. Its price tails are polynomial, (C0/gap)n, so pushing a binary price to 0.999 costs 3.4× LMSR. As an expert router it satisfies an exact regret identity (settlement term ≤ C0 plus Bregman terms), but under regime switches it shows no advantage over Hedge (negative result). Symmetric pools, no fees. Pure-Python, 10 tests.

07

Paying contributors

Buying compute, data and model improvements: holdout markets, Shapley payments, contests and races. Topic page →

holdout-market4 tests

Paying for improvements, not for overfitting

Paying for model improvements against a hidden holdout: telescoping budget, a payment-feedback overfitting attack (paid 0.15 while true loss worsens 0.37), and the Ladder fix with its measured cost.

Abstract Code →

A model-improvement market paying holdout-loss decreases: the budget telescopes, but naive payment feedback lets a data-less adversary be paid while the published model's true loss worsens; a Ladder-style threshold removes the attack at a measured cost to honest small contributors. Stylised.

data-valuation-replication9 tests

What does submitting copies earn under Shapley payments?

Shapley and leave-one-out payments under replication: Shapley pays every extra copy even when worthless, saturating at stand-alone value ((n+2)/2× honest), naive evaluators hand over the pot, LOO pays copies 0 but distributes 1/(n+1), dedup underpays lookalikes by 45%.

Abstract Code →

Paying contributors of data or gradients by Shapley value rewards replication even when copies add zero information: in a Bayesian mean-estimation game the replicator's payment rises with every copy to its stand-alone value, exactly (n+2)/2 times the honest payment against n unit-precision others (5.5× at n=9). If the evaluator treats copies as independent the replicator's pot share tends to 100%; leave-one-out pays true copies exactly zero but distributes only 1/(n+1) of the pot; collapsing duplicates fixes it but underpays independent look-alikes by 45%. Exact computation checked against permutation brute force. Stylised.

shapley-sampling9 tests

How should Shapley payments be sampled and audited?

Auditing sampled Shapley payments: exact estimator variances in a saturating game, permutation sampling is exactly efficient but stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (zero for equal contributors) at up to 7% budget error, antithetic reversal gives 1.6× lower RMSE, Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× conservative.

Abstract Code →

In a saturating contribution game v(S)=1−exp(−Σwi) every estimator variance is exact. Permutation sampling always pays out exactly v(N) but is noisy; size-stratified sampling has 6–8× lower variance (exactly zero for equal contributors) yet misses the pot by up to 7% in a run; reversing each permutation cuts RMSE 1.6× at no cost; Hoeffding sample counts are 4–5× larger than needed, and stratification finds the top-3 payees with about 4× fewer samples. Stylised, n≤10.

contest-precision11 tests

How precise should a training-contest leaderboard be?

Winner-take-all training contests scored on a noisy holdout: effort V a_n √m/s with a_2 = a_3 = 1/(2√π) exactly, a precision ceiling V/σ² ≤ λ_max(n) beyond which no pure equilibrium exists (below the zero-rent limit), and the resulting optimal holdout size.

Abstract Code →

In a winner-take-all contest ranked on a noisy holdout of m samples, equilibrium effort is V·an√m/s with a2=a3=1/(2√π) exactly, but the formula stops being an equilibrium once V/σ² passes a ceiling (12.35, 7.78, 6.11, 5.60, 5.80 for n=2, 3, 5, 10, 20) that sits below the zero-rent limit and falls to half of it at n=20. The organiser's optimal holdout is min(mcap, (wVan/2sκ)²): when evaluation is cheap the ceiling, not cost, binds. Quadrature checked against Monte Carlo and brute-force best replies. Stylised.

compute-procurement9 tests

What does it cost to buy decentralised compute?

Buying k units of decentralised compute by reverse auction: exact VCG payment k(k+1)/(n+1) is exactly 2× winners' cost, optimal reserve is exactly v/2, first-price equilibrium matches by revenue equivalence.

Abstract Code →

Reverse auction for k compute units from n devices with private costs: the truthful threshold auction pays exactly k(k+1)/(n+1), twice the winners’ true cost for every n and k (also with a reserve), the buyer-optimal reserve is exactly v/2 (worth up to +1.03 utility in thin markets, nothing once v≥2), and the pay-as-bid equilibrium has closed form and matches revenue (1.3334 vs 1.3333). Stylised.

speed-race12 tests

What does it cost to make workers race?

Paying the first k of n finishers makes speed a contest: π'(1)=(1−k/n)(H_n−H_{n−k}), equilibrium speed R(n−k)(H_n−H_{n−k})/(nc), exact round time nc/((n−k)R); paying all finishers buys no speed, a budget favours winner-take-all until an accuracy floor k_min binds, and recruiting more workers barely speeds the round.

Abstract Code →

If a round pays the first k of n finishers a prize R and workers buy speed at cost c per unit rate, the win probability’s slope at the symmetric point telescopes to (1−k/n)(Hn−Hn−k), so equilibrium speed is R(n−k)(Hn−Hn−k)/(nc) and the round time is exactly nc/((n−k)R). Paying every finisher buys no speed at all; for a fixed budget, speed alone wants winner-take-all (0.10 at k=1 versus 3.2 at k=16 for n=32), and only the statistical floor on k justifies more winners. Recruiting more workers barely helps: total speed bought saturates at kR/c. Exponential races, linear cost, symmetric risk-neutral workers; equilibrium checked on a grid.

race-heterogeneity13 tests

Who drops out of a race when workers have unequal costs?

Paying the first k of n finishers when costs differ: proof of the π'(1) telescoping identity, exact exit rule (slow workers idle iff c_s/c_f ≥ n_f/(n_f−k), never for k ≥ n_f), cost ratio 4 excludes slow workers for k ≤ 3 of 4 fast, convex costs make headcount buy speed.

Abstract Code →

If only the first k of n finishers are paid, a slow worker entering at a vanishing rate wins with probability rate × E X(k) of the fast workers, which gives an exact exit rule: workers with cost ratio cs/cf ≥ nf/(nf−k) stay out entirely, and paying k ≥ nf never excludes anyone (checked by best-entry payoffs at thresholds 4/3, 2, 4). At cost ratio 4 with four fast workers, k ≤ 3 shuts the slow ones out and k=4..7 readmits them (share of prizes 0.21→0.46 against a fair 0.5). The note also proves the telescoping identity behind the symmetric race and shows that with convex speed cost, headcount does buy speed. Two cost types, exponential races, grid-checked equilibria.

private-data-market8 tests

How much accuracy can a market buy from contributors who value their privacy?

Buying private data with a telescoping log-score market: payment equals information, best Gaussian-mechanism noise in closed form, participation iff κa<1 so precision is capped at λ/(cΔ²) for any number of contributors, and early arrivals over-collect (1–22% welfare loss).

Abstract Code →

A market pays each contributor the log-score gain of a public Gaussian belief for releasing a statistic plus Gaussian-mechanism noise, so the expected payment is exactly the information released, ½λln(1+τ/a). The best noise is a closed-form quadratic root, and participation is possible if and only if κa < 1 with κ = cΔ2/λ: precision is capped at λ/(cΔ2) however many contributors arrive, approached geometrically at rate 2σ2/(2σ2+κ), and total payout is at most ½λln(1/(κa0)). Early arrivals add too little noise (1.5–5×; 1–22% welfare loss against a planner), and admitting small data holders first lifts final precision from 28.0 to 34.2. Checked against grid search and 106-run Monte Carlo. Stylised.

08

Decentralised training systems

Gossip, local SGD, pipelines, checkpoints and shared rollouts on unreliable, heterogeneous workers. Topic page →

ratelimit-burst7 tests

How far over its limit can a rate limiter be pushed in a true rolling window?

How far over its limit can a rate limiter be pushed in a true rolling window? Adversarial search over fixed window, sliding log, sliding-window counter, token bucket and leaky bucket: only the sliding log holds the limit; the sliding counter admits up to about 1.5 L and the buckets nearly 2 L, and under Poisson overload at 1.5x load 39-47% of rolling windows exceed the limit for fixed window and buckets. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A stylised free-choice study of five limiters configured as L requests per window W, by adversarial search on an integer tick clock and a Poisson overload test. Only the sliding log never admits more than L in a rolling window. The sliding-window counter admits up to about 1.4–1.5L (1.40, 1.45, 1.48 for W = 20, 40, 100), and token and leaky buckets admit 1.90–1.98L; fixed window reaches 2L. At 1.5× offered Poisson load, 47% of rolling windows exceed L for fixed window, 39% for the buckets, 8.8% for the sliding counter and none for the sliding log. The searches give lower bounds, not proofs; one client, no distributed state.

gossip-consensus7 tests

What can one stubborn node do to gossip training?

Pairwise gossip for decentralised training: exact contraction (n−2)/(2(n−1))≈½ per matching round (~20 rounds at any n), noise floor (n−1)(n−2)s²/n, one stubborn node captures consensus at rate 1−1/(n(n−1)), trust-region clipping caps drift at τ/(n(n−1)) per step.

Abstract Code →

Pairwise gossip averaging as a stand-in for all-reduce: disagreement contracts by exactly (n−2)/(2(n−1)) ≈ ½ per matching round (about 20 rounds at any n), the noise floor is (n−1)(n−2)s²/n (matched to 0.3%), a single stubborn node captures the honest mean at exact rate 1−1/(n(n−1)), and a trust-region clip turns capture into linear creep of at most τ/(n(n−1)) per step. Stylised.

local-sgd-bias8 tests

What does infrequent averaging do to the answer?

Local-SGD/DiLoCo-style averaging on heterogeneous quadratics: exact fixed point with saturating weights 1-(1-ηa_i)^H, non-monotone bias to the unweighted mean, exact a_i/w_i correction, step-count inflation moves the fixed point 0.50→0.91, wall-clock-optimal sync interval.

Abstract Code →

Local-SGD / DiLoCo-style averaging of heterogeneous quadratic workers has a closed-form fixed point: a weighted mean of the workers' optima with weights 1−(1−ηai)H that saturate, so it is exactly unbiased at H=1, forgets curvature as H grows (converging to the unweighted mean), and is non-monotone in between. Weighting by ai/wi removes the bias exactly; if the server trusts claimed step counts, a low-curvature worker moves the fixed point from 0.50 to 0.91 by claiming 100 steps instead of 5, tying communication savings to verified work. Wall-clock-optimal H under a bias tolerance is 5.7× faster than H=1 at moderate comm cost, with a non-interval feasible set. Noise formulas match Monte Carlo. Stylised.

churn-checkpointing8 tests

How often should preemptible workers checkpoint?

Checkpoint interval for preemptible decentralised training: exact Lambert-W optimum independent of restart cost, Young/Daly overshoot 5–25%, flat within 2×, synchronous efficiency wall (50% at n≈691), flaky workers cut throughput 5×.

Abstract Code →

Exact checkpoint interval under Poisson churn: w* = (1+W0(−e−1−λC))/λ, independent of restart cost, with Young/Daly overshooting by 5–25%; intervals within 2× cost under 3.5%; a synchronous job on n workers restarts at rate nλ so efficiency falls to 50% near n≈700, and admitting flaky workers cut throughput five-fold. Stylised.

pipeline-replication11 tests

Should a pipeline replicate stages or skip them?

Replicate or skip? pipeline stages on unreliable workers: exact binomial drop law, replicas cannot beat the shared-domain floor (1−ρ)^L, a 4-stage skip budget halves workers for a 1e-3 drop rate (240 → 96), cost-optimal design shifts from skipping to replication as skips get costly.

Abstract Code →

A microbatch crosses L stages held by workers that come and go. The drop probability is the exact binomial tail P(Bin(L,q)>s) with stage outage q = ρ + (1−ρ)(1−a)r, so replicas cannot lift success above the shared-domain floor (1−ρ)L: at L=48, ρ=10−3 no r reaches a 1% drop rate, but allowing one skipped stage makes r=3 enough. At a=0.9 a four-stage skip budget cuts the workers for a 10−3 drop rate from 240 to 96; under a per-skip quality loss κ the cost-optimal design is skip-heavy for cheap skips and moves to replication as κ grows (gain over no-skip 2.9× down to 1.08×). Independent outages, multiplicative skip penalty. Stylised.

hetero-pipeline8 tests

How should a model be cut across devices of unequal speed?

Cutting a model across heterogeneous devices: exact greedy bottleneck partition (matches DP, with memory caps), W/V ≤ T* < W/V + m·w_max/V, speed-blind splitting costs exactly v̄/v_min (2.4× at σ=0.5), device order is the residual decision (sorts no better than arbitrary, swap search within 1.1%), memory inverse to speed costs 1.7×.

Abstract Code →

For a fixed pipeline order, greedy filling is an exact test of a target stage time (agreeing with an independent dynamic program, with and without memory caps), and every order satisfies W/V ≤ T* < W/V + m wmax/V. A speed-blind equal split costs exactly v̄/vmin times the lower bound (2.40× at log-speed spread 0.5, 8.25× at 1.0) while speed-aware cutting stays within 1.4% at 240 layers. What is left is the device order: at 14 layers and 6 devices the worst order is 1.34× the best, fast-first and slow-first sorts do no better than an arbitrary order (all about 1.16× optimal), and pairwise-swap search gets within 1.1%; the penalty fades to 1.03× at 224 layers. Memory that shrinks as speed grows inflates the bottleneck 1.7×. No communication cost, static speeds.

straggler-backup10 tests

What does it cost to skip the slowest workers?

Waiting for the fastest k of n workers: exact order-statistic round times (Pareto mean finite iff n−k+1 > 1/α), exact SGD time-to-accuracy with a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× over wait-for-all at s=0, 1.12× at s=32), joint step tuning, and the exact selection bias of the speed filter with Horvitz–Thompson correction.

Abstract Code →

Waiting for the fastest k of n workers has exact round time s + (Hn−Hn−k)/μ for exponential tails, and for Pareto tails the mean is finite iff n−k+1 > 1/α, so with α ≤ 1 waiting for everyone has infinite expected round time. For SGD on a quadratic the time to accuracy has a minimum k and an interior optimum (34× faster than waiting for all at zero fixed cost, 1.12× at large fixed cost). If speed correlates with data, the fastest-k average is biased by Σ(πi/k−1/n)θi; Horvitz–Thompson reweighting removes it but only pays when the bias is large.

rollout-commons7 tests

Does a bigger swarm learn more from shared rollouts?

Rollout sharing in swarm RL as a public-goods game: Nash gives every agent a lone agent's learning level whatever N (total effort caps at (a/c−1)/θ) while efficient welfare is 4.5× at N=256; at θ=1 one agent generates; a Pigouvian matching subsidy (fraction θ(N−1)/(1+θ(N−1)) of cost) implements the optimum; junk beats honesty iff c−ε > p(τ+F).

Abstract Code →

Not without incentives. With diminishing returns and a peer-rollout discount θ, symmetric Nash play gives every agent exactly the learning level of a lone agent whatever the swarm size (total effort caps at (a/c−1)/θ), while the efficient level grows linearly in N: welfare per agent is 4.5× higher at N=256. At θ=1 a single agent generates everything. A Pigouvian matching subsidy covering θ(N−1)/(1+θ(N−1)) of cost implements the optimum exactly, and junk rollouts beat honesty iff c−ε > p(τ+F).

stale-rollouts7 tests

How stale can a shared rollout be before it is worthless?

Stale off-policy rollouts in swarm RL: exact importance-weight moments (E w²=e^{δ²}, ESS fraction e^{−δ²}), closed-form truncation bias/variance verified by simulation, best cap cuts shift-estimation MSE 1.9× at δ=1 and ~750× at δ=3, and the staleness window √ln(1/ρ)/drift.

Abstract Code →

With Gaussian policies whose mean has moved by δ standard deviations, the importance weight has exact moments E w = 1 and E w² = eδ², so the effective-sample fraction is e−δ² (0.37 at δ=1) and a learner needing fraction ρ accepts a lag of √ln(1/ρ)/drift policy versions. Truncating weights has closed-form lost mass, bias and variance (matched by simulation); the best cap cuts the mean-shift estimator’s MSE 1.9× at δ=1, 12.8× at δ=2 and about 750× at δ=3, and finite-sample ESS is optimistic once weights are heavy-tailed. Equal-variance Gaussians, one statistic.

forgetting-law9 tests

How fast does a shared model forget a task, and does splitting it into modules help?

Exact catastrophic-forgetting law for sequential training on random low-rank tasks: (r/d)(1−r/d)(ρᵏ−λᵏ) rises then vanishes, uniform module routing dilutes it but sharing wins on seen-plus-fresh loss, conflicting tasks leave a floor 2rτ²/d.

Abstract Code →

Training to convergence on random rank-r tasks in Rd is a projection, and the expected loss on a task learned k tasks ago is exactly (r/d)(1−r/d)(ρk−λk): zero when learned, a peak (0.044 at d=12, r=3, lag 2.5) at a lag near 0.7d/r, then decay because the tasks agree; matched by simulation to the third decimal. Routing tasks to m modules dilutes both rates by m and cuts short-horizon forgetting (5.9× at T=4, m=8) but a single shared model minimises seen-plus-fresh loss at every horizon tried, and two modules forget more than one at T=12. With conflicting tasks forgetting has a floor 2rτ²/d that only task-specific modules remove. Stylised: linear regression, exact convergence, isotropic tasks.

merge-law7 tests

How should independently trained modules be merged, and how much does parallel training buy?

Merging independently trained modules on random low-rank tasks: exact residual 1−2amp+a²(mp+m(m−1)p²), optimal scale 1/(1+(m−1)p) (averaging stalls at (1−p)², unscaled sum diverges), harmonic 1/m decay, parallel speedup only logarithmic (8.9× at m=16, d/r=8).

Abstract Code →

Averaging m modules trained to convergence on random rank-r tasks has an exact residual error 1−2amp+a2(mp+m(m−1)p2) with p=r/d, needing only isotropy. The optimal scale is 1/(1+(m−1)p) and leaves (1−p)/(1+(m−1)p): plain averaging stalls at (1−p)2 (0.78 vs 0.47 at m=8, d/r=8) and unscaled task arithmetic diverges (56 at m=64). The decay is harmonic, not geometric, so m parallel workers give a wall-clock speedup that grows only logarithmically (8.9× at m=16, 17× at m=64) and halves in efficiency near m≈d/r×2.5. Seen and fresh losses are closed forms matched by simulation. Stylised: linear regression, exact convergence, consistent isotropic tasks.

replay-law8 tests

When should a continual learner replay an old task, and does a fixed schedule beat random replay?

Exact expected forgetting under replay schedules in sequential training on random low-rank tasks: 2×2 matrix recursion matches simulation, one replay is best at the forgetting-peak lag yet removes only 25–42%, a fixed period beats random replay only below ~1.2–3 peak lags, halving forgetting needs rate 0.25 (d=12, r=3) to 0.015 (d=128, r=1).

Abstract Code →

Replaying a task alongside each fresh one is a joint projection, so the expected loss on a tracked task is an exact product of 2×2 matrices for any schedule (matched to simulation at every step; recovers the no-replay law). One replay is best at the forgetting-peak lag — 5 at d=32, r=4; 89 at d=128, r=1 — yet removes only 25–42% of total forgetting (replaying at step 1 barely helps at small r/d). A period longer than the peak lag never touches the peak, and a fixed period beats random replay at the same rate only below roughly 1.2–3 peak lags (e.g. 1/8 at d=32, r=4, but random wins at 1/12). Halving forgetting needs a rate 0.25 at d=12, r=3 and 0.015 at d=128, r=1; tasks with 2r≥d are fully recovered by one replay. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, one tracked task.

replay-memory8 tests

How much of an old task must a continual learner store, and is it better to replay a little often or a lot rarely?

Partial replay when only m of an old task's r examples are stored: exact 2×2 law interpolating no replay and full replay, best-step saving nearly linear in m/r, and at a fixed example budget a few large replays beat many small ones by only 0.1–6 points.

Abstract Code →

If only m of an old task’s r examples are stored, replaying them with a fresh task is “project out the stored subspace, then take a plain step in dimension d−m”. That gives an exact 2×2 mean-state matrix interpolating no replay (m=0) and full replay (m=r, matched to replay-law to 12 digits), agreeing with simulation at every step. One replay at its best step recovers a fraction of the full saving that is nearly linear in m/r (0.23, 0.47, 0.72 at ¼, ½, ¾ for d=12, r=4; within 0.004 of m/r at d=128, r=8). At a fixed rate, half the memory buys 57–65% of the saving. At a fixed budget of examples per step, one large replay beats many small ones, but only by 0.1–2 points of total forgetting in wide models and up to 6 in a tight one (d=12, r=4), so buffer size matters more than schedule. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, one tracked task.

router-impurity8 tests

When continual-learning tasks conflict, how much does a task-aware router of modules actually buy?

Task-aware routing when continual-learning tasks conflict: the long-run floor is (2r/d)[τ_w²+τ_b²(1−Purity)] with purity = 1 − the router's Gini impurity, random modules buy nothing, a perfect router removes (m−1)/(K−1) of the between-cluster floor, and a 10% routing error gives back 36%.

Abstract Code →

With cluster-structured conflicts, the long-run loss on an old task is exactly (2r/d)[τw² + τb²(1 − Purity)], where Purity is one minus the router’s expected Gini impurity (matched to simulation within 0.3–2.3% across six routers). Random routing to any number of modules leaves the whole floor; a perfect router onto m modules removes exactly (m−1)/(K−1) of the between-cluster floor, so half needs 5 of 8 clusters’ worth of modules; and a routing error q costs 2q of impurity at first order (10% error returns 36% of the shared-model floor at K=8, 25% returns 59%). Purity is auditable with an unbiased pair-collision estimator. Stylised: realizable linear regression, exact convergence, Gaussian cluster centres, hard routing.

outer-momentum9 tests

How should the outer optimiser and sync interval be set when workers run H local steps per round?

DiLoCo-style outer momentum: H inner steps precondition the outer quadratic (κ_H ≈ κ/H), exact per-mode rates, optimal momentum falls 0.88 → 0.01 with H (fixed 0.7/0.9 Nesterov needs 4–8× more rounds), and the wallclock-optimal sync interval is H* ≈ C (sync cost in inner steps), worth ≈ √C/2.

Abstract Code →

On a quadratic, H inner steps make the outer optimiser see curvatures 1 − (1 − ηa)H, which saturate at 1: the outer condition number shrinks from κ to about κ/H (1000 → 16.1 at H=64). Per-round rates are exact 2×2 spectral radii (matching literal simulation), the tuned heavy-ball outer step puts every mode at exactly √β*, and the best momentum falls from 0.88 at H=1 to 0.01 at H=1024, so a fixed Nesterov 0.7/0.9 needs 4–8× more rounds. With a sync costing C inner steps, the wallclock-optimal interval is H* ≈ C, worth about √C/2 over syncing every step (16× at C=1000), while plain averaging has no interior optimum. Stylised: noiseless quadratic with a shared Hessian.

noisy-local-sgd9 tests

How much gradient noise survives in DiLoCo-style local SGD, and how should the outer step, momentum, worker count and sync interval be set against it?

Noise floor of DiLoCo-style local SGD: exact stationary loss αV(1+β)/((1−β)s(2(1+β)−αs)), independent of H at α=1, momentum free at equal effective step, near-linear speedup in M, and a noise-limited sync interval that grows as the floor target falls.

Abstract Code →

On a quadratic with M workers, H noisy inner steps and a heavy-ball outer step, the stationary variance per mode is exactly αV(1+β)/((1−β)s(2(1+β)−αs)) with V the averaged inner noise and s = 1 − (1 − ηa)H, matching literal simulation to 0.2%. At α = 1 the floor is independent of H; for small α more local steps shrink it by less than a factor of 2. Momentum costs no extra floor at equal effective step (and lowers it at large steps), workers give near-linear speedup (331× at M = 256, α still below 1), and unlike the noise-free case the best sync interval grows as the noise-floor target falls (H* = 5, 11, 38 at C = 10), up to 41× faster than syncing every step. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared Hessian, fixed α.

partial-participation11 tests

What happens to local SGD when workers drop in and out?

Local SGD when workers drop in and out: exact floors for participant averaging (E[1/K|K≥1]) and expected-count normalisation (stable iff αsc<2), at matched speed the fixed normaliser is quieter by E[K]E[1/K] at small steps, and reliable workers bias the fixed point unless inverse-propensity weighted.

Abstract Code →

Each of N workers joins a round with probability p. Averaging the participants has exact stationary variance αVwm/(s(2−αs)) with m = E[1/K | K≥1]; dividing by the expected count instead is stable only for αs < 2/c, c = 1+(1−p)/(Np), and cannot contract faster than 1−1/c per round (0.22 at N=32, p=0.1). At matched speed the fixed normaliser is quieter at small steps by E[K|K≥1]·E[1/K|K≥1] (1.34×), and averaging wins only at fast rates. Reliable workers bias the fixed point (0.467 instead of 1.000 in our example) unless displacements are inverse-propensity weighted. Matched to simulation within 0.5%. Stylised.

compressed-sync9 tests

What does compressing the pseudo-gradient cost local SGD, and is it better than syncing less often?

Local SGD with compressed displacements: exact floor (1+ω) and stability limit αs(1+ω/N)<2 for rand-k (more workers restore the step, not the floor), closed form for norm-scaled quantisation, and at equal bytes syncing less often beats compressing.

Abstract Code →

Unbiased compression of each worker's displacement (rand-k, relative variance ω) gives an exact stationary variance αVw(1+ω)/(N s((2−αs)−αsω/N)) and shrinks the stable outer step to 2/(s(1+ω/N)): more workers restore the step (0.47 → 2.44 for ω=99, N=16 → 256) but never the floor, which stays (1+ω)×. Norm-scaled (QSGD-style) quantisation has a closed form through one scalar T = E|d|2; at equal error energy its loss equals coordinate-wise at H=1 and is about 10% worse at H=16, with the stiff mode's variance doubling. For equal bytes, syncing 1/ρ times less often leaves the floor unchanged at α=1 while keeping a fraction ρ multiplies it by 1/ρ. Matched to simulation within 2%. Stylised: quadratic, shared curvature (no client drift), unbiased compressors only.

delayed-outer11 tests

How much outer step does overlapping communication with compute cost, and how many rounds should be in flight?

Overlapping communication in local SGD with τ-round-late outer updates: exact stable step 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) (shrinks ~1/τ), double-root rate τ/(τ+1), exact noise floor matched to simulation, free at small steps, wall-clock-optimal delay ⌈L/T_c⌉ (1.9–7.5× faster than no overlap).

Abstract Code →

Applying the averaged displacement τ rounds late obeys zτ+1 − zτ + c = 0 with c = αs, so the stable step is exactly c < 2 sin(π/(4τ+2)) ≈ π/(2τ+1): 2, 1, 0.62, 0.45 for τ = 0…3, shrinking like 1/τ. The fastest single-mode rate is the double root τ/(τ+1), and the stationary noise floor is an exact Yule–Walker solve (closed form (1+c)/((1−c)c(2+c)) at τ = 1) that matches literal delayed-DiLoCo simulation to 0.3%. Delay is free at small steps (+1% at α = 10−3, τ = 4) but multiplies the floor by 3.9× at c = 0.8. At an equal floor each delay round costs only about 6% more rounds, so the wall-clock-optimal delay is exactly ⌈latency / compute time⌉ (1.9–7.5× faster than no overlap). Stylised: constant delay, identical workers, quadratics, no momentum.

error-feedback-sync9 tests

Does error feedback rescue the noise floor that compressed local SGD loses?

Error feedback in compressed local SGD: exact stability limit 2(2−ρ)Nρ/(Nρ²+4(1−ρ)) and closed-form floor that returns to the uncompressed one at small steps (unbiased compression pays 1/ρ), dropping is biased to the send-rate-weighted mean and the residual removes it at a variance price.

Abstract Code →

Workers keep the unsent part of their displacement and add it to the next message. On a quadratic with random sparsification the second moments close exactly: stability requires αs < 2(2−ρ)Nρ/(Nρ2+4(1−ρ)) — half the unbiased limit for a single worker, above the uncompressed limit for large cohorts — and the floor has a closed form that returns to the uncompressed one at small steps (1.08× at ρ=¼ where unbiased compression pays 4×) while the mean keeps its speed. What the residual buys is unbiasedness: dropping converges to the send-rate-weighted mean, feedback to the true mean, but at a variance that only pays off for very small steps. Top-k is simulation only; stylised quadratics.

heterogeneous-steps9 tests

How should a server weight workers that ran different numbers of inner steps?

Weighting workers that ran different numbers of inner steps: exact floor α²Σw²V/(r(2−r)), worker information I∞·tanh(λH/2) saturates, optimal weights span ≤2× so equal weights lose ≤9/8 (measured ≤1.09) while step-proportional weights lose up to 1.76× per mode and 10.5× on three modes.

Abstract Code →

With worker i running Hi steps, weighted averaging has exact floor α2Σwi2Vi/(r(2−r)), r = αΣwisi. One worker's information is I∞tanh(λH/2): H=8 carries 20% of the ceiling and H=64 93%, so a fast device is worth far less than its step count. Information-optimal weights span at most 2×, hence equal weights lose at most 9/8 (measured ≤1.09), whereas step-proportional (FedAvg-style) weights lose up to 1.76× per mode and 10.5× on three modes when one worker in eight is 256× faster. Matched to simulation within 1%. Stylised: quadratic, shared optimum (no client drift), fixed Hi.

robust-outer11 tests

What does a median or trimmed-mean outer step cost local SGD, and what does it buy against Byzantine workers?

Median and trimmed-mean outer aggregation in local SGD: exact linear loop with floor and bias split, π/2 variance price with no attackers, bounded worst-case bias Φ(z)=1/(2(1−ε)) that more workers cannot average away but a longer inner loop shrinks.

Abstract Code →

Because the median and trimmed mean commute with shifts, the outer loop stays exactly linear: floor αVwv/(s(2−αs)) plus a bias Vwm2/s2, with the same stability limit as averaging. With no attackers the median costs N·Var = 1.35 to 1.56 (→ π/2). With a fraction ε of attackers its bias is bounded (Φ(z) = 1/(2(1−ε)): 0.18 noise-sigmas at ε = 1/8) and beats averaging once the attack offset exceeds about 1.4 sigmas; more workers shrink only the variance part (total loss 0.103 → 0.102 from N=8 to 128), while a longer inner loop shrinks the bias (39× from H=1 to 256). Trimming exactly the attacker count is worse than the median. Matched to simulation within 1.3%. Stylised: quadratic, Gaussian noise, shared curvature, constant-offset attackers.

09

Digital twins & sim-to-real

What a simulated clone of a physical system is worth for training and validating controllers: transfer regret, validation, and randomization. Topic page →

stereo-twin14 tests

A stereo twin that adds Gaussian noise to depth gets the median right: what does it get wrong about over-range errors, safety margins and averaging compared with real disparity-space noise?

Gaussian-depth-noise stereo twin vs real disparity-space noise: median exact, gated mean biased by ≈s², over-range errors up to 191× more frequent at 40 m, a twin 3σ margin exceeded 10× as often, mean-depth averaging floors while averaging disparity converges (negative result at the 60 m range floor). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Real sensor: disparity noise σ = 0.25 px on a 700 px, 0.12 m rig (matches only above 1 px, so 84 m), depth = reciprocal of disparity; twin: Gaussian depth noise with the linearised sd. The median is exact, but the (gated) mean is biased by about s2 (+1.5% at 40 m) and over-estimates of distance are far more common than the twin says: at 40 m P(depth > 1.5Z) is 0.0026 vs 10−5 (191×), and a twin mean + 3σ margin is exceeded 10× as often as designed. Matching the variance leaves 41× on that tail. Averaging 1024 frames of depth floors at 1.5% error where the twin predicts 0.4%, whereas averaging disparity converges; at 60 m the range floor loses 5.5% of looks and flips or removes these effects (reported as a negative result). Stylised: Gaussian i.i.d. disparity noise, no outliers or calibration error.

slosh-twin12 tests

A rigid-body twin of a cart carrying liquid predicts no slosh: how wrong is that, what does a slosh-safe move cost, and what does a stale frequency calibration do to it?

A rigid twin of a cart carrying liquid predicts zero slosh: minimum-time move leaves 10.7 cm (10× tolerance), slosh-safe move is 55% slower, and a full-tank frequency calibration fails at low fill (28 s vs 8.7 s recalibrated; tuning-free bound 24.7 s).

Abstract Code →

Real cart: 80 kg body with a damped spring-mass slosh mode (20 kg liquid, 0.5 Hz at full fill); twin: one rigid mass. The twin gets the centre of mass exactly (RK4 error ~10−14 m) but predicts zero slosh; for a bang-bang rest-to-rest move the real residual is 4μa0sin2(ωT/4)/ω2, matched by exact propagation and RK4. The twin’s minimum-time move (3 m, 4.90 s) leaves 10.7 cm of slosh, 10× a 1 cm tolerance; the fastest move meeting it takes 7.60 s (55% slower) because zero-residual times are whole multiples of two slosh periods. Calibrating ω at a full tank is harmless down to half fill (−5% frequency, 9.5 mm) but at 25% fill the smallest safe null-tuned move takes 28 s vs 8.7 s recalibrated, worse than the tuning-free bound 24.7 s; at fixed acceleration the first unsafe null order is exactly ⌊asin(√ρ)/(π|ε|)⌋+1. Stylised: one linear slosh mode, bang-bang force, no shaper optimisation, no nonlinear slosh.

shaper-twin9 tests

Can an input shaper make a liquid-carrying cart’s move robust to a stale slosh-frequency calibration, and how fast can it be?

Input-shaped moves of a liquid-carrying cart: ZV/ZVD residual sin(πε/2), sin²(πε/2) exactly multiplies the bang-bang residual, so a stale frequency calibration that breaks the null-tuned move (28 s) is harmless to a 5.9 s ZV move; closed-form tolerated error and a fill-band design that spends the tolerance on a shorter shaper.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to slosh-twin. Convolving the twin’s bang-bang acceleration with a ZV or ZVD shaper multiplies the undamped residual exactly by V(ε) = |sin(πε/2)| or sin2(πε/2), ε the frequency error (verified against exact propagation to 10 digits), while distance and the acceleration cap are preserved. Designed at a full tank, both shapers keep the 1 cm tolerance at every fill from 100% to 10% (ε down to −9.5%; worst residual 4.8 mm ZV, 0.6 mm ZVD) in 5.90 s and 6.90 s, where the null-tuned move needs 8 s at half fill and 28 s at 25% and below. Closed forms give the largest tolerated |ε| (e.g. 10.7% for ZV at half fill). Searching the design frequency for a fill band [0.1, 1] yields a 5.85 s ZV move, but only by detuning to spend the whole tolerance (worst residual 9.88 mm, no margin). Stylised: one linear slosh mode, ideal actuator, no nonlinear slosh.

twin-transfer12 tests

What is a digital twin worth for training a controller?

What a digital twin is worth for training a controller: exact LQ sim-to-real regret with a stability cliff, a validation blind spot (zero score gap yet mistrained control without probing), and a twin worth exactly σ²/(vδ²) real samples at any accuracy.

Abstract Code →

In a scalar linear-quadratic plant the twin-trained gain has exact deployment regret, asymmetric with a stability cliff: underestimating actuation to 0.21× is infinitely costly while 2× over costs 0.22. A twin can score perfectly on passive logs (log-score gap exactly 0) yet mistrain the controller, and closed-loop logs are blind along Δa = kΔb, so validation needs designed probing. Used as a ridge prior, a twin with bias δ is worth exactly σ2/(vδ2) real probe steps at every accuracy target (22 steps at δ=0.3), and removes small-sample divergence (3.1% to 0 at n=10). Matched to simulation within 1–4%. Stylised.

randomized-twin9 tests

How wide should domain randomization be, and what does it buy?

Domain randomization over a twin, exactly: cliff-limited width, quartic price when the twin was right, cliff pushed out ~15%, but uniform-average training is not minimax and the best width tracks the prior.

Abstract Code →

Randomizing the twin's input gain over ±ε trains a more conservative gain (monotone in ε; small-width law kε−k* = −(εb)2Jkbb/(6Jkk)) at a quartic price when the twin was right, and moves the deployment stability cliff out by about 15%. At 2.3× the twin's gain the nominal controller has regret 84 versus 1.4 at ε=0.9. But uniform-average training is not minimax: its worst-case regret exceeds the nominal gain's for ε ≤ 0.7, and the best width equals the prior's half-width, paying off only when the prior reaches the cliff. Stylised.

twin-upkeep13 tests

What does it cost to keep a digital twin in sync with a drifting plant, and is probing worth it?

Keeping a digital twin in sync with a drifting plant: closed-form Kalman tracking variance and control regret (matched to simulation), a frozen twin loses half its edge in ln 2/(2(1−ρ)) steps, probing never pays for one drifting parameter, and a two-parameter closed-loop blind direction gives a mean-field dither law ν* ∝ q^{1/6} that self-exciting certainty-equivalent control mostly makes unnecessary.

Abstract Code →

A Kalman twin tracks a drifting actuator gain from the closed-loop data the controller already produces. Its steady-state predictive variance is a closed-form quadratic root (m = q/2 + √(q2/4 + qσ2/v) for a random walk), matching closed-loop simulation to 1–3%, and control regret is ½Jkk(dk*/db)2m (0.00447 predicted vs 0.00466 simulated). A calibrate-and-freeze twin loses half its edge over the population mean after ln 2/(2(1−ρ)) = 34.5 steps. For one drifting parameter a dedicated probing budget never pays (information price 0.70 vs marginal value ≤ 0.04); for two, the closed-loop blind direction makes a fixed-gain twin unobservable and the mean-field optimal dither scales exactly as q1/6, yet simulation shows the controller’s own gain jitter supplies most of that excitation, so the mean-field law is an upper bound. Stylised.

twin-recalibration10 tests

How often, and how long, should a digital twin be re-identified as the plant drifts?

Re-identifying a drifting twin by dedicated experiments: closed-form interval T*∝q_d^{−2/3} with downtime, noise and drift regret exactly equal at the optimum, excess ∝q_d^{1/3}, a 4× drift misjudgement costs ≤26%, but the second-order optimum destabilises 0.7–15% of cycles and a safe schedule is 37–200× worse than an always-on Kalman twin.

Abstract Code →

For a twin refitted from dedicated experiments rather than filtered from operating data, the second-order-optimal schedule is closed-form: interval T* = (4cσ2/(vρqd2))1/3, with experiment downtime, estimation noise and drift regret exactly equal at the optimum, so excess cost scales as qd1/3 (fitted slope 0.333) and 10× cheaper experiments lower it only 2.2×. Misjudging the drift rate by 4× costs at most 26%. But the second-order optimum is unsafe: 0.7–15% of its cycles destabilise the loop, and a schedule with failure probability ≤ 10−3 costs 1.2–16× more and is 37–200× worse than an always-on Kalman twin. Stylised.

twin-elicitation8 tests

What should you pay a digital-twin provider for?

What to pay a digital-twin provider for: cost-paid twins differ from Brier-paid ones, certainty-equivalence loss is quartic in spread, payment caps make the elicited twin jump at a closed-form threshold, and Brier mispays probing by 15×.

Abstract Code →

A provider paid Brier score on the twin’s parameter reports its posterior mean; one paid the deployed control cost reports the Bayes gain, which is more conservative (0.778 vs 0.823 at posterior sd 0.3, mean 1) and equals domain randomization under the provider’s own uncertainty. Certainty equivalence costs a quartic in spread (16× per doubling); reports with equal squared error have regret ratios of 1.3–24×; a payment cap makes the elicited gain jump at a closed-form threshold M* (19.3 in the example) that decides whether rare catastrophic plants are priced in; and Brier under- or over-pays probing by a 15× spread in decision value per unit variance. Stylised.

A Gaussian-mixture e-process on the closed-loop residual audits a deployed twin continuously: it false-alarms 2.4% of the time against 58% for a z-test checked every step. Detection delay follows ≈ 2[ln(1/α)+½ln(1+τ2nU)]/(Δ2U) with U the controller’s own excitation (simulation 0–18% earlier); expected regret accumulated before detection is nearly independent of the gap (8–10 while per-step regret spans 38×); an expensive-control operator needs 11× longer to catch the same gap; and added probing pays only for gross errors (true gain above 2.25× or below 0.35× the twin’s), with the rule failing at the near-cliff edge. Stylised.

What does a Gaussian-clutter radar simulator do to a CFAR detector's false-alarm rate?

A CA-CFAR threshold set in a Gaussian-clutter twin and deployed in gamma-textured (K-distributed) clutter has an exact false-alarm law, matched to direct simulation to ~1%. At design 10−4 the real rate is 9× (ν=5) to 30× (ν=2) too high, and 50× to 358× at 10−6; restoring it costs 1.9–3.7 dB of threshold at 10−4. If texture is shared across the window CFAR is unaffected, so the twin must model spatial correlation. A moment fit of ν from 1000 real clutter cells brings the median to 1.1× (90th percentile 2×), versus ~106 cells to threshold empirically. Stylised: no target, no measured data.

Does a more robust CFAR survive a Gaussian-clutter twin? CA, OS and log-t all inflate 8–44× at design 1e-4 (no detector escapes), a known-scale oracle inflates as much as CA (the test cell's own texture), and CA detects best at equal real Pfa after repair.

Abstract Code →

Four window detectors (cell-averaging, order-statistic at ranks 3N/4 and N/2, log-t) are calibrated in a Gaussian-clutter twin and deployed in gamma-textured clutter. None is meaningfully more robust: at design 1e−4 the false-alarm inflation is 30–44× at ν=2 and 8–9× at ν=5, and the ranking flips with ν and design rate. A known-scale oracle with no window noise inflates 2.88× at 1e−2, ν=2 against cell-averaging’s 3.02×, so most of the error is the test cell’s own texture, which reference cells cannot see. After repairing each threshold to the design rate, cell-averaging detects best everywhere (Rayleigh target, 20 dB, ν=2: 0.758 vs 0.744, 0.732, 0.703), and the twin’s promised detection probability is overstated (0.70 vs 0.43 at 15 dB). No interfering targets, so order-statistic detectors are tested away from their home ground. Stylised.

handover-twin6 tests

What does a light-tailed simulated human do to a collaborative robot's timeout?

When a collaborative robot should give up waiting for a human: J'(τ)=S(τ)(w−c·h(τ)) makes exponential/Weibull simulated humans corner-only (never abort), 3.7% regret in the base case rising to 37–81% for heavy tails and cheap aborts, plug-in lognormal fit regret 1/n (delta method within 11%).

Abstract Code →

A robot that waits for a human and aborts after τ has cost J(τ) = wE[min(T,τ)] + cP(T>τ), with slope S(τ)(w − c·h(τ)). Simulated humans with constant or increasing hazard (exponential, Weibull) therefore have only corner-optimal timeouts and, when aborting costs more than the mean wait, never give up. Against a lognormal human (σ=1.2, an assumed model) the interior optimum is 9.4 s and the light-tailed twin’s regret is 3.7% of the optimum, rising to 37% (σ=1.6) and 81% (σ=2) for heavier tails and cheap aborts. A lognormal twin with the right mean and σ off by 0.2 recovers all but 0.5%. Fitting the correct family from n real trials costs regret ∝ 1/n, matched by the delta method to within 11% (0.0323 at n=10, 0.00034 at n=1000). Stylised: scalar i.i.d. response time, one fixed timeout, no real human data.

A grid cell committed when log-odds built with a twin's sensor model reach ±A has, under the real sensor, an exact error set by the Lundberg exponent θ* (equal to 1 for a correct twin) with a rigorous optional-stopping sandwich. A twin whose free-space false-hit rate is 0.05 against a real 0.15 turns a 10−3 design into 1.45×10−2 (14.5×, matched by simulation; 260× at 0.30), and an optimistic occupied hit rate (0.8 vs 0.6) gives 26×. Stylised: one independent-beam cell.

Demonstrations logged as applied (actuator-clipped) actions bias a linear clone even in a perfect twin: at an actuator limit of 1 the clone gain is 0.58 against the expert’s 0.96 and its real cost is 9.8% higher, with the exact Gaussian-state gain k0 P(|k0x|<U) from Stein’s lemma. Twin errors act through the states they visit and can help: 0.25× noise cuts the gap to 0.002, 2× raises it to 0.75, and a loose twin limit of 3 nearly removes it. Log-state coverage narrower than half the saturation width recovers the expert, while DAgger with applied-action labels converges to a worse gain (0.5575, gap 0.169 vs 0.141). Stylised: scalar plant, population-level fit, no real logs.

A teacher that sees the true state is trained in a twin and cloned into a student that sees only a noisy sensor. Least-squares cloning attenuates the gain to gP/(P+s), where P is the demonstration state variance, so the student depends on the twin only through its process-noise-to-sensor-noise ratio. A twin with a quarter of the real process noise yields a lazy student with excess cost 0.36 (s=0.5) to 1.11 (s=2) against 0.005 to 0.10 from an exact twin, 2.8–3.6× worse than on-policy DAgger in the same twin. A scalar unstable plant is controlled by the LQR gain designed in a twin with no measurement delay. When does a forecast-ensemble twin send the UAV to the wrong place, or make the update worse?

A UAV samples from a corridor to cut forecast error over a region it cannot enter, with sites and Kalman gain taken from a twin’s covariance; the real error after the update is exact (Joseph form, checked against simulation). A matched twin cuts the real error 22%; a twin whose correlation length is 2× too long claims −65% and delivers +28%, because updates are harmful beyond a closed-form radius (ln 2/(ℓr−2−ℓt−2))1/2. What does a deterministic-duration twin of a lab workcell promise, and how many stations does it buy?

A batch is split over k parallel stations with a serial arm handover; a twin running every step at its mean picks k = √(W/a) = 8 and promises 16 min. The real makespan uses the exact expected maximum of gamma branches (checked against harmonic numbers and simulation): with exponential branches it averages 1.86× the promise, only 2.6% of runs finish every branch within its mean, and the 95% quantile is 3.03× the promise. Whether the twin also buys the wrong layout depends on how variability scales with splitting: task-level variability makes it under-buy (optimum 12, 24.7% regret on the 95% quantile), while a chain of random unit steps cancels the effect so k = 8 stays optimal yet the real makespan is still 6–59% above the promise. Fitting the branch-time shape needs about 5 real durations to fix the decision and about 50 to make the predicted makespan accurate to 1%. Stylised: one fork-join stage, i.i.d. gamma branches.

grasp-twin7 tests

How firmly should a robot grip when its friction twin is too clean?

Abstract Code →

A pinch grasp slips if μF < w0 and crushes if F exceeds a fragility limit; with log-normal friction and crush force the expected loss is a sum of two normal CDFs in ln F and its optimum solves a quadratic. A twin whose friction spread is 0.1 instead of 0.3 grips softer, claims a risk of 1.1×10−5 and delivers 0.069 (4.0× the optimum; 11.6× at spread 0.05). A near-zero-spread twin has a flat zero-risk plateau, so its ‘optimal’ force is a tie-break: real slip 0.50 at the lower edge, 0.015 at the upper. Biased friction costs ≈ ½J″Δx² (85% of the optimum at −0.3 in log-friction), and a widened randomisation width can cancel a known bias but costs 1.5× the optimum if the bias is of opposite sign. A plug-in from n real friction measurements has regret matched by the delta method within 5% for n ≥ 50. Stylised: static friction threshold, chosen parameters, no contact dynamics or reactive re-grasp.

uav-energy-twin7 tests

How much battery should a UAV carry when its twin has a constant wind?

Battery reserve of a UAV leg planned in a constant-wind twin: cruise speed nearly right (regret 0.1%) but the energy claim is low by exactly artanh(x)/x (3.5%) and a battery sized to it depletes in 50% of real flights; 5% depletion needs a 39% margin, and the twin speed stalls once wind spread exceeds v−μ.

A leg flown at airspeed v against a headwind that is uniform across flights costs P(v)/(v−w) in energy per distance; a constant-wind twin has no spread. Its cruise speed is nearly right (1.100 vs the real optimum 1.123, regret 0.10%), but its energy claim is low by exactly artanh(x)/x with x = a/(v−μ) (3.5% here), and a battery sized to that claim runs out in 50% of real flights (42% with a 5% margin). A 5% depletion target needs a 39% margin and 1% needs 44%, in closed form, and the real-optimal speed trims only 39.2% to 37.6%. The speed error itself grows to 6.4% of the optimum at wind half-width 0.6, and the twin speed meets a stalling wind (infinite energy) once the half-width exceeds v−μ = 0.80. Refitting the twin to n = 50 logged winds beats the constant-wind speed in 97% of fits. Stylised: one leg, constant airspeed, wind fixed within a flight, chosen parameters, no gusts or turn-back.

loopclosure-twin11 tests

What does a too-clean odometry twin do to a SLAM loop-closure gate?

A SLAM loop-closure gate tuned in a too-clean odometry twin: exact chi-square gate costs and closed-form optimal gate, real noise 2× the twin's rejects 38% of true closures (claimed 2%) at 4.4× the claimed cost, pessimistic twins are not safe either, and ~59 ground-truthed closures repair it.

A back end accepts a loop closure when its squared residual is below a gate; true closures are N(0, s2I), aliased ones are wider, and the cost is a weighted sum of two chi-square probabilities with a closed-form optimal gate in 2-D. A twin whose odometry noise is half the real value picks a gate that claims a cost of 0.094 and 2.1% of true closures rejected; in reality it rejects 38.2% (checked against simulation), costs 4.4× the claim and has 62% regret; a conventional α = 1% gate rejects α1/ρ2 = 32%. A too-pessimistic twin (ρ = 0.5) is not safe either (145% regret), regret depends strongly on how costly a false closure is, a fixed inflation factor is a bet on the true noise, and re-fitting the variance from about 59 ground-truthed closures brings regret under 1% of the twin’s. Stylised: isotropic Gaussian 2-D residuals, hard gate, known costs, no real odometry data.

loop-closure-twin8 tests

What does an odometry twin that is too clean do to a loop-closure gate?

A scalar position filter is tuned in a twin with drift variance T and gates loop closures by a chi-square test on its own covariance. With every closure accepted the real posterior variance is exact (1.47×, 2.14×, 4.03× the twin’s claim for real/twin drift-sd ratios 1.5, 2, 3; simulation within 1%), and genuine closures fail the 99% design gate 5% of the time at ratio 2. With the gate on, rejection compounds into lock-out: real error is 9–16× the ungated value at ratio 2 and 56–182× at ratio 3, growing with horizon. The gate halves error against aliased closures when the twin is right (0.52 vs 1.27) but is 8× worse than no gate at ratio 2 (13.9 vs 1.72), and a gate retuned with the real drift beats no gate only up to ratio 2. Stylised: scalar error, Gaussian drift, simulated not measured.

rendezvous-twin8 tests

How often should a mapping team rendezvous when its twin's odometry drift has no bias?

Abstract Code →

Robots reset their dead-reckoning error at rendezvous; the real error variance is s2t + b2t2 (white noise plus a per-run bias rate), but a twin fitted on short-horizon increments sees only the first term, so it plans a rendezvous every 10 and claims a peak error std of 3.16. The real optimum solves a cubic; at a bias/noise ratio ρ = 0.1/0.3/1/3 the twin's interval has 0.19/1.35/8.65/34.6% regret, the real error is exactly √(1+ρ) times the claim, and under an error budget the twin breaches it for 8–55% of every cycle. In the pairwise frame used for map merging a shared bias cancels (twin regret 5.3% → 0.10% at bias correlation 0.9). Repair needs ground-truth error at a long lag as well as a short one and about 5–10 runs to beat the twin reliably. Variance law and pairwise law checked by Monte Carlo. Stylised: one-dimensional Gaussian error, constant per-run bias, perfect reset.

odometry-twin10 tests

What does a simulator tuned on one-step odometry noise get wrong about drift, relocalisation and loop closure?

A traversal has a persistent bias plus white noise, so real error after T steps has variance σ12(ρT2+(1−ρ)T); a twin fitted to one-step increments, identical for every ρ, predicts σ12T and is off by exactly 1+(T−1)ρ. With 5% of step variance persistent, the twin’s relocalisation interval is 3.4× too long (real miss probability 51.6% against a claimed 5%), and a 3σ loop-closure gate tuned in it accepts true closures with probability 0.64 at T = 200 instead of 0.997; in a closed loop the rejections let error run away (RMS 8.8 m against 0.17 m calibrated). A calibrated gate accepts 97–99% of aliased closures once drift uncertainty exceeds the alias offset, and a variance ratio fitted at one loop length does not transfer to others. Stylised: 1-D Gaussian, assumed one-step-fitted twin, no real odometry data.

safety-twin9 tests

How wrong is a safety margin certified in a Gaussian-disturbance simulator when real gusts are heavy-tailed?

A stabilised vehicle must stay in a corridor for T = 200 steps; the twin’s disturbances are Gaussian, the real ones Student-t with the same variance, so a variance fit cannot tell them apart. The twin’s certificate is exact (a union bound over its stationary tail), yet at the margin certified for δ = 0.01 the real failure probability is 0.29 (ν = 3) to 0.052 (ν = 8), and the margin the real system needs at δ = 0.001 is 7.3× to 1.25× the twin’s, a ratio that grows as δ shrinks. dropout-twin7 tests

How wrong is the thinnest obstacle a lidar twin certifies as detectable when real beam dropout is clustered?

A thin obstacle covers m adjacent lidar beams and is detected if at least k return. The twin drops beams independently at 10%; the real sensor drops them in bursts (a Markov chain with the same rate and lag-1 correlation λ). The exact miss law is a small DP, and for k = 1 the real/twin ratio is (1 + λ(1−p)/p)m−1. At the width certified for miss 10−3 (m = 3) the real miss is 0.041 (λ = 0.6) to 0.067 (λ = 0.8), and the claimed detection range is 4× to 8.3× too long. Inflating the drop rate to match one width is wrong at the others. Stylised: one scan, a simulated ‘real’ sensor, no lidar data.

twin-certification11 tests

Can a digital twin shorten a real-world safety certification?

Can a twin shorten a real-world safety certification? Worst-case size of any k ≤ c rule is exactly P(Bin(n,ε) ≤ c), so a twin prior cannot cut real trials at a fixed level (299 exact zero-failure trials; twin prior reaches 133 only at size 0.26); wrong twins inflate size or block certification.

Abstract Code →

Certifying a failure rate p < ε from n real trials with a twin-derived prior. The worst-case false-certification probability of any ‘certify iff k ≤ c’ rule is exactly P(Bin(n,ε) ≤ c), so by Karlin–Rubin the twin cannot cut real trials at a fixed level: at ε=0.01, δ=0.05 the exact test needs 299 zero-failure trials, a twin prior reaches 133 only at worst-case size 0.26, and the exact test held to the same size needs the same n (1057 vs 1057 for 90% power at p=ε/3). A weakly informative Jeffreys bound is already anti-conservative (size 0.147 at 191 trials). Stylised: one Bernoulli failure rate, no continuous margins.

It does not remove the twin’s own model error bk ~ N(0,τ2): the quoted-minus-real bias is −eKτ2/√(τ2+s2) (formula −0.531, simulated −0.530 at τ=0.5), so only real trials of the chosen plan give an honest real-cost quote. A pick skill is retried until success. The twin draws attempts independently at p = 0.6; in the “real” system each object has a latent success probability (Beta, same mean), so single-attempt validation cannot tell them apart while attempts on one object are correlated. Real failure after k attempts is exactly ∏(b+j)/(a+b+j), a power law k−a against the twin’s geometric law (matched to simulation). selection-twin9 tests

How optimistic is the best of K controllers chosen in a noisy digital twin?

twin-evaluation7 tests

How many real rollouts does a biased digital twin save when evaluating a robot policy?

Evaluating a robot policy with a biased twin as a control variate: unbiased whatever the twin's bias (+0.700 twin-only vs +0.001), exact variance σ²((1−ρ²)/n+ρ²/N), ρ=η for a faithful twin but √η for a noise-free one (1.33× vs 2.0× real-sample gain), worth-it threshold c_T/c_R<(1−√(1−ρ²))²/ρ² (0.072 at ρ=0.5), and 86–125 vs 164 real episodes per policy to rank correctly when twin bias favours the wrong one.

Abstract Code →

Using the twin as a control variate keeps the estimate unbiased whatever the twin's bias (twin-only error +0.700 vs +0.001) with exact variance σR²((1−ρ²)/n + ρ²/N). Real and twin cannot share execution noise, so ρ is set by the observed scenario context: a faithful twin gets ρ=η but a noise-free twin gets ρ=√η (1.33× vs 2.0× real-sample equivalent at η=0.5). A twin is worth its compute only if cT/cR < (1−√(1−ρ²))²/ρ² (0.072 at ρ=0.5), and where twin bias favours the wrong policy, twin-only ranking is wrong while 86–125 real episodes per policy give a 90% correct order against 164 real-only. Stylised: Gaussian returns, exact context replay, no robot data.

twin-pilot6 tests

How big a pilot decides whether a biased digital twin is worth using?

How big a pilot decides whether a biased twin is worth using: threshold ρ*=2√r/(1+r) with a gain linear in ρ−ρ*, so wrong calls are frequent but cheap (regret 0.004–0.016 at ρ=0.5), decision-regret law f·slope·(1−ρ*²)²/(2m) (ratio 0.63→1.00 for m=10→160), plug-in allocation ≈0.27–0.30/m, and an adaptive two-stage design that stays unbiased (|bias| ≤ 0.002) with 0.946–0.955 coverage.

Abstract Code →

The twin pays iff its correlation with the real return exceeds ρ*=2√r/(1+r) (0.426 at cost ratio r=0.05), and the gain is linear in ρ−ρ* there, so a small pilot's wrong calls are frequent but cheap (probability 0.36–0.11 at ρ=0.5 for m=10–160 pairs, regret 0.004–0.016 of real-only variance). Decision regret follows f·slope·(1−ρ*2)2/(2m) (simulated/law 0.63 at m=10, 1.00 at 160) and plug-in allocation costs ≈0.27–0.30/m extra variance. The adaptive two-stage design (pilot reused) stays unbiased (|bias| ≤ 0.002 against twin bias 0.7) with 95% intervals covering 0.946–0.955. Stylised: Gaussian returns, exact context replay, asymptotic law, no robot data.

crn-twin8 tests

Does giving two policies the same seed in a digital twin actually pair them?

Seed-paired (common random numbers) policy comparison in a twin: correlation is exactly lost to random-stream desynchronisation (flat score 0.95→0.77, terminal score 0.36→0.001 at q=0.05→0.3), a sizing trap (power 0.11–0.85 vs nominal 0.90), and counter-keyed draws restore ρ=1.

Abstract Code →

Common random numbers pair two policies only while their read pointers into the random stream stay aligned. If one policy consumes an extra draw with probability q per step, the paired correlation is exactly ρ = ∑t∑d Bin(t,q)(d) wtwt+d/∑wt² (matched to simulation within 0.012). A flat 20-step score keeps ρ=0.95/0.77 at q=0.05/0.3, but a terminal-only score has ρ=(1−q)T (0.36/0.001). Sizing a comparison as if seeds stayed synchronised (n=12) gives power 0.85 to 0.11 against a nominal 0.90; keying each draw by (episode, step) restores ρ=1. Stylised: Gaussian per-step noise, policies differing only in draw consumption, no robot data.

timestep-twin9 tests

What overshoot does a controller tuned in a fixed-step digital twin really have?

What overshoot a controller tuned in a fixed-step twin really has: exact per-step decay laws for explicit/semi-implicit/implicit Euler, damping bias flips sign at ζ=1/√2 (explicit, implicit), a 10% twin target delivers 0.105–0.192 real overshoot (implicit/semi-implicit) or 0.036–0.091 (explicit), error first order in h, Richardson repair.

Abstract Code →

A twin's integrator adds or removes damping the plant does not have. Per-step pole moduli are exact (real e−hc; explicit 1−hc+h²k; semi-implicit 1−hc; implicit 1/(1+hc+h²k)), and the first-order damping bias of explicit and implicit Euler changes sign at ζ=1/√2 (measured 0.742→0.711 and 0.675→0.703 as h falls 0.2→0.025). Tuned to 10% overshoot in the twin, the real plant overshoots 0.105–0.192 (semi-implicit and implicit, h=0.05–0.4) while forward Euler is conservative (0.091–0.036); at a 1% target the semi-implicit twin under-claims by up to 4.9×. The excess halves with h (first order); Richardson extrapolation of the twin’s overshoot at fixed gain recovers the real value to 0.0003–0.0012, and re-tuning with substeps costs ×4 to ×32. Stylised: one linear oscillator, textbook integrators (not any engine’s scheme), overshoot read from samples, no robot data.

scenario-twin10 tests

What does a too-narrow scenario generator do to a digital twin's estimate of a rare failure?

A too-narrow scenario generator in a twin makes rare-failure estimates silent: reweighted variance finite iff s²>½, 0.6× width claims 2e-7 for a real 1.2e-3 and reports zero failures in all runs, optimal width ≈1.05·a needs 38× fewer runs than plain Monte Carlo, and a defensive real-prior mixture is finite but no better.

Abstract Code →

With real scenarios x~N(0,1), failure iff x>a, and a twin generator of width s, the raw twin claims Q(a/s) and the reweighted (importance-sampling) estimate has per-sample second moment sτQ(a/τ), τ2=s2/(2s2−1), finite only for s2>½. In a braking example (P=1.2×10−3) a generator 0.6× too narrow claims 2.1×10−7 and reported zero failures in all 4,000 simulated runs of 2,000 scenarios; a wide one over-claims but reweighting repairs it, with optimal width ≈1.05a needing 2,179 runs for 10% error against 83,459 for plain Monte Carlo. A defensive mixture with the real prior makes a narrow twin's variance finite but no better than plain Monte Carlo.
