A spectrum-matched white twin is always conservative, real/twin = a(a+kd)/(a2+akd+kp) < 1 (0.71 at a=1). Fitting the OU rate from logged wind recovers the real variance (within 1% at 105 samples). Stylised: linear loop, Gaussian gusts, no wind data.

multipath-twin16 tests

A free-space radar twin ignores ground-bounce lobing: how wrong is it, and can a two-ray twin with a slightly wrong target height be worse?

Free-space radar twin vs two-ray ground-bounce lobing: detection fraction exactly 2/3 at the free-space range edge, real detects 44% beyond it, a two-ray twin with height error δh disagrees ≈4h_rδh/(λr) and is worse than free space at short range, a height-jitter ensemble scores Brier 0.119 vs 0.197 deterministic. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Two-ray detection 16 sin4u, u=2πhrht/(λr): lobe-mean gain exactly 6 and a detected phase fraction 1−(2/π)asin((c/16)1/4), exactly 2/3 at the free-space range edge. The real system misses 20% of ranges inside the free-space range and detects 44% of those beyond it. A deterministic two-ray twin with height error δh disagrees ≈4hrδh/(λr) (0.200 at 0.5 m, matching simulation) and is worse than free space at short range; a height-jitter ensemble scores Brier 0.119 against 0.197 deterministic and 0.533 free space. Stylised: perfect reflection, flat earth, hard threshold, no radar data.

glint-twin17 tests

A point-target radar twin of two unresolved scatterers: it has the right median, so what does it get wrong, and does averaging looks converge where it says?

Point-target radar twin of two unresolved scatterers under ideal monopulse: real mean is exactly the strong scatterer and median exactly the power centroid, outside-span probability arccos(r)/π, a variance-matched Gaussian twin is 27× too optimistic at a 3σ gate (r=0.9), averaging looks floors at bias 2r²/(1+r²) where the twin predicts √(var/N), and the median beats the mean for r≥0.477. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Ideal monopulse on two unresolved scatterers (strong 1, weak r, random phase) gives Y=(1−r2)/(1+r2+2rcosφ): the mean is exactly the strong scatterer and the median exactly the power centroid, variance 2r2/(1−r2), and the estimate lies outside the target span with probability arccos(r)/π. A variance-matched Gaussian centroid twin gets the median right and the mean wrong by 2r2/(1+r2), is 27× too optimistic at a 3σ gate at r=0.9, and predicts √(var/N) for averaged looks where the real mean floors at that bias (0.90 vs 0.09 at N=1024); the median converges and beats the mean on variance for r≥0.477. Stylised: noise-free ideal monopulse, two scatterers, no radar data.

shot-twin7 tests

A constant-variance Gaussian camera twin of Poisson photon counting: which dark/bright decision rule does it teach, and what does that cost on the real sensor?

Constant-variance Gaussian camera twin of Poisson photon counting: the real Bayes threshold is the logarithmic mean, the twin's the arithmetic mean (7.28 vs 8.00 for 4 vs 12), a detector tuned in it has 1.25–1.83× the optimal error and 23× at λ0=200 (λ1=2λ0), and a square-root twin recovers the optimum in 8 of 9 pairs. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

For Poisson counts the Bayes dark/bright threshold is the logarithmic mean (λ1−λ0)/ln(λ1/λ0); a Gaussian twin with one matched variance puts it at the arithmetic mean (7.28 vs 8.00 for 4 vs 12), and a square-root twin lands in between at (A+G)/2. A detector tuned in the arithmetic twin has 1.25× the optimal real error at (4,12), 1.83× at (10,30) and 1.74× at (50,100), and with λ1=2λ0 the penalty grows to 23× at λ0=200, while the twin’s own predicted error stays within 1.8× of the optimum; the square-root rule recovers the optimal integer rule in 8 of 9 pairs. Stylised: ideal Poisson counts, no read noise, no camera data.

sidelobe-twin17 tests

A radar twin whose targets occupy a single range cell: how far around a strong target does the real matched filter ghost, and does tapering fix it?

Single-cell radar twin vs a real matched filter: exact Rician ghost false alarms (0.020 at 20 dB, 1.0 at 30 dB for rect vs the twin's 1e-6), ghost zone radius growing √10 per 10 dB, taper gain exactly sidelobe difference + ENBW loss, and a 60 dB Hamming zone 6× Hann's despite the lower peak sidelobe. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A lone strong target through a matched filter alarms at neighbouring cells with an exact Rician probability where the point-response twin says Pfa0=10−6: at the rect peak sidelobe (−13.3 dB) it is 0.020 at 20 dB SNR and 1.0 at 30 dB, and the ghost zone radius grows √10 per 10 dB (3 to 331 cells for 20–60 dB). Tapers raise the ghost-free SNR by exactly the sidelobe-level difference plus the ENBW loss (20.0 dB Hann, 30.8 dB Hamming) at 1.5–1.6× mainlobe width, but ordering by peak sidelobe misleads at very strong targets: Hamming’s 1/x far sidelobes give a 42-cell zone against Hann’s 7 at 60 dB. A weak target beside a 40 dB one is ‘detected’ with Pd=1.0 where the empty cell alarms with probability 1.0. Stylised: white output noise, no CFAR or clutter, no radar data.

interleave-twin10 tests

A link twin with independent packet loss says to send repeats back to back: what does burstiness do to repetition coding for shared maps, and what does spacing buy?

Independent-loss link twin vs a bursty loss chain for repeated map updates: exact residual p·q_g^(r−1), the twin's 5 back-to-back copies leave 81–311× the claimed loss at λ=0.5–0.8, spacing needs 6–36 slots for two copies, and with ≤8 copies the best design is 12–154 slots of latency vs the twin's 4.

Abstract Code →

An update is sent as r copies g slots apart and is lost only if all are. Against a two-state loss chain with the same marginal rate p = 0.2 and lag-1 correlation λ, the exact residual is p(p + λg(1−p))r−1 against the twin’s pr. The twin’s 5 back-to-back copies for 10−3 give a real residual of 0.026 at λ = 0.5 and 0.10 at 0.8 (81× and 311× the claim); two copies need spacing of 6 to 36 slots to come within 10% of the twin. With at most 8 copies the minimum-latency design is 12 to 154 slots (λ = 0.5 to 0.95) against the twin’s 4, and with at most 4 copies no spacing reaches 10−3. A counter-case: with no copy budget and a long deadline, back-to-back copies still beat a few spaced ones. Stylised: simulated link, known stationary parameters, no radio traces.

fog-twin15 tests

A lidar twin without atmospheric loss overstates range in fog: by how much, how sensitive is it to a mis-set extinction, and what does it do to a driving policy?

Clear-air lidar twin vs fog: detection range W(αr0)/α overstated by exactly e^{αr}, range error is W/(1+W)<1 times the extinction error, a policy sized on median fog is violated 50% of the time (5%-quantile range: 5%, 43.5% slower), and one extinction calibrated on a bright target fails for dark ones in patchy fog. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Detection range solves reαr = r0, i.e. r = W(αr0)/α; the clear-air twin overstates it by exactly eαr (×2.32 at 200 m visibility) and a relative extinction error moves range by the elasticity W/(1+W) < 1. With lognormal episode-to-episode fog a policy sized on the median fog is violated 50% of the time (mean fog 34%), the 5%-quantile range gives exactly 5% at a 43.5% speed cost, and in patchy fog one extinction calibrated on a bright target underestimates dark targets by up to 29% (calibrated on a dark one, bright targets are overestimated 61–168%). Stylised: hard threshold, Beer–Lambert medium, no lidar data.

rain-twin9 tests

Is a clear-air or mean-rain-rate radar twin right when rain comes in cells?

Clear-air or mean-rain-rate radar twin vs intermittent storm-cell attenuation: Jensen gap 1.52× in the rain-rate power law, Lambert-W mean-rate range reached by only 39% of real fields, mean-matching barely helps, a rain ensemble scores Brier 0.038 vs 0.101 clear air. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Radar detection range under intermittent rain attenuation. The power law in rain rate has a Jensen gap (1.52× the mean-rate attenuation), so a mean-rate twin (closed-form Lambert W range, 18.84 km) is reached by only 39% of real storm fields; matching the mean attenuation barely helps (Brier 0.054 vs 0.055). A rain ensemble scores 0.038 vs 0.101 for clear air, and long cells flip the mean-rate twin from optimistic to pessimistic. Stylised: simulated rain, illustrative coefficients, no radar data.

runlength-twin11 tests

How long must a real test run be when its length was sized in a twin with the wrong plant pole?

Real test-run length sized in a wrong-pole twin: exact autocorrelated-cost variance, 3.8× too short (coverage 0.69 vs 0.95) or 2.1× too long depending on the real closed-loop pole, and a pilot-run repair that under-sizes half the time.

Abstract Code →

A gain designed in a twin whose pole is m× the real one is validated on hardware for a run length chosen in the twin. The variance of the time-averaged cost of a Gaussian AR(1) loop is exact and depends on the closed-loop pole through (1+ρ)/(1−ρ), ρ=ac2, so the twin-sized run is 3.8× too short at m=2, r=0.1 (3,177 vs 12,110 steps; real coverage of a ±5% claim 0.69 vs 0.95 nominal, simulated 0.68) and 2.1× too long at m=1.5, r=5; an oscillating (negative-pole) loop averages as slowly as a sluggish one. Sizing from a real pilot’s lag-one autocorrelation is close to median-unbiased but under-sizes about half the time. Stylised: scalar linear-Gaussian, fixed known gain, normal-approximation interval.

aliasing-twin9 tests

What does a radar twin with unlimited unambiguous velocity over-certify?

What a radar twin with unlimited unambiguous velocity over-certifies: exact wrapped-Gaussian bias (−V at μ=V) and MSE with a bias² floor so averaging widens the gap (7.9× → 2.1×10³ at μ=0.8V, n=1→10⁴), safe speed ≈V+sΦ⁻¹(tol/2V), and prior-unwrapping failure 2Φ(−V/√(s²+s_p²)) needing prior error ≤ 0.26V.

Abstract Code →

A pulsed Doppler radar reports radial velocity modulo 2V; a twin that renders velocity as a real number never aliases. The real bias of a wrapped return is an exact Gaussian tail series (−V at speed V, −2V beyond) and the real MSE has a bias2 floor, so averaging widens the gap to the twin's claim s2/n: at V=10, s=1 and speed 8 the real/claimed MSE is 7.9× for one return and 2.1×103 for 104. Speeds with |bias| ≤ 0.1 reach only 87%, 74% and 48% of V for noise 0.5, 1, 2. Unwrapping against a prior has exact failure probability 2Φ(−V/√(s2+sp2)) and stays within 10% of the twin's claim only for prior error ≤ 0.26V. Stylised: one radial channel, Gaussian noise, simulated radar.

twin-ladder6 tests

Which rungs of a ladder of digital twins are worth running?

Which rungs of a multi-fidelity twin ladder to run: exact nested-estimator variance, a cheaper rung pays iff ρ₂/ρ₁ > 2√r/(1+r) (step correlation, 0.943 for halved cost), using all rungs can be worse than none (1.41× real-only at q=0.9) while the best subset gets 0.83, and a timestep-ladder plant shows 0.156 of real-only variance (0.204 single twin) collapsing to the cheapest twin when disturbance replay is only 90%.

Abstract Code →

For twins of decreasing cost and fidelity used as nested control variates the variance is exact, σ2Σ(ρi2−ρi+12)/mi, and a cheaper rung pays below a twin already in use iff ρ2/ρ1 > 2√r/(1+r) (0.943 for halved cost, 0.575 for a 10× drop), the single-twin threshold applied to the step correlation. Using every rung is not best (q=0.99, r=0.5, six rungs: 0.284 of real-only variance vs 0.196 for the best two; q=0.9 makes all rungs 1.41× worse than real-only while the best subset gets 0.83), and 10 of 336 paying grid points are infeasible. On a saturated PD mass-spring timestep ladder the best ladder reaches 0.156 of real-only variance (0.204 for the best single twin), collapsing to the cheapest twin at 90%/70% disturbance replay (0.52/0.89 simulated); a coarser rung diverged in 2 of 20,000 contexts. Stylised: one plant, known correlations, step-count costs.

watchdog-twin12 tests

A heartbeat twin that drops packets independently: how often does the real bursty link trip a missed-beat watchdog, and what timeout is safe?

I.i.d.-loss heartbeat twin vs a bursty Gilbert link: a 5-missed-beat watchdog false-trips every 3.4e6 ticks in the twin but every 235–990 on the real link, worst at burst length ≈ m (mean time to trip ≈ e·m/p), and a 1e6-tick target needs m = 16–154 instead of the twin's 5. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

At 5% mean loss a watchdog that e-stops after m = 5 missed heartbeats false-trips once in 3.4×106 ticks (18.7 h at 50 Hz) in the i.i.d.-loss twin but every 235–990 ticks (5–20 s) on a two-state bursty link with mean burst 2–50, from an exact recursion checked against enumeration and Monte Carlo. The error is not monotone in burst length: it is worst at L ≈ m, where the mean time to trip is only ≈ em/p. For a 106-tick target the twin picks m = 5 (0.10 s to detect a dead link) while the real link needs 16–154 (0.3–3.1 s) growing linearly in L, and with L unknown no affordable timeout guarantees it. Stylised: Gilbert channel, plain miss counter, no link traces.

gate-twin14 tests

A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: does an innovation gate help or hurt the real estimator, and what does it do after a jump?

Gaussian-sensor twin vs a real sensor with outliers under an innovation gate: the twin says the gate costs 8.5% MSE, the real sensor gains 3.0× from it, the worst outlier scale for a gated filter is finite (κ≈4) while ungated error grows as κ², and a gate locks out recovery from a jump for ≈76·D² steps. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

With a Gaussian-sensor twin an innovation gate (z = 2.58) costs 8.5% of the update MSE, since every gated measurement is good data; with 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the same gate cuts the MSE 1.74 → 0.58 (3.0×) while still passing 28% of the outliers. The ungated error grows like κ2 in the outlier scale, the gated error is bounded and worst at a finite κ* ≈ 4, and a better-tuned gate width gains only 0–6%. After a jump D in a random-walk state the gate rejects the correct measurements and re-convergence takes ≈ 76D2 steps (30,512 at D = 20) against 30 with no gate. Exact post-update MSE checked by quadrature and Monte Carlo. Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, simplified covariance rule in the jump experiment.

groundeffect-twin12 tests

A twin without ground effect: where does a landing altitude loop go wrong?

Rotorcraft altitude twin without ground effect vs real thrust gain 1/(1−(R/4z)²): hover sits 18 mm high at one rotor radius (twin: 0), and a delayed loop with 28% twin headroom goes unstable at 0.54 rotor radii. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

With the constant-power ground-effect multiplier G(z) = 1/(1−(R/4z)2) a gravity-feedforward altitude hold sits above its target by 2.7, 17.7 and 30.2 mm at 3, 1 and 0.6 rotor radii (twin: 0), 0.9% to 50% of the height. A sampled loop with one-sample delay that the twin gives 27.6% gain headroom at every height loses it as the vehicle descends: the real margin is 1.19 at one radius and reaches the stability boundary at 0.54 radii, confirmed by a nonlinear simulation; the undelayed thrust-gradient stiffness matters, since scaling the gain alone misses the instability. Negligible above about two radii. Stylised: point mass, closed-form ground-effect model, no rotor lag.

deadtime-twin10 tests

What does a linear photon-counter twin of a SPAD lidar miss about dead time?

Linear photon-counter twin of a SPAD lidar vs dead time: half the flux reported at nτ=1, a paralyzable-detector ambiguity (one reading, two fluxes, 12.7× apart at mτ=0.2), first-photon range bias −N/(2√π)σ saturating near −2σ (−22.6 cm at N=10, σ=1 ns) that does not average out, and a Coates correction that removes it. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

An ideal counter twin reads flux linearly; a real detector with dead time τ reports half the flux at nτ=1 (non-paralyzable) or 36.8% (paralyzable), and the paralyzable curve peaks at 1/e, so one reading has two fluxes (0.259 or 2.543 at mτ=0.2; a twin is 12.7× too low on the high branch). First-photon timing of a Gaussian pulse is biased early by −N/(2√π)σ at small N (exact) and saturating near −2σ: −0.28σ at N=1 and −1.50σ at N=10 (−22.6 cm for σ=1 ns) while the spread shrinks to 0.62σ, so it is bias, not averaging noise. A Coates correction of the first-photon histogram restores the mean to within 0.02σ. Stylised: one pulse, no background light, afterpulsing or crosstalk.

flyingpixel-twin13 tests

What ghost ranges does a single-ray lidar twin never produce at a depth edge?

Single-ray lidar twin vs a finite beam with merged pulses at a depth edge: ghost-range band exactly 2Φ⁻¹(1−ε/D) beam widths (2.56 at ε/D=0.1, none at ε≥D/2), shifts and narrows for unequal brightness, matches a scan simulation to 0.3%, and a 3-of-5 persistence filter still passes 80–99% of ghosts.

Abstract Code →

A one-ray twin returns the near or the far surface at a depth edge; a real beam with a Gaussian footprint and merged return pulses reports an energy-weighted range in free space. The ghost band is exactly 2Φ−1(1−ε/D) beam standard deviations wide for equal energies (2.56 at ε/D = 0.1, 4.65 at 0.01, none once ε ≥ D/2), checked against a direct scan to 10−4, and shifts toward the near side and narrows when the far wall is brighter (1.67 at a 100× energy ratio). A scan with an edge every ≈ 100 beams has a ghost fraction equal to the prediction to within 0.3%, and a 3-of-5 persistence filter on a static robot passes 80–99% of ghosts because they come from geometry, not noise. Stylised: hard merge threshold, 1-D footprint, centroid detector, no real scans.

chirp-twin9 tests

What does an FMCW radar twin without range–Doppler coupling get wrong about a moving target?

FMCW range–Doppler coupling: a twin that reads true range misses a bias of f_D T cells (0.6–4.8 at 30 m/s), signal-level check ≤1e-4 cells, wrapped-Doppler compensation is worse than none on half of the over-range speeds, and a ±60° stationary scene leaves 0.71κv position bias plus 0.46κv distortion.

Abstract Code →

A sawtooth chirp radar reads a moving target’s range as R + κv, κ = fcT/B; the twin reads R. A signal-level beat-tone simulation matches the formula to ≤ 10−4 range cells, and the bias is fDT cells independent of bandwidth: 0.6, 3.1 and 4.8 cells (9 cm, 46 cm, 2.9 m) at 30 m/s for fast 77 GHz, mid 77 GHz and slow 24 GHz ramps. Within the unambiguous speed it is under half a cell, but compensating with the radar’s own wrapped Doppler is worse than doing nothing on exactly half of the over-range speeds. For a stationary scene (±60°) a centroid fit absorbs 0.71κv of along-track position error and leaves 0.46κv rms distortion. Stylised: single up ramp, noise-free tone, no radar data.

corridor-twin8 tests

Does a well-featured twin overstate scan-matching accuracy in a corridor, where the scan cannot see the along-track direction?

Scan matching in a corridor: along-track information is exactly zero without door frames, 1.6–6× a room's along-track sd with them; a filter fed the room twin's covariance has NEES 432–1535 over a blind span, and the exact covariance holds only inside a ~0.2 m basin. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

In a bare corridor the point-to-line information matrix is exactly singular along the track and the matcher returns its initial guess; door-frame stubs every 20/10/5/2 m give an exact along-track sd of 8.1/6.3/3.9/2.2 mm (MC 7.3/6.2/4.3/2.4), 1.6–6× a well-featured room's 1.35 mm, while lateral accuracy (≈ 0.8 mm) is unchanged. A Kalman filter fed the room twin's 1.9 mm covariance across a 20 m blind span has NEES 432 (1 cm/step odometry) and 1535 (2 cm/step) against 0.75 for the exact-covariance filter; the exact covariance is valid only inside a matcher basin of ≈ 0.2 m, and the covariance-aware filter is still overconfident at re-entry (NEES 2–8). Stylised: simulated 2D lidar, one-dimensional filter.

particle-twin11 tests

A twin whose sensor never produces outliers: how many particles does a bootstrap filter need, and is the average effective sample size the right thing to size on?

Gaussian-sensor twin vs outliers for a bootstrap particle filter: exact ESS fraction c₀e^{−ay²}, the mean ESS barely moves (0.671 vs 0.645) while P(ESS<1%) rises 120× (2.5e-4 → 3.1e-2), a twin-sized N=528 fails 4.4% of real steps, and posterior-mean error is 45–421× the twin's.

Abstract Code →

For a bootstrap particle filter the large-N effective-sample-size fraction is exactly c0 e−ay² in the measurement y (c0 = 0.866, a = 1/6 at P = R = 1). With 5% real outliers at 10× the noise scale the mean ESS fraction barely moves (0.671 in the twin, 0.645 real, at every dimension), but P(ESS < 1% of N) goes from 2.5×10−4 to 3.1×10−2 (120×). Sizing N = 528 for ESS ≥ 50 at 1% failure in the twin fails 4.4% of real steps, and the particle posterior mean's error against the exact Kalman update is 45× to 421× the twin's for N = 50 to 1000, falling barely at all with N. The large-N formula is checked against quadrature and simulation and fails once Nρ is small (reported). Stylised: scalar update, simulated outliers, no resampling dynamics.

Can a fixed inflation radius stand in for a rectangular robot's footprint in a narrow gap?

Point/circle/calibrated-inflation footprint twin vs a rectangular robot with heading error in a narrow gap: exact pass probability 2Φ(θ*/σ)−1, circle twins are step functions, a 95%-calibrated inflation is 0.17 m too small at 3× the heading error, 10-gap missions succeed 0.60 where the twin says 1.

Abstract Code →

A 1.0×0.5 m robot with Gaussian heading error crossing a gap: pass probability is exactly 2Φ(θ*/σ)−1 with θ* = asin(g/R)−atan(W/L) (matches a corner-geometry Monte Carlo within 0.0013). Inscribed- and circumscribed-circle twins are step functions (always pass / always fail below 1.118 m); an inflation calibrated to 95% at σ = 0.05 is 0.17 m too small at σ = 0.15 (real pass 0.49), and ten-gap missions succeed only 0.60 of the time where the twin says 1. Stylised: simulated robot, Gaussian heading error, no sensing error.

ransac-twin6 tests

If a twin gives every scene the same inlier fraction, how many RANSAC iterations does it say we need, and is that enough when real scenes vary?

RANSAC iteration budget from a fixed-inlier-fraction twin (17 for 99%) vs scenes with beta-binomial inlier counts: exact failure 1.3–30% at that budget, 99% needs 19–458 iterations or is unreachable for κ≤2; stylised, line fitting only.

Abstract Code →

With N = 100 correspondences, minimal sample 2 and 50% mean inliers, the twin's budget for 99% success is 17 iterations. If the real scene inlier count is beta-binomial with concentration κ, the exact failure at 17 iterations is 1.3% (binomial variation only), 7.0% (κ = 10) and 14.1% (κ = 4); restoring 99% takes 19, 58 and 458 iterations, and for κ ≤ 2 no budget exists because scenes with fewer than 2 inliers cannot succeed. Exact values match a sampler, and an end-to-end noisy line fit goes from 0.9% to 12.6% slope failures at κ = 4 (1.8% with the larger budget, still above 1%). Stylised: assumed scene law, line fitting only, no real data.

occlusion-twin11 tests

Can a lidar twin give each beam an independent visibility probability, or do neighbouring beams share occluders?

Lidar twin with independent per-beam visibility vs a Poisson occluder field: beams closer than an occluder diameter share occluders, exact blind probability by inclusion–exclusion over union lengths, 8 beams at 25 cm blind 0.0815 vs the twin's 0.0039 (20.9×), the twin is exact once spacing ≥ 2ρ, an occluder-field ensemble matches. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

For a Poisson field of occluders of radius ρ, beams a distance s apart are both clear with probability exp(−μ(2ρ+min(s,2ρ))), which equals p2 exactly when s ≥ 2ρ; any set of beams has the closed form exp(−μ·union length). An independent-beam twin therefore matches the mean number of clear beams but understates the variance and the blind probability: with 8 beams at 25 cm and single-beam visibility 0.5 (occluder diameter 1 m) the exact blind probability is 0.0815 against the twin’s 0.0039 (20.9×, 97× at 5 cm), and reaching a blind probability of 0.01 needs 16 beams instead of 7 (not reachable with 16 at 10 cm). The twin is exact once the spacing exceeds the occluder diameter, and an ensemble twin that samples occluder fields reproduces the exact value (0.0815 vs 0.0815 ± 0.0006). Stylised: one-dimensional lateral projection, binary opaque occluders, no lidar data.

sag-twin9 tests

A battery twin with no internal resistance: how much endurance and how large a burst does the real, sagging cell actually give?

Battery twin with no internal resistance vs a real sagging cell: endurance exactly (1+√(1−u))/2 of the twin's (0.5 at the fold), 9–94% of charge stranded at the voltage cutoff, a burst of 0.5 fails below 51% charge where the twin's floor is 0 (a flat 20% reserve covers only a third of the full-charge limit), and a constant-derate refit errs +12% to +473% off its fit power. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A UAV battery twin that keeps the open-circuit voltage curve but drops the series resistance overstates endurance by exactly 1/η(u) with η = (1 + √(1−u))/2 (up to 2× at the maximum-power fold, beyond which the real cell cannot deliver the power at all while the twin still quotes an endurance). With droop and a voltage cutoff, real/twin endurance is 0.86, 0.57, 0.30 at normalised power 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 9%, 37%, 66% of the charge is stranded. The deliverable burst power falls linearly with charge, so a burst of 0.5 fails below 51% charge where the twin's floor is zero, a flat 20% reserve covers only a third of the full-charge limit, and keeping a 0.6 burst deliverable leaves 35% of the twin's cruise time. A constant derate fitted at one power errs by +12% to +473% elsewhere, but the resistance is identified to 1–2% from tens of voltage–current samples, and a full-charge fit misses resistance that grows as the cell empties (endurance +42% to +85% too high). Stylised: simulated cell, linear curves, constant-power load, no polarisation or self-heating.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-twinc2st on a stylised pendulum (Coulomb friction, Student-t sensor noise). The rejection threshold is the 95th percentile of the exact twin’s own null, and power is the share of replicates above it. For a Coulomb error of 20% the paired error test (same start angles, noisy real vs noise-free twin) has power 0.76 at 50 trajectories and 0.98 at 100, while the boosted-tree C2ST has 0.04 and 0.25 and needs about 200 to reach 1.00. For a 10% error the paired test stalls at 0.09–0.20 for every n up to 800 (a plausible but untested cause: the squared heavy-tailed noise has infinite variance), while the C2ST reaches 0.62 at 200 and 1.00 at 400. For Gaussian instead of Student-t noise of the same sd the paired test has power 0.04–0.07 at every n, the C2ST with second-difference features 0.92 at 50. Caveat: the null threshold comes from 60 replicates, and a check on fresh null replicates falsely rejected 0–29% of the time (nominal 5%), so power at small n is approximate. Stylised, simulated, 24 replicates per cell.

Follow-up to free-c2stpower, where a paired error test stalled at 0.09–0.20 power for a 10% Coulomb-friction error under Student-t(3) sensor noise. Which robust paired test still catches a wrong digital twin when noise has infinite variance or whole runs go bad? Follow-up to free-robustpaired on the same stylised pendulum (10% Coulomb-friction error, n = 50–200 matched trajectories, 400 null replicates). With Student-t(2) cells (infinite variance) the mean squared residual has power about 0.05 at every n, while median and trimmed squared residuals reach 1.00 and a Huber loss with a MAD-estimated scale reaches 0.70–1.00 (0.20–0.53 with the scale fixed at 0.02). Which paired test of a digital twin survives both heavy-tailed cells and whole bad runs? Abstract Code →

Follow-up to free-robusttails, which found no single robust statistic won against both Student-t(2) cells and 10%-of-runs-10×-noisier bad runs. Here each trajectory’s squared residuals are summarised robustly (median or 20%-trimmed mean), then the per-run values are summarised robustly across runs. On the same stylised pendulum (10% Coulomb error, n = 50–200, 400 null replicates) the trimmed-then-trimmed statistic has power 0.99–1.00 under t(2) cells and when t(2) cells sit inside bad runs, 0.86 / 0.95 / 1.00 under bad runs alone, and 0.84 / 0.99 / 1.00 under Gaussian noise, against 0.91 / 0.99 / 1.00 for the per-run mean-squared median; the best single-level statistics reach only 0.10–0.28 or 0.15–0.38 in the case they fail. Follow-up to free-c2stexact on the stylised pendulum twin. A throttle controller inverts a twin whose thrust is linear around hover; the real thrust is quadratic. The realised acceleration is exactly acmd+acmd2/(4g): climbs over-deliver, descents under-deliver, and the throttle floor is reached at acmd=−2g. At ζ=0.7 the climb overshoot rises from 0.046 to 0.095 while the descent falls to 0.027 for a step of p=ωn2|x0|/g=4; gentle steps (p≤0.5) change overshoot by under 1.1 points. Follow-up to thrust-twin. Exact steady-state MSE of a scalar Kalman filter run at the wrong process noise qa = λq, matched to simulation within 1%. Averaging a policy’s return over n randomised scenarios, compared across iid, Latin hypercube, randomly shifted Halton and shifted Rd lattice samplers, against exact means. Latin hypercubes keep the n−0.5 rate (MSE cut 1.6–12×). Shifted Halton improves the rate for smooth returns (slope −0.92 at d = 2, MSE 149× lower at n = 1024) and keeps a 4–24× gain on a discontinuous success-rate return, shrinking as the number of randomised parameters grows. Abstract Code →

Follow-up to free-qmcdr. The shifted Rd lattice’s error exponent at d = 5 is −0.45 ± 0.01 over six seed strings, no better than iid, so it is not a seed fluke; across d = 2…8 it dips at 5 between −0.72 and −0.61 neighbours, so it is not a smooth dimension effect; a generator built from √pj reaches −0.66 at d = 5. How long does a float32 twin of a chaotic system shadow the float64 one, and do its statistics survive? Lorenz-63 and Rössler integrated with the same RK4 scheme in float32 and float64 from the same start. The Lyapunov exponent (0.8995 vs 0.8997) and long-run time averages agree within sampling error (|z| < 1.2, 200 members), and a float16 run showed no detectable bias on 100 members either. Does a float32 simulation of a bouncing, chaotic system lose its statistics? Sinai billiard against float64

Abstract Code →

A point particle in a unit square with a circular obstacle (Sinai billiard), event-driven with specular reflection, run in float32 and float64 from the same start. The first different surface is hit exactly one collision after the position departs, at every error size tried. Mean free path (0.45296 vs 0.45325) and the circle's share of collisions agree within sampling error (|z| < 0.6), and match Cauchy’s exact mean free path 0.45321; no particle escaped and the direction vector’s length drifted by about 10−5 after 2000 collisions. Abstract Code →

Installs Yosys, Icarus Verilog and Verilator, records versions, and synthesises adders, a multiplier and a FIFO to a generic gate library: a ripple-carry adder is 5W−3 gates deep 2W−1, and the operator form + gets the same depth with a few more gates. A SAT miter proves the two adders equivalent and rejects a deliberately broken one. Stylised: gate counts, not silicon area; OpenROAD and a PDK are not yet part of the flow.

chip-rtl-probe9 tests

Which check catches an RTL bug: lint, random simulation or a formal equivalence proof?

What lint, random simulation and a Yosys equivalence proof each catch, on 12 small RTL tasks (companion to chip-rtl-loop); mutation probe shows 30 of 389 rejected bugs are caught only by the formal proof. Session-written attempts, not an LLM benchmark.

Abstract Code →

A harness (a proposer writes Verilog; lint, random-vector simulation and a Yosys equivalence proof score it) with 12 small tasks. One attempt per task written by the session agent (not an LLM benchmark) passed every stage at round 0, so the loop never had a failure to use. Of 414 single-point mutants of those designs, lint rejects 56, simulation 303 and only the formal proof 30 (7.7% of the 389 rejected), while 25 pass everything. A no-LLM random-mutation repair baseline fixes 11/36 broken designs within 4 proposals and 22/36 within 16. Toy: tiny modules, bounded 10-cycle proof for sequential tasks, syntactic mutants.

chip-rtl-loop4 tests

How much does simulation and formal feedback help a proposer repair small Verilog designs?

Lint, simulation and formal-equivalence feedback for Verilog repair on nine small tasks; 6/9 pass at round 0 and 9/9 after one round, with the session as proposer (anecdotal, not an LLM benchmark).

Abstract Code →

A checker (Verilator lint, Icarus lockstep simulation against a golden model, Yosys SAT proof for combinational tasks) scores nine small tasks. With the session itself as proposer, 6 of 9 pass from the spec alone and all 9 after one round of mismatch feedback; the three failures were a Gray encoder written as a decoder, a logical shift on a signed value and a combinational pulse that should be registered. Anecdotal: one attempt per round, one proposer who also wrote the tasks, no resampling baseline, simulation only for sequential tasks. Not an LLM benchmark.

chip-repair-baseline7 tests

What does a no-model baseline repair when a scripted RTL checker is the only feedback?

No-model mutation-repair baseline for a scripted Verilog checker (compile, lint, simulation, SAT miter) on ten small tasks: 9/20 one-fault cases repaired in 60 evaluations; the session agent passed all ten first try, so the feedback loop is unmeasured. Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A companion to chip-rtl-loop: a four-stage checker (compile, lint, simulation, SAT miter) over ten small Verilog tasks, with a random-mutation hill-climbing baseline that uses no model. Given 1, 2 or 3 injected faults and 60 checker evaluations, the baseline repairs 9/20, 4/20 and 4/20 cases. The session agent (Claude) passed all ten tasks on its first attempt, so the feedback rounds were never exercised and no pass-rate-versus-rounds curve is reported. Preliminary: tiny tasks, one attempt, mutation faults unlike a language model's mistakes, and the optional API proposer is untested.

chip-ppa-loop7 tests

Does a rewrite proposer beat a parameter sweep on area and depth when every rewrite must be proved equivalent?

Equivalence-gated area/depth rewrites of a 16-bit adder and 6x6 multiplier against a no-model parameter sweep; best adder 0.85x the reference cells×depth, tied by the sweep, no multiplier gain (stylised, gate counts).

Abstract Code →

A loop in which rewrites of a 16-bit adder and a 6×6 multiplier must be proved equivalent to the reference by a Yosys miter before a generic-gate ABC script scores cells and depth. With nine attempts written by the session agent (not an LLM benchmark; two were seeded faults the gate rejected), the best adder is a 4-bit carry-select at 0.85× the reference cells×depth, the same circuit family as the best config of a no-model parameter sweep, so a random sweep of the same budget never beats it (ties in 63 of 200 seeds). No multiplier rewrite beat a * b. Stylised: gate counts, not layout; one tool version; two designs.

chip-scaling4 tests

How does generic-gate area grow with bit width for adders, shifters, popcount and multipliers?

How generic-gate cells and depth scale with bit width for seven arithmetic blocks: adder, comparator and mux are near-linear, the multiplier quadratic (exponent 2.19), and adder depth grows ~2&times;W (stylised, generic gates).

Abstract Code →

Seven behavioural blocks synthesised by Yosys 0.33 to generic gates at widths 4–64. Cell counts for the adder, comparator, equality and 4:1 mux are close to linear in width (fitted exponent 1.00–1.13); the multiplier is quadratic (2.19 overall, 2.06 on the largest widths); the barrel shifter sits at 1.27–1.35. Logic depth scales differently from cells: the default-script adder's depth grows about 2×W (7 to 125) while the comparator's grows slowly (5 to 16). Preliminary: five widths, one tool version, generic gates rather than library area, no confidence intervals.

chip-constmul6 tests

Does writing a fixed-weight multiplier as shift-and-add with canonical signed digits beat Yosys's x * K?

Fixed-weight multipliers for all 255 8-bit constants: Yosys's x * K tracks binary shift-add (Pearson 0.97 with set bits), and a canonical-signed-digit form has 33% fewer generic-gate cells at similar depth (every form proved equivalent).

Abstract Code →

For every 8-bit constant K (1–255), an 8-bit input is multiplied three ways — the * operator, binary shift-add, and canonical-signed-digit (CSD) shift-add/subtract — and scored by Yosys 0.33 in generic gates; every variant is proved equivalent to the operator form by a miter. The operator tracks binary shift-add (cells correlate 0.97 with the number of set bits of K, 0.65 with CSD digits). CSD uses 75.7 mean cells against 112.9 for the operator (33.0% fewer; fewer cells for 230 of 255 constants, worse for 14) at similar mean depth (20.0 vs 19.6); K=255 drops from 222 to 30 cells. Preliminary: one tool version, one ABC script, generic gates rather than library area, one input width, no shared sub-sums across constants.

chip-mcm6 tests

Does sharing sub-sums across a bank of fixed-weight multipliers cut gates beyond per-constant shift-and-add?

A bank of fixed-weight multipliers sharing sub-sums (multiple-constant multiplication): 9% fewer generic-gate cells than per-constant signed-digit shift-add at 2 constants and about 20% fewer at 8 and 16 (43% fewer than Yosys's *), every form proved equivalent; random constants, not trained weights.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to chip-constmul: one 8-bit input feeds a bank of M random 8-bit constants (M = 2, 4, 8, 16; 40 banks each), written three ways — the * operator, per-constant canonical-signed-digit (CSD) shift-add, and a greedy shared-sub-sum (MCM) form — scored by Yosys 0.33 in generic gates, every variant proved equivalent to the operator form. Sharing uses 9% fewer cells than per-constant CSD at M = 2 and about 20% fewer at M = 8 and 16 (690 vs 866 at M = 16; 43% fewer than the operator), fewer in 130 of 160 banks and more in 2. Adders removed in the source predict cells saved (Pearson 0.875, about 15 cells per adder). Sharing also recovers the depth CSD loses on large banks (28.2 vs 33.2 at M = 16). Preliminary: random rather than trained weights, one greedy heuristic, one tool version, generic gates rather than library area.

chip-cutheadroom7 tests

How many gates could an exact 4-input rewriter still remove from Yosys/ABC netlists?

How many gates an exact 4-input rewriter could still remove from real Yosys/ABC netlists: none in 28 of 30 runs (1 gate in two), even where the default script beats plain mapping by 25 to 42%, so the flow's gains are not local.

Abstract Code →

chip-exact4 found Yosys/ABC about 1.2 gates above the proven minimum on isolated 4-input functions. Here every gate of six small netlists (adder, multiplier, comparator, popcount, shifter, priority encoder) under five ABC flows is checked against that exact minimum over all its 4-leaf cuts, counting only logic a local replacement could delete. The disjoint headroom is 0 gates in 28 of 30 runs and 1 gate in the other two, even though the default script cuts 25–42% of the gates of plain mapping on add16 and prio16: the flow’s gains are not local, so an exact small-cone rewrite proposer would find almost nothing. Stylised: six blocks, gate count with free inverters, one Yosys build; replacement circuits were not constructed.

chip-exact45 tests

How many gates above the proven minimum does Yosys/ABC use for 4-input logic?

How far above the SAT-proven minimum gate count Yosys/ABC lands on 4-input logic: the default flow is exactly optimal on only 34% of sampled functions (mean 1.19 gates above, max 4), and a heavier script is worse.

Abstract Code →

The exact minimum 2-input gate count of every 4-input Boolean function (222 NPN classes, by SAT) against what Yosys/ABC returns on 884 sampled functions. The default flow is exactly optimal on only 34% and averages 1.19 gates above the minimum (max 4); the best of seven scripts per function reaches 38%. A heavier resyn2 script is worse (1.72), and the count changes with which negated or permuted form of the same function is synthesised. One Yosys version, generic gates, 4 inputs only. Preliminary.

Does the ABC synthesis script matter as much as the written RTL structure for adder and multiplier area and depth?

Sweeps five ABC scripts over five adder and eight multiplier structures (all proved equivalent): the script moves cells&times;depth by up to 1.75&times; for one adder, while all eight multiplier structures score identically (stylised, generic-gate).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to chip-ppa-loop: five ABC scripts are applied to five written 16-bit adder structures and eight 6×6 multiplier structures, each proved equivalent to its reference by a Yosys miter. For the adder, cells×depth moves by up to 1.75× with the script for one structure and 1.18–1.94× across structures for a fixed script; the best pair is 0.48× the default-script plain adder. All eight multiplier structures score identically under each script, yet the script alone moves them by 1.17×. Stylised: two designs, one Yosys version, generic-gate counts rather than layout.

Does the order or naming of equivalent Verilog change what Yosys and ABC synthesise?

Whether equivalent Verilog that differs only in wire names, statement order or the order of added operands synthesises to the same size: names and statement order never change cells&times;depth, operand order does for one carry-select adder (up to 1.43&times;, a 17% better result than the earlier sweep's best; stylised).

Abstract Code →

Provably equivalent rewrites of generated adder and multiplier RTL (random wire names, shuffled statements, shuffled order of added operands; 864 scored variants, every text proved equivalent to its reference) are scored under three ABC scripts. Names and statement order never change cells×depth. Operand order changes one carry-select adder by up to 1.43× within a script, and its best variant under dch is 17% better than the best adder chip-abc-sweep reported, so that earlier best was one draw from a distribution the text controls. Five other structures are unaffected. Stylised: two designs, one Yosys version, 12 seeds, generic-gate counts, cause not yet traced.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to chip-abc-orderpass, which only ran uniform orders. 400 random mixed variants of a 16-bit carry-select adder (each of the 7 a + b + const chains in its own random operand order; all proved equivalent to the reference) are scored under three ABC scripts. The set of blocks whose two chains both start with a, b predicts the Yosys adder count after opt in 400 of 400 variants and fixes the cells × depth: all 8 possible sets occurred, and each had exactly one score per script. The effect is not additive: sharing only block 1 costs 1.38× under dch_map, only block 3 costs 1.00×. Stylised: one adder, Yosys 0.33, a generic-gate library, no place and route.

Which Yosys pass makes the operand order of a + b + constant change the synthesised adder?

Finds the Yosys pass behind chip-abc-order's operand-order effect: opt_merge shares a+b between the two carry-select sums only when both are written with a and b first (4 of 36 operand orders); removing it widens the spread (up to 3.2&times;), so it was hiding variation. One adder, stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to chip-abc-order. All 36 operand orders of a 16-bit carry-select adder's a + b + const chains (each proved equivalent to the reference) are run through synth one pass at a time. The cell counts first diverge in opt_merge: when a block's two sums both start with a and b, one shared a + b is kept (7 adders instead of 10), which happens in 4 of 36 orders. Cells×depth then takes only two values per ABC script, and the shared netlist is 1.20–1.28× larger under dch_map and resyn2_map but 0.92× under Yosys's default script. Removing opt_merge does not remove the dependence: the spread over orders widens to 1.44–3.17×. Stylised: one adder, Yosys 0.33, generic-gate cells×depth, no place and route.

Does letting Yosys share a common a + b make adders smaller under every ABC script?

Tests whether letting Yosys share a common a + b shrinks adders: fewer cells in 54 of 55 design/script pairs but often deeper; stylised, Yosys 0.33.

Abstract Code →

Eleven small adder-shaped designs whose outputs all contain a + b are written once so opt_merge shares the sum and once so it cannot (each pair proved equivalent). Scored under five ABC scripts, sharing gives fewer cells in 54 of 55 pairs (median ratio 0.76–0.85), but is deeper in 6–9 of 11 designs, so cells × depth favours it in 7–9 of 11. The sign flip seen on the 16-bit carry-select adder in chip-abc-orderpass does not appear. Stylised: generic gates, Yosys 0.33, no place and route.

Writing the shared a + b sum of a carry-select adder by hand (explicitly, or as an incrementer) gives the same netlist Yosys already finds; attaching the constant to b first defeats the sharing and is 17-22% smaller under ABC's optimising scripts (stylised, Yosys 0.33).

Abstract Code →

Six equivalent 16-bit adder styles (each proved against a + b with a Yosys miter) are scored with three ABC scripts. Writing the shared sum by hand (p = a + b, y = p + 1) or as an incrementer (y = x + 1) gives exactly the netlist opt_merge finds for the plain a + b + 0 / a + b + 1 text (cells×depth 2090 / 1232 / 1665), so a hand common-subexpression rewrite is a no-op. Attaching the constant to b first, a + (b + k), defeats the sharing: 2268 / 1024 / 1300, 17–22% smaller under the two optimising scripts and 9% larger under yosys_default. One design, one tool version (0.33), generic gates. Stylised.

A follow-up to chip-abc-sweep and chip-ppa-loop: the earlier proposer files and a 16-adder and 8-multiplier sweep are scored under five ABC scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equivalent to its reference (none failed). A follow-up to chip-ppa-logic: its 34 equivalent candidates for popcount, leading-zero count (clz16) and absolute difference are re-scored under five ABC scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equivalent to the reference (none of 170 failed). On clz16 the verdict flips with the script: the no-model sweep wins under the default and dc2 scripts (344, 405), while a session-written nibble-combine file wins under three others (216–336 against the sweep’s 344–462); the overall best is 0.35× the reference’s default score. Only carry-save forms win, under dch (0.91×) and a resyn2-style script (0.94×); the overall best is 0.93× the reference under its own best script. A follow-up to chip-ppa-mac: the same 17 candidates for a 4×4 unsigned multiply-accumulate are mapped to SkyWater SKY130 HD cells with ABC under four scripts, and every mapped netlist is proved equal to the reference (none failed). An exhaustive 800-point table of SKY130 areaxdelay over ABC pass sequences for the MAC (optimum 11% below the best earlier script; needle-like landscape), with random search, hill climbing and session-written proposals compared at equal budget (stylised, preliminary).

A follow-up to chip-ppa-sky130mac: every one of 800 (design, ABC pass sequence of length ≤3) points is evaluated, so the optimum is known: 1062 µm2·ns for the carry-save MAC, 11% below the best earlier script, and its netlist is proved equal to the reference. How do MAC-lane count and bit width trade area against latency in a tiny quantised-MLP accelerator?

Parameterised MAC-lane accelerator for an 8-8-4 quantised MLP, bit- and cycle-exact against NumPy in Icarus; lanes x bit-width sweep puts the cells-times-cycles minimum at 4 lanes (stylised, generic-gate counts).

A generator for an 8-8-4 integer MLP engine with P multiply-accumulate lanes and 4-, 6- or 8-bit weights, simulated in Icarus Verilog and matched bit for bit and cycle for cycle against an integer NumPy reference in all 12 configurations. Synthesised with Yosys to generic gates, latency falls from 110 to 20 cycles as lanes go from 1 to 8 while area grows about 3× to 4×, so cells×cycles is smallest at 4 lanes for every width. 6 bits matched float accuracy on the toy task; 4 bits lost about 3 points. How far do synthesis-only area and delay sit from placed-and-routed numbers on SKY130?

Abstract Code →

Thirteen small designs (adders, multipliers, FIFOs) pushed through generic gate counting, Yosys/ABC mapping onto the SKY130 HD library, and an OpenROAD flow with placement, clock tree, global routing and timing repair. Generic gate count stays within 5.1–5.8 um² per gate for combinational logic but is about 3× higher per gate for FIFOs, whose flops dominate; mapping makes a ripple and a + adder identical. Layout adds 0–28% area (most where timing needs repair), and wires add 3–19% to delay before repair. The ABC clock target did not change the netlist at all. Stylised: tiny designs, one corner, global-route parasitics only, no detailed route or DRC, nothing about a fabricated chip.
