One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

chip-mac-lanes4 tests

Which MAC-lane count is best for a tiny quantised MLP if every P from 1 to 20 is built and checked?

Builds and RTL-checks every MAC-lane count P = 1 to 20 on the F-16-4 network (F = 16, 32): the best P is 8 and 16, no non-power-of-two wins, and P above 16 only adds cells (stylised, generic-gate counts).

Abstract Code →

Every MAC-lane count P = 1–20 of chip-accel's engine on an F-16-4 quantised network (F = 16, 32), all 40 designs simulated in Icarus Verilog bit for bit against an integer NumPy reference with measured cycles equal to the formula, then scored with Yosys. The best P is 8 at F = 16 and 16 at F = 32, so the earlier hand-picked sweep already contained the optimum; P > 16 only adds cells at equal cycles, and no non-power-of-two P wins (best is 44–62% behind). Cell count is far from monotone in P (F = 32: P = 15 has 2.4× the cells of P = 16), a possible generator artefact left untested. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

chip-systolic-hidewide6 tests

Does the MAC-engine lead survive a wider hidden layer (H = 16) and more MAC lanes?

Widens the hidden layer to 16 (F = 16, 32) and lets the MAC engine reach P = 16: the best MAC engine still beats the best systolic array, by 1.30x and 1.27x in cells-times-cycles per vector, and at F = 32 its best lane count is again the largest tried (negative, stylised, generic-gate counts).

Abstract Code →

The chip-systolic-hidden comparison repeated on an F-16-4 quantised network (F = 16, 32; 4-bit weights), all 8 array configurations matched to an integer NumPy reference in Icarus Verilog and scored with Yosys against MAC-lane engines up to P = 16. A negative result: the best MAC engine wins at both F, by 1.30× and 1.27× in cells×cycles per vector. At F = 32 the best lane count (P = 16, 3% ahead of P = 8) is again the largest tried, so its optimum may lie further out. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

chip-systolic-p327 tests

Does the MAC-engine lead survive MAC lanes up to P = 32 and arrays up to R = 4?

Extends the hidden-16 comparison to MAC lanes up to P = 32 and arrays up to 4x8 with every design simulated: the best MAC engine still wins, by 1.30x and 1.28x in cells-times-cycles per vector; P = 32 adds no cycles over P = 16 (negative, stylised, generic-gate counts).

Abstract Code →

The chip-systolic-hidewide comparison (F-16-4 quantised network, F = 16, 32) extended to MAC engines with P up to 32 lanes and arrays up to 4×8 and 2×16, every design simulated in Icarus Verilog against an integer NumPy reference and scored with Yosys. A negative result: the best MAC engine still wins, by 1.30× and 1.28× in cells×cycles per vector. P = 32 adds no cycles over P = 16 (only 16 hidden outputs) and a 0.7% cell-count difference at F = 32; 4×8 does not beat 2×8. One network family, one seed, gate counts only; no layout or power.

chip-systolic-abcrobust3 tests

Does the MAC engine beat a systolic array under every ABC script, not just Yosys's default?

Re-scores chip-systolic-p32's 20 designs under five ABC scripts: the best MAC engine beats the best systolic array in all ten F x script cases, by 1.28x to 1.60x (negative for arrays, stylised, generic-gate counts).

Abstract Code →

The 20 designs of chip-systolic-p32 (six output-stationary arrays and four MAC-lane engines on an F-16-4 quantised network, F = 16, 32), each simulated against an integer NumPy reference and then scored with Yosys under five ABC scripts. A negative result for arrays: the best MAC engine wins in all ten F × script cases, by 1.28× to 1.60× in cells × cycles per vector, so the size of the lead depends on the script but the ranking does not. Stylised: one network, one seed, generic-gate counts, no layout.

chip-macp32cells4 tests

Is P = 32 being smaller than P = 16 at equal cycles a real effect or a synthesis artefact?

Re-synthesises the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines (same cycles) with three seeds and three Yosys flows: the sign of the cell-count gap depends on the flow, with swings of 1-10%, so chip-systolic-p32's 0.7% ranking is not reliable (artefact-sensitive, stylised, generic-gate counts).

Abstract Code →

chip-systolic-p32 found the 32-lane MAC engine smaller than the 16-lane one although both take the same cycles. Re-synthesised with three model seeds and three Yosys/abc flows at F = 16 and 32, the sign depends on the flow: P = 32 is smaller in all 6 cases under two flows and larger in all 6 under a four-gate library, by 47 to 699 cells (1–10%). That swing is far above the 0.7% margin used to rank the best design earlier, so that ranking should be discarded. Three seeds, one tool version, generic-gate counts only; the mechanism is not traced.

chip-p32netlist3 tests

At which Yosys stage does the P = 32 versus P = 16 cell gap appear?

Counts cells of the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines after the word-level, bit-level and abc stages: the 32-lane engine is bigger at the word level, about 500 cells smaller after techmap, so the chip-macp32cells gap is set before abc (localised, mechanism unexplained, stylised).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to chip-macp32cells. Counting cells of the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines (identical cycles, F = 16, three seeds) after the word-level, bit-level and abc stages of one Yosys script: the 32-lane engine is 640–770 cells larger at the word level but about 500 cells smaller after techmap, and abc only trims the gap to 270–410. The sign is therefore set before abc runs. Which pass removes the extra lanes was not identified. Preliminary; one Yosys version, generic-gate counts.

chip-p32passes5 tests

Which Yosys pass flips the P = 32 versus P = 16 cell gap?

Runs the Yosys fine passes one at a time on the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines: the P = 32 versus P = 16 sign flips (+2,100 to about -120 cells) at the first opt -fast after techmap, before any abc, and chip-p32netlist's pre-abc label is corrected (Yosys 0.33's -run :abc includes abc -fast). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to chip-p32netlist. Running the fine passes of Yosys 0.33 one at a time on the 16- and 32-lane MAC engines (identical cycles, F = 16, three seeds): the 32-lane engine is still about 2,100 cells larger after techmap and 114–125 cells smaller after the next opt -fast, before any abc; abc -fast adds about 400 more. It also corrects the earlier project: Yosys 0.33’s -run :abc runs abc -fast, so its “pre-abc” column was post-abc. Localised to a pass, not explained; one Yosys version, generic cell counts. Stylised.

11

Robot manufacturing loops

Can general-purpose robot arms make and assemble things, planned and checked in simulation first? Assembly sequences, insertion and cells, with every claim kept to the simulator. Topic page →

robofab-sequence10 tests

Which assembly orders survive a better checker?

Assembly-order planning for a printed gearbox: exact subset DP, collision-only admits 10.6% of orders but support checking leaves 0.077%, the collision-only optimum is infeasible, greedy disassembly needs 4 direction changes vs 1 optimal. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Exact subset dynamic programming over assembly orders for a twelve-part printed gearbox, checked at three fidelity levels. Collision-only admits 4,227,168 of 39,916,800 orders (10.6%); adding quasi-static support leaves 30,760 (0.077%), and the collision-only optimum is infeasible once support is checked. Greedy disassembly needs 4 insertion-direction changes against an optimum of 1; one order written by the session agent (a single attempt, not a benchmark) passes with 2. Stylised axis-aligned boxes, no physics engine.

robofab-settle7 tests

Does a quasi-static support rule agree with a physics engine?

MuJoCo settle tests of all 2,048 partial gearbox assemblies vs the quasi-static support rule: 95.6% agreement, 81 mutual-support false accepts and 10 bore-capture false rejects, valid-order count unchanged at 30,760. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Validates the support rule of robofab-sequence against MuJoCo settle tests on all 2,048 partial assemblies of the printed gearbox. The rule agrees on 1,957 (95.6%): 81 states it accepts topple because a part can count as resting on a part that rests on it, and 10 it rejects hold because a gear bore captures the shaft. An acyclic-support variant reaches 99.5% (fitted on the same states). The count of valid orders is unchanged at 30,760 for three friction values, so this product's conclusions survive. Stylised boxes, static release, one product.

robofab-insert6 tests

Does an insertion policy tuned in one simulator survive a better one?

Peg-in-hole search policies tuned by CEM in MuJoCo at three fidelity levels or with domain randomisation: tuned on the simplest level 0.91 success there but 0.53 / 0.26 on a stiffer-contact / held-out level; training on the stiffer level or with randomisation gives 0.43–0.46 held-out and cannot be ranked with 5 seeds. Stylised, sim-to-sim.

Abstract Code →

Cross-entropy-tuned five-parameter peg-in-hole search policies in MuJoCo, trained on three simulator fidelity levels or with domain randomisation and tested on all three plus a held-out parameter set. Tuned on the simplest level, success is 0.91 there but 0.53 on the stiffer-contact level and 0.26 on the held-out one; training on the stiffer level or with randomisation gives 0.43–0.46 on the held-out set, and with 5 seeds the two cannot be ranked. No seed exceeds 0.61 on the held-out level. Toy planar task; sim-to-sim only.

robofab-program10 tests

How much of the gap between “the twin passes” and “it fails for real” does each twin fidelity close?

Session-written pick-and-place programs checked in a kinematic SCARA twin at three fidelities against a held-out reference: of 69 reference-failing injected-bug mutants the levels reject 38, 46 and 60 with no false alarms; misses are unmodelled effects (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A kinematic SCARA pick-and-place twin at three checking levels (geometry; plus joint, payload and deadline limits; plus stochastic grasp error, grip build-up and slip) against a held-out reference twin. Of 162 injected-bug mutants of three programs, 69 fail the reference; the levels reject 38, 46 and 60 of them, with no false alarms. The misses are effects the checker does not model, so the rates reflect how the reference was built. Four programs written by the building session: three failed the reference as drafted, and one failure (payload at long reach) was invisible to all three levels. Stylised, kinematic only, no language-model API called.

robofab-cell9 tests

Which resource limits a small robot-printer-inspection cell, and does the busiest one tell you what to upgrade?

Discrete-event twin of an arm, printers and an inspection station: printers have the highest utilisation at every size, yet at 6 printers an extra arm saves 10.9 min vs 2.3 for an extra inspection station; dispatch rules trade makespan for flow time; a mean-value twin is optimistic. Stylised, illustrative parameters.

Abstract Code →

A discrete-event twin of one arm, 1–8 printers and one inspection station (30 parts, 200 replications, illustrative times). Printers have the highest utilisation at every size, yet at 6 printers an extra arm saves 10.9 min of makespan against 2.3 for an extra inspection station, because a printer is held while it waits for the arm. Dispatch rules trade makespan for mean flow time as textbook scheduling predicts, and a mean-value twin underestimates the stochastic makespan by 1–133 min. Stylised; parameters are invented, not measured.

robofab-cell-bound8 tests

Where is the bottleneck of an arm, printer and inspection cell?

Discrete-event twin of an arm, 3D printers and an inspection station: a utilisation bound names the bottleneck (printers to 10, the arm from 12, ~12.7 good parts/h) and the simulation sits 10–11% below it near the switch; a 25% faster arm lifts 11.34 to 12.68 parts/h at 12 printers, a second inspector nothing (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A hand-written discrete-event twin of one arm that loads and unloads P 3D printers, plus an inspection station with reprints, against a utilisation bound. The bound names the bottleneck (printers up to 10 printers, the arm from 12, about 12.7 good parts/h) and the simulation reaches it within 1–2% far from the switch but sits 10–11% below it at 10–12 printers. A 25% faster arm lifts throughput from 11.34 to 12.68 parts/h at 12 printers while a second inspector does nothing; arm dispatch rules made no measurable gain, and WIP beyond one job per printer plus one only lengthens flow time. Stylised parameters of my choosing, no travel or breakdowns, 20 seeds.

robofab-cell-mva8 tests

Does exact queueing analysis predict a robot-printer cell's throughput better than a utilisation bound?

Exact mean value analysis of the arm, printers and inspection network against a discrete-event twin: a few per cent off for exponential times, up to 11% low for less variable ones, better than the utilisation bound in most real-semantics rows, and it overshoots saturation at high work in process. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Mean value analysis of a closed arm, printers and inspection network, checked against a hand-written discrete-event simulation that adds one departure from product form at a time (illustrative times, 20 seeds). The code matches the exact Markov-chain solution on small networks. With exponential times MVA is within −6% to +4% of simulation; with less variable times it is up to 11% low. With printers held while waiting for the arm, MVA beats the utilisation bound at 4, 8 and 12 printers but not at 16, and it overshoots the saturation plateau at high work in process (9.8 against 8.6 parts/h at 8 printers). Stylised, simulation-only; no physical cell.

robofab-cell-cv6 tests

Where does exact queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell stop working?

Coefficient-of-variation sweep and a measured printer stall share for the arm-printer-inspection queueing model: MVA's error crosses zero near cv 1 while the utilisation bound stays high, and held-printer capacity times (1 − stall) reproduces the saturated rate at 4 and 8 printers. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the mean-value-analysis project: a coefficient-of-variation sweep (0–2, lognormal times, 4–16 printers, 20 seeds) and a directly measured printer stall share (finished parts waiting for the arm). At 12 printers the MVA error runs from −6.2% to +8.4% and crosses zero near cv 1, while the utilisation bound stays 8–25% high. Stall is small (about 4.6% at 8 printers), but holding the printer through load and unload plus the stall reproduces the saturated rate at 4 and 8 printers (8.59 against 8.56 ± 0.09). Stylised, illustrative times, simulation only.

robofab-cell-monitor8 tests

Is a print-failure camera worth it in a robot-arm 3D-printer cell?

Is a print-failure camera worth it in a robot-arm printer cell? Blind printing against abort-on-failure: +6 to 10% good parts per hour at 2 to 10 printers, none once the arm limits the cell; break-even false-stop rate. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Adds mid-print failures (0.3 per printing hour) to the arm, printers and inspection cell and compares blind printing with a camera that aborts a failing print after a delay, including false stops, against an analytic bound and a 40-seed discrete-event simulation. With a 10 min delay the camera adds 6–10% good parts per hour at 2–10 printers, 4.5% at 12 and 0.8% at 16 where the arm limits the cell; the gain falls with detection delay (11% for an instant camera, about 0.5% at 80 min), vanishes between 0.1 and 0.2 false aborts per printing hour, and grows with the failure rate (28% at 1.0 per hour). Stylised: memoryless failures, a fixed detection delay, no real detector or measured farm.

robofab-cell-detector9 tests

Where should a print-failure detector's alarm threshold go in a robot-arm 3D-printer cell?

Where should a print-failure detector's alarm threshold go in a robot-arm printer cell? A look every 2 min makes a z = 2 threshold 19 to 23% worse than blind printing; the best z is 3 to 3.5, worth +6% (d' = 2) to +11% (d' = 4). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Replaces the monitor project's fixed detection delay with a detector that looks at a print every few minutes and has a Gaussian score (separation d′) and an alarm threshold z, and asks which z maximises good parts per hour, with an exact analytic bound and a 40-seed discrete-event simulation (6 printers, 0.3 failures per printing hour, looks every 2 min). A threshold that sounds strict (z = 2, 2.3% false alarms per look) makes the cell 19–23% worse than blind printing for every detector quality, because a 60 min print is looked at 30 times; the best z is 3–3.5, and the gain over blind printing is +5.8% at d′ = 2, +9.7% at 3 and +11.3% at 4, and within noise below d′ of about 1. Stylised: looks are independent, which real consecutive frames are not.

robofab-cell-fescsweep4 tests

Where does a flow-equivalent-server decomposition of a robot-printer cell go wrong as the inspector speeds up or slows down?

Where does the flow-equivalent-server decomposition of a robot-printer cell err as the inspector speed varies? Error is 0 for fast and slow inspectors but peaks at −2% to −5% just below the knee where inspector and subsystem rates match, ten times the earlier 0.3% mean. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the decomposition project, which reported a 0.32% mean error at one inspection time. Sweeping the inspection time from 0.1 to 100 min in 10 stylised cells (2–6 printers, Erlang-4 print time, illustrative times) against the exact Markov chain, the decomposition’s error is 0.000% for a fast inspector and at most 0.52% for a very slow one, but peaks at −2.2% to −5.0% (mean −3.2%) just below the knee t* = 1/H(N), where the inspector alone matches the subsystem’s rate (0.81–0.99 t*, grid-limited). It is never positive, and smaller cells err more. The explanation (ignored correlation between inspection queue and subsystem state) is untested. Stylised: one job class, exponential load, unload and inspect times.

robofab-cell-fesc5 tests

Can a flow-equivalent-server decomposition predict a robot-printer cell's throughput without enumerating its states?

Can a flow-equivalent-server decomposition predict a robot-printer cell without enumerating its states? Mean error 0.3% (max 1.6%) against the exact Markov chain in 42 settings, where plain MVA is off by up to 20%. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the exact Markov-chain project: Norton’s theorem applied to the same stylised cell (one arm, 2–6 printers held through load and unload, one inspector; Erlang print time; illustrative times). The arm-and-printers subsystem is solved exactly at each population and replaced by one load-dependent server. Over the same 42 settings the mean absolute error against the exact chain is 0.32% (maximum 1.57%), against 6.8% (up to 20.3%) for plain mean value analysis and 4.3% for the held-printer variant; in five cells of 8–12 printers it is 0.09–0.31%. It underestimates in 38 of 42 settings because the cell is not product form. The subsystem chain is about a tenth the size of the full chain, but both solve in under a second here, so no speed claim. Stylised: one job class, exponential load, unload and inspect times.

robofab-cell-ctmc6 tests

Is the error of queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell from print-time variability or from the cell's structure?

Is the error of queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell from print-time variability or from structure? An exact Markov chain says structure: cv 1 to 0.33 moves throughput by at most 0.71%, while plain MVA overshoots up to 20% beyond the printer count.

Abstract Code →

An exact Markov-chain solution of a stylised cell (one arm, 2–6 printers held through load and unload, one inspector; Erlang print time, cv 0.33–1; illustrative times) used as a noise-free reference. It matches a simulation in 10 settings (largest |z| 1.73). Changing the print-time cv from 1 to 0.33 moves the exact throughput by at most 0.71%, so the error of mean value analysis is structural: plain MVA is within 0.6% when work in process equals the printer count but overshoots by up to 20.3% beyond it (mean error 12.8% at twice the printers), and held-demand MVA is 2.8% off at saturation but −5% to −12% off at low load. One job class, exponential load, unload and inspect times. Stylised, simulation-only.

robofab-cell-held5 tests

Does holding the printer through load and unload fix queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell?

Does adding load and unload time to the printer's demand fix MVA of the robot-printer cell? Mixed: it cuts the error at saturation (2.9% against 8.2%) but raises it elsewhere (7.3% against 3.6%), so overall plain MVA is better (4.7% against 6.2%). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the variability-sweep project: mean value analysis with the printer demand increased by the arm’s load and unload time, compared with plain MVA and two utilisation bounds against the simulated cell (cv 0.3 and 1.0, 4–16 printers, four loads, 20 seeds, 32 settings; illustrative times). The repair helps only at saturation (mean absolute error 2.9% against 8.2% for plain MVA) and hurts elsewhere (7.3% against 3.6%), so over all settings plain MVA is better (4.7% against 6.2%). A mixed result: no single demand setting is right across loads. Stylised and simulation-only.

robofab-cell-stall5 tests

Does an arm-wait-aware printer demand fix queueing analysis of a robot-printer cell?

Does adding the arm's queueing delay (a fixed point, no fitted parameter) to the held printer's demand fix MVA of the robot-printer cell? No: it underpredicts in all 32 settings and is worse overall (7.9% mean error against 6.2% for held-demand and 4.7% for plain MVA). Negative result. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the held-printer project: the printer’s demand is increased by the arm’s queueing delay, found as a fixed point from the arm’s own queue with no fitted parameter. Against the simulated cell (cv 0.3 and 1.0, 4–16 printers, four loads, 20 seeds, 32 settings; illustrative times) it underpredicts throughput in every setting and is worse overall: mean absolute error 7.9%, against 6.2% for held-demand MVA and 4.7% for plain MVA. At saturation it ties held demand (3.1% against 2.9%) but on the other 24 settings it is worse (9.5% against 7.3%). A negative result: a demand-side patch to product-form MVA is the wrong tool here. Stylised and simulation-only.

robofab-cell-blocking5 tests

Can a blocking-aware correction to queueing analysis predict a robot-printer cell across loads?

Can a blocking-aware correction to MVA predict the held-printer robot cell across loads? A fitted stall helps only at saturation (1.4% error) and worsens other loads (8.5%); keeping latency apart from capacity gives 3.6% against plain MVA's 4.7% on the design grid, but only ties plain MVA (3.4% against 3.5%) on a held-out job mix. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the held-printer project: held demand plus a fitted stall (printers waiting for the arm to unload them) helps only at saturation (1.4% mean error) and double-counts load and unload time elsewhere (8.5%). A predictor that keeps latency (plain demand plus stall) apart from capacity (held demand plus stall) scores 3.6% against 4.7% for plain MVA on 32 design settings, but ties plain MVA on a held-out job mix (3.4% against 3.5%) and still underestimates by up to 8% at moderate load. Stylised; illustrative times; 20 seeds.

robofab-selfparts8 tests

Can a parallel-jaw arm assemble its own gripper?

Can a parallel-jaw arm assemble its own toy gripper? A complete order exists only once the jaw opens to the widest part (30 mm); a top-down-only arm accepts 120 of 720 orderings against 384 with sideways moves; pad thickness changes nothing (negative). Stylised boxes.

Abstract Code →

Exhaustive search over assembly orders of a seven-part toy gripper (axis-aligned boxes) by a modelled arm with a parallel-jaw grasp check, three approach-direction models and a swept jaw opening. No complete order exists below a 30 mm opening, the width of the widest part; above it, 384 of 720 orderings are valid when parts may be slid sideways and 120 when strictly top-down. Jaw-pad thickness from 2 to 10 mm changes nothing (a negative result for this geometry). Stylised single design, no reach, force or fasteners; simulation only.

robofab-bootstrap6 tests

Can a printed gripper assemble its own next generation?

Can a printed gripper assemble its own next generation? With fixed-size jaw pads a gripper builds a copy only at scale &ge; pad thickness in mm (4 mm pads: scale 4); a stroke cap of S mm needs 30&middot;pad &le; S; seeds of 130 and 140 mm sustain a chain, 60 and 100 mm decay. Largely algebraic given an assumed opening; stylised.

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to the self-parts project: the arm that builds generation k+1 is the printed gripper of generation k, with an assumed jaw opening of 32s − 2t mm for fixed-size pads of thickness t. Exhaustive assembly search gives a required opening of exactly 30s mm, so a gripper can build a copy only at scale s ≥ t (scale 4 for 4 mm pads), and a stroke cap S admits one only if 30t ≤ S. Seeds of 130 and 140 mm sustain a chain; 60 and 100 mm seeds shrink and stop. Largely algebraic given the assumed opening; one toy design; simulation only.

robofab-reach7 tests

How long an arm does it take to assemble its own toy gripper?

How long an arm does it take to assemble its own toy gripper? A planar two-link arm needs 60–140 mm links as the tray moves 40–400 mm away, and a 90° elbow limit more than doubles it (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A planar two-link arm on a turntable must reach a pick, place and lift point for each of the six free parts of the seven-part toy gripper from robofab-selfparts. With equal links and a 100 mm shoulder height the shortest arm is 60–140 mm per link as the tray moves from 40 to 400 mm away; an elbow limit of 90° raises it from 80 to 180 mm and 60° admits none up to 600 mm. Stylised: wrist point only, no collisions, payload or wrist orientation; results sit on a 10 mm grid.

robofab-reachorder5 tests

Does the assembly order change the arm an arm needs to build its own gripper?

Does the assembly order change the arm needed to build its own gripper? Across all 384 valid orders the shortest arm is identical in every setting tried (negative result, stylised).

Abstract Code →

Combines the order search of robofab-selfparts (384 valid orders) with the two-link reach model of robofab-reach, letting each part’s lift height clear whatever is already assembled. Negative result: for every valid order the shortest arm is the same (for example 80 mm per link at a 100 mm shoulder and 120 mm tray gap, 120 mm at a 200 mm shoulder), because the cover’s own lift point bounds every order and the tray distance dominates. Stylised: wrist point only, 10 mm link grid, 20 mm base grid.

robofab-grasp6 tests

Can friction hold each printed part of a gripper?

Can friction hold each printed part of the toy gripper? The simulated minimum jaw force matches the m·g/(2μ) bound to within 5% over 33 cases and is at most 0.1 N, so the jaw opening, not friction, is the constraint (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-selfparts: for each of the six free parts of the toy gripper and each grasp axis that fits a 30 mm jaw opening, the smallest jaw force that holds the part against gravity by friction, from the bound m g/(2μ) and from a MuJoCo simulation, at μ = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8. Over 33 cases the two agree to within 5%, and the force needed is at most 0.1 N, so in this model the jaw opening, not friction, is the binding constraint. A check on the simulator set-up rather than a new result. Stylised: static hold only, boxes, assumed density and friction, no tipping or insertion loads.

robofab-armaccel10 tests

Does arm torque or jaw friction limit how fast an arm carries a printed part?

Does arm torque or jaw friction limit how fast an arm carries a printed part? With 0.12 m links and 5 N m the carries take 0.06–0.10 s and the cover needs 1.25 N per jaw (21× static); grip binds below about 0.5 N (stylised, bound extrapolated beyond 40 m/s²).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-graspmove and robofab-reach: a planar two-link arm with assumed masses carries each of the six free parts of the toy gripper on a min-jerk joint move, as fast as an assumed joint torque limit allows. With 0.12 m links and 5 N m the carries take 0.06 to 0.10 s and the 5.95 g cover needs 1.25 N per jaw, 21× its static force; a jaw force under about 0.5 N makes the grip, not the arm, the limit. A larger arm is slower at a fixed torque. Stylised: assumed masses and torques, and the grip bound, simulated only up to 40 m/s2 earlier, is applied beyond that range.

robofab-armbang14 tests

How much carry time does a time-optimal move save over min-jerk, and what does it cost the jaws?

How much carry time does a time-optimal move save over min-jerk, and what does it cost the jaws? On the robofab-armaccel arm the six-part total falls by 21 to 29% while the jaw-force bound rises 1.2 to 2.4 times (stylised, assumed parameters).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-armaccel: the same planar two-link arm carries the six free parts of the toy gripper along the same joint-space line, once with min-jerk and once with the time-optimal speed profile under an assumed joint torque limit. Over nine arm and torque cases the six-part total time falls by 21–29%, but the per-jaw force bound rises 1.2–2.4×. Stylised: every parameter except the geometry is assumed, the grip bound is not re-simulated above 40 m/s2, and the path is fixed.

robofab-jawcap23 tests

How fast can an arm carry a printed part when the jaw force is capped as well as the joint torque?

How fast can an arm carry a printed part when the jaw force is capped as well as the joint torque? On the robofab-armbang arm the time-optimal move still beats min-jerk by 17 to 43% under caps of 1.25 to 10 times the static hold force, and a tight cap makes the torque limit irrelevant (stylised, assumed parameters).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-armbang: the time-optimal speed profile along the joint-space line is solved with an added cap on the per-jaw force bound (a quadratic constraint on the path acceleration), at 1.25–10× the static hold force, and compared with the fastest min-jerk move meeting the same two limits. Over nine arm and torque cases the time-optimal six-part total is 17–43% shorter, most when the cap is tightest, and at the tightest cap the torque limit no longer changes the time. Stylised: every parameter except the geometry is assumed, the caps are multiples of a friction hold force, the grip bound is not re-simulated above 40 m/s2, profiles overshoot the limits by up to 3%, and the path is fixed.

robofab-jointspeed29 tests

Does a joint-speed limit erase the time-optimal carry's advantage over min-jerk?

Does a joint-speed limit erase the time-optimal carry's advantage over min-jerk? On the robofab-jawcap arm it grows it: 28 to 46% shorter under speed limits of 6 to 1 rad/s, tending to the 47% set by the min-jerk profile shape (stylised, assumed parameters).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-jawcap (stylised, preliminary): a peak joint-speed limit is added to the torque and jaw-force limits of a planar two-link arm carrying printed parts. Over three arm sizes, three jaw caps and speed limits of 6 to 1 rad/s, the time-optimal profile is 28 to 46% shorter than min-jerk meeting the same limits (18 to 34% without a speed limit), and the saving tends to 1 − 1/1.875 = 47%, a property of the min-jerk profile shape, so a trapezoidal baseline would show less. All parameters are assumed; the speed limits are round numbers, not an actuator rating.

robofab-trapezoid37 tests

Is the time-optimal carry's speed-limited advantage just the min-jerk profile's shape?

Is the time-optimal carry's speed-limited advantage just the min-jerk shape? Against a tuned trapezoidal-velocity move it is only 0.4 to 2.9% at speed limits of 2 and 1 rad/s (46% over min-jerk), and 8.7 to 22.5% with no speed limit (stylised, assumed parameters).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-jointspeed (stylised, preliminary): the min-jerk comparator is replaced by a trapezoidal-velocity move with a tuned ramp fraction, under the same torque, jaw-force and joint-speed limits. Over three arm sizes, three jaw caps and speed limits of 6 to 1 rad/s, the time-optimal profile beats the best trapezoid by only 0.4 to 2.9% at 2 and 1 rad/s (0.4 to 0.8% at 1 rad/s), against 46% over min-jerk, so the earlier ceiling was mostly the comparator. Without a speed limit it still wins by 8.7 to 22.5%. The smallest ramp fraction tried (0.01) binds in most tight-limit rows, so the small gap is bounded by the grid. All parameters are assumed; the speed limits are round numbers, not an actuator rating.

robofab-scurve42 tests

How much of the time-optimal carry's edge survives a jerk-limited (S-curve) profile?

Does rounding the trapezoid's corners (a jerk-limited S-curve) change the time-optimal carry's edge? An S-curve is never faster than the trapezoid and costs 0.0 to 2.0% (half-jerk) or 0.0 to 7.0% (full-jerk) at speed limits of 2 and 1 rad/s, but 1.4 to 33.7% with no speed limit (stylised, assumed parameters).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-trapezoid (stylised, preliminary): the trapezoid's acceleration corners are rounded into jerk-limited S-curves (half- and full-jerk ramps) under the same torque, jaw-force and joint-speed limits. In none of 45 speed-limited rows is an S-curve faster than the trapezoid; at speed limits of 2 and 1 rad/s it costs 0.0 to 2.0% (half-jerk) or 0.0 to 7.0% (full-jerk), and the time-optimal profile is 1.3 to 9.2% faster than the full-jerk one. With no speed limit the S-curves cost 1.4 to 33.7% and the time-optimal profile is 22.5 to 36.8% faster than the full-jerk one. Jerk is limited by profile shape, not an absolute bound, and the ramp grid is coarse. Simulated only.

robofab-scurvefine46 tests

At tight joint-speed limits, is the time-optimal carry's edge over a trapezoid real or an artefact of the ramp grid?

Checks robofab-scurve on a finer ramp grid: sampling a 0.2% ramp is needed or the trapezoid wrongly beats the time-optimal solver; with it the time-optimal edge at 2 and 1 rad/s is −0.3 to +0.9%, below the solver's own ~0.5% node-count error (stylised, negative on the old figure).

Abstract Code →

A check on robofab-scurve (stylised, negative on its old figure). Refining the ramp-fraction grid alone makes the trapezoid beat the time-optimal solver by up to 1.8%, because the 201-point torque check misses the acceleration peak of a 0.2% ramp. With extra samples inside each ramp the time-optimal edge at 2 and 1 rad/s is −0.3 to +0.9% (old figure 1.3 to 1.5%), and raising the solver from 400 to 6400 nodes moves one row by 0.5%, as large as the whole edge. Jerk-limited profiles are still never faster than the trapezoid. Only the speed-limited rows were re-run, and every parameter is assumed.

robofab-edgeconv47 tests

Once the solver is converged, is the time-optimal carry's edge over a tuned trapezoid still positive in all twelve speed-limited rows?

Re-solves the time-optimal carry at 400, 1600 and 6400 nodes in all 12 speed-limited rows of robofab-scurvefine: once converged the edge over a tuned trapezoid is positive everywhere, +0.1 to +0.9% (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-scurvefine (stylised). Re-solving the time-optimal carry at 400, 1600 and 6400 nodes lowers the six-part total by 0.01 to 0.46%, and the edge over a ramp-resolved trapezoid, negative in 7 of 12 rows at 400 nodes, becomes +0.11 to +0.88% in every row at 6400. A one-step extrapolation moves it by at most 0.03 percentage points. The trapezoid's own ramp grid is not re-converged, which can only shrink the edge, and every parameter is assumed.

robofab-rampopt49 tests

Does tuning the trapezoid's ramp fraction beyond a grid shrink the time-optimal carry's edge, and is it still positive?

Golden-section tuning of the trapezoid's ramp fraction shrinks the time-optimal carry's edge to +0.05 to +0.28% (still positive in all 12 rows; stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-edgeconv (stylised). Golden-section refinement of the trapezoid's ramp fraction lowers its six-part total by 0.00 to 0.60% across the twelve speed-limited rows. With the solver at 6400 nodes the time-optimal edge, +0.11 to +0.88% over the grid-tuned trapezoid, falls to +0.05 to +0.28% over the refined one, still positive in every row. The smallest edges are comparable to the solver's residual discretisation error, so their sign is not firmly established. One planar arm, assumed parameters, no motor dynamics; simulated only.

robofab-motorconv28 tests

Is the motor-line edge of the time-optimal carry converged in solver nodes?

Repeats the robofab-motorcurve motor-line rows with the time-optimal solver at 400, 1600 and 6400 nodes: the edge over the tuned trapezoid moves by at most 0.28 points from 1600 to 6400 (the 0.08 m, k = 2, w0 = 4 row rises from 4.98 to 5.26%), and the missing cover profile was a node-count limit. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to robofab-motorcurve (stylised, preliminary). The same nine rows and five motor no-load speeds are solved at 400, 1600 and 6400 nodes. From 1600 to 6400 nodes the six-part time-optimal total changes by at most 0.29% and the edge over the tuned trapezoid by at most 0.28 points, so the 3.5 to 28.6% range stands. The exception is the 0.08 m, k = 2 row at w0 = 4, whose edge rises from 4.98% to 5.26%. The cover part that had no profile at w0 = 4 was a node-count limit: it solves at 6400 nodes. Limits: three node counts only, toy arm, assumed motor line.

robofab-motorcurve58 tests

Does the time-optimal carry's edge over a tuned trapezoid survive a motor torque-speed line?

Re-solves the nine torque- and jaw-bound robofab-torquebound rows with a motor torque-speed line (no-load speed 4 to 20 rad/s): the time-optimal carry stays faster than the tuned trapezoid in all 45 cells, but its edge ranges 3.5 to 28.6% (9.0 to 22.9% under a constant limit), shrinking where a jaw cap binds and growing where only torque does. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to robofab-torquebound (stylised, preliminary). The same nine torque- and jaw-bound rows are re-solved with each joint's torque limit falling linearly with speed, 5 N m × (1 − |speed|/w0), for no-load speeds w0 of 20, 10, 6 and 4 rad/s. The time-optimal carry stays faster than the tuned trapezoid in every one of the 45 cells, but its edge is no longer one number: 3.5% to 28.6%, against 9.0% to 22.9% under a constant limit. Where a jaw cap binds on the smaller arms the edge shrinks as w0 falls (22.9% to 5.0% for the 0.08 m arm, k = 2); where only torque binds it grows (9.0% to 28.6% for the 0.2 m arm). The constant-limit profiles reach joint speeds up to 139 rad/s, which no motor does. One planar arm, assumed parameters, a linear motor model, not checked in MuJoCo; simulated only.

robofab-peakcheck60 tests

Is the trapezoid's duration in the torque- and jaw-bound rows set by peaks a sparse check never looked at?

Re-checks the nine torque- and jaw-bound robofab-torquebound rows with a dense trapezoid peak check (10,000 whole-move samples, 1,000 per ramp, both sides of the acceleration corners): trapezoid totals move by under 0.16% and the time-optimal edge stays 9.5 to 23.0%, so the large edge does not rest on unseen trapezoid peaks. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to robofab-torquebound (stylised, preliminary). The nine torque- and jaw-bound rows are re-solved with a trapezoid check of 10,000 whole-move samples, 1,000 per ramp and both sides of the acceleration corners, against 201 plus 160 per ramp before. The six-part trapezoid totals change by between −0.15% and +0.15%, the time-optimal edge stays 9.5% to 23.0% (9.4% to 23.0% before), and the dense answers hold at ten times the density with an estimated missed peak of at most 0.25% of a limit. The large edge does not rest on unseen trapezoid peaks. One row goes the other way (dense trapezoid 0.15% faster) and its cause is not investigated. Stylised toy arm; no hardware.

robofab-mujocotorque5 tests

Do the robofab carry results survive an independent physics engine?

Re-checks the 108 trapezoid and time-optimal carry profiles of the robofab-torquebound rows against MuJoCo inverse dynamics: the hand-written two-link torques agree to 1.8e-5 N m, peaks are within 0.73% of the 5 N m limit (stylised, joint torques only).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to robofab-torquebound (stylised, preliminary). The two-link arm behind every robofab carry result is rebuilt in MuJoCo and the 108 actual profiles (best trapezoid and time-optimal, nine rows, six parts each) are checked with MuJoCo inverse dynamics. The hand-written joint torques agree to at most 1.8e-5 N m against a 5 N m limit, so the 9 to 23% edge is not an artefact of a dynamics bug. Where only torque binds, MuJoCo puts the trapezoid's peak at up to 5.037 N m (0.73% over) and the time-optimal profile's at up to 5.011 N m (0.21% over). An open-loop replay drifts up to 0.023 rad and 1.4 mm. Joint torques only: the jaw-force bound and motor model are not checked. Planar toy arm, assumed parameters; simulated only.

robofab-torquebound50 tests

Does the time-optimal carry's edge over a tuned trapezoid survive when torque or the jaw cap binds?

Re-checks the torque- and jaw-bound rows of robofab-scurve (no speed limit) with a converged solver and denser trapezoid ramp sampling: the time-optimal carry is still 9.4 to 23.0% faster than the tuned trapezoid in all 9 rows, and the edge is stable to solver node count (under 0.1%) and rises by at most 0.4 points with denser sampling. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to robofab-toppconv (stylised, preliminary). The nine no-speed-limit rows of robofab-scurve (three arm sizes, jaw cap 2×, 5× or none, six printed parts each) are recomputed with the time-optimal solver at 400 to 25600 nodes and the trapezoid on a fine ramp grid with 40 and 160 extra samples per ramp. The time-optimal carry is 9.4% to 23.0% faster than the trapezoid in every row; the solver is converged to within 0.004% by 6400 nodes, and denser ramp sampling slows the trapezoid by 0.05% to 0.5%, raising the edge by at most 0.4 points. So, unlike the sub-1% edge under a speed limit, the torque- and jaw-bound gap is not a resolution artefact in this toy. A trapezoid-only comparison on assumed parameters; not a claim about real arms.

robofab-toppconv48 tests

Once the time-optimal solver's node count is converged, how big is its edge over a tuned trapezoid?

Re-solves the time-optimal carry of robofab-scurvefine at 400 to 25600 nodes in all 12 rows: converged to 0.02% by 6400 nodes, the 400-node answer was up to 0.5% pessimistic, and the converged edge over a ramp-resolved trapezoid is 0.11 to 0.88% in every row; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to robofab-scurvefine: all 12 rows (three arm sizes, jaw cap 5× or none, joint speed limit 2 or 1 rad/s, six printed parts each) are re-solved at 400, 1600, 6400 and 25600 nodes. The totals change by at most 0.02% between 6400 and 25600 nodes, while 400 nodes is up to 0.5% pessimistic, which explains the negative “edges” there (7 of 12 rows). At 25600 nodes the time-optimal profile is faster than the ramp-resolved trapezoid in every row, by 0.11–0.88%. The observed convergence order is noisy (1.1–3.2). Stylised and preliminary; the trapezoid side’s ramp sampling is not varied.

robofab-graspmove7 tests

How hard must the jaws squeeze while the arm moves?

How hard must the jaws squeeze while the arm moves? Simulated minimum force matches the m·sqrt((g+a)²)/(2μ) bound within 7% over 77 cases and is at most 0.3 N at 40 m/s²; a contact time constant that passes the static test reports slip at any force once the jaws accelerate (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-grasp: the jaw assembly accelerates upward or sideways at up to 40 m/s2 and the smallest holding force is compared with the bound m√((g+aup)2+aside2)/(2μ) at μ = 0.5. Over 77 cases the two agree to within 7%, and the heaviest part needs at most 0.3 N, so friction is still not the constraint. A fidelity finding: the contact time constant used for the static test (0.004 s) reports slip at any force once the jaws accelerate; 0.0005 s is needed. Stylised: boxes, rigid pads, assumed density and friction.

robofab-graspfast6 tests

Does the jaw-force bound still hold at arm accelerations of 100 to 800 m/s²?

Does the jaw-force bound still hold at arm accelerations of 100 to 800 m/s²? With fine MuJoCo contact settings the minimum force is 0.89–1.02× the bound over 39 cases; the earlier settings fail above 200 m/s² (stylised, prescribed acceleration, no arm).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-graspmove and robofab-armaccel, which applied the bound m√((g+aup)2+aside2)/(2μ) beyond the 40 m/s2 it had been tested to. Here a MuJoCo jaw assembly with prescribed constant acceleration (40 to 800 m/s2) holds three printed parts of a toy gripper. With a 0.05 ms timestep and 0.1 ms contact time constant the simulated minimum force is 0.89 to 1.02 times the bound over 39 cases (median 1.00); with the earlier settings no force up to 60 N holds a part at 400 or 800 m/s2, a contact-lag artefact. Stylised: rigid box pads, one friction coefficient, no arm dynamics or trajectory.

robofab-solrefmap5 tests

How fine must the MuJoCo contact settings be for a moving grasp?

How fine must MuJoCo contact settings be for a moving grasp? On all seven toy-gripper parts, solref 0.2 ms and below reproduce the jaw-force bound (0.98–1.04×) at 100–800 m/s²; 0.5 ms fails at 400 and above, and the adequate value falls with acceleration (stylised, upward load only).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-graspfast. On all seven printed parts of a toy gripper, a jaw assembly accelerating upward at 100, 400 and 800 m/s2 needs a simulated minimum force of 0.98–1.04 times the bound at contact time constants of 0.2 ms and below (63 cases). At 0.5 ms the bound is matched at 100 m/s2 but no force up to 60 N holds any part at 400 or 800. A scan on one part shows the largest adequate time constant falls with acceleration and is not a single threshold on their product. Stylised: upward load only, rigid box pads, one friction value, no arm.

robofab-solreftimestep6 tests

Is it the contact time constant or the timestep that breaks a moving grasp?

Is it solref or the timestep that breaks a moving MuJoCo grasp? On a 24-cell grid only 6 cells hold; a coarse step always fails, a finer step does not rescue a marginal solref, and solref 0.1 ms holds at steps of 0.1 ms and below (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-solrefmap. On the cover part of a toy gripper accelerating upward at 400 and 800 m/s2, a MuJoCo jaw-force test holds in only 6 of 24 cells of a grid of contact time constant (0.5, 0.3, 0.2 ms) and timestep (0.4 to 0.05 ms). A coarse timestep always fails, probably because MuJoCo raises the effective constant to twice the timestep. A finer timestep does not rescue a marginal constant (at 800 m/s2 and 0.2 ms only a 0.1 ms step holds, finer ones fail for an unexplained reason), while a 0.1 ms constant holds at every step of 0.1 ms and below. Stylised: one part, upward acceleration only, rigid box pads, no arm.

robofab-solrefsafe8 tests

Is MuJoCo's refsafe clamp what breaks a moving grasp at a coarse timestep?

Does MuJoCo's refsafe clamp break a moving grasp at a coarse timestep? Switching it off changes 7 of 32 grid cells' outcomes (11 hold on, 10 off), 10 runs go unstable, and the non-monotone timestep behaviour survives (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-solreftimestep, which only read the documentation on the refsafe flag. The same jaw-force test (cover part, 400 and 800 m/s2) is run over contact time constants of 0.5 to 0.1 ms and timesteps of 0.4 to 0.05 ms with the flag on and off. 11 of 32 cells hold with it on and 10 of 32 with it off, and the two settings disagree in 7 cells. With it off, 10 runs end in a solver instability, so the clamp protects some cells and costs others, and the non-monotone timestep behaviour survives with it off. Stylised: one part, upward acceleration only, rigid box pads, no arm.

robofab-graspoffset6 tests

Does an off-centre centre of mass need a harder grasp?

Does an off-centre centre of mass need a harder grasp? Ball-pad elliptic-cone bound matches MuJoCo within 1.1% (5× force at 20 mm offset); flat-pad MuJoCo lies between an equal-split and a best-split corner-contact bound (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-liftload, whose torque bracket was inconclusive. A 20 mm cube is pinched with its centre of mass shifted 0 to 20 mm in the pad plane. For ball pads (one point contact, an assumed torsional friction coefficient of 2 mm) the elliptic-cone bound matches MuJoCo within 1.1% and the needed force rises 5× (0.097 to 0.50 N). For flat pads the twist is resisted at the corner contacts: MuJoCo lies between an equal-split upper bound and a best-split lower bound at all eight offsets, and needs 0.39× the ball-pad force at 10 mm. The result is insensitive to the rotation tolerance (1, 3, 10°). Stylised: rigid pads, assumed friction, static hold only.

robofab-liftload7 tests

Does the friction-grasp bound survive lift acceleration and an off-centre centre of mass?

Does the friction-grasp bound survive lift acceleration and an off-centre centre of mass? Scaled bound matches MuJoCo within 6% over 66 cases; the torque bracket for an off-centre bar is inconclusive and depends on the rotation tolerance (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-grasp. With a constant lift or sideways acceleration applied as an effective gravity, the simulated minimum jaw force for the six free parts of the toy gripper stays within 6% of the scaled bound m √((g+az)2+at2)/(2μ) over 66 cases, at most 0.21 N. These parts are symmetric, so they test no torque. For a 10×10 mm bar held at one end the torque bracket is inconclusive: with a 5° rotation tolerance MuJoCo holds with less force than the lower bound in 11 of 12 cases, and with 1° the longer bars do not hold at 20 N. Stylised: constant load, boxes, assumed density and friction, thresholds chosen by me.

robofab-sliprate7 tests

Is the off-centre bar result in robofab-liftload a grasp effect or solver creep?

Is the off-centre bar result in robofab-liftload a grasp effect or solver creep? The bar creeps at about 3.7 deg/s from 0.3 to 3 N in MuJoCo, with a rate set by contact settings, so the earlier verdict reflects the simulator (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-liftload that replaces its pass/fail threshold with the bar’s rotation rate. A 10×10×40 mm bar held at one end creeps at about 3.7 deg/s from 0.3 to 3 N and still 2.2 deg/s at 20 N, so no force stops it. The rate scales with the contact time constant and drops tenfold when impratio goes from 1 to 10; torsional friction lowers it 2.5–3×. Free drops occur only at 0.1 N. The earlier verdict reflects simulator settings, not the grasp. Stylised: one engine, boxes, assumed density and friction.

robofab-slipcrit5 tests

Does a rate-based "holds" criterion make a MuJoCo grasp verdict independent of solver settings?

Does a rate-based "holds" criterion make a MuJoCo grasp verdict independent of solver settings? No: the minimum holding force still varies 33x to 400x or more across contact settings, like a 1 degree tolerance (negative, stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-sliprate. Judging a bar held at one end by its extrapolated creep over a 3 s hold (under 2 mm) instead of a rotation tolerance does not help: across eight MuJoCo contact settings the minimum holding force varies by 33× to 400× or more, about as much as under a 1° tolerance. Only a loose 5° tolerance is stable, and only for bars up to 40 mm. Negative and preliminary: the settings, not the criterion, drive the verdict. Stylised, one engine, no physical grip.

robofab-slipthresh6 tests

Is any rate threshold settings-robust for a MuJoCo grasp "holds" verdict?

Is any rate threshold settings-robust for a MuJoCo "holds" verdict? Spread falls with the allowed tip speed and is 1.6 only at a loose 20 mm/s (0.5 s, 10 mm); 242.7 to 400 at 2 mm/s or less (stylised, preliminary).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-slipcrit that sweeps the rate criterion’s task time (0.5–10 s) and tip bound (1–10 mm) over four bars and eight MuJoCo contact settings. The worst-case spread of the minimum holding force falls with the allowed tip speed: 242.7–400× at 2 mm/s or less, 89.4× at 3.3–5 mm/s, 20× at 10 mm/s and 1.6× only at 20 mm/s (0.5 s, 10 mm), a loose threshold; 10 s holds fail at every bound. Robustness comes from a loose threshold, not a better criterion. Stylised and preliminary: one engine, boxes, assumed density and friction.

robofab-slipmu8 tests

Does the loose 20 mm/s “holds” threshold stay settings-robust at other friction and under lift?

Does the loose 20 mm/s "holds" threshold stay settings-robust at other friction and under lift? It is the only threshold under 5x spread in all six conditions (1.6 to 4.5), every other is at least 20x (stylised, preliminary).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-slipthresh, repeating its 16-threshold sweep at friction 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8, with and without a 5 m/s2 lift acceleration. The loose 20 mm/s threshold (10 mm in 0.5 s) is the only one with a worst-case spread of the minimum holding force under 5× in all six conditions: 1.6× in four, 2.7× at mu 0.5 with lift and 4.5× at mu 0.3 with lift. Every other threshold is at least 20×. Robustness comes from looseness, and it weakens at low friction under load. Stylised, one engine, no physical grip.

robofab-barimpratio8 tests

Does a stiffer friction cone make the held-bar result in robofab-liftload threshold-free?

Does a stiffer friction cone make the held-bar result threshold-free? Creep falls about as 1/impratio (3.66 to 0.004 deg/s); from impratio 10 the 1 and 5 degree forces agree within 26%, and MuJoCo needs 0.67 to 1.17 times the old torque bracket's lower bound (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A follow-up to robofab-sliprate, which traced the bar’s creep to MuJoCo’s contact settings. Raising the impratio option from 1 to 1000 cuts the creep of a 10×10×40 mm bar held at one end from 3.66 to 0.004 deg/s, roughly as 1/impratio. From impratio 10 the minimum holding forces for 1° and 5° tolerances agree within 26% in all 12 cases, so the answer no longer depends on the threshold. The simulated force is below the uniform-pressure torque bracket in 10 of 12 cases (0.67–1.17× its lower bound) and 1.15–1.67× a point-contact bound built on the five contacts per pad MuJoCo reports. One engine, one bar section, no torsional friction. Stylised and preliminary.

robofab-tolstack9 tests

How much clearance does a printed two-pin cover need to assemble, and how wasteful is worst-case stacking?

How much clearance does a printed two-pin cover need to assemble, and how wasteful is worst-case stacking? At position sd 0.10 mm and size sd 0.05 mm, 99% yield needs 0.62 mm diametral clearance and a ±3σ worst-case stack asks for 2.0 mm (stylised, assumed process spreads).

Abstract Code →

Monte Carlo of a printed base with two pins and a cover with two holes, each centre with a Gaussian position error and each diameter a Gaussian size error, translation-only assembly (exact two-disk test). With exact sizes, yield is 1 − exp(−c2/(8σp2)) (tested against simulation). For position sd 0.10 mm and size sd 0.05 mm, 99% yield needs 0.62 mm nominal diametral clearance and 99.9% needs 0.77 mm, while a ±3σ worst-case stack asks for 2.0 mm (3.0–3.4× the 99% requirement and 2.5–2.8× the 99.9% one across the six unbiased cases); a 3σ root-sum-square rule lands at 0.9990–0.9998 yield where the holes are unbiased. A hole bias adds to the needed clearance one for one. Assumed process spreads, not measured; two pins, no rotation, stylised.

12

Ambient AI assistant

An always-on, audio-first assistant: when it should speak, and how fast and cheaply the pipeline runs on a device. Simulation first, no real recordings. Topic page →

ambient-pipeline7 tests

How much latency and memory does an open-model voice pipeline cost on a CPU, and what reply time does it leave?

CPU voice pipeline (Silero VAD, Whisper tiny.en, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Piper) on synthetic speech: per-stage latency/RTF/memory and a reply-latency budget of 0.9–1.5 s at 200–800 ms endpoint hangover, ~0.7 s of it compute. Server CPU, not a phone.

Abstract Code →

A streaming Silero VAD, Whisper tiny.en (int8), Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit) and Piper chain on four CPU cores, on six synthetic sentences. VAD costs 0.15 ms per 32 ms frame, ASR 306 ms per segment (RTF 0.11), the first LLM sentence 267 ms, the first TTS chunk 88 ms, and the models add about 740 MB. End of speech to first audio is 0.94–1.55 s at 200–800 ms endpoint hangover, of which about 0.7 s is compute; a 200 ms hangover already cut one utterance in two, and a 0.5 s target is impossible once the hangover alone exceeds it. Stylised: synthetic clean speech, one server CPU not a phone, batch ASR, LLM answer quality not evaluated.

ambient-interject9 tests

When should an always-on assistant speak, and does a policy tuned in a simulator keep its annoyance budget in a real room?

When an always-on assistant should speak: wake, keyword, threshold and learned policies at equal annoyance, and what breaks when the simulator's room differs from the real one

Abstract Code →

Simulated 10 s listening windows (needs at 3%, an intent score with d′ = 2, wake-phrase and keyword signals) compare interruption policies at equal annoyance. A wake word is precise (0.69) but catches 15% of needs; adding a keyword reaches 53% recall at 28.7 false interruptions per hour (0.72 for the wake word). At a budget of 1 false per hour a score threshold reaches recall 0.26 and a logistic policy that also uses the keyword and wake flag 0.33; recall at that budget climbs from 0.17 to 0.82 as d′ goes from 1 to 4. Tuned to 1 false per hour, policies keep the budget when only the need side shifts (weaker detector, rarer needs) but run at 3.6–3.9 per hour when the no-need background shifts (noisier score, more wake false alarms); 16 labelled hours restore it for the noisier score, and no threshold can for a wake detector that alone causes 3.5 false per hour. Stylised: independent windows, Gaussian scores, chosen costs, no real conversations.

ambient-asrnoise6 tests

How much does speech-recognition error hurt an always-on assistant's trigger policies at equal annoyance?

How much speech-recognition error hurts an always-on assistant's trigger policies at equal annoyance: from word error rate 0 to 0.5 a two-word wake phrase loses 74% of its recall and a transcript-reading threshold 76%, an acoustic-only score about 54%, and the transcript policy falls behind the acoustic one at WER 0.3 to 0.4 if its separation shrinks as (1-WER)^2 (stylised).

Abstract Code →

The ambient-interject world with an ASR word error rate (WER) entering each signal by assumption: a two-word wake phrase needs both words right, a keyword one, a transcript-reading intent score loses separation as (1−WER)k, an acoustic score is unaffected. At 2 false interruptions per hour, going from WER 0 to 0.5 cuts the wake phrase's recall from 0.151 to 0.039 (−74%) and the transcript threshold's from 0.365 to 0.089 (−76%), while the acoustic threshold falls from 0.189 to 0.087. With k = 1 the transcript policy stays marginally ahead at WER 0.5; with k = 2 the acoustic policy overtakes it at WER 0.25–0.4. Thresholds tuned at WER 0 stay under the false-interruption budget when deployed at higher WER. Stylised: the WER-to-signal mapping is assumed, not fitted to real recognition, and ASR confidence is not modelled.

ambient-cluster7 tests

When moments of need cluster in time, does a cooldown, a boost or a back-off help an always-on assistant at equal annoyance?

When moments of need cluster in time, does a cooldown, boost or back-off help an always-on assistant at equal annoyance: an episode-aware boost gains up to 0.05 recall under strong clustering, a cooldown always loses recall, back-off is a wash; stylised simulation.

Abstract Code →

Needs are made to cluster with a hidden episode/quiet chain (overall rate fixed at 3% of 10 s windows), and a plain score threshold is compared with three stateful rules at the same budget of false interruptions per hour, paired over 10 seeds. With strong clustering an episode-aware boost (lower the threshold after an accepted answer) raises recall by 0.039 at 1 false/h and 0.054 at 4 (0.467 to 0.521); a cooldown after speaking loses recall everywhere, up to 0.066; a back-off after a dismissal is within noise or slightly negative. Without clustering nothing helps. At the 1 false/h budget the boost also overshoots the budget slightly (1.19 vs 1.11). Stylised: false alarms are independent of the episode state, feedback is exact and immediate, every distribution is chosen, no real conversations.

ambient-memory9 tests

Under a storage limit, which transcripts should an on-device assistant keep, and what survives?

What an on-device assistant should keep from a week of simulated transcripts: BM25 retrieval, extractive summaries and byte-limited retention policies (stylised)

Abstract Code →

Seven simulated days of 1500 utterances each with 6 planted facts per day. BM25 finds every fact (hit@5 = 1.00) when the key words are rare, which is the easy case. With the store limited to 10% of the week, dropping oldest or random utterances keeps 0.11 and 0.10 of the facts; keeping the highest mean-IDF utterances keeps 0.93, because the facts are rare-word lines by construction. An importance-ranked extractive summary at 5% of a day holds 85% of its facts, against 3% for the first lines. Index build 0.04 s, query 1.9 ms on one container CPU. Stylised: synthetic words, lexical queries, no paraphrase, no speech errors. Produced with AI assistance.

Which parts of an always-on Android listening service can be tested without a phone?

Abstract Code →

A plain-Kotlin core (frame re-chunking, an energy-gate voice detector with hangover and pre-roll, an utterance segmenter that never emits silence, and a headset route policy that pauses rather than falling back to the phone mic) with 7 unit tests, which pass when compiled with Kotlin 2.0.21 and run through a test shim. The Android foreground-service shell is unbuilt: no SDK was usable, so no latency, battery or accuracy numbers exist. Synthetic square-wave frames only. Produced with AI assistance.

ambient-glance10 tests

When is a glance better than speech for an always-on assistant?

When a glanceable display beats speech for an always-on assistant: a stylised utility model over noise, company, free eyes and message length, with sensitivity and twin-gap checks

Abstract Code →

A stylised expected-utility model chooses between speech, a glanceable display and silence by noise, other talkers, free eyes and message length; a Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.001. A glance wins in about half of 84 grid contexts, and the look rate, the number a simulator is least able to supply, drives the twin gap (up to 0.036 utility per message). Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-urgency9 tests

Abstract Code →

A stylised expected-utility model adds three urgency classes (deadlines of 120, 20 and 6 s) and a chime-plus-glance mode to the speech, glance and silence choice. Chime-plus-glance is the best mode in 62% of normal and high-urgency contexts and raises mean utility per message from 0.351 to 0.417 (partly by construction, since high-urgency messages carry twice the weight); a Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.002. The look and reaction rates drive the twin gap (up to 0.018 utility per message). Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-speculate9 tests

How much reply latency can an always-on assistant hide by starting its pipeline before the speaker has finished?

How much reply latency starting the ASR/LLM/TTS chain during the end-of-speech hangover hides, from the measured ambient-pipeline stage times and an assumed within-turn pause model (hold-until-endpoint vs eager; extra runs per turn)

Abstract Code →

Using the measured ASR, LLM and TTS times from ambient-pipeline (a 682 ms median chain on one server CPU, six synthetic utterances), the reply pipeline starts after S ms of silence instead of after the full end-of-speech hangover H and the reply is held until H confirms the turn is over. Holding saves exactly min(chain, H − S): at H = 1000 ms the median reply falls from 1744 to 1061 ms, at the price of 0.7 to 1.9 extra pipeline runs per turn depending on S, and the just-in-time start S = H − chain is the cheapest that hides everything. Pause durations inside a turn are assumed (five lognormal settings, not data); with median 400 ms pauses no hangover up to 1.2 s keeps cut-offs under 10%. Closed forms agree with a Monte Carlo check.

ambient-semend8 tests

Can a sentence-completeness cue let an always-on assistant stop waiting so long before it replies?

Can a sentence-completeness cue let an always-on assistant stop waiting so long before it replies: a stylised two-hangover endpointer cuts the mean wait from 913 to 574 ms at a 10% cut-off budget if no pause sits at a complete point, but only to 837 ms if half do; cue and pauses assumed.

Abstract Code →

A stylised signal-detection model: the endpointer waits a short hangover Hs after a sentence the cue calls complete and a longer Hl otherwise. With medium pauses (2 per turn, median 250 ms, assumed) and a 10% cut-off budget, a fixed hangover is 913 ms; a cue of quality d = 2 cuts the mean wait to 574 ms if no pause sits at a complete point, but only to 837 ms if half of them do, because the cue is blind to those. With long or widely spread pauses, where a fixed hangover is 1.9 to 2.6 s at a 5% budget, d = 3 gives 571 to 873 ms. The cue, the pause model and the share of clause-boundary pauses are assumed, not measured; only the 682 ms reply chain is measured. Closed forms agree with a Monte Carlo check.

ambient-rechime9 tests

How many repeated earbud tones before a glance are worth their annoyance, by urgency, tone gap and masking, in the ambient-urgency utility model (stylised)

Abstract Code →

A stylised extension of the urgency model lets the assistant repeat a tone up to four times, 3 s apart, each noticed independently and cancelled once the wearer looks. Choosing the number of tones per context raises mean utility per message from 0.387 (plain glance or one tone) to 0.409; two tones give most of it, and the gain is nil for low urgency and 0.062 for high urgency (partly built in by the weights). Always repeating is barely better than one tone. A Monte Carlo check agrees with the closed form to 0.002. Tones are assumed independent and annoyance flat per tone, and every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-misread8 tests

How accurate must an always-on assistant's urgency label be before acting on it beats ignoring it?

How accurate an urgency label must be before an always-on assistant should act on it: naive, Bayesian and label-ignoring policies in the ambient-urgency utility model (stylised)

Abstract Code →

In the stylised urgency model, perfect urgency knowledge is worth 0.034 utility per message. Acting naively on a noisy label stops being worse than ignoring it at about 70% accuracy with uniform errors (about 53% if errors only hit neighbouring classes), and at 70% it loses in 18 of 48 contexts. A Bayesian reading of the label never loses to ignoring it when the prior and confusion matrix are known, but a prior that over-weights high urgency drops it below ignoring the label. Every parameter is a round figure of mine: nothing is fitted or measured.

ambient-confest6 tests

How many audited messages does an always-on assistant need before it can trust a noisy urgency label?

How many audited messages an assistant needs to estimate a noisy urgency label's confusion matrix and prior well enough to act on it: about 50 at moderate accuracy, with smoothing helping at tiny audit sets (stylised)

Abstract Code →

Extending the stylised urgency-label model, the assistant estimates the label’s class mix and confusion matrix from n audited messages and then acts by Bayes’ rule. With maximum-likelihood estimates, n = 10 is worse than ignoring the label (mean utility 0.363 against 0.382 at 70% label accuracy); n = 50 recovers 76% of the gain of knowing the true parameters and n = 200 recovers 92%. Add-one smoothing cuts the spread at tiny n but costs a little at high accuracy. Stylised: round-number utilities, uniform label errors, noise-free audit labels.

ambient-noisyaudit7 tests

What does a noisy auditor do to an assistant that learns its urgency label’s reliability from audits?

What a noisy human auditor does to an assistant that learns its urgency label's reliability from audits: taking audit labels as truth biases the estimate and loses 8% to 69% of the label's gain at a 0.9 to 0.7 auditor, and correcting for a known auditor accuracy recovers it (stylised)

Abstract Code →

Extending the stylised urgency-label model, the audit labels are themselves wrong. Taking them as truth biases the estimated label accuracy (0.57 instead of 0.70 with a 0.8-accuracy auditor) and does not improve with more audits: the policy loses 47% of the label’s gain over ignoring it at label accuracy 0.7, and 31% at 0.9. A 0.9 auditor costs only 8–14%. Maximum likelihood over the unseen true class, given the auditor’s accuracy, recovers the true-parameter value, but it needs that accuracy known (not identifiable from one auditor) and is no better at 50 audits with a poor auditor. Stylised; both label and auditor are made-up uniform-error matrices.

ambient-goldaudit7 tests

How many gold-labelled audits replace noisy ones when the auditor’s accuracy is unknown?

Abstract Code →

Extending the stylised noisy-audit model, 200 or 1000 audits from a 0.8-accuracy auditor read as truth give mean utility 0.387–0.388 (label accuracy 0.7) and do not improve with n, while 25 gold audits already match them and 10 do not. Pooling noisy with gold audits as truth is worse than gold alone. Fitting the mix, the label matrix and the auditor’s matrix jointly by EM, with 10 gold and 200 noisy audits, reaches 0.4054 against 0.4066 for the true parameters at label accuracy 0.9 (gold alone: 0.3955). The advantage vanishes by 200 gold audits. Stylised: uniform-error matrices, one auditor accuracy, EM started at the true value, round-number utilities.

How should a fixed audit budget be split between gold-labelled and noisy audits?

How to split a fixed audit budget between gold and noisy audits when gold costs 3 to 30 times more: all-noisy is worst or near-worst in all 12 cells, 25% on gold with a joint EM fit is within 0.0009 of the best, and all-gold loses when gold is expensive (stylised)

Abstract Code →

Extending the stylised gold-audit model with a price: a gold audit costs 3, 10 or 30 noisy audits, with budgets of 200 and 1000. Spending everything on noisy audits read as truth is the worst or near-worst split in all 12 cells (0.387–0.388 at label accuracy 0.7). There is no single best share, but 25% of the budget on gold, fitted jointly with the noisy audits by EM, is within 0.0009 of the best in every cell and 50% within 0.0016. When gold is expensive, all-gold is worse (0.3843 at B = 200, cost 30). Stylised: uniform-error matrices, one auditor accuracy, round-number utilities.

Can the assistant learn its urgency label's reliability from two noisy auditors with no accuracy known (Dawid-Skene), and what does a wrong assumed auditor accuracy cost: over-trusting the auditor loses 31% of a 0.9 label's gain, and Dawid-Skene reaches within 0.0005 of the oracle at n = 1000 (stylised)

Abstract Code →

Extending the noisy-audit model, a wrongly assumed accuracy for a 0.8-accuracy auditor costs 31% of a 0.9 label’s gain if the auditor is trusted fully, 17% if assumed 0.9 and 6% if assumed 0.6 (about 39–47% at either extreme for a 0.7 label). What does Dawid-Skene do when the two auditors share their errors: it over-trusts them (auditor accuracy read as 0.909 for a true 0.8 at half shared) and loses part of its edge over trusting one auditor, falling to equal it when the second auditor is a copy, never below it (stylised)

Abstract Code →

Extending the two-auditor model, the second auditor copies the first with probability ρ (each stays 0.8 accurate). Dawid–Skene reads their agreement as correctness: the accuracy it assigns auditor 1 rises from 0.80 to 0.91 at ρ = 0.5 and 1.00 at ρ = 1. At label accuracy 0.9 its policy utility falls from 0.4066 (ρ = 0) to 0.4026 and 0.3992, where it equals taking one auditor as truth, and never goes below that in this model; an oracle told auditor 1’s accuracy is unaffected. ambient-dshard7 tests

What if the two auditors only share errors on hard messages, and can a hardness-aware EM fix Dawid–Skene?

A fraction h of messages is hard for both auditors (accuracy 0.5 or chance) and the rest easy, with each auditor still 0.8 accurate overall. Dawid–Skene again over-trusts the auditors (0.84 for a true 0.8 at h = 0.3, hard accuracy 0.5), but the utility cost is far smaller than with copying: at label accuracy 0.9 its policy utility is 0.4060 against 0.4066 for the true parameters. Only in the extreme cell (30% of messages at chance, the rest perfectly easy) does it fall to the naive estimator’s 0.3992, and it never goes below it. A hardness-aware EM with an informed start recovers the classifier’s matrix and the policy utility at the population level, but the hard share itself is not identified: different starts fit the same joint distribution with P(hard) from 0.24 to 0.35. Stylised, simulated results only.

Extending the hard-message model to three auditors (each 0.8 accurate overall, a fraction h of messages hard for all). A hardness-aware EM now recovers the hard share at the population level (P(hard) 0.300 from four informed starts, where two auditors left 0.24–0.35), but only loosely from samples (sd 0.07 at n = 1000) and a poor start still lands on a degenerate fit. Plain Dawid–Skene gets worse with more auditors: in the extreme cell (30% of messages at chance) it reads them as 0.85 accurate and its policy utility falls to 0.3912 at label accuracy 0.9, below the naive estimator’s 0.3992; the hardness-aware EM stays at the true-parameter 0.4066. Fitting the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model from 8 grid starts (none near the truth) and keeping the highest-likelihood fit recovers the hard share at the population level (P(hard) 0.300), where a single poor start stays at 0.500 with a lower likelihood. Testing h = 0 in the three-auditor hardness-aware Dawid–Skene model. Under the null the likelihood-ratio statistic has median about 5 and 95th percentile about 13, so the chi-square cutoffs 3.84 and 5.99 reject 62–72% and 35–49% of null data sets. A parametric bootstrap (39 refits) rejects 7/60 and 0/60 under the null and detects h = 0.3 reliably at n = 1000 (100%) but only 37% at n = 200 with hard accuracy 0.5; h = 0.1 is undetectable. Stylised, 60 draws per cell.

A larger null-only check of the parametric-bootstrap test from ambient-hlrt (B = 39): 200 data sets with no hard messages at each of n = 100, 200 and 500. Rejection at nominal 5% is 11/200, 9/200 and 8/200 (exact 95% intervals all contain 0.05) and at 10% is 20, 16 and 19 of 200; mean p is about 0.5. The earlier 7/60 at n = 200 looks like noise. Does the bootstrap test of “no hard messages” stay valid when the auditors differ in accuracy?

Can an always-on assistant learn when to speak from accept/dismiss feedback alone, and what does it cost in dismissals?

A simulated assistant learns an interruption policy online (greedy, ε-greedy or Thompson-sampled logistic model) from the user’s reaction only when it speaks. A stylised follow-up to ambient-bandit: the assistant speaks with a known probability (ε-greedy) and refits its model with each labelled window weighted by 1/propensity. Mostly negative: exploration itself costs more utility than the learning gains at every ε tried, weights up to 500 make the weighted fit unstable at small ε (a standard deviation across seeds of tens of utility units per hour), and the weighting did not rescue the uninformed-prior or the drift scenarios. ambient-crossfit5 tests

Does cross-fitting the outcome model help capped doubly robust learning from an assistant’s own feedback?

Does fitting the doubly robust outcome model out-of-sample (2-fold cross-fitting) help the capped correction: no, a negative result; differences are within seed noise or worse, and the unclipped collapse at ε = 0.002 persists (1.53 vs 0.26 utility/h); stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-drclip. The outcome model behind the doubly robust pseudo-labels is fitted on the other half of the windows (2-fold cross-fitting) instead of on the same data, with the inverse-propensity correction capped at 5, 20, 100 or not at all. Negative result: with an informed prior the cross-fitted and in-sample fits are within about 0.1 utility/h of each other wherever the cap is finite, and the unclipped collapse at ε = 0.002 remains (1.53 vs 0.26 utility/h, against 12.71 for the oracle). With an uninformed prior the gaps are large but have no consistent sign (cross-fitting is better in some cells, worse in others) and both variants stay far below the biased fit. Simulated windows with costs chosen by me; no claim about a real user or device.

ambient-capcv5 tests

Can the doubly robust cap be chosen by validation on an assistant’s own logs?

Can the capped doubly robust cap be chosen by 4-fold IPS validation on the log: with an informed prior it matches the best fixed cap within seed noise, with an uninformed prior it does not rescue learning; stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-crossfit. The cap on the inverse-propensity correction is chosen from {2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, ∞} by 4-fold validation, scoring each candidate with an uncapped inverse-propensity estimate of its utility. With an informed prior the chosen cap matches the best fixed cap to within seed noise (12.23 against 12.19 utility/h at ε = 0.005; 11.45 against 11.84 at 0.002, with a wider spread). With an uninformed prior it does not rescue learning (between −21 and −1 utility/h with seed standard deviations of 24–51, against about 12 for a randomly sampled log), and the validation score is noisy enough that chosen caps scatter across the grid. Stylised, simulated only; 20 seeds, no significance tests.

ambient-drvalid7 tests

Does a doubly robust validation score choose the doubly robust cap better than an IPS score?

A doubly robust validation score does not pick the DR cap better than IPS with the same 4 folds (equal with an informed prior, mixed with the uninformed one); 8 random folds with the DR score is best in all three uninformed cells but still far below the label-matched control (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, mostly negative follow-up to ambient-capcv.
