Replacing the inverse-propensity validation score with a doubly robust one, on the same 4 folds, changes nothing with an informed prior and gives mixed results with the uninformed one (seed standard deviations of 20–51 utility/h). A doubly robust score on 8 random folds is the best selector in all three uninformed cells, but remains far below a label-matched control (about 12 utility/h against −11 to 6); score, fold count and fold type changed together, so the cause is untested. Simulated, independent windows only; preliminary.

ambient-drablate7 tests

Which of score, fold count and fold type made cap selection better in ambient-drvalid?

Ablating the three changes in ambient-drvalid (score, fold count, fold type): in the uninformed cells random folds help more than the DR score (IPS on 8 random folds is as good as DR on 8), no factor wins everywhere, and every selector stays far below the label-matched control (stylised, negative).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, mostly negative ablation of ambient-drvalid: all 8 combinations of validation score (IPS or doubly robust), folds (4 or 8) and fold type (contiguous or random) choosing the doubly robust cap, 20 seeds. With an informed prior all eight are within 0.2 utility/h. With the uninformed prior, random folds are the most consistent help: at ε = 0.02 the 4-fold IPS selector gives −1.4 (std 24) against 5.6 (std 7.3) with random folds, and IPS on 8 random folds (6.3) matches DR on 8 random folds (5.9). At ε = 0.005 the DR score is worse than IPS on contiguous folds (−26.9 vs −17.7) and no selector is clearly best; seed standard deviations are 5–55. Every selector stays far below the label-matched control (about 12). Simulated, independent windows, no significance tests.

ambient-drrepeat8 tests

Do repeated random fold assignments stabilise validation-based cap selection?

Repeated random fold assignments for cap selection in the ambient-assistant world (follow-up to ambient-drablate): averaging 5 assignments helps the IPS-score selector at ε = 0.02 (3.5 → 5.3 utility/h) and nothing else beyond noise; stylised, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, mixed follow-up to ambient-drablate: averaging the cap-selection score over 5 random fold assignments (instead of one) with an uninformed prior, 20 seeds. At ε = 0.02 it lifts the IPS-score selector from 3.5 to 5.3 utility/h and halves its seed spread; at smaller ε it changes nothing beyond noise. Single-assignment results differ from the earlier project's, showing how much one fold permutation can matter. Every selector stays far below the label-matched control (about 12). Simulated and stylised only.

ambient-exploreonly5 tests

Does fitting only on the windows an assistant explored at random fix learning from its own feedback?

Fitting only on the windows an assistant explored at random fixes the uninformed-prior failure of learning from its own feedback (11.99 vs −13.08 utility/h at ε = 0.02), at an exploration cost (stylised)

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-labelmatch and the reweighting and doubly robust fixes after it. The deployed learner already draws a random sample for free: the windows it spoke on only because its ε coin came up. Fitting on those windows alone, unweighted, reaches 11.99 utility/h at ε = 0.02 and 12.25 at 0.05 with an uninformed prior, against −13.08 and −71.85 for the fit on every spoken window (oracle 12.71; 20 seeds), and as a learner it earns 6.49/h online at ε = 0.005 against −2.04. Exploration costs dismissals (online utility falls at larger ε), and with an informed prior the plain fit is better at small ε. Stylised simulation only.

ambient-falsewake6 tests

How many false wakes a day does an always-on trigger get when its frame scores are correlated, and what does requiring m frames in a row buy?

How many false wakes a day does an always-on trigger get when its frame scores are correlated? Exact grid-chain rates for "m frames in a row" on AR(1) scores, checked by Monte Carlo: a threshold set by the independent-frames rule gives 613 / 4,793 / 20,993 wakes a day (not 1) for m = 2 / 3 / 5 at phi = 0.9, while a single-frame threshold is nearly unaffected. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A stylised new question for track 2. A trigger fires after m consecutive 10 ms frames at or above a threshold, on Gaussian AR(1) background scores. Setting the threshold so that Pm = 1 per day (independent frames) is nearly right for m = 1 (0.78 wakes a day at φ = 0.9) but wrong and unsafe for m ≥ 2: at φ = 0.9 it gives 613, 4,793 and 20,993 wakes a day for m = 2, 3, 5. Exact rates from a grid Markov chain match Monte Carlo (largest |z| 1.69), and the threshold that really gives one a day is 2.0–2.5 sd higher. The score is a model, not a real wake-word detector, and no audio was used. Stylised.

ambient-wakeburst9 tests

How bursty are an always-on trigger's false-wake counts, and does a lockout help?

How bursty are an always-on trigger's false-wake counts? On AR(1) frame scores the Fano factor is near 1 (1.05–1.5), but a 5% window-to-window drift in noise scale lifts it to about 9 for m = 3 (38 at 10%); a 10 s lockout cuts it to 2.5 but also cuts the mean by a third. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-falsewake. On Gaussian AR(1) frame scores, wake counts per 1,000 s window are close to Poisson (Fano factor 1.05–1.5 at φ = 0.9–0.95). A window-to-window drift in the noise scale is what makes them bursty: a 5% lognormal drift lifts the Fano factor to about 9 for m = 3 while moving the mean only 4%, and 10% drift gives 38. A 10 s lockout cuts the Fano factor (9.8 to 2.5 with drift) but also cuts the mean by a third; a sub-second lockout changes little. The score is a model, not a real wake-word detector, and the drift is assumed. Stylised.

ambient-driftwindow10 tests

How does the burstiness of an always-on trigger's false-wake counts grow with the counting window when the noise level drifts for hours?

How does the Fano factor of false-wake counts grow with the counting window when the noise level drifts for hours? At 5% persistent drift (about 3 h correlation time) it grows from 1.9 at 100 s to about 150 at 28 h, against a flat 1.9 for independent drift. Stylised; the drift is assumed.

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-wakeburst, which drew a fresh noise level per window. With a noise scale that drifts persistently (log-scale AR(1), 5% sd) the Fano factor of false-wake counts rises with the window instead of staying flat: about 1.9 at 100 s for any correlation time, then 14, 110 and 150 at 16, 256 and 1,024 blocks (28 h) for a 2.8 h correlation time, and 620 at 28 h for a 28 h correlation time, while the mean moves only 5%. A Poisson-given-scale (Cox) model, checked against a frame-level simulation (4.7 vs 4.7 and 44 vs 44), and a closed form (mean error 2% on the busy trigger, worst 11%) explain it. The drift is assumed, not measured, and the ‘rare’ trigger is one wake per 500 s, not one a day. Stylised.

ambient-gatesimd3 tests

Do a dual-MAC energy loop and a divide-free threshold make the Cortex-M4 voice gate cheaper?

Do a dual-MAC energy loop and a divide-free threshold make the Cortex-M4 voice gate cheaper: 17-37% fewer instructions with the block-minimum floor, slower without it, RAM doubled; decisions unchanged (emulator counts, synthetic audio)

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-gatem4. With the block-minimum floor the SMLALD energy loop cuts executed instructions per frame by 17% at -Os and 37% at -O2, but without it the gate gets slower (64-bit ring entries), RAM doubles and code grows by about 60%. A divide-free sum-domain threshold matched the original decision on all 36,000 frames per configuration and removes the only library call; the divide itself is not counted, so its saving is unmeasured. Emulator instruction counts on synthetic audio, not cycles and not hardware.

ambient-gatem43 tests

What does the adaptive voice gate cost on a Cortex-M4, in flash and instructions per frame, and is the block-minimum floor worth it?

What does the adaptive voice gate cost on a Cortex-M4? ambient-gatefw's C gate built with clang for Thumb-2 and run in an emulator: bit-exact, about 250 bytes of code, 3237 instructions per frame exact and 2096 with the block-10 floor, because the energy sum dominates. Instructions, not cycles; stylised.

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-gatefw. Its C gate is built with clang for Cortex-M4 (Thumb-2, soft float) and run frame by frame in an emulator on ambient-gateroc’s synthetic audio. It is bit-exact with the Python reference, takes 236–258 bytes of code at -Os, and its only library call is the 64-bit divide, once per frame. The exact gate executes 3237 instructions per 20 ms frame at -Os; the block-10 floor executes 2096, a 35% cut, because the 320-sample energy sum (about 1980 instructions) is the floor under the saving. Instructions are not cycles, the divide is not counted, and nothing ran on hardware. Stylised.

ambient-gatefw6 tests

Can a noise-adaptive voice gate fit in about 120 bytes of RAM on a pendant microcontroller, and does a cheaper noise floor cost battery life?

Can a noise-adaptive voice gate fit in about 120 bytes of RAM on a pendant microcontroller? C port of ambient-gateroc's adaptive energy gate, bit-exact with the Python reference; a block-minimum noise floor cuts state from 1020 to 120 bytes and comparisons per frame from 249 to 24, moving modelled battery life by at most 0.07 h. Synthetic audio, host build only.

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-gateroc. Its adaptive energy gate (open when a 20 ms frame is at least 4× the minimum energy of the last 5 s) is ported to plain C99 and checked frame by frame against the Python reference. The exact 250-frame floor needs 1020 bytes of state and about 244 comparisons per frame. Keeping one minimum per block of 10 frames cuts that to 120 bytes and about 24 comparisons, flips 0.02–0.08% of gate decisions, and changes mean recall by at most 0.0002 and modelled battery life by at most 0.07 h (of about 82–90 h) on synthetic audio, 20 seeds × 4 rooms. Limitations: synthetic audio only; host gcc struct sizes and comparison counts, not measured cycles on an ARM core; battery hours inherit the ambient-wearable model.

ambient-preroll7 tests

How much pre-roll buffer does an energy-gated audio pendant need to stop clipping the first word, and what does it cost in RAM and battery?

How much pre-roll buffer does an energy-gated audio pendant need to stop clipping the first word? Synthetic audio: no gain in quiet rooms, in the loudest room onset recall 0.866 → 0.980 → 0.999 at 0, 5 and 25 buffered frames (0, 3.1, 15.6 KB) for 90 → 81 → 70 modelled hours; a too-deaf gate is not rescued (stylised)

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-gateroc, which did not measure onset clipping. On synthetic speech over background noise at −60 to −30 dBFS (20 seeds × 120 s per room), a noise-adaptive gate opens on the first frame in quiet rooms, so a pre-roll ring buffer buys nothing and costs battery (82.4 h to 76.9 h at 5 frames). In the loudest room it opens 2.3 frames late on average, and onset recall (first 500 ms of each utterance) goes 0.866, 0.980, 0.999 for 0, 5 and 25 buffered 20 ms frames (0, 3.1, 15.6 KB), at 90.0, 81.1 and 69.7 modelled hours. A gate set too deaf (k = 8) is not rescued: 50 frames lift onset recall only from 0.610 to 0.877. Pre-roll and hangover cost the same per frame and protect different ends of an utterance. Synthetic audio, a stylised power model, no hardware.

ambient-gateroc8 tests

Does a fixed energy-gate threshold survive different rooms on an always-on audio pendant, and what does an adaptive one buy in battery life?

Does a fixed energy-gate threshold survive different rooms on an always-on audio pendant? Synthetic audio, 20 seeds x 4 background levels: any fixed threshold that keeps speech recall >= 0.9 leaves the gate open all the time in the loudest room (57.6 h, no gating gain), while one adaptive threshold (4x a 5 s running-minimum floor) gives 82-90 h at recall 0.89-1.00 in all four; stylised, nothing measured on hardware

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to ambient-wearable. Synthetic harmonic ‘speech’ bursts (−36 to −20 dBFS) over pink-ish background noise at −60, −50, −40 and −30 dBFS plus short transients (20 seeds × 120 s per room) are passed through a Python port of the pendant’s energy gate (checked frame by frame against the compiled C), and the gate-open fraction is turned into battery hours with the same power model. Any fixed threshold that holds worst-room speech recall at 0.9 or more ((−30 dBFS or lower)minus;34 dBFS or lower on the grid I swept) stays open nearly all the time in the loudest room, giving 57.6 h, the always-streaming figure. One adaptive threshold (4× a 5 s running-minimum noise floor) gives 82–90 h at recall 0.89–1.00 in all four rooms. Within a single room the two trade-off curves are almost the same; the adaptive gate’s gain is that one setting transfers. Stylised: synthetic audio, uniform one-microphone model, assumed power parameters, nothing measured on hardware or real speech.

ambient-wearable8 tests

What limits the battery life of a pendant-style always-on audio wearable?

What limits battery life in a pendant-style always-on audio wearable: stylised nRF52840-class power model (mic floor ~170 h; speech-gated ~105 h vs 59 h always streaming) plus a 74-byte VAD gate that compiles for Cortex-M4; no hardware measured

Abstract Code →

A stylised average-current model for an nRF52840-class pendant with a 150 mAh cell, built from a few vendor figures read on 2026-10-13 plus labelled assumptions. The always-on microphone is the floor (about 170 h alone); gating codec and radio on speech at a 30% speech fraction gives about 105 h against 59 h for always streaming. A 74-byte energy-gate routine compiles for Cortex-M4. Nothing is measured on hardware, the datasheets were not read in full and there is no numeric comparison with Omi.

13

Self-replicating manufacturing

How close can a small shop get to making copies of its own machines? Closure, growth and what to build next, in models that run on a CPU. Topic page →

selfrep-closure8 tests

How much of a RepRap printer can a growing seed shop make itself?

Part, mass and cost closure of the RepRap Prusa Mendel (iteration 2) for three seed shops: printer alone makes 18 of 51 part lines (35%), plus router and laser 43%, assumed-mass closure 22%; casting helps only with brass bushings. Mass and cost inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The RepRap Prusa Mendel (iteration 2) bill of materials (51 part lines, from the RepRap wiki) against three seed shops. A printer alone makes 18 of 51 lines (35%); adding a CNC router and laser cutter reaches 43% of lines and, under assumed masses and costs, about 22% of mass and 16% of cost; casting helps only if brass bushings replace LM8UU bearings (45% of lines, 24% of mass). Motors, electronics, rods, bearings and fasteners stay vitamins. Stylised: the wiki gives no masses or prices, so those inputs are assumed and shown with a sensitivity range, process assignments are judgement, and only the printer is decomposed.

selfrep-nextmachine6 tests

Which machine should a seed shop add next, and does a greedy rule find it?

Which machine a printer-only seed shop should add next under a budget: greedy closure-per-price vs exhaustive search; same choice on the real 3-machine instance, optimal in 72–94% of 500 synthetic instances. Machine prices assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Builds on the selfrep-closure part model. Choosing among a CNC router, laser cutter and casting setup under a budget, a greedy closure-per-price rule matches exhaustive search at every tested budget on the real three-machine instance (router first, then casting only if brass bushings replace LM8UU). On 500 random synthetic instances greedy is optimal in 72–94% of cases and loses up to about 38% of the closure gain in the worst case. Stylised: machine prices, masses and costs are assumed placeholders, machines have no bills of materials of their own, and the synthetic instances are random.

selfrep-growth9 tests

How fast does a replicating printer shop grow when its vitamins must be bought?

Discrete-event and fluid growth of a replicating printer shop with imported vitamins: doubling time falls roughly as 1/budget until machine time binds (about 53 h in the simulation), failed builds cost about 1/(1-f), and closure helps most when imports bind. All inputs assumed; Lackner and Wendt comparison not done. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Builds on the selfrep-closure part model. A discrete-event simulation of a fleet of printers that each build copies of themselves, checked against a closed-form fluid model. With a small import budget the doubling time falls almost in proportion to the budget (about 455 h at 4 units/h, 120 h at 16/h); above a crossover fleet size N* = BW/V machine time binds and doubling flattens near the 50 h build time. Failed builds raise the doubling time by about 1/(1−f), and raising closure helps most when imports bind. Every input (print rate, assembly time, costs, budget, failure rate) is assumed and the fleet is homogeneous. Stylised. The comparison with Lackner and Wendt’s growth model is not done.

selfrep-reinvest8 tests

When should a replicating shop stop copying itself and start making goods?

Optimal split of a replicating printer shop's time between copies and goods: copy flat out, then switch one e-folding time (about 50 h) before the horizon; constant splits get 9–27% of that value, smooth ramps no better. Cash-limited cases switch about 50 h from the end. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Builds on the selfrep-growth fleet model. A fluid optimal-control model splits machine time between building copies and making goods, scored on the total value of goods over 600 h. Copying flat out and then switching to goods one e-folding time (1/k = W/(1−f), 50 h with no failures) before the horizon matches the closed form; the best constant split earns only 9–27% of that value, and smooth ramps are no better than the sharp switch. When imports or goods sales fund vitamins, cash binds throughout and the switch lands about 50 h from the end. Every input is assumed, the fleet is a continuous fluid, goods demand is unlimited and the final fleet is worth nothing. Stylised. Piecewise policies are local search, not a proof of optimality.

selfrep-materials10 tests

How much imported material can recycling save a self-replicating printer shop?

Mass and energy balance of plastic and aluminium recycling for one RepRap copy (stylised, assumed process parameters): vitamins stay about 75% of imported mass, recycling the shop's own scrap cuts imports a median 3%, and only retired-machine plastic changes the plastic import much.

Abstract Code →

Builds on the selfrep-closure part list. A stylised steady-state mass and energy balance for building one more RepRap Prusa Mendel, with shredding and re-extrusion of plastic and remelting of aluminium offcuts. With assumed process parameters, vitamins stay about 75% of imported mass for the largest shop (82% for the printer alone), and recycling the shop’s own scrap cuts imports by a median 3% (5–95% over parameter draws: 1–6%). Only plastic from retired machines changes the filament import much, and then the assumed recycled-share cap decides the result. Limitations: every yield, loss and energy figure is an assumption, recycling machines are not counted, and recycled-plastic quality is not modelled.

selfrep-recyclers8 tests

How many printer copies does it take for a shop's recycling machines to repay their own imports?

Payback of recycling machines with their own assumed part lists (stylised): about 100 printer copies on the shop's own scrap, 12–31 if retired machines' plastic is recycled.

Abstract Code →

Builds on selfrep-materials. A shredder, a filament extruder and an aluminium furnace are given assumed part lists, split into vitamins and parts the shop can make. With the shop’s own scrap only, the plastic pair needs 99–116 printer copies to avoid as much imported mass as it costs (91–164 over part-mass draws) and the furnace about 94. Plastic from retired machines cuts this to about 12–31 copies, depending on an assumed recycled-share cap. Limitations: part lists and masses are placeholders, mass is the only currency (cost, time and energy are ignored), and retirement is a scenario knob. Stylised.

selfrep-costpayback8 tests

Does pricing a shop’s imports, instead of weighing them, change when its recycling machines repay themselves?

Recycler payback priced instead of weighed (stylised, assumed prices): plastic pair 98–111 printer copies on own scrap, furnace 203, 10–26 with retired plastic.

Abstract Code →

Builds on selfrep-recyclers with assumed round-number prices for feedstock and for each vitamin of the machines. The plastic shredder and extruder repay in 98–111 printer copies on the shop’s own scrap (median 99, 45–235 over price draws), close to the mass-based 99–116, while the aluminium furnace worsens from 94 to about 203 copies because aluminium is cheap per kilogram. Recycling retired plastic brings the plastic pair to 10–26 copies. Stylised: every price and part list is an assumption, and labour and energy costs are ignored.

selfrep-singulararc8 tests

What is the closed form of a replicating shop’s smooth switch from copying to goods, and does it match dynamic programming?

Closed-form optimal copy share for a replicating printer shop with a saturating goods market (Pontryagin singular arc: goods output grows linearly, last 1/k hours all goods); earns 99.96–100% of the dynamic-programming policy's value. Necessary conditions only; all inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Builds on selfrep-satmarket. With concave revenue a c(1 − e−g/c), Pontryagin’s principle gives three arcs: copy flat out, a singular arc on which goods output grows linearly at rate kc, then goods only for the last 1/k hours. The entry time solves one scalar equation. In the Euler model the open-loop policy earns 99.96–100.00% of the dynamic-programming policy’s value over 7 market sizes and 4 failure shares. The conditions are necessary, not a proof of optimality, and depend on the assumed exponential revenue form. Stylised.

selfrep-satmarket8 tests

When the goods market saturates, does a replicating shop’s bang-bang switch turn smooth?

Reinvestment of a replicating printer shop when the goods market saturates, checked by dynamic programming: bang-bang is optimal with linear revenue, but with market capacity below about 10^4 machine-hours per hour the optimum ramps the copy share down over 90–300 h and bang-bang loses 4.5–7%. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Builds on the selfrep-reinvest fluid model, with concave goods revenue a c(1 − e−g/c) and a backward dynamic programme (Bellman) as a check on the local-search policies. With a large market the optimum is still copy-then-switch; once market capacity c is below about 104 machine-hours per hour the optimal copy share ramps down over 90–300 h, bang-bang loses 4.5–7% of the optimum and a logistic ramp recovers all but 1–1.5%. Slower growth from failed builds sharpens the switch again. Every input is assumed and the saturation form is a convenient choice; cash never binds. The DP value is the optimum of a discretised problem, within a few tenths of a percent of its simulated policy where it is accurate and several percent in near-linear cases. Stylised.

selfrep-wearout8 tests

What fleet can a replicating printer shop sustain when its machines wear out?

Fleet a replicating printer shop sustains when machines wear out (stylised, assumed inputs): short-lived machines die out from one seed; recycling gains need a correction for builds cut short.

Abstract Code →

Extends the selfrep-growth fleet model with random machine lifetimes (Weibull) and a recovered share of vitamin value at retirement. With assumed inputs and a vitamin budget of 4 units/h, a lone seed machine died out in every run when mean life was 200 h or less (20% of runs at 500 h, 3% at 2000 h), while the fluid model predicted a small stable fleet; survivors held about 10 machines at 500 h. Wear-out lifetimes are safer than constant hazard at the same mean. The fluid equilibrium over-predicts fleet size at high recycling (235 vs 73 simulated at 95% recovery); charging for builds cut short by retirement closes the gap (76), though that correction was added after seeing the discrepancy. Stylised: every input is assumed.

selfrep-extinction6 tests

Can an exactly solvable birth-death chain explain why short-lived printer fleets die out?

Exact mean extinction time of a wearing-out printer fleet as a birth-death chain (stylised, assumed inputs): explains the die-outs in kind, within about 35% only after a post-hoc fix.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-wearout. The fleet is a birth-death chain with an absorbing state at zero, and its mean extinction time is solved exactly and checked against a closed form and Monte Carlo. From one seed machine it grows from 358 h (mean life 100 h) to 3967 h (200 h) to 41,602 h (300 h), but the wear-out simulation dies out 1.8–2.5× sooner. Scaling births by the chance a build outlives its machine brings the two within about 35% for a lone seed (16–18% at 200–300 h), a fit made after seeing the gap; it is 1.7–1.9× too short for four seeds at 300 h. Stylised, with assumed inputs; the 500 h rows are unusable.

selfrep-repairpay5 tests

Does paying for spares late rescue the long repair queue of a printer shop?

Does paying for spares at service start rescue the long repair queue of a printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): yes, an unbounded queue then beats never repairing (488 against 458 at one bench) and queue caps stop mattering.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-repairlabour. That project found an unbounded repair queue is dead stock (414 working machines against 458 for never repairing, one bench, B = 40) when spares are bought at breakdown. Buying them when a bench frees up instead reverses it: 488 against 458, and 572 against 504 with four benches. The queue is as long (about 3400 machines) but ties up no vitamins, and capping it no longer helps (caps of 1–200 all give 484–492 at one bench; no standard errors computed, so no optimum cap is claimed). Stylised: assumed inputs, first-come service, a machine unaffordable at its turn is retired.

selfrep-repairlabour7 tests

What happens to a repairing printer shop when repairs need labour?

Repair labour as a limit on a repairing printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): with few repair benches an unbounded queue of broken machines is dead stock and does worse than never repairing; capping the queue recovers most of the gain.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-repair. Repairs need one of K benches; broken machines queue after buying spares. The pre-run prediction that the working fleet is about min(import limit, K·L/h) fails: with B = 40 and one bench the fleet is 414 against a cap of 40, because most breakdowns are never served and the queue (2915 machines) is dead stock. An unbounded queue with one bench is worse than never repairing (414 against 458); retiring a breakdown when 1–20 machines already wait gives 487–492. Stylised: assumed inputs, benches are a count with no wages, no corrected closed form.

selfrep-repair8 tests

When is repairing a printer worth more than building a new one?

Repair versus replacement in a replicating printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): repair wins iff its cost share is below its success probability, but only if spares are held back from new builds.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-wearout. Machines break down at a constant rate and the shop may spend spare-part vitamins to repair one instead of retiring it. A vitamin-balance formula predicts repair gives a bigger fleet exactly when the repair cost share is below the repair success probability; a discrete-event simulation with assumed inputs puts the crossing at that value, within about 9% of the formula in that sweep, but only when spares are held back from new builds (without a reserve the fleet was 70 against a formula value of 157). Repair also cuts die-out from one seed at short lifetimes (for example 55% against 100% at a mean life of 100 h) but does not remove it. Stylised: assumed inputs, memoryless breakdowns, repair returns the machine to new, no printed spares.

selfrep-spares7 tests

How much does making its own spare parts cut the cost of repairing a printer?

How much making its own spare parts cuts a printer shop's repair cost (stylised, assumed inputs): the printer alone makes none of the wear parts, so in-house spares barely move the fleet; the breakdown rate matters more.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-repair. The spare-part cost share of a repair is derived from the Prusa Mendel’s wear parts (belts, bearings, hot end, switches), each with an assumed life, and from which of them a seed shop can make. The printer alone makes none and adding a router and laser cutter makes only the pulleys, so the share stays near 0.021 and the fleet is unchanged (62.5 vs 63.0 machines, against 7.3 with replacement only). Swapping the linear bearings for a printed bushing lowers the share to 0.019, but if the bushing lasts half as long the fleet falls to 43, so breakdown rate matters more than where the spare comes from. Stylised: every life and cost is assumed.

selfrep-sparehours3 tests

Does a printer shop lose its printed-bushing gain once a printed spare takes print hours?

Does charging printed spares their print hours erase the printed-bushing gain (stylised, assumed inputs): the fleet ignores waits up to ~500 h per repair because it is import-limited, and the gain was within noise anyway.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-spares. A repair that needs a printed bushing waits extra print hours (mean-downtime approximation in the unchanged selfrep-repair simulation). At the assumed inputs the working fleet is flat up to about 500 h of wait per repair (62.7 vs 64.2 machines with none) and falls at 1000 h (58.5) to 36.0 at 5000 h, because the fleet is import-limited, not downtime-limited. The bushing’s gain over stock bearings (+1.8) was already inside the run-to-run spread. Stylised, assumed inputs; printing does not compete with building for machine time.

selfrep-extinction-kits7 tests

Is the lone-printer die-out an early birth-death accident?

Exact Markov-chain test of why a lone replicating printer dies out (stylised, assumed inputs): about a fifth die before a fleet forms at 500 h mean life; wear-out lives remove it.

Abstract Code →

Tests the extinction explanation left open by selfrep-wearout with an exact continuous-time Markov chain of the same shop (Poisson vitamin kits, exponential builds and lives). With assumed inputs and a budget of 4 units/h, the chain gives a 0.194 chance that a lone seed machine is lost before the fleet reaches 6 machines at 500 h mean life (simulation 0.198 ± 0.006), of which 0.162 is the seed retiring before its first copy; relaxing the Markov assumptions moves this by at most about 0.03. Wear-out lives (Weibull shape 2 or more) cut it to under 3%. Exact mean extinction times for small equilibrium fleets match simulation (1464 h against 1511 ± 50 h at 200 h life), but with regular kits and lognormal builds long times roughly double, so the chain is a lower guide there. Stylised: every input is assumed; simulated only.

selfrep-extinction-qsd4 tests

Can a quasi-stationary approximation predict how long a small printer fleet lasts?

Quasi-stationary approximation of how long a small replicating-printer fleet lasts (stylised, assumed inputs): within 5% of the exact mean time once a correction for early die-out is applied, poor for the shortest lives.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-extinction-kits. The slowest decay rate of the exact Markov chain gives a quasi-stationary estimate 1/λ0 of the mean extinction time. Stylised, with assumed inputs, it overshoots a lone seed machine by 1.2 to 1.9 times (2388 h against 1465 h exact at 200 h life), but multiplied by the exact chance the fleet survives its start it lands within 5% in four of seven cases (for example 0.999 at 500 h life) and fails where the fleet rarely survives (ratio 1.4 at 200 h life, 42 at 75 h). Seed fleets help only up to the quasi-stationary time: 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 seeds give 1465 / 1983 / 2388 / 2666 h at 200 h life. The survival correction was chosen after seeing the overshoot, so it is a post-hoc fit. Stylised: every input is assumed; simulated only.

selfrep-reconcile4 tests

Why do two exact extinction chains of the same printer shop disagree?

Reconciles the two exact extinction chains of the lone printer shop (stylised, assumed inputs): the fleet-size chain is 1.5 to 7 times longer; adding the kit wait fixes small fleets but over-corrects large ones.

Abstract Code →

Two sibling chains of the lone replicating printer shop, one on fleet size and one on machines and vitamin kits, give different mean extinction times for the same inputs. Stylised, with assumed inputs, the fleet-size chain is longer by 1.5 to 7 times because its birth law min(n/W, a) lets machines and kits never wait for each other. A fixed-in-advance repair that adds the two waits matches the kit chain within 5% when the fleet stays at 1 to 3 machines, but falls 24 to 60% below it for larger fleets, where kits pool in stock. No law right in both regimes was derived.

selfrep-redesign5 tests

Which part substitutions cut a printer's vitamins most, within a performance budget?

Which assumed part substitutions (printed bushings and nuts, wooden rods) cut the Prusa Mendel's vitamins most under a penalty budget: all seven take closure from 43/22/16% to 60/36/48% (lines/mass/cost); best set depends on the assumed penalties. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-closure that changes the machine instead of the shop. Seven assumed substitutions (printed bushings and nuts, wooden rods, a printed drive) are searched exhaustively, greedily and at random under an assumed penalty budget. All seven together take the Prusa Mendel’s vitamin lines from 29 to 19 and closure from 43/22/16% to 60/36/48% (lines/mass/cost) for the printer, router and laser shop; mass closure stays below 36% because motors, electronics and threaded rods remain. Cost closure responds most, and the best set depends on the assumed penalties. Stylised: substitutions, masses and penalties are all assumed and no part was tested.

selfrep-rodbeam6 tests

What does a wooden rod cost a printer in stiffness?

Beam model of the Prusa Mendel's smooth rods: a wooden rod sags 20 times a steel one at 8 mm and needs about 17 mm to match it, and selfrep-redesign's assumed dowel mass was twice the geometric one (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Replaces the assumed penalty of selfrep-redesign’s wooden-rod substitution with Euler–Bernoulli beam theory. At 8 mm a hardwood rod sags 20× a steel one (the modulus ratio) and a printed PLA rod 80×; matching steel stiffness needs about 17 mm of hardwood, outside the printer’s 8 mm hardware, while a 1–2 mm sag tolerance needs 9–11 mm. The earlier 30 g per dowel was about twice the geometric 13.8 g, moving mass closure from 35.8% to 34.6%; thicker dowels raise closure again, a quirk of counting imported feedstock as makeable. Stylised: properties and the 5 N load are assumed and no rod was tested.

selfrep-rodmodes5 tests

What natural-frequency target does a printer’s rod have to meet, and what does a wooden rod cost?

Carriage natural frequency on the Prusa Mendel's smooth rods: a vibration target, not a sag limit, sets the rod diameter; hardwood needs about twice steel's diameter (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-rodbeam that derives the rod spec from a vibration target instead of an assumed sag limit. A carriage mass on a simply supported rod (Rayleigh estimate with the 17/35 effective rod mass) gives a first mode of 42 Hz for 8 mm steel but 10 Hz for hardwood and 5 Hz for printed PLA, for an assumed 0.3 kg carriage. Matching steel’s frequency needs about 16 mm of hardwood, close to the sag-matching 17 mm; at equal frequency the dowel is 1.9–2.1× the steel diameter. Stylised: carriage mass and material constants are assumptions, one mode, no damping or bushing play.

selfrep-alurod6 tests

Does an aluminium rod fit the printer where a wooden one cannot?

Aluminium rods in the printer redesign: matching a steel rod's sag takes 10.4 mm aluminium (fits the assumed 12 mm holders) against 16.9 mm hardwood (does not), at 39.5% vs 37.8% mass closure (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-rodbeam that adds aluminium bar, cut to length on the router, as a rod substitution in selfrep-redesign. To match the sag of the 8 mm steel rod (0.19 mm at the assumed 5 N) aluminium needs 10.4 mm, inside the assumed 12 mm holder limit, while hardwood needs 16.9 mm and does not fit. Mass closure of the all-substitutions redesign is 39.5% with aluminium at a 0.2 mm spec, 37.8% with wood and 28.7% with steel rods kept as vitamins; the shop imports about 170 g more stock than with wood. Stylised: moduli, load and limit are assumed, and the surface of cut aluminium bar is taken to be adequate for the bushings.

selfrep-alufreq6 tests

How stiff a rod does a frequency target need, in aluminium and in wood?

Sizing printer rods to a first-mode frequency target instead of a sag spec: at 0.3 kg aluminium reaches 40 Hz with 10.0 mm (fits the assumed 12 mm holders) where hardwood needs 16.0 mm (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-alurod and selfrep-rodmodes: rods of the printer redesign are sized to a first-mode frequency target (Rayleigh estimate, assumed 0.3 kg carriage) instead of a sag spec. Aluminium reaches 40 Hz with 10.0 mm, inside the assumed 12 mm holder limit, where hardwood needs 16.0 mm; within 12 mm the highest reachable frequency is 56 Hz for aluminium and 23 Hz for hardwood. Closure by mass rises with the target only because thicker stock counts as makeable, while imported stock grows from 1946 g to 2596 g. Stylised: one mode, assumed carriage mass, moduli and holder limit.

selfrep-alufring6 tests

How thick must a printer rod be to keep carriage ringing small at a given acceleration?

Rod diameter from an acceleration and ringing budget: at 3 m/s² with abrupt steps steel needs 7.3 mm, aluminium 9.6 mm, hardwood 15.5 mm; a 20 ms force ramp cuts aluminium at 5 m/s² from 10.9 to 8.9 mm (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-alufreq: the rod diameter is derived from an acceleration and a 50 µm ringing tolerance (one-mode oscillator, assumed 0.3 kg carriage and damping ratio 0.01) instead of a bare frequency target. At 3 m/s² with abrupt steps steel needs 7.3 mm, aluminium 9.6 mm and hardwood 15.5 mm; ramping the force over 20 ms cuts aluminium at 5 m/s² from 10.9 to 8.9 mm. Stylised: one mode, assumed damping, nothing measured.

selfrep-sensitivity4 tests

Which assumed input of the replicating-printer growth model does the doubling time depend on most?

Which assumed input of the replicating-printer growth model moves its doubling time (Sobol indices, stylised, assumed ranges): budget and vitamin cost together carry ~90% of the variance when imports bind; when machine time binds, failure, print rate, budget and price are comparable.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-growth: variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity of the fluid-model doubling time to print rate, assembly time, vitamin cost, import budget and build-failure probability over assumed ranges. Import-limited (4/h): budget and vitamin cost carry about 0.45 and 0.43 of the variance of ln T, failure 0.11, print rate and assembly time none. Time-limited (64/h): budget, vitamin cost, failure and print rate are comparable (0.25–0.28). The fluid model overstates budget sensitivity at 64/h against the discrete-event model (elasticity −0.45 vs −0.02). Stylised, with assumed ranges and inputs.

selfrep-terminal6 tests

How does a resale value for the finished fleet move the switch from copies to goods?

A resale value s per machine at the horizon shortens the goods phase from one e-folding time 1/k to 1/k − s/a; at s ≥ a/k the shop never switches. Grid optimum matches the closed form. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-reinvest. Giving each machine left at the horizon a value s shortens the goods phase from one e-folding time 1/k to 1/k − s/a, so the switch moves later; at s ≥ a/k (50 per machine with no failures, 29% of the assumed vitamin cost) the shop copies to the end. The grid optimum of the Euler simulation agrees with this closed form to within 1 h, and ignoring a terminal value of 12.5–50 per machine costs 3–26% of the optimum. Every input is assumed; cash is free and demand unlimited. Stylised.

selfrep-terminalmarket5 tests

Does a resale value for the finished fleet still end copying late when the goods market saturates?

A resale value s per machine with a saturating goods market (DP): at capacity c = 1000 machine-hours per hour the copy phase runs to the horizon once s is 12.5 (a quarter of a/k), and the policy that ignores s earns 14% of the optimum; the DP loses to bang-bang by under 1% where the fleet is large, so it is a lower bound there; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-terminal and selfrep-satmarket: a backward dynamic programme with terminal reward s per machine on the saturating-market fluid model (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). With a linear market the DP reproduces the closed-form switch of selfrep-terminal. As the market capacity c falls, a small s moves the optimum from an early switch to copying until the horizon (c = 1000: switch near 400 h at s = 0, none at s = 12.5), and a policy tuned for s = 0 earns only 14% of the optimum. Where the final fleet is large the DP is not reliable: a bang-bang switch beats its policy by up to 0.7%, so it is a lower bound there. Stylised and preliminary; the resale value is assumed and does not itself saturate.

selfrep-dpgrid4 tests

Is the dynamic-programming table for the replicating shop with a resale value converged, and can its policy be trusted?

Grid-convergence check of the terminal-value DP: the policy's value is stable to about 0.15% from 800 to 1,600 grid points while the table value rises from 8–13% (400 points) to 2–3% (1,600) below it; a stylised fluid model, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-terminalmarket, which found its DP table up to about 10% below the value of its own policy. This project refines the log-spaced fleet grid from 100 to 1,600 points and tries a second interpolation rule (linear in fleet size instead of in log fleet size), on the same fluid model (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). The simulated value of the DP policy changes by only about 0.15% between 800 and 1,600 points and stays within 0.2% of the best bang-bang switch, while the table value approaches it from below roughly in proportion to 1/(grid points): about 8–13% low at 400 points and 2–3% low at 1,600. The table is therefore a slowly converging lower bound, not a certificate; a first-order extrapolation puts it within about 0.8% of the bang-bang value in the three cases tried, but that rests on two grids. The cause of the bias is not diagnosed. Stylised fluid model, preliminary.

selfrep-exactdp5 tests

How much does a smooth copy-then-sell policy beat a single switch for the replicating shop, certified without interpolation?

An interpolation-free DP (the table equals its own policy's value to 1e-14): with no resale value and a saturating market a three-phase policy beats the best single switch by 4.7% (c = 1e4) to 7.1% (c = 1e3), while a resale value of 50 makes one switch optimal; a stylised fluid model, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-dpgrid, whose DP table sat 2–13% below the value of its own policy. This project chooses a control set whose steps land exactly on a geometric fleet grid, so no interpolation is needed and the table equals the policy value to 1e-14. On the same fluid model (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed) a single copy-then-goods switch is optimal when machines keep a resale value of 50 each. With no resale value and a saturating goods market, a three-phase policy (full copying, an intermediate share, then goods) beats the best switch by 4.7% (capacity 1e4) and 7.1% (capacity 1e3); with a resale value of 12.5 and capacity 1e4 the gain is 6.5%, and only appears once the control set is fine enough. Stylised, with a fixed Euler step and no cash constraint; preliminary.

selfrep-resalecurve6 tests

How does a falling resale price for the finished fleet change when the shop stops copying?

A resale price for the finished fleet that falls with market depth m (stylised): with an unsaturated goods market the switch moves from 574 h (linear) to 549 h (m = 1e3) and a single switch matches the DP; with a saturating goods market the DP beats the best switch by up to 14%.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to selfrep-terminalmarket: the fleet is sold at the horizon for sm(1 − e−N/m), so the first machine fetches s and the price falls with market depth m (W = 50 h, failure 0, horizon 600 h, all inputs assumed). With an unsaturated goods market a shallower resale market moves the optimal switch from 574 h (linear) to 549 h (m = 103), and a single switch matches the DP. With a saturating goods market (c = 104) the DP policy beats the best single switch by up to 14%. The DP table value is not a certificate (it overstates at 400 grid points); simulated policy values are reported. Stylised and preliminary; both market curves are assumed, not fitted.

selfrep-judgement5 tests

How much do the RepRap closure numbers depend on which parts a shop is judged able to make?

How much the RepRap closure numbers depend on which parts a shop is judged able to make (stylised, assumed inputs): buying all optimistic lines cuts mass closure from 22% to 17%; making the motors in-house would add 22 points.

Abstract Code →

Flips the make-or-buy judgements behind selfrep-closure. Buying all five optimistic lines (washers, GT2 pulley, MDF bed, brass bushing) cuts the largest shop to 17% mass and 11% cost closure, the printer-alone level, and no single line moves mass closure by more than 2.4 points. Granting a missing capability matters far more: making the NEMA17 motors in-house would add 22 points of mass closure, the 370 mm threaded rods 10. Monte Carlo (judged lines kept with probability 0.5, arguable vitamins granted with 0.1; arbitrary): mass closure 18–35% (5–95%). Stylised; masses and costs are assumed placeholders.

selfrep-partpool11 tests

Does sharing part jobs across printers make a replicating printer shop double faster than one copy per printer?

Does sharing part jobs across printers beat one copy per printer (stylised, assumed inputs): a pool serving the oldest copy first doubles in 43.2 h against 51.1 h with no import limit, about half the gap to the fluid 34.7 h; with imports binding all policies agree.

Abstract Code →

Tests the explanation given in selfrep-growth for the gap between its fluid (34.7 h) and discrete-event (about 53 h) doubling times. A part-level simulation of the Prusa Mendel's 44 printed parts plus assembly compares one copy per printer with a shared pool of part jobs. With no import limit the pool that always serves the oldest copy doubles in 43.2 h against 51.1 h (15% faster), closing about half of the gap; a pool that advances all copies together equals one-copy-per-printer, and under an import budget all three agree. Stylised: every input is assumed, parts are uniform, no plate packing or failed prints.

selfrep-platepack8 tests

How many parts should a replicating printer print per plate to double its shop fastest?

How many parts per print plate double a replicating printer shop fastest (stylised, assumed inputs): with no changeover one part per plate wins (43.2 h doubling), with 0.25 h per plate four parts (46.4 h), with 0.5 to 1 h eleven parts; pooled fleets stay 7.6 to 15.5% ahead of one copy per printer.

Abstract Code →

Groups the Prusa Mendel's 44 printed parts k to a plate in the selfrep-partpool simulator, with an assumed per-plate changeover of 0 to 1 h. With no changeover one part per plate is best (43.2 h effective doubling for a pooled fleet); at 0.25 h the best plate holds 4 parts (46.4 h), at 0.5 h and 1 h it holds 11 (47.8 h and 49.6 h). Pooling keeps an edge over one copy per printer (7.6–15.5%), and large plates cost it the pooling gain: at one plate per copy both policies coincide. Stylised: every input, including the changeover, is assumed, the BOM has no real part masses and plates are full and identical.

14

Simulation-first design

Designs written as code, simulated, optimised and exported as manufacturing files with an open toolchain, on a CPU. Topic page →

simdesign-bracket8 tests

Can a parametric L-bracket be sized by finite elements for minimum mass and come out printable?

Parametric L-bracket sized by 2D finite elements (scikit-fem) for minimum mass under a stress limit: differential evolution 19.6 g vs random 25.6 g vs grid 31.4 g at equal budget, exported as STL with a printability check. Assumed material inputs. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A 2D plane-stress scikit-fem model of an L-bracket with a filleted inner corner (arm width, fillet radius, depth) under a 100 N tip load. Differential evolution reaches 19.6 g against 25.6 g for random search and 31.4 g for a grid at 144–150 evaluations each, under a 20 MPa stress and 4 mm deflection limit. The design is exported as a binary STL and checked for minimum wall and overhang. Stylised: material properties and limits are assumed, the optimum stress rises about 7% on mesh refinement (just over the limit), the sharp-corner stress diverges, and the thin optimum was not checked for out-of-plane buckling.

selfrep-coverscale5 tests

Does greedy substitution search still work when the printer-redesign list grows past seven items?

Does greedy substitution search still work past seven items (synthetic instances, assumed generator): 96–100% of the exact optimum on average but optimal in only 33–95 of 100 instances; 64 random evaluations fall to about 89% at 24 items.

Abstract Code →

A synthetic, preliminary test (100 instances per cell, assumed generator) of budgeted weighted coverage, the shape of the printer-redesign search, for 7 to 24 substitutions with 0 to 0.9 overlap. Greedy gain-per-penalty stays at 96–100% of the exact optimum on average but is exactly optimal in only 33–95 of 100 instances, with a worst case of 49.6%. Local search is best on average (about 99.5%); 64 random evaluations are perfect at 7 items and fall to about 89–90% at 24, so small-list random baselines flatter themselves. Nothing here uses the real bill of materials. Computed only.

selfrep-alusearch7 tests

Does an aluminium rod change which printer redesign the penalty-budget search picks?

With an aluminium rod option priced by sag, the penalty-budget search of the printer redesign picks the 12 mm aluminium rod and reaches 40.0% mass closure at budget 2.0 against 33.1% with the wooden rod (41.4% against 35.8% at full budget); the penalty curve is assumed and the metric favours heavy stock; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary search over 448 designs: a rod choice (steel, hardwood or aluminium at 8, 10 or 12 mm) times subsets of six other part substitutions, with a rod penalty tied to mid-span sag by an assumed log curve. At every budget from 0.5 up the best mass-closure design uses the 12 mm aluminium rod: 40.0% at budget 2.0 against 33.1% for the wooden-rod search of selfrep-redesign, and 41.4% against 35.8% at full budget. The choice sits at the assumed holder limit because the closure metric counts heavier bar stock as makeable, so it says little about the best rod. The pick held for penalty scales from 0.05 to 1. Computed only; nothing was built.

selfrep-stockmass6 tests

Does the best printer redesign change when imported bar stock counts as an import, not as made?

Scoring the printer redesign by the mass the shop must still import (vitamins plus raw stock) instead of closure: the best design imports 5.85 kg against 6.72 kg for the baseline, while the closure-maximising 12 mm aluminium pick imports 6.79 kg (stylised; yield and prices assumed).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary re-scoring of the 448-design search of selfrep-alusearch: the score is the mass (or cost) the shop must still import per printer copy, vitamins plus raw stock at an assumed 0.8 yield. The import-mass minimiser reaches 5.85 kg against 6.72 kg for the steel-rod baseline, with the light 8 mm hardwood rod; the earlier closure-maximising pick (12 mm aluminium) imports 6.79 kg, no better than baseline. By import cost the 12 mm aluminium rod stays best (147.5 against 173.3). Yield, stock price and penalties are assumed; computed only.

selfrep-learnfirst7 tests

Which imported part should a printer-replicating shop learn to make first?

Which imported printer part to learn to make first (stylised, assumed inputs): by mass or cost the NEMA17 motor (+22 and +26 points of closure, first in 90% and 76% of draws with masses and costs scaled 0.5x to 2x), by unit count the M8 nut; by lines every vitamin ties.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary ranking of the 29 parts the printer + router + laser shop of selfrep-closure still imports, by the closure gained if that one part became makeable (free and certain, so an upper bound). By mass or cost the NEMA17 stepper motor is first (+22 and +26 points) and stays first in 90% and 76% of 2,000 draws with every assumed mass and cost scaled 0.5× to 2×; by unit count the M8 nut leads, and by distinct lines every vitamin ties. Three lines buy +52 points of cost closure but +39 of mass. Masses, costs and makers are assumed; difficulty of learning is not modelled.

selfrep-capability7 tests

Which process capabilities should a printer-replicating shop learn when one capability unlocks several imported parts?

Which process capabilities (lathe, winding, heat treatment, ...) a printer-replicating shop should learn when one capability unlocks several imported parts (stylised, assumed efforts): a lathe is the best first buy by mass (+31 points for effort 4), winding plus stamping by cost (+30 for effort 8), and exact capability sets beat part-by-part picking by up to 10 points, but the choice is fragile to the assumed efforts.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to selfrep-learnfirst. Each of the 29 imported printer parts needs a set of assumed process capabilities (lathe, heat treatment, winding, stamping, grinding, ...) with an assumed effort each, paid once however many parts share it; all 512 capability sets are enumerated exactly. A lathe with threading is the best first buy by mass (effort 4, +31 points of mass closure but only +10 of cost); winding plus stamping is best by cost (effort 8, +30). Exact capability sets beat picking parts one at a time by up to 10 points at the same real cost, but with efforts scaled 0.5× to 2× the nominal choice stays affordable and optimal in only 20–28% of draws. The efforts and the part-to-capability map are the project’s own assumptions; the controller electronics stays imported.

selfrep-capsequence6 tests

In what order should a printer-replicating shop learn its process capabilities?

In what order a printer-replicating shop should learn its process capabilities (stylised, assumed efforts): the exact best order over all 362,880 beats walking the budget frontier (54 to 73% of the optimum over 24 weeks); a gain-per-week bundle rule comes within 0 to 6%.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to selfrep-capability: a shop learns capabilities one at a time, so the choice is an order, scored by closure-weeks (closure held while still learning). With the assumed efforts, all 9! orders are covered exactly. The best order differs from walking the budget frontier, which scores only 54–73% of the optimum over 24 weeks; a gain-per-week bundle rule is within 0–6%, a one-capability-at-a-time rule 69–80%. The optimal order is moderately fragile to the efforts (within 1% of the optimum in 39–88% of draws scaled 0.5×–2×). Efforts and the capability map are assumptions; nothing was built.

simdesign-topopt7 tests

Can Sigmund's 99-line topology optimisation be reproduced in Python and carried through to a printable part?

Python reproduction of Sigmund's 99-line SIMP topology optimisation (cantilever, half-MBB; filter removes 11.5% checkerboards) with the density field exported as a mirrored, extruded STL; stylised 2D compliance only.

Abstract Code →

A Q4 plane-stress SIMP code with the 99-line sensitivity filter and optimality-criteria update, tested against Hooke's law and finite-difference sensitivities. It gives truss-like cantilever (compliance 351.9 → 52.4) and half-MBB (1007.0 → 203.3) designs. Without the filter 11.5% of 2×2 cells are checkerboards; with it none, at the same compliance within 0.03%. The thresholded MBB design is one connected body and is written as an extruded, mirrored STL. Stylised: dimensionless 2D compliance only, no stress or 3D check, not compared with the published codes.

simdesign-loadrobust5 tests

How much stiffness does a topology-optimised cantilever lose when the real load points a different way than the model assumed?

How much stiffness a topology-optimised cantilever loses when the real load direction differs from the modelled one: 1.57× at 60° and 2.58× at horizontal for the nominal design; a multi-load design at 0, ±60° cuts the worst case to 2.00× for 0.6% nominal cost; stylised 2D, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Optimises a 48×24 cantilever (volume fraction 0.4) for a straight-down tip load and for weighted sums over several load directions, then analyses each design under load angles from −90° to 90° against the design optimised for that angle alone. The nominal design is within 5% for tilts up to 30°, but 1.57× off at 60° and 2.58× at horizontal. A {0, ±60°} multi-load design cuts the worst case to 2.00× for 0.6% on the nominal load, and {0, ±90°} to 1.88× for 2.9%; no single topology is stiff in every direction. Stylised 2D, one mesh, one run per design; preliminary.

simdesign-heaviside7 tests

Does a density filter with Heaviside projection close the gap between a topology-optimised density field and the black-and-white part?

Density filter and Heaviside projection added to the SIMP code: the optimiser's compliance matches the thresholded part's to 0.1% (sensitivity filter: 10% off) but the parts are equally stiff within 0.9%; β continuation needed (β=64 from the start: 344.8 vs 192.1); a minimum-length-scale check found no advantage (negative); stylised 2D.

Abstract Code →

Adds a density filter, a tanh Heaviside projection and β continuation to the SIMP code of simdesign-topopt. On a 90×30 half-MBB beam the sensitivity and density filters leave 26–34% grey elements and a model compliance 10–15% above the thresholded part’s; with projection the two agree to 0.1% (192.1 vs 192.0). The thresholded parts are equally stiff within 0.9% (190.3–192.0), so the gain is an honest model, not a stiffer part. Starting at β = 64 without continuation gives 344.8 against 192.1. A minimum-length-scale check did not separate the formulations (negative): a single projection does not by itself fix a physical minimum feature. Stylised: 2D dimensionless compliance, one problem, one run per setting.

simdesign-robust3 tests

Does a topology-optimised beam survive a 0.2 threshold error, and what does the robust formulation cost?

Does a topology-optimised beam survive a 0.2 threshold error? The plain Heaviside design disconnects when eroded on all three meshes; the robust eroded/blueprint/dilated design stays at 224–226 (14–16% above nominal) for 0.8–3.4% more nominal compliance, but shows no minimum-length-scale gain (negative; stylised).

Abstract Code →

Adds the eroded / blueprint / dilated robust projection formulation to the SIMP code of simdesign-heaviside and tests both on a half-MBB beam at three mesh sizes, each design judged at projection thresholds 0.7, 0.5 and 0.3. The plain Heaviside design fails when eroded on every mesh (a member disconnects; compliance 105–109 against about 190), while the robust design stays at 224–226 eroded, 14–16% above its nominal value. The nominal compliance costs 0.8–3.4% more and the run about 2.5× the time. A minimum-length-scale gain was not shown (negative): feature sizes match Heaviside’s to within a pixel. Stylised: 2D dimensionless compliance, one problem, one run per setting, a density threshold standing in for etch error.

simdesign-robustradius3 tests

Does the filter radius or the threshold gap set the minimum feature size of a robust topology-optimised beam?

Does the filter radius or the threshold gap set a robust beam's minimum feature size? A gap of 0.1 already stops the erosion failure (eroded compliance 255–276 against 187–200 nominal; plain design disconnects), but solid feature size is 3 px at both radius 4 and 6 (negative; stylised, one mesh).

Abstract Code →

Sweeps filter radius (2, 4, 6 elements) against threshold gap Δη (0, 0.1, 0.2) on a half-MBB beam, 120×40 elements, nine designs each judged at thresholds 0.7, 0.5 and 0.3. A gap of 0.1 already stops the erosion failure: eroded compliance 255–276 against 187–200 nominal, where the plain Heaviside design disconnects (107–109). The radius does not give a clean length-scale control by the opening-rule measure: solid feature size is 3 px at both radius 4 and 6. Stylised: one problem, one mesh, one run per cell, integer-pixel measure.

simdesign-robustmesh3 tests

Does the minimum feature of a robust topology-optimised beam follow the filter radius when the mesh is refined?

Does the minimum feature follow the filter radius once the mesh is refined? No: at 180×60 it is 5 px at radii of 6, 9 and 12 px; across meshes it grows with the grid (1, 3, 5 px), not the radius (negative; two poor 60×20 robust runs reported; stylised).

Abstract Code →

Repeats the simdesign-robustradius sweep on 60×20 and 180×60 meshes with the filter radius held at 1/30, 1/20 and 1/15 of the beam length, plain Heaviside against the robust eroded / blueprint / dilated design (12 runs, one each). On the 180×60 mesh the minimum solid feature is 5 pixels (2.8% of the beam) at all three radii, 6, 9 and 12 elements; on 60×20 it is 1–3 pixels. With the earlier 120×40 runs the feature in pixels grows with the mesh (1, 3, 5) and not with the radius, so it is set by the grid here, not by the filter (negative for radius control; one problem, coarse integer measure). Two robust runs on the 60×20 mesh ended at poor blueprints (compliance about 740 against about 195), reported as such. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless.

simdesign-robustmove6 tests

Does the optimality-criteria move limit decide whether a robust topology optimisation survives its beta steps?

Does the move limit decide whether a robust topology optimisation survives its β steps? Yes here: at 0.2 five of nine cases failed (blueprint compliance up to 4× the best), at 0.1 and 0.05 none (stylised; mechanism not tested).

Abstract Code →

Diagnoses two unexplained poor runs from simdesign-robustmesh. The robust eroded / blueprint / dilated half-MBB design is rerun at move limits 0.2, 0.1 and 0.05 over nine mesh-and-radius cases (27 deterministic runs). At 0.2, the value every earlier project used, five of nine blueprint compliances are more than 1.5× the best (e.g. 742 against about 200 on 60×20); at 0.1 and 0.05 none are. The failing runs show worst-case compliance jumping up to 400× in one iteration after β reaches 32–64. The mechanism (a thin member breaking when the eroded field sharpens) is a hypothesis, not tested. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless, one problem.

simdesign-robustadapt4 tests

Can an adaptive move limit that shrinks after a compliance spike rescue a robust topology optimisation as well as a fixed small one?

Can a move limit that halves after a compliance spike rescue a robust topology optimisation? Partly: fixed 0.2 failed 5 of 9 cases, fixed 0.05 none, the adaptive rule 2 of 9, because it reacts after the damaging step (stylised, one run per cell).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-robustmove. The same nine robust half-MBB cases are run with three move-limit rules (27 deterministic runs): fixed 0.2, fixed 0.05, and an adaptive rule that starts at 0.2 and halves after any iteration whose worst-case compliance jumps more than 3×. Fixed 0.2 fails (blueprint compliance > 1.5× the best of the three) in 5 of 9 cases, fixed 0.05 in none, adaptive in 2 of 9. The rule reacts only after the damaging step, so it rescues some cases and not others; in one 120×40 case its blueprint is fine but its eroded compliance is 2 839 against 284 for the fixed small move. Stylised: 2D, one problem, one run per cell.

simdesign-retry4 tests

Does rolling back a robust topology-optimisation step that spikes compliance, and redoing it at half the move, beat shrinking the move afterwards?

Does rolling back a robust topology-optimisation step that spikes compliance and redoing it at half the move beat shrinking the move afterwards? Mostly: fixed 0.2 failed 5 of 9 cases, adaptive 2, retry 1, fixed 0.1/0.05 none, but retry never beat fixed 0.05 (stylised, one run per cell).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-robustadapt. The same nine robust half-MBB cases are run with five move-limit rules (45 deterministic runs): fixed 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, the earlier adaptive rule, and reject-and-retry, which discards a step whose worst-case compliance jumps more than 3× and redoes it at half the move. Blueprint failures: fixed 0.2, 5 of 9; adaptive, 2; retry, 1; fixed 0.1 and 0.05, none. Retry costs at most 2% more evaluations but never beat fixed 0.05, and on eroded-design quality it is 1.22× the best on average (fixed 0.1 hides one eroded design 25× worse that the blueprint test passes). Stylised: 2D dimensionless, one problem, one run per cell.

simdesign-stuck4 tests

Can penalty continuation free SIMP topology-optimisation starts that stay stuck in a different local optimum?

Can penalty continuation free SIMP starts stuck in a different local optimum? No: it sends all 5 stuck starts of 20 to one design (c 204.01) worse than the 202.83 three reach by running longer at p = 3. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-startsconverge. Half-MBB 60×20, p = 3: after 1200 iterations 5 of 20 random starts still differ from the uniform-start design in at least 1% of elements. Penalty continuation (p = 1, 2, 3) frees none of them: all five collapse onto one design, 20.4% different from the uniform-start one, with compliance 204.01 versus 203.29 for the uniform start. Simply running 1200 more iterations at p = 3 takes three of them to 202.83, about 0.6% better than continuation. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless compliance, one mesh, 20 seeds.

simdesign-startsconverge4 tests

Is the start-dependence of fixed-penalty SIMP topology optimisation just slow convergence?

Is the start-dependence of fixed-penalty SIMP just slow convergence? Over 1200 iterations the median of 20 random starts reaches the uniform-start design (0.0% of elements differ, from 3.9% at 150), but the compliance spread only falls 1.43% → 0.85% (stylised, 2D, one mesh).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-starts. Half-MBB 60×20, p = 3, one uniform and 20 random starting fields (noise ±0.3), each run 1200 OC iterations and snapshotted at 150, 300, 600 and 1200. The median random start ends at the uniform-start design (0.0% of elements differ at 1200, 3.9% at 150) and the pair disagreement falls from 15.4% to 0.5%, but the compliance spread only falls from 1.43% to 0.85% and holes still range 2–5, so a minority of starts stay in a different, slightly worse local optimum. Stylised: 2D, one mesh, one noise level, stuck starts not counted.

simdesign-starts6 tests

How much does a SIMP topology optimisation depend on its starting density field, and does penalty continuation remove it?

How much does a SIMP topology optimisation depend on its starting density field? With a fixed penalty, final compliance spreads 1.4–2.8% over 30 random starts and 2–23% of elements change state; with penalty continuation the spread is 0–0.4% (stylised, 2D, 150 iterations).

Abstract Code →

Half-MBB, volume 0.5, p = 3, 150 sensitivity-filtered OC iterations, 30 random starting fields at each of three noise levels on two meshes, with and without penalty continuation (1 → 3). With a fixed penalty the final compliance spreads by 1.4–2.8% (max/min − 1) and the 0/1 design differs from the uniform-start design in a median 2–23% of elements, with 2–10 enclosed holes. With continuation the spread is 0.0% on 60×20 (identical topology from every start) and at most 0.4% on 90×30. On 90×30 the uniform start, which the 99-line code uses, is worse than 25–28 of 30 random starts at fixed penalty. Stylised: 2D, dimensionless, 150 iterations (not run to convergence), one problem, two meshes.

simdesign-contlength5 tests

How short can SIMP penalty continuation be and still remove the dependence on the starting density field?

How short can SIMP penalty continuation be and still remove the start dependence? A ramp of 25 iterations or fewer leaves much of it (worst start differs in 16–23% of elements, 27–31% for a fixed penalty); 50 iterations cuts compliance spread to 0.01–0.23%, and a 112-iteration ramp is most repeatable but ends at a worse compliance (stylised, 2D, 150 iterations).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-starts. Half-MBB, volume 0.5, final p = 3, exactly 150 OC iterations, random starts (noise ±0.3; 20 on 60×20, 12 on 90×30), with the penalty ramped 1 → 3 over 0, 6, 12, 25, 50, 75 or 112 iterations. Ramps of 25 iterations or fewer leave most of the start dependence of a fixed penalty (worst start differs from the uniform-start design in 31% and 27% of elements on the two meshes): for ramps of 6–25 it is still 17–23% (60×20) and 16–20% (90×30), and compliance spreads 0.5–1.3%. At 50 iterations the spread falls to 0.01% (60×20) and 0.23% (90×30); at 75 the median disagreement is 0.0–0.3%. A 112-iteration ramp is the most repeatable but gives a worse final compliance (203.55 against 203.08 on 60×20; 197.3 against 196.6 on 90×30), because few iterations remain at full penalty. Stylised: 2D, one problem, two meshes, 150 iterations, not run to convergence.

simdesign-fidelity6 tests

When does a cheaper beam model pick the same design as 3D finite elements?

Cantilever sizing with Euler–Bernoulli, Timoshenko, 2D and 3D finite elements: stress agrees everywhere, deflection differs; cheap models land within ~5% of the 3D depth, unsafe when narrow and stubby (Euler–Bernoulli) and oversized when wide (plane stress). Stylised, assumed material.

Abstract Code →

A rectangular cantilever is sized for minimum mass under a tip-deflection and a top-fibre stress limit with Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theory, 2D plane-stress and 3D finite elements (scikit-fem), and each design is judged by the 3D model. Stress read away from the clamp agrees across models; deflection does not. Over 12 length–width cases the cheap models choose a depth within about 5% of the 3D optimum: Euler–Bernoulli is unsafe for narrow, stubby beams (up to 1.05× the deflection limit), while Timoshenko and plane stress are up to about 5% too heavy for wide ones, where plane strain stiffens the beam. Stylised: assumed material, a coarse 3D reference whose deflection still moves about 0.4% under refinement, no stress concentrations, nothing measured.

simdesign-llm6 tests

How do design proposals from a language-model agent compare with CMA-ES, Bayesian optimisation and random search at an equal simulation budget?

Session-agent design proposals vs CMA-ES, Bayesian optimisation and random search on a bracket sized by finite elements, 40 evaluations each: agent 23.0 g vs 32–39 g baseline medians (best known 22.4 g); the agent had prior knowledge, n = 1, not an LLM benchmark. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The finite-element bracket of simdesign-bracket, with tighter limits (15 MPa, 2.5 mm), is sized for minimum mass with 40 simulator calls per method. The proposer is the session agent itself, writing four rounds of ten designs by hand from the scores (no API key; not a reproducible LLM benchmark). It reaches 23.0 g against medians of 32.2 g (Bayesian optimisation), 33.3 g (CMA-ES) and 39.0 g (random) over 20 seeds, with 22.4 g best known from 1,845 evaluations; no baseline seed beat it. Stylised and weak evidence: n = 1, the agent used mechanics and the sibling project’s results as a prior, baselines were untuned, the stress constraint is mesh-sensitive, assumed material.

simdesign-dfm12 tests

What do manufacturing rules cost a sized bracket on FDM, CNC routing, laser cutting and casting?

Manufacturability rules (FDM, CNC routing, laser cutting, sand casting) added to the sized L-bracket: the mass price of each rule set against the same material with no rules (casting +43% from its even-section rule, CNC +24% from plate stock, laser and FDM ~0); designs overshoot the stress limit by 17–26% on a fine mesh (stylised, assumed rule values).

Abstract Code →

The L-bracket of simdesign-bracket is sized for minimum mass under a stress and a deflection limit with and without each process’s rules (tool radius, plate or sheet gauges, minimum walls, draft, an even-section rule), in the same material, so the ratio isolates the rules. Sand casting pays +43% (best of three seeds), driven by its wall-ratio rule rather than draft; CNC routing +24%, from the thinnest plate on the stock list; laser cutting and FDM about nothing, within optimiser noise (three seeds spread over 20%). Re-solved on a fine mesh, every chosen design exceeds its stress limit by 17–26%. Stylised: rule values and materials are assumed, the model is 2D, nothing was built. Exports an STL and DXF profiles.

simdesign-holes9 tests

How much does a bolt hole cost a tension plate, and which rule sets its width?

Tension plate with a required bolt hole sized under net-section, Kt = 3 and finite-element stress models and per-process hole rules (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A flat plate carrying one required hole is sized for minimum mass under a working-stress limit with three stress models (net section, a fixed Kt = 3, and 2D finite elements over d/W) and with per-process hole rules (minimum hole, centre-to-edge distance, ligament, stock thickness). FE reproduces the large-plate limit of Kt = 3 as the hole shrinks. Ignoring the concentration gives plates 1.9–2.7× overstressed where stress binds; Kt = 3 is safe but 8–26% heavier for FDM. Where an edge-distance rule binds (CNC routing, laser from 8 mm, casting from 8 mm) the stress model is irrelevant and the plate is 2–4× stronger than needed. Stylised: rule values, load and materials are assumed, 2D plane stress, no bolt contact or fatigue, mesh not fully converged (about 1% low), nothing built.

simdesign-coverweight8 tests

Does weighting parts by mass change which shop process, and which machine, matters?

Does weighting parts by mass change which shop process, and which machine, matters? With a tip load FDM covers 0.30 of parts by count and 0.58 by mass, the laser-versus-CNC order flips, and at budgets 600–800 exhaustive search picks the laser cutter by count but the casting setup by mass (one seed). Stylised, assumed rules and prices, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-processcover: coverage of a sampled bracket family by FDM, CNC, laser and casting, with each part weighted by arm volume (a same-material mass proxy) instead of counted equally. With a tip load, FDM alone covers 0.30 of parts by count and 0.58 by mass, casting 0.22 and 0.46, laser 0.18 either way, and the laser-versus-CNC order flips. At budgets 600–800 on one seed, exhaustive search picks the laser cutter by count but the casting setup by mass; for the large-part family at 800 it picks the CNC router by count and casting by mass. Stylised: assumed rules and prices, one density, single-seed machine choice. Simulated only.

simdesign-flipseeds5 tests

Do the mass-weighting machine-choice flips of simdesign-coverweight survive across seeds?

Do the mass-weighting machine-choice flips of simdesign-coverweight survive across seeds? Over 20 seeds, log flips from the laser cutter (count) to the casting setup (mass) in 20/20 at budgets 600–800, large only at 800, small never; the 1100–1400 flips are near-ties (≤0.26 points). Stylised, assumed rules and prices, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-coverweight, whose machine-choice flips between count and mass weighting came from one seed. Over 20 fresh seeds of 20 000 sampled brackets and three assumed machines, family log picks the laser cutter by count but the casting setup (or, in 2 seeds at 800, the CNC router) by mass in 20 of 20 seeds at budgets 600 to 800 (95% Wilson interval 0.84 to 1.00; about 2.1 points of mass-weighted coverage given up), family large flips only at budget 800 (20 of 20), and small never flips. The log flips at 1100 and 1400 split 10 of 20 but lose at most 0.26 points, a near-tie. The intervals cover sampling noise only; rules, prices and the volume mass proxy are assumptions. Stylised; simulated only.

simdesign-pricebands5 tests

How wide are the budget bands where mass weighting changes the machine choice when prices are uncertain?

How wide are the budget bands where mass weighting changes the machine choice when prices are uncertain? With ±20% independent price noise the log flip band widens from budgets 600–800 to 500–1000 but softens at its edges (about one half), and large's single nominal flip at 800 shows up in only 44% of price draws. Stylised, assumed rules and prices, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to simdesign-flipseeds, whose count-vs-mass machine-choice flips sat exactly on thresholds set by assumed round prices. Machine prices (800, 600, 300) are scaled by independent U(1−s, 1+s) factors, 400 draws over 8 samples of 20 000 sampled brackets. For family log the flip band widens from budgets 600–800 to 500–1000, but its edges soften to about one half; large's single nominal flip at 800 appears in 44% of draws at s = 0.2 and spills to 700 and 900; small never flips. Near-tie flips never lose more than 0.5 points. Stylised: assumed prices and rules, uniform independent noise, arbitrary 0.5-point materiality threshold.

simdesign-processcover10 tests

Which share of a bracket family can each shop process make, and which machine should a shop add next?

Share of a sampled bracket family each shop process can make under the simdesign-dfm rules: geometry alone adds nothing beyond FDM (negative), with a tip-load requirement the processes separate (FDM alone 30%, +casting +laser 41%) and the best next machine depends on budget and part size, where greedy sometimes loses 1–2 points to exhaustive search (stylised, assumed rules).

Abstract Code →

Using the assumed rules of simdesign-dfm (FDM, CNC routing, laser cutting, casting) as feasibility checks on 20 000 sampled bracket feature sets, geometry alone gives a degenerate answer: FDM covers 89% and no other process covers anything FDM cannot, so no machine adds coverage (a negative result).
