With a tip-load requirement of 1–1000 N and closed-form beam checks the processes separate: FDM alone covers 30%, adding casting and a laser cutter 41%, and the best next machine depends on the budget and on the part sizes. Greedy selection from selfrep-nextmachine is sometimes 1–2 coverage points below exhaustive search. Stylised: all rule values, working stresses and prices are assumed, the beam check ignores fillet stress concentration, and nothing was made.

simdesign-meshmargin4 tests

Does a mesh-aware stress margin change what manufacturing rules cost a sized bracket?

Re-runs simdesign-dfm with a stress knock-down and a finer search mesh, checking designs at h = 0.7 mm: the price ordering (casting ~1.4, CNC ~1.23, FDM 1.0) survives the mesh, the laser-cutting price does not (1.01–1.22, noisy), and a 1.3 margin leaves designs at 0.88–1.02 of the limit (stylised, assumed rule values).

Abstract Code →

The process-rule search of simdesign-dfm is repeated with a coarse mesh, a coarse mesh with the stress limit divided by 1.3, and a finer mesh, and every design is re-solved on a finer check mesh. The ordering of the mass prices survives: casting about 1.4, CNC routing about 1.23, FDM 1.0 by construction. The laser-cutting price does not (1.01 to 1.22 across settings, with only two seeds). A margin of 1.3 leaves the designs at 0.88 to 1.02 of the limit on the check mesh, at a 17at a 20–35% mass costndash;35% mass cost. Stylised: the peak stress is not converged even on the check mesh, rule values are assumed, and nothing was made.

simdesign-patchstress5 tests

Does a patch-averaged stress converge under mesh refinement where the peak element stress does not?

Compares peak and patch-averaged von Mises stress under mesh refinement on the L-bracket: the peak rises 18–41% from h = 2.5 to 0.55 mm while a 3 mm patch average moves 1–6%, but it reads only 0.45–0.69 of the peak so needs its own limit (stylised, assumed values).

Abstract Code →

On four L-bracket designs solved on five meshes (h = 2.5 to 0.55 mm), the peak von Mises stress rises by 18–41% while a 3 mm patch average moves by 1–6%. The peak is not monotone along the sequence, so a two-mesh check can mislead. The patch average is not conservative: it reads 0.45–0.69 of the fine-mesh peak and would need its own calibrated limit. Stylised: 2D plane stress, one load case, a non-nested mesh family, assumed material, nothing made.

simdesign-patchsearch4 tests

Does a patch-averaged stress change what manufacturing rules cost a sized bracket?

Repeats the process-rule bracket search with a 3 mm patch-averaged stress instead of the peak: the ordering of mass prices (casting > CNC > laser ≈ FDM) holds, the laser price spread across seeds shrinks from 0.16 to under 0.005, and designs overshoot their limit by 2–12% on a fine mesh against 19–34% for the peak (stylised, assumed values, uncalibrated limit).

Abstract Code →

The minimum-mass bracket search under FDM, CNC-routing, laser-cutting and casting rules is repeated with a 3 mm patch-averaged stress in place of the peak element stress, using the same numeric limit, then every design is re-solved on a fine check mesh (h = 0.55 mm). The ordering of the mass prices survives (casting 1.35, CNC 1.23–1.27, laser 1.03–1.05, FDM 1.0), and the laser-cutting price, which varied from 0.99 to 1.15 across three seeds under the peak measure, varies by under 0.005. Patch-searched designs exceed the limit by 2–12% on the fine mesh, against 19–34% for peak-searched designs, but they are lighter only because the same numeric limit is a looser test; the patch limit is uncalibrated. Three seeds, assumed rules and material, stylised 2D.

simdesign-filletfloor6 tests

Is the shrinking laser-cutting price scatter under the patch stress caused by the near-sharp fillet floor?

Tests whether a near-sharp fillet floor explains the laser-cutting price scatter seen in simdesign-patchsearch: it does not (peak-stress designs already use 7.6–14.3 mm fillets, so floors of 0.2 and 1 mm give identical designs); the patch-stress price is steady (sd 0.006–0.011) at every floor, and the cause of the peak scatter is not identified (negative, five seeds, stylised).

Abstract Code →

A negative result (stylised). Raising the laser-cutting inner-fillet floor from 0.2 to 1 and 3.175 mm over five seeds does not explain the scatter in the mass price of the rules: the peak-stress designs already use fillets of 7.6–14.3 mm, so the 0.2 and 1 mm floors give identical designs (sd of the price 0.063), and under a 3 mm patch average the price is steady (sd 0.006–0.011) at every floor. The cause of the peak-stress scatter is not identified. Limits: five seeds, one process and load, uncalibrated limit, assumed values, 2D plane stress.

simdesign-gaugebudget8 tests

Where does the peak-stress price scatter of laser-cutting rules come from?

Follow-up to simdesign-filletfloor: the peak-stress price scatter of laser-cutting rules (sd 0.063) sits in the 2 mm gauge sub-search, not the fillet floor; a four-times search budget cuts it to 0.025 but not monotonically, so several nearby optima are plausible but not shown (five seeds, stylised).

Abstract Code →

A stylised follow-up to the fillet-floor negative result. Keeping the best mass of each of the ten stock-gauge sub-searches shows that the scatter in the rules mass (price 0.990–1.145 over five seeds) sits in the 2 mm gauge: in one seed that sub-search found nothing feasible and the 3 mm gauge won, giving the 1.145 outlier, while gauges of 3 mm and above agree across seeds to within 0.05 g at four times the budget. Quadrupling the search budget cuts the price sd from 0.063 to 0.025, but not monotonically, the no-rules twin moves too, and the 2 mm gauge still spreads over 2 g, so the data are consistent with several nearby optima there, not proof of it. Five seeds, one process and load case, 2D plane stress, assumed rules. Simulated only. Produced with AI assistance.

simdesign-holepatch6 tests

Does a patch-averaged stress give a mesh-converged stress concentration for a bolt hole?

Patch-averaged stress for a bolt hole in a tension strip: nearly settled under mesh refinement already, matches Kirsch's disc averages, needs its own limit (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A strip in tension with a central circular hole is solved by finite elements on meshes of 48 to 768 points around the hole, and the pointwise peak of σxx is compared with its average over a disc of 0.1 to 0.5 hole radii, for d/W from 0.05 to 0.4, and with Kirsch’s analytic field. The peak is already nearly settled for a smooth hole (0.3% change over the last refinement; the patch measures 0.0–0.1%), and at d/W = 0.05 the patch values match Kirsch’s disc averages to within 0.4%. The patch reads 65–91% of the peak, so it needs its own limit. One coarse mesh (d/W = 0.4, 96 points) is an unexplained outlier for every measure. Stylised; linear plane stress, no allowable calibrated.

simdesign-kirsch6 tests

How far below the exact stress concentration does a finite-element peak stress sit, and how fast does it close?

Checks the finite-element peak stress at a circular hole against Kirsch's exact 3× concentration: the element-centroid peak sits 27% (coarse) to 1.1% (fine) below it and closes only at first order, while hole-edge vertex values are within 1% (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A plate with a circular hole under tension has an exact peak stress of 3× the remote stress (Kirsch). On a graded quarter-plate mesh with exact-solution tractions (48 384 elements at the finest), the usual element-centroid peak sits 27% below it on the coarsest mesh and 1.1% below on the finest, closing only at first order, while the field itself converges at second order: the shortfall is sampling position, not solver error. Reading the stress at the hole-edge vertices instead is within 1% on every mesh. Stylised 2D plane stress, one geometry, regular mesh; the numbers do not transfer to other fillets.

simdesign-gaugescatter8 tests

What causes the peak-stress price scatter of laser-cutting rules in the bracket search?

The peak-stress price scatter of laser-cutting rules is a missed search at the narrow 2 mm gauge (1 seed in 20), not a cost of the rules; stylised, mesh effects untested.

Abstract Code →

A diagnostic with a negative-for-the-rules answer (stylised). The high price in one of five seeds (1.15 vs 1.00–1.01 in the others) is a missed search, not a cost of the laser rules: the 2 mm sheet gauge, which wins, has a feasible region of only 13 of 900 grid cells, and the rules sub-search missed it in 1 of 20 seeds (the rule-free twin in 0 of 20). Feasible 2 mm results fall in two mass groups (33.3–34.0 g and 35.3–35.6 g) whose cause is not identified. Mesh effects were not tested. Stylised 2D plane stress; assumed rules and loads.

simdesign-gaugerestart5 tests

Do search restarts remove the missed 2 mm sub-search in the laser-cut bracket problem?

A second DE restart or a doubled population removes the missed 2 mm sub-search (0 misses in 40 runs against 1 in 20 at baseline) and shifts results to the lighter of two mass groups at about twice the cost; stylised, 2.5 mm search mesh only.

Abstract Code →

A small search-effort experiment (stylised). At the 2 mm sheet gauge, one differential-evolution run missed the narrow feasible region in 1 of 20 seeds; a second independent run or a doubled population missed in 0 of 40 runs each, at about twice the finite-element solves. Results also shift from an even split towards the lighter of two mass groups (to 70–75% with a restart, 85–95% with the larger population), consistent with the heavier group being a local optimum of the search. Zero misses in 20 does not prove a zero miss rate, and the 2 mm region is itself a coarse-mesh effect, so the lower masses are not better physical designs.

simdesign-gaugebasins5 tests

Are the two mass groups of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket search two separate basins?

The two gauge-2 mass groups differ in web width w (about 14.3–14.9 against 15.2–15.6 mm), not fillet radius, and the lighter group matches ragged isolated feasible pockets on the 2.5 mm mesh rather than a second broad basin; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small diagnostic (stylised, preliminary). The lighter and heavier groups of gauge-2 search results differ in web width (about 14.3–14.9 against 15.2–15.6 mm), not in fillet radius. A coarse grid shows one connected feasible region, but a 0.1 mm scan shows the feasible set is ragged in width: isolated feasible pockets lie below a contiguous region, and the lighter group matches those pockets. This is consistent with a coarse-mesh stress artefact rather than two broad basins, a mechanism not tested here. Twenty seeds, one process, one mesh; nothing was built.

simdesign-pocketmesh5 tests

Do the isolated feasible pockets of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket survive mesh refinement?

The isolated feasible pockets of the gauge-2 bracket scan (web width below 15.4 mm) vanish when the mesh is refined from 2.5 to 1.5 mm and the smallest feasible width rises by about 1 mm; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small mesh-refinement scan (stylised, preliminary). Scanning web width in 0.1 mm steps at four fillet radii on 2.5, 2.0 and 1.5 mm meshes, the isolated feasible widths below 15.4 mm seen on the 2.5 mm mesh are absent at 1.5 mm, and the smallest feasible width rises from about 14.4–14.8 to 15.6–15.7 mm. This is consistent with the lighter search group being a coarse-mesh artefact, but the boundary was still moving, so convergence is not shown. No search was rerun on the finer meshes. Simulated only.

simdesign-meshconverge6 tests

Does the feasible boundary of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket converge when the mesh is refined to 0.5 mm?

On meshes of 1.0 and 0.5 mm no width in the usable 15.0–16.0 mm window of the gauge-2 bracket scan is feasible (one point at 0.75 mm), and the lowest peak stress rises 11–14% from 1.5 to 0.5 mm; negative, stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A negative result (stylised, preliminary). Scanning web width from 15.0 to 16.0 mm (the slenderness rule forbids wider) at four fillet radii on 1.5, 1.0, 0.75 and 0.5 mm meshes, the feasible widths found at 1.5 mm are all infeasible at 1.0 and 0.5 mm under the 100 MPa peak-stress limit, with a single feasible point at 0.75 mm. The lowest peak stress rises 11–14% from 1.5 to 0.5 mm and is still creeping up, so convergence is not shown. One gauge, one load, a peak measure at a near-sharp fillet floor; no search was run on the fine meshes.

simdesign-lbuckle3 tests

Does the 1.5 mm bracket clear buckling when the whole L is one 3D body with a flexible corner?

The whole 1.5 mm L-bracket as one 3D body clears the buckling floor under the design load (factor 4.01 vs closed-form 3.47) but not with the load reversed (2.25, below 3); sharp corner, ideal sheet, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, one design). Meshing the whole L of the 1.5 mm, w = 18.4 mm design from simdesign-bucklebound as one hexahedral body, the lowest buckling factor under the design load (vertical arm in tension) is 4.01, above the closed-form 3.47 and the floor of 3. With the load reversed (arm in compression) it falls to 2.25, below the floor, a case the moment-only formula cannot see. Refinement moved the factors by under 2%. No fillet, no imperfections.

simdesign-revwidth4 tests

How wide must the 1.5 mm L-bracket be to clear the buckling floor when the load is reversed?

Widening the 1.5 mm L-bracket web from 18.4 to about 22.6 mm lifts the reversed-load buckling factor from 2.27 to the floor of 3, at +5.9 g (+19%) plate mass; buckling only, sharp corner, ideal sheet, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small finite-element sweep (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, buckling only). Reusing the whole-L 3D eigenbuckling model of simdesign-lbuckle, the reversed-load factor of the 1.5 mm bracket rises from 2.27 at w = 18.4 mm to 3.0 at w ≈ 22.5–22.6 mm (coarse root 22.47, finer-mesh bracket 22.54–22.62), about 0.22 per extra millimetre. The plate mass rises from 30.7 to 36.6 g (+19%). Stress, slenderness and minimum-wall limits were not rechecked at the wider web, the floor of 3 is an assumption, and the corner is sharp.

simdesign-gaugelayers3 tests

Do the reversed-load buckling widths of the L-bracket change with more element layers through the thickness?

More element layers through the thickness (1 to 4) move the L-bracket's reversed-load buckling factor by at most 1.2% and the width needed for the floor of 3 by at most 0.07 mm at 1.5 to 3.0 mm gauges, so the thicker-sheet designs of simdesign-revgauge stand; coarse in-plane mesh, sharp corner, ideal sheet, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, coarse in-plane mesh). Raising the number of hexahedral layers through the sheet from one to four moves the whole-L reversed-load buckling factor at the simdesign-revgauge root widths by at most 1.2% (3.0 mm gauge; under 0.7% at 1.5 to 2.5 mm) and the width needed for a factor of 3 by 0.07 mm or less (2.0 mm: 11.84 to 11.77 mm, 27.4 g). The thicker-sheet mass ranking of that project is not an artefact of a single through-thickness layer; its other doubt, a web barely wider than the sheet is thick, stands.

simdesign-fwdcheck3 tests

Do the reversed-load buckling-limited L-bracket designs also pass the forward-load buckling, stress and deflection checks?

Under the forward 100 N load the four reversed-load buckling-limited L-brackets all clear buckling (factor 4.7 to 5.6), but only the 1.5 mm design also meets the 100 MPa and 4 mm limits; the 2.5 and 3.0 mm designs fail by 2 to 8 times, and the 2.0 mm design passes only on the coarse mesh (95.7 vs 144.9 MPa finer). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic steel, sharp inner corner, assumed limits). Under the forward 100 N load the four lightest designs that clear the reversed-load buckling floor (1.5 to 3.0 mm sheet) all have forward buckling factors of 4.7 to 5.6, so buckling does not bind. But only the 1.5 mm, 22.5 mm design meets the 100 MPa stress and 4 mm deflection limits; the 2.5 and 3.0 mm designs exceed them by 2 to 8 times, and the 2.0 mm design passes only on the coarse mesh (95.7 MPa against 144.9 MPa on a finer one). The thicker sheet's mass saving is therefore not feasible under these limits.

simdesign-revgauge4 tests

Is a thicker sheet lighter than a wider 1.5 mm web for clearing the reversed-load buckling floor?

At the reversed-load buckling floor of 3, a 2 mm sheet needs a web of about 11.8 mm and weighs 27.5 g against 36.6 g for 1.5 mm at 22.6 mm; 2.5 mm gives 20.5 g; buckling only, one element layer through the thickness, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small finite-element sweep (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic sheet, sharp inner corner, buckling only, one element layer through the thickness). Reusing the whole-L 3D eigenbuckling model of simdesign-lbuckle, the smallest web width that lifts the reversed-load factor to 3 falls from 22.6 mm at 1.5 mm sheet to 11.8 mm at 2 mm and 6.8 mm at 2.5 mm, so the plate mass at the floor falls from 36.6 g to 27.5 g (−25%) and 20.5 g (−44%). Thick, narrow webs are where the model is weakest, and forward load, stress and minimum-wall rules were not rechecked, so this is an indication, not a design.

simdesign-minwall7 tests

Does relaxing the 1.2 mm minimum-wall rule open thinner sheet gauges for the laser-cut bracket, or is the buckling floor what binds?

Relaxing the 1.2 mm minimum wall of the laser-cut bracket: it does not open 1.0 mm sheet by itself (the buckling floor binds); with floor 1 and wall ≤ 1.0 mm a 24.8 g design appears (unvalidated closed form).

Abstract Code →

A small optimiser study (stylised, preliminary; the buckling factor is an unvalidated ideal-bar closed form). Relaxing the minimum wall from 1.2 to 1.0 or 0.8 mm changes nothing at 1.5 mm (31.0 g in every cell) and does not by itself open 1.0 mm sheet: with a buckling-factor floor of 3 no design exists at 0.8 or 1.0 mm (the widest allowed web reaches a factor of only 1.5 at 1.0 mm). With a floor of 1 and a minimum wall of 1.0 mm or less, a 1.0 mm design appears at 24.8 g (w = 22.7 mm, factor 1.33, 2 of 3 seeds), 20% under the 1.5 mm optimum, but a factor of 1.33 from an ideal-bar formula is no margin. Simulated results only.

simdesign-buckle153 tests

Does the lightest 1.5 mm bracket design clear buckling in a converged 3D eigenbuckling model?

A through-thickness-converged 3D eigenbuckling model agrees with the closed-form buckling factor of the lightest 1.5 mm bracket design to under 1% (3.49 vs 3.47, so it clears the floor of 3); the horizontal-arm formula is about 18% conservative; one design, ideal bar, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small finite-element check (stylised, preliminary; ideal elastic clamped arms, one design). Meshing the 1.5 mm, w = 18.4 mm design from simdesign-bucklebound with hexahedra at three resolutions, including two layers through the thickness, the governing vertical-arm buckling factor is 3.49 against 3.47 from the closed form (ratio 1.020 → 1.007 on refinement), so the design clears the floor of 3. The horizontal-arm formula is about 18% conservative. Nothing was made or tested.

simdesign-bucklebound5 tests

What changes when the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness ceiling of the laser-cut bracket is replaced by a buckling-factor floor?

Replacing the w/b ≤ 8 ceiling with a closed-form buckling-factor floor makes the 1.5 mm laser-cut gauge feasible (31.0 g, about 13% lighter than the best 2 mm design) and changes nothing at 2 and 3 mm; at 1 mm the minimum-wall rule, not buckling, blocks every design; stylised, unvalidated factor, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small optimiser study (stylised, preliminary; the buckling factor is an unvalidated closed form). Minimising mass over web width and fillet radius at four sheet gauges with differential evolution (three seeds, mesh 1.5 mm): the old ceiling makes the 1.5 mm gauge infeasible, while a buckling-factor floor of 1 or 3 yields a 31.0 g design (w ≈ 18.4 mm, factor 3.5), about 13% lighter than the best 2 mm design (35.8 g). At 2 and 3 mm the three guards agree to 0.1%. At 1 mm no design is feasible under any guard because the 1.2 mm minimum-wall rule, not buckling, rejects it. Mass is the only objective; nothing was made or tested.

simdesign-webbuckle4 tests

Does lateral-torsional buckling justify the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness rule of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket?

A closed-form lateral-torsional buckling check of the laser-cut bracket arms (stylised, unvalidated by FE): at 2 mm gauge the governing safety factor is 6.9–9.0 for w = 16–20 mm, so the widths of simdesign-widerweb are not buckling-limited, and the factor rises with w, opposite to the w/b ≤ 8 rule; at 1 mm the old rule admits designs below 1.

Abstract Code →

A closed-form check (stylised, preliminary, not validated against a shell or 3D model). Treating each bracket arm as an ideal elastic flat bar, the lateral-torsional buckling safety factor at the 2 mm gauge is 6.9–9.0 for web widths of 16–20 mm, so the wider webs of simdesign-widerweb are not buckling-limited under this model. The factor rises with width, the opposite direction to a w/b ceiling; at a 1 mm gauge the old rule would admit w up to 8 mm, where the factor is 0.41. The two textbook coefficients were checked numerically; real sheet imperfections, residual stress and corner flexibility are left out. Calculated only.

simdesign-webshell3 tests

Do the closed-form buckling factors of the laser-cut bracket arms agree with a 3D eigenbuckling model?

A 3D scikit-fem eigenbuckling check of the bracket-arm closed forms (stylised, mesh not converged): within about 1% for the governing vertical arm, conservative by 6–29% for the horizontal arm at the 2 mm gauge.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary comparison of two idealised models (mesh not fully converged). A 3D scikit-fem linear-buckling model of each bracket arm, checked against the Euler column, gives a critical load within about 1% of the closed form for the governing vertical arm (end moment) at web widths of 8–25 mm at the 2 mm gauge. For the horizontal arm (tip load) the closed form is conservative: the 3D model is 6% higher at w = 8 mm and 29% higher at 25 mm. The governing safety factors (3.2, 7.0, 11.9) therefore support the conclusion of simdesign-webbuckle. Imperfections, residual stress, corner flexibility and plasticity are left out. Simulated only.

simdesign-shellconverge2 tests

Does refining the mesh of the 3D eigenbuckling check change how the closed-form bracket-arm buckling factors compare?

Mesh refinement of the 3D eigenbuckling check of the bracket arms (stylised): refining length, width and thickness lowers every FE/closed-form ratio by 0.9–1.3 points, so the governing vertical arm agrees with the closed form to within 1% (ratio 0.99–1.00 at the finest mesh).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary mesh study of the model in simdesign-webshell. Refining the quadratic-hexahedron mesh in length, width and thickness lowers the finite-element critical load every time, by 0.9–1.3 percentage points of the closed-form value in total at web widths 8, 16 and 25 mm (2 mm gauge); thickness and width refinement dominate and length refinement contributes under 0.1 point. On the finest mesh (72×8×2) the governing vertical arm sits at 0.992, 0.996 and 1.002 of the closed form, so the two agree within about 1% and the earlier fine-mesh ratios were slightly high. The horizontal-arm closed form stays conservative (ratios 1.046, 1.135, 1.279). Only two refinement levels per direction, so no convergence rate or extrapolated limit is claimed. Simulated only.

simdesign-shellaspect2 tests

At what bar slenderness does the 3D eigenbuckling model agree with the slender-beam closed form?

How the 3D eigenbuckling model compares with the slender-beam closed form as a bar gets longer (stylised): the finite-element load is 14.5%, 7.4%, 3.8% and 2.1% above it at l/w = 3, 6, 12, 24.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary scan of one steel bar cross-section (8×2 mm, tip shear, clamped end) at l/w = 3, 6, 12 and 24 on a fixed element size. The finite-element critical load sits 14.5%, 7.4%, 3.8% and 2.1% above the Timoshenko–Gere closed form, so the gap shrinks roughly in proportion to w/l and is consistent with a short-bar effect rather than mesh error. One cross-section and one cross-section mesh; no refinement at the longer lengths.

simdesign-volscale4 tests

How much stiffer than a uniformly thinned plate is a topology-optimised part, and how does that depend on volume fraction?

How much stiffer a thresholded topology-optimised part is than a uniformly thinned plate across volume fractions (stylised): 26–31% lower compliance at v = 0.3–0.5, shrinking to 14% at 0.8, and disconnected designs below that on coarse grids.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary study of two 2D plane-stress problems (cantilever 60×20, half-MBB 90×30). Thresholded 0/1 SIMP designs have 26–31% lower compliance than a plate thinned uniformly to the same volume at v = 0.3–0.5, the advantage shrinking to about 14% at v = 0.8; fits give C ∝ v−0.8 against v−1 for the plate. At low volume on these grids the design is disconnected and the comparison fails. One run per point, coarse grids, variable-thickness reference.

simdesign-shellorder1 tests

At what rate does the 3D eigenbuckling model converge under uniform mesh refinement?

Observed convergence order of the 3D eigenbuckling model on a short bar (stylised): three uniform meshes give order ≈ 2.6 and a Richardson limit FE/closed-form ratio 1.137, so the gap to the closed form is not discretisation error.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary study of one short steel bar (24×8×2 mm, tip shear). Three uniformly refined hexahedral meshes give an observed order of about 2.6 and a Richardson limit of 9618 N, 0.12% below the finest mesh. The limit is still 13.7% above the slender-beam closed form, so the gap is not discretisation error (plausibly shear deformation and clamp warping; untested). One geometry, one mesh triple.

simdesign-buckleguard7 tests

What does it cost to replace the w/b ≤ 8 rule of the laser-cut bracket with a buckling-factor guard?

Replacing the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness rule of the laser-cut bracket with a lateral-torsional buckling factor ≥ 3 lets the optimiser use the 1.5 mm gauge at w ≈ 18.7 mm, 31.3 g instead of 35.9 g (about 12% lighter), and the guard does not bind at that optimum; the result depends on the assumed factor (no feasible design for factors ≥ 5 at that gauge); stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary optimisation study (closed-form buckling check, assumed rules, material and load). Replacing the w/b ≤ 8 slenderness rule with a lateral-torsional safety factor of at least 3 lets the differential-evolution optimiser use the 1.5 mm gauge at w ≈ 18.7 mm: 31.1–31.4 g against 35.8–36.0 g under the old rule, about 12% lighter (three seeds each). The guard does not bind at that optimum; the stress limit does. The result depends on the assumed factor: no feasible 1.5 mm design was found for a factor of 5 or more. Simulated only; edge crippling, imperfections and cutting stress are not modelled.

simdesign-loadbind11 tests

When does the buckling guard of the laser-cut bracket start to bind as load and arm length change?

Sweeping tip load (50–400 N) and arm length (60–120 mm) of the laser-cut bracket: the buckling-factor ≥ 3 guard binds only at 120 mm arms (unguarded optimum has factor 1.9; 69 g vs 59 g), while the old w/b ≤ 8 rule costs 14–25% in mass in five of six cases (stylised, two seeds).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary sweep (closed-form buckling check, assumed rules, material and loads; two seeds). Over tip loads of 50–400 N and arms of 60–120 mm, a lateral-torsional factor ≥ 3 guard binds in only one of six cases: 120 mm arms, where the unguarded optimum has a factor of 1.9 and the guard costs 16% in mass (69 g vs 59 g). The old w/b ≤ 8 rule was 14–25% heavier than the buckling guard in five of six cases. Gauge steps make mass non-smooth in load; the result moves with the assumed factor.

simdesign-edgescan7 tests

How sharp is the feasible edge of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket web at 0.1 mm resolution, and is it mesh noise?

A 0.1 mm scan of the feasible edge of the gauge-2 bracket web (nine mesh/radius cases): peak stress is not monotone in w, with residual jitter of 0.9–2.4 MPa about a quadratic trend, the same size as the 0.1–1.7 MPa gap to the 100 MPa limit just below each edge, so the edge is a band of about 0.5 mm and the earlier refinement shift is not separated from mesh noise; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small scan (stylised, preliminary). Re-scanning web width w in 0.1 mm steps (15.5–17.5 mm) at three radii and three meshes, the peak von Mises stress is not monotone in w in any of the nine series. Its residual jitter about a quadratic trend is 0.9–2.4 MPa, shrinking with refinement, and the stress just below each feasible edge is only 0.1–1.7 MPa over the 100 MPa limit, so the edge is a band of about 0.5 mm and the refinement shift reported in simdesign-widerweb is not separated from mesh noise. The source of the jitter is not identified. Simulated only.

simdesign-widerweb5 tests

Do wider webs of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket stay feasible on fine meshes when the slenderness rule is relaxed?

With the assumed slenderness limit raised from 8 to 12.5, gauge-2 bracket webs of 16–17 mm and wider are feasible at h = 1.5, 1.0 and 0.75 mm; refinement from 1.5 to 1.0 mm moves the lightest feasible width up 0.5 mm (about 1 g, 3%); stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small scan (stylised, preliminary). With the assumed slenderness limit w/b raised from 8 to 12.5, web widths of 15 to 20 mm at fillet radii 8, 12 and 14 mm are feasible under the peak-stress measure from w = 16.0–17.0 mm upward at every mesh tried (h = 1.5, 1.0 and 0.75 mm), so the empty fine-mesh feasible sets of simdesign-meshconverge came from the rule window. Refinement from 1.5 to 1.0 mm raises the lightest feasible width by 0.5 mm (about 1 g, 3%) at all three radii; at 0.75 mm it is unchanged at two radii and falls back one step at r = 14 mm, so the shift is not resolved beyond about one scan step. The relaxed rule stands in for out-of-plane buckling, which the 2D model cannot see, so these designs are not validated. Simulated results only.

simdesign-gaugepockets5 tests

Do the isolated feasible pockets of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket survive mesh refinement?

The isolated feasible pockets below w = 15 mm at the 2 mm laser-cut gauge vanish at 2.0 and 1.5 mm element size, and the smallest feasible w moves up (14.4 to 15.6 mm at r = 14 mm); stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A small mesh-refinement scan (stylised, preliminary). The isolated feasible web widths below 15 mm that appear at 2.5 mm element size vanish at 2.0 and 1.5 mm, and the smallest feasible width moves up (14.4 to 15.6 mm at fillet radius 14 mm). Mesh convergence was not reached, and a stress peak at a corner is itself mesh-sensitive, so the least-mass design on the search mesh is optimistic.

Is the narrow 2 mm laser-cut bracket region a mesh artefact?

The narrow 2 mm laser-cut bracket region is a mesh effect: all 39 designs feasible at h = 2.5 mm fail the stress limit at h ≤ 1.5 mm (peak 1.09–1.27× higher, still rising at 0.75 mm); stylised, negative for the search mesh.

Abstract Code →

A negative result for the search mesh (stylised). All 39 gauge-2 bracket designs that were feasible on the 2.5 mm search mesh (19 under laser rules, 20 for the no-rules twin) are infeasible on finer meshes (1.5, 1.0, 0.75 mm): the peak von Mises stress is 1.09–1.27× higher at 0.75 mm and is still rising, at the point where the fillet meets the arm. Does a patch-averaged stress make the 2 mm laser-cut bracket region mesh-independent?

A 3 mm patch-averaged stress converges with the mesh (≤2.2% change from h = 1.0 to 0.75 mm) where the centroid peak does not, and all 39 gauge-2 designs stay feasible; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Preliminary, stylised 2D plane stress. On the 39 gauge-2 bracket designs that fail the stress limit on fine meshes under the element-centroid peak, a 3 mm patch-averaged stress changes by at most 2.2% between 1.0 and 0.75 mm meshes (the centroid peak rises up to 9.7%), and all 39 stay feasible at every mesh size, with a median of 84–86 MPa on the finest mesh. The verdict flips because the criterion is less strict, not because the model changed; whether a patch average is an adequate design rule was not shown, and no fine-mesh design search was run.

Does the L-bracket's peak stress at the fillet tangent point converge under graded mesh refinement? Yes for four designs: it flattens at 1.09–1.14× its 1.5 mm value (0.0–1.1% change over the last 4× refinement down to 0.025 mm), so the 2 mm region's mesh dependence is a resolution effect; the 16/15/2 design is marginally over 100 MPa when converged; stylised 2D, no reference solution.

Preliminary, stylised 2D plane stress. Uniform meshes left the element-centroid peak stress of the 2 mm laser-cut bracket still rising. Under a 3 mm patch-averaged stress rule the least-mass laser-cut bracket is the same on a 2.5 mm and a 1.0 mm mesh (gauge 2: 32.31 vs 32.33 g), while the centroid-peak rule leaves no feasible gauge-2 design on the fine mesh; the patch value hardly sees the fillet radius; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Preliminary, stylised 2D plane stress. On a 20×20 grid over arm width and fillet radius, the least mass of a feasible laser-cut bracket under a 3 mm patch-averaged stress rule is the same on a 2.5 mm and a 1.0 mm mesh (2 mm sheet: 32.31 vs 32.33 g; 3 mm: 40.81 vs 40.81 g). Under the element-centroid peak rule the 2 mm sheet has no feasible design on the fine mesh and the 3 mm sheet needs 10.8% more mass. The catch: the patch value hardly depends on the fillet radius (94–102 MPa for r from 0 to 15 mm against a peak of 126–264 MPa), so the rule cannot tell a sharp corner from a generous fillet. simdesign-rank5 tests

Do cheap beam and 2D models rank candidate cantilever designs like 3D finite elements?

Do cheap beam and 2D models rank cantilever designs like 3D finite elements? Yes on 3 seeds of 80 designs: Kendall τ 0.987–0.996 and the 3D-best design always ranked first, even though single-design merit is off by up to 14%; stubby sections agree least; stylised, one load case.

Abstract Code →

Stylised. 80 random cantilever designs per seed (3 seeds) are ranked by stiffness per mass with Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theory and 2D plane-stress FE, and compared with a 3D finite-element reference (scikit-fem). Single-design merit is off by up to 14% (Euler–Bernoulli, stubby sections), yet every cheap model ranks the designs almost identically: Kendall τ 0.987–0.996 with 3D, 3D’s best design always ranked first, top-8 overlap 7 or 8 of 8. Stubby designs agree least (τ 0.96–0.99). Limits: one load case, assumed material, a coarse 3D reference, no stress or constraints in the ranking.

15

Engineered clothing

Fashion from an engineering point of view: what garments cost to make, and what materials, mechanics and electronics could do for clothes. Topic page →

garment-teardown7 tests

Where does a designer coat's price go, and what does a $20 to $50 replica keep?

Bottom-up cost model for a lined coat applied to two reported designer prices: modelled factory cost is under 15% of price, the assumed markup chain does not close the gap, and a $20–50 replica needs very cheap cloth and labour. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A bottom-up cost model for a lined woven coat (fabric from pattern area and marker efficiency, trims, sewing minutes times wage, overhead, brand and retail multipliers) applied to two reported designer prices. Under assumed inputs the factory cost is $186–248 for a $2,850 trench and $469–551 for a $3,850 coat, under 15% of the price in every wage scenario, and the assumed multipliers do not close the gap. A cheap-cloth replica costs $46–100 to make; only a very lean case reaches $29–34. Stylised: every cost input is assumed, prices are from search snippets, and fit and durability are not scored.

garment-pattern-fit8 tests

Can a cheap cloth drape score how well a flat pattern fits a body, and is a fitted pattern body-specific?

Position-based cloth drape scores a flat skirt-tube pattern on two synthetic elliptical bodies by strain and waist ease; the best waist is near the body's waist perimeter and a pattern fitted to one body fits the other clearly worse. Stylised; strains depend on mesh and solver.

Abstract Code →

A flat skirt-tube pattern is draped by position-based-dynamics cloth on two synthetic elliptical-section bodies and scored by circumferential strain and waist ease. The best waist is close to the body’s waist perimeter (×1.01 and ×1.03); tighter patterns strain, looser ones leave ease. A pattern optimised for one body costs 2.1–2.9 on the other against own optima of 0.15–0.75 (arbitrary cost units). Stylised: the body is a stack of ellipses, the cost weights are assumptions, the hem optimum sits at the edge of the search range, and the optimum cost moves from 0.75 to 1.34 on a finer mesh.

garment-nesting8 tests

How much cloth does marker making waste, and do annealing and exact methods beat greedy nesting?

Marker making as strip packing: on 20 random 8-box markers, shelf heuristics leave 17–20% extra length vs the exact optimum, annealing 0.5%; on two stylised garments, polygon nesting beats box packing at equal budget. Stylised; no seam allowance or multi-ply.

Abstract Code →

Marker making as strip packing. On 20 random 8-box markers an exact MILP proves optimality on 19; shelf heuristics (NFDH, FFDH) are on average 20% and 17% longer than optimal, bottom-left 7.3%, and simulated annealing over placement order 0.5%. On two stylised garments (a shirt and a four-gore skirt, no seam allowance, one ply) true-polygon nesting with 180° turns beats bounding-box packing at the same annealing budget in every case, by about 5–9% for the shirt and 9–43% for the skirt. Stylised: the shapes are invented, polygon results have no exact reference, and the raster is conservative.

garment-markercost6 tests

What do seam allowance and mixed sizes do to marker efficiency, and what does that do to a garment's cloth cost?

A 1 cm seam allowance cut the stylised shirt's marker efficiency from 0.69 to 0.63 and the skirt's from 0.71 to 0.51; mixing three sizes in one marker shortened it 9%; swapped into the cost model, trench cloth rises from $26 to $33–41 at $7/m². Stylised; sensitivity, not a coat measurement.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to the nesting and cost-teardown projects. Adding a 1 cm seam allowance to stylised pieces lowered marker efficiency from 0.69 to 0.63 for a shirt and from 0.71 to 0.51 for a four-gore skirt (the skirt mostly loses its interlocking gores); nesting three shirt sizes in one marker was 9% shorter than three separate markers. Swapping the measured efficiencies into the teardown formula moves a $7/m2 trench’s cloth cost from $26 (assumed 0.80) to $33–41. Stylised: invented outlines, one ply, small annealing budget (differences of a few cm are noise), and the coats were not nested, so the cost step is a sensitivity, not a measurement.

garment-cutplan7 tests

How much cloth does a cutting plan save by mixing sizes in one marker, and is the saving real?

Cutting-order planning for a 3-size stylised shirt: laying several garments per marker saves 9–11% of cloth over one per marker; mixing sizes adds 0.4–3.7% in sample, but re-nesting the chosen markers with fresh seeds leaves +0.09%, so it is within nesting noise. Stylised; invented shapes.

Abstract Code →

Cutting-order planning as an exact integer program (marker mixes and plies) over 34 nested markers of a stylised three-size shirt. Laying several garments per marker saves 9–11% of cloth against one garment per marker on 20 random orders. Mixing sizes adds a further 0.4–3.7% in sample, but re-nesting the markers the plan picked with fresh seeds leaves a +0.09% difference: the gain is within annealing noise (about 5%) and partly selection of luckily short markers. Stylised: invented shirt, linear size grading, small annealing budget, mixes of at most four garments, free setup cost.

garment-nestcost6 tests

How far is a fixed 0.80 marker efficiency from a nested coat, and what does the difference do to the cost model?

Nesting a stylised coat's 10 shell and 5 lining pieces with a 1.5 cm seam allowance gives marker efficiencies of 0.68–0.73 (shell) and 0.59–0.68 (lining) at three cloth widths, below the fixed 0.80 in garment-teardown; its trench FOB moves +9% to +15% at the teardown's own areas. Stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to the nesting and cost-teardown projects (stylised, preliminary). A coat drawn as 10 shell and 5 lining polygons, grown by a 1.5 cm seam allowance and nested by annealing at cloth widths of 110, 140 and 150 cm, gives marker efficiencies of 0.68–0.73 for the shell and 0.59–0.68 for the lining, against the fixed 0.80 assumed earlier (0.77–0.82 without allowance). Transplanted into the teardown trench model, the efficiency alone raises factory cost by about $20–30; the larger uncertainty is the pattern area, which these invented pieces do not settle. One ply, one size, my own shapes, no exact reference.

garment-sizeset6 tests

How many clothing sizes does it take to fit a population, and does a regular S-M-L grid waste them?

How many sizes fit a population? On a stylised synthetic bust/hip population (+-4 cm), an exact size run beats a regular grid by 12 to 25 points at correlation 0.9 but not on fresh people at correlation 0; greedy is within 3.7 points of optimal (stylised, preliminary).

Abstract Code →

Stylised and preliminary: a synthetic bust and hip population (assumed means 95 and 100 cm, sd 8 cm, no survey data) with a fit tolerance of ±4 cm. Choosing k sizes to fit the most people is maximum coverage; solved exactly (integer program), greedily and as a regular grid on 300 people, 3 seeds. At bust–hip correlation 0.9, exact sizes fit 12–25 points more people than the best grid and 6 sizes reach 80%; greedy is within 3.7 points of exact. At correlation 0 the gap is small, and on 20,000 fresh people the exact set is no better than the grid, so the optimiser overfits small samples. Limits: Gaussian two-measurement population, pass/fail box fit, no cost of extra sizes.

garment-sizestretch5 tests

How many clothing sizes does a stretch fabric save?

How many sizes does a stretch fabric save? On a stylised synthetic bust/hip population, 10% usable stretch cuts the sizes needed for 80% fit from 6 to more than 8 down to 2 or 3; an idealised upper bound (preliminary).

Abstract Code →

Stylised and preliminary: follow-up to the size-set project on a synthetic bust and hip population (assumed means 95 and 100 cm, sd 8 cm, no survey data). A body fits a garment if it is at most 8 cm smaller and no more than stretch larger than the nominal size, in both measurements; the best k sizes are found exactly (integer program). Sizes needed to fit 80% fall from 6 to more than 8 with no stretch to 2–3 at 10% and 1 at 20%, and the loss on fresh people shrinks too. The stretch model is idealised: usable stretch is far below rated stretch, so these are upper bounds.

garment-thermal11 tests

How much comfort can an infrared-transparent or gating textile buy, and which fabric properties matter?

Fanger/ISO PMV and a two-node model extended with fabric infrared transmittance, emissivity and solar absorptance: indoors, transmittance 0→0.8 is worth ~2.4 °C of comfort at 28 °C; in sun, absorptance dominates. Stylised; assumed fabric properties, no reference for the optical extension.

Abstract Code →

A Fanger/ISO 7730 PMV model and a Gagge-style two-node model extended with fabric infrared emissivity and transmittance, solar absorptance and vapour permeability. The no-optics PMV matches an open-source ISO implementation to 0.006 over 144 cases. Indoors without sun, infrared transmittance (0 to 0.8) is worth about 2.4 °C of comfort at 28 °C, more than cutting insulation from 0.7 to 0.3 clo (1.8 °C), but makes a 16 °C room feel 7.3 °C colder; in sun, solar absorptance (7.7 °C span) dominates the infrared properties. Stylised: assumed fabric properties, a parallel-path radiation model with no reference data, and recalled two-node constants.

garment-twonodecheck3 tests

How far is the repository's two-node thermal model from an open-source implementation of the Gagge model?

Cross-checks garment-thermal's two-node model against pythermalcomfort over 108 conditions: core temperature within 0.25 °C, skin temperature mean 0.6 °C (up to 2.1 °C) apart; a comparison of implementations, not of people.

Abstract Code →

Runs the two-node model from the thermal-comfort project against pythermalcomfort over 108 conditions (18–36 °C, 30–80% humidity, 1–2 met, 0.3–1 clo). Core temperature agrees within 0.25 °C everywhere; skin temperature differs by 0.58 °C on average and up to 2.1 °C, mostly in cool air; evaporative loss differs by up to 14 W/m2 in hot humid air. The direction of change with insulation and humidity agrees in 23 of 24 cases. This compares two implementations, not either against people; causes of the skin-temperature gap are untested and the optical extension is not covered.

garment-twonodealign3 tests

Which design choices explain the gap between the repository's two-node model and an open-source Gagge implementation?

Switches nine design choices one at a time between garment-thermal's two-node model and pythermalcomfort's: variable skin mass fraction, convection coefficient and vasodilation gain explain most of the 0.58 °C skin-temperature gap; a comparison of implementations, not of people.

Abstract Code →

Rebuilds the two-node model with nine switchable choices (body area, constants, convection, clothing radiation, skin mass fraction, vasodilation gain, sweat caps, update order, step count), each set to the repository's version or to the pythermalcomfort version read from its source. With all nine set to the reference's, the model matches it to 0.008 in every output over 108 conditions. Switching one at a time, the skin-temperature gap (mean 0.58 °C) falls most with the variable skin mass fraction (to 0.36), the convection coefficient (0.43) and the vasodilation gain (0.44); body area, constants, update order and step count each change it by under 0.01 °C. A comparison of two implementations, not of either against people; the effects interact, so the attribution depends on the order.

garment-twonodeoptics4 tests

Do the fabric-optics conclusions of the thermal-comfort model survive a different two-node implementation?

Adds garment-thermal's fabric optics (infrared transmittance, emissivity, solar absorptance) to the switchable two-node model and re-runs the comparisons under pythermalcomfort's choices: property rankings agree in all four scenarios, sizes within 3% at 28 °C but up to ~2× apart in cool air and in sun; a comparison of implementations, not of people.

Abstract Code →

Adds infrared transmittance, outer emissivity, solar absorptance, radiant temperature and solar load to the switchable two-node model and compares each property’s effect under the repository’s design choices and under those of pythermalcomfort. Over four stylised scenarios the properties rank identically by dry-heat-loss effect; sizes agree within 3% in a 28 °C room but differ by up to about 2× in cool air (traced mostly to the variable skin mass fraction) and in sun (convection coefficient); the one sign change is under 0.1 °C. The reference has no optics, so its optical terms are my own linearised construction without an external check. A comparison of implementations, not of people or measured fabrics.

garment-twonodesteady4 tests

Do the fabric-optics effects on thermal comfort change once the two-node model reaches steady state?

The fabric-optics comparison of garment-twonodeoptics run to steady state instead of one hour: the cool-room disagreement between design choices mostly vanishes (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Re-runs the switchable two-node comparison of fabric optics (infrared transmittance, emissivity, solar absorptance, insulation) for 24 h of model time instead of one hour (stylised, preliminary). In the 28 C room, with hot walls and in sun the one-hour effects are already steady. In the 16 C room the one-hour disagreement between the repository’s design choices and those of pythermalcomfort (ratio 1.9–2.7) shrinks to 0.89–0.98 at steady state, so it was mostly a transient-speed difference. A model fixed point, not a claim about people; no fabric or person was measured.

garment-twonodegate4 tests

Do the closed and open bounds of an infrared-gating textile survive other two-node design choices and steady state?

The closed-to-open bounds of an infrared-gating textile from garment-thermal hold under both two-node choice sets and at steady state: opening the gate cools skin by 0.20–0.25 C at 31 C and keeps it 1.4–1.5 C cooler at 16 C; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Re-runs the two fixed states of a gated textile (infrared transmittance 0.15 closed, 0.8 open) from an earlier model in the switchable two-node comparison, under two sets of design choices and at 3 h and steady state (stylised, preliminary). Opening the gate lowers skin temperature by 0.20–0.25 C in a 31 C room and 1.4–1.5 C in a 16 C room, and moves 5.5–6.2 W/m2 from evaporation to dry loss at 31 C; the choice sets differ by about 0.05 C there. Limits: two fixed states with no switching dynamics, evaporative heat loss rather than sweat mass, no validation against people.

garment-twonodeswitch5 tests

What does a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile do that its fixed closed and open states do not?

A skin-temperature-triggered infrared-gating textile with hysteresis and actuation lag settles to a fixed closed or open state under constant rooms (no chatter, lag only delays the start); gains need changing conditions; stylised, preliminary, mostly null.

Abstract Code →

Adds a skin-temperature-triggered gate (hysteresis band, first-order actuation lag) to the switchable two-node comfort model (stylised, preliminary). In constant 31, 24 and 16 C rooms over 3 h the gate settles into one of the two fixed states with at most one change, so it cannot beat the best fixed state; a 10 min lag only delays the start (open 94% vs 98% of minutes at 31 C). Threshold placement matters more: a 32–35 C band opens under one set of design choices and never under the other. A mostly null result; it needs changing conditions to show value. No fabric or person was measured.

garment-twonodestep4 tests

When the room temperature steps, does a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile beat its fixed states and approach an oracle?

Under a single step in room temperature, a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile beats both fixed states after a step up and tracks an oracle schedule closely (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodeswitch. One step in room temperature at minute 90 of 180 in the switchable two-node model, scored by mean |skin temperature − 33.7 C| (a proxy, not a comfort index). After a step to a hotter room the gate beats both fixed states and lies within about 0.02within about 0.02–0.07 C of an oraclenbsp;C of an oracle that knows the schedule; after a step to a cooler room it gains little, and a 10 min actuation lag can make it worse than staying closed. Transmittances are assumptions; no fabric or person was measured.

garment-twonodemet4 tests

When the metabolic rate steps from rest to walking, does a thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile beat its fixed states?

A step in metabolic rate (rest to walking) instead of room temperature for the thermostat infrared-gating textile: at 24 C the gate beats both fixed states under one choice set and ties fixed closed under the other, at 28 C staying open is as good as any policy, and a 10 min lag erases the gain after walking stops; stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodestep. One step in metabolic rate (1 to 2 met, or back) at minute 90 of 180 in the switchable two-node model, scored by mean |skin temperature − 33.7 °C|. In a 20 °C room the gate never opens; at 24 °C it beats both fixed states under this repository’s choice set and ties fixed closed under the reference’s; at 28 °C staying open is as good as any policy; after walking stops a 10 min actuation lag erases most of the gate’s gain. Bands were not tuned and results depend on the choice set. Not a claim about any real textile.

garment-twonodeheld4 tests

If a thermostat infrared-gating band is tuned on some rooms, does it still help in rooms it never saw?

Tuning the thermostat infrared-gating band on training rooms and testing on held-out rooms: a narrow band just below 33.7 C carries over (about 0.01 to 0.06 C better than the untuned band) but chatters, up to 24 switches in 180 min (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodemet. A skin-temperature gate band is tuned by exhaustive grid search on rest-to-walk and walk-to-rest steps in 22, 24 and 26 C rooms, then scored unchanged on held-out rooms (23, 25, 20 and 28 C). The tuned band (a narrow 33.6–33.7 C) beats the untuned 33.2–34.2 C band and both fixed states on both held-out sets under both choice sets, by 0.01 to 0.06 C against the untuned band. It also beats the four-schedule oracle on training scenarios, because the oracle is restricted, and it chatters (up to 24 switches in 180 min) with instant, free switching, so the gain may not survive actuation lag or cost. Six training and eight held-out scenarios from one model; no real fabric or person.

garment-twonodelag5 tests

Does a tuned infrared-gating thermostat survive an actuation lag and a cost per switch?

Retuning the thermostat infrared-gating band with an actuation lag (0 to 10 min) and a cost per switch: lag cuts the gain over never switching from 0.23 to 0.15 C (stylised), a switch penalty widens the band and stops the chatter, and under one choice set the tuned band can lose to the untuned one.

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodeheld. The skin-temperature gate band is retuned by exhaustive grid search for each actuation lag (0, 2, 5, 10 min) and each cost per switch (0, 0.01, 0.03 C), then scored on held-out rooms. A 10 min lag cuts the tuned gate’s gain over never switching from 0.23 to 0.15 C (“between” rooms, this repository’s choice set). A switch penalty widens the band and removes the chatter. The tuned band is not always better: under the reference choice set it loses to the untuned band by up to 0.035 C in 3 of 24 cells, and once to never switching (0.052 C). Six training and eight held-out scenarios, assumed lags and penalties, one model; no real fabric or person.

garment-twonodeprop5 tests

Does a proportional infrared-gating textile beat the on/off thermostat gate?

A proportional infrared-gating transmittance against the tuned on/off thermostat gate: a negative result, within 0.010 C in every cell because the tuned ramp collapses to nearly on/off, and a softer ramp costs 0.02 to 0.07 C (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary, negative follow-up to garment-twonodelag. A transmittance that ramps linearly with skin temperature is tuned by exhaustive search (72 bands) for each actuation lag (0 to 10 min) and scored on held-out rooms against the tuned on/off gate. Proportional wins in 5 of 16 cells and every difference is within 0.010 C: the search picks bands only 0.1 to 0.2 C wide, i.e. nearly on/off. Forcing a softer ramp (at least 1.4 C wide) costs 0.02 to 0.07 C. Switching is free in this run, so a switch penalty could change the answer. Six training and eight held-out scenarios; no real fabric or person.

garment-twonodepen5 tests

At what switching penalty does a proportional infrared gate beat the on/off thermostat gate?

Prices actuation in equal units (one full close-open swing = 1) and asks when a proportional infrared gate beats the on/off gate: it wins in 52 of 80 held-out cells, by tenths of a degree at most, and the gain reverses in the outside rooms at the highest penalty (stylised, preliminary).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodeprop. Both gates are retuned on training rooms for each actuation lag and a per-swing penalty (one full close-to-open swing = 1 for either gate; the penalty scale is an assumption), then scored on held-out rooms. The proportional gate has the lower cost in 52 of 80 cells, by at most 0.096 C on a proxy of order 0.3–1.5 C; at the highest penalty the gain holds in the between rooms (8 of 8) but mostly reverses in the outside rooms (2 of 8). Simulated comfort, not a claim about any real garment.

garment-twonodewide4 tests

Is the outside-room reversal of the proportional infrared gate a training-range artefact?

Retunes both infrared gates on a wider set of rooms: the proportional gate's outside-room reversal is partly a training-range artefact

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodepen. Both gates are retuned on a wider set of rooms (20–28 C instead of 22–26 C) and scored on rooms held out of both. At the highest penalty, proportional wins 7 of 8 cases at 21 and 27 C when tuned wide, against 4 of 8 when tuned narrow, so the reversal is partly an artefact of the training range. At 18 and 30 C the gates differ by at most 0.007 C, which this model cannot resolve. Two penalties only; simulated comfort, not a claim about any real garment.

garment-twonodeperson4 tests

Does an infrared-gating band tuned for one person and clothing level still work for other clothing and body sizes?

Tunes both infrared gates on one person and clothing level and scores them on other clothing and body sizes; clothing matters, body size barely does

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodewide. Both gates are tuned on one person (0.5 clo, 70 kg) and scored unchanged on other clothing levels and body sizes. Body size barely matters (retuning gains at most 0.002 C), clothing does: retuning an on/off band for 1.2 clo gains up to 0.375 C, while the proportional gate's gap stays at most 0.075 C. Proportional wins every cell except three at 0.3 clo and penalty 0.1. Mass and height enter the model only through body area and heat capacity; simulated comfort, not a claim about any real garment.

garment-twonodeopt4 tests

How far is the thermostat-driven infrared-gating textile from the best possible switching schedule when the room temperature steps?

A grid search for the best open/closed switching schedule under a room-temperature step shows one toggle suffices and the thermostat gate sits within 0.02 °C of it after a step up, but up to 0.11 °C after a step down (stylised).

Abstract Code →

A stylised, preliminary follow-up to garment-twonodestep. Exhaustive search over open/closed schedules (at most 3 toggles on a 10 min grid, instant actuation) in the switchable two-node model, scored by mean |skin temperature − 33.7 C| (a proxy, not a comfort index). One toggle is enough (more improve the score by at most 0.001 C). The best toggle is not always at the step: it is early or late after a step down. The gate is within 0.02 C of the optimum after a step up but 0.06–0.11 C away after a step down (0.18 with 10 min lag in one case). One person, two assumed transmittances, a coarse grid; not a claim about any real garment.

garment-comfortcost7 tests

What does a degree of comfort cost in fabric?

Joins garment-thermal comfort shifts to garment-teardown costs: only one fabric treatment helps in each scenario, levers combine sub-additively, and at assumed premiums a degree costs $0.5 to $19 on a replica trench but $3 to $114 on a designer one. Stylised; premiums assumed.

Abstract Code →

Joins the thermal comfort model to the garment cost chain for five fabric levers (infrared transmittance, low emissivity, white, thinner, thicker cloth). Levers combine sub-additively (infrared-transparent plus thin: +2.58 °C jointly, +3.25 summed), and in each scenario only one treatment helps, so a price premium sets cost, not ranking. At assumed premiums the treatments cost $0.5 to $19 per °C on a $20–50 replica trench and $3 to $114 on a designer one, because the retail chain multiplies the premium about 6×. Stylised: every premium and the thickness pricing are assumed, not quoted, and the comfort model has no reference for its optical extension.

garment-wearmix7 tests

Does a fabric lever still pay once you weight it by where the garment is worn?

Weights garment-comfortcost's fabric levers by wearing time and adds a gated infrared lever: a fixed infrared-transparent shell pays only with a warm-room majority (above 75.5% of time against the cool room), white never harms, and the gate is chosen only when it costs about the fixed shell's premium or less. Stylised; premiums and wearing shares assumed.

Abstract Code →

Weights the comfort benefit of fabric levers by wearing time across a warm room, sunny outdoors and a cool room, and adds an idealised gated infrared lever. A fixed infrared-transparent shell has positive expected benefit only if the warm room takes more than 75.5% of wearing time (against the cool room); white never harms and has the best benefit per dollar in all four mixes tried. Across 66 wearing mixes the best garment changes with the mix, and the gate is chosen in 65 of 66 mixes at the fixed shell's premium but in 18 of 66 at twice it and none at four times. Stylised: premiums, gate cost and wearing shares are assumed, and the gate is an upper bound.

garment-learning9 tests

How many home-sewn coats before the labour cost per coat settles?

How many home-sewn replica coats until labour cost settles? On a Wright learning curve (assumed first coat 4× an experienced operator, rate 0.85) it takes 20 coats to get within 2× of factory time; the first coat stays under $50 only if your time is valued at ≤$1.45/h. Learning parameters assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Applies a Wright learning curve (unit time falls by a fixed share per doubling of output) to the replica trench coat of garment-teardown ($43 materials, 76 experienced-operator minutes). With an assumed first coat 4× experienced time and an 85% rate it takes 20 coats to get within 2× of experienced time; with 8× and 90% it takes about 9,100, so the answer is set by the two assumed parameters. The first coat stays under $50 only if the sewer’s time is valued at $1.45/h or less ($4.28/h for the 100th). In a factory run the learning surcharge is under 8% after 200 coats. Stylised: learning rates are assumed, not measured.

garment-costperwear7 tests

How much longer must a $2,850 coat last to beat a $56 replica on cost per wear?

How much longer must a $2,850 coat last than a $56 replica to win on cost per wear? About 46× with no resale and equal care; needs a median life near 3,100 wears to win half the time. Lifetimes, care and resale assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Combines the modelled replica costs and reported prices of garment-teardown with an assumed durability layer. With no resale and equal care the $2,850 trench must outlast a $56 replica by about 46× (52× for the $3,850 coat). With lognormal lifetimes (log-sd 0.5) and a 60-wear replica, the designer coat needs a median life near 3,100 wears to win half the time and wins about 6% of the time at 1,000; designer care of $1 per wear pushes the needed median to about 73,000. Lifetimes, care and resale are all assumed, not measured. Stylised.

garment-wearpair5 tests

Is a second garment better than a dearer single one?

Is a second garment better than a dearer single one? A shell-and-layer pair beats the best single garment at the same budget in 54 of 66 wearing mixes at $50 and $100 (mean +0.49 C and +1.02 C) once thin cloth is removed; the apparent $20 gain is an artefact of thin cloth's negative assumed cost. Stylised; premiums and wearing shares assumed.

Abstract Code →

Lets the wearer own two garments (a shell and a layer) and wear whichever is most comfortable in each of three scenarios, searching all lever pairs under one total added-retail budget on the replica trench. With thin cloth allowed the pair beats the best single garment in 58 of 66 wearing mixes at $50, but the apparent $20 gain is an artefact: thin cloth has a negative assumed cost that funds the second garment. With thin cloth removed the gain is 0 at $20, +0.49 °C (54 of 66 mixes) at $50 and +1.02 °C at $100, usually a warm-weather infrared-transparent shell plus a cold-weather thick low-emissivity coat. Stylised: premiums, wearing shares and fabric properties are assumed, garments are not stacked, and no real garment was measured.

garment-wearwrong6 tests

How often can a wearer pick the wrong garment before a second garment stops paying?

How often can a wearer pick the wrong garment before a second garment stops paying? With random wrong picks the pair's edge over one garment holds (+0.57 C at 30% error, $100); if every mistake is the worst option it falls from +0.55 to +0.09 C (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Re-runs the two-garment wardrobe search of garment-wearpair with a wearer who picks a wrong option in a share e of scenarios, re-optimising each purchase at each e (replica trench, 66 wearing mixes, thin cloth removed). If a wrong pick is a random wrong option the pair’s edge holds (+0.55 C at e = 0, +0.57 C at 0.3, $100 budget), because errors hurt a single garment’s all-or-nothing choice more than an overlapping pair. If every mistake is the worst owned option the $100 edge falls to +0.09 C at e = 0.3, with a break-even e of median 0.72 and as low as 0.04. At $50 the edge is negligible either way. Stylised: error rates and premiums are assumed, no wearer behaviour was observed, and the conclusion flips between the two error models.

garment-optics8 tests

How much conductive yarn does an RF-shielding fabric need, and how fast does breakage ruin it?

RF-shielding weave model: 54–87 dB sheet shielding but the aperture bound caps it (36 dB at 2.4 GHz for 1 mm pitch, ~15 dB at 28 GHz); yarn breakage tracks 1/(1−2f) and conduction fails near 50% broken. Stylised; plane wave, ideal crossings, RF part only.

Abstract Code →

A thin-sheet shielding model of a conductive square weave (sheet resistance, aperture bound, metal mass) plus a Monte Carlo of random yarn breakage. Every design tried has a sheet shielding of 54–87 dB, but the aperture bound limits it: 36 dB at 2.4 GHz for a 1 mm pitch, about 15 dB at 28 GHz. Breakage raises resistance as the effective-medium estimate 1/(1−2f) up to 30% broken segments and the weave stops conducting near 50% (bond percolation). Stylised: plane wave, ideal crossings, recalled constants, no measurement; covers only the RF part of the optics milestone.

garment-contactres6 tests

Does contact resistance at yarn crossings matter for an RF-shielding fabric?

Contact resistance at yarn crossings in the RF-shielding weave: no effect on an intact fabric, but with 20% of yarns broken a contact equal to one segment raises sheet resistance 22% and ten segments 2.3×. Stylised; contact values are a sweep, not measured.

Abstract Code →

A two-layer resistor network of a conductive weave: warp and weft touch only through a contact resistor at each crossing, and yarn segments break at random. On an intact fabric the contacts carry no current, so they have no effect at all. Once yarns break they carry the bypass currents: with 20% of segments broken, the median sheet resistance is 1.74 segment-resistances with perfect contacts, 2.11 with contacts equal to one segment, 4.07 at ten and 16.7 at a hundred. For a stylised stainless weave that is 59.6 dB against 52.3 dB at ten segments (thin-sheet only, aperture limit excluded). Stylised: contact values are a sweep, not measurements; one lattice size, 20 draws, independent breaks.

garment-flexdamage9 tests

Does it matter where an RF-shielding fabric is damaged, and whether worn contacts go with the breaks?

Correlated damage in the RF-shielding weave: worn contacts next to breaks (rc×10) raise the median sheet resistance at 20% broken from 2.05 to 3.03 segments; a fold band across the current direction at the same mean breakage leaves 57 of 60 draws open, while a fold along it helps. Stylised; wear multiplier is a sweep, not measured.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to the contact-resistance model, on a 24×24 conductive weave with 60 draws per cell and bootstrap intervals. When contacts next to a broken yarn are worn (contact resistance ×k), the median sheet resistance at 20% broken and a base contact of one segment rises from 2.05 segment-resistances (k = 1) to 3.03 (k = 10). Clustering matters more: a fold band across the current that holds the mean break fraction fixed but breaks 4× as often inside the band leaves the weave open in 57 of 60 draws at 20% broken, while the same band along the current direction lowers the resistance to 1.43. Stylised: square lattice, one lattice size, a rule-of-thumb wear multiplier rather than a measured one, no flexing physics, and no measurement.

garment-thincolor8 tests

How thin must a coating be to colour a fibre without dye, and how fragile is that colour?

Thin-film transfer-matrix structural colour on a nylon-like substrate: 6-pair stacks reach 99% reflectance with 2–3 g/m² of oxide but blue-shift 48 ΔE by 60° incidence, and 10% layer-thickness error moves hue by ΔE≈10. Stylised; flat substrate, no dispersion.

Abstract Code →

A transfer-matrix model of dielectric quarter-wave stacks on a flat nylon-like substrate, with colour computed under an equal-energy illuminant. Six-pair stacks reach 99% reflectance with 2–3 g/m2 of oxide and saturated colour, but the peak blue-shifts from 620 to 540 nm by 60° incidence (ΔE76 48), and 10% layer-thickness error moves hue by ΔE≈10 while roughly preserving chroma. Stylised: flat substrate, constant indices, no fibre scattering.

garment-stackopt5 tests

Can an optimiser cut the angle shift of a structural-colour coating, and what does it give up?

Optimising 8-layer thin-film stacks for low angle shift at fixed colour: Nelder–Mead restarts cut mean ΔE76 shift from 12.4 to 1.4 (red) and 25.9 to 5.6 (blue) at 3000 evaluations, beating random search and differential evolution, at the cost of chroma and ~1.8–2.5× oxide mass. Stylised; flat substrate, no tolerance.

Abstract Code →

Eight-layer thin-film stacks on a flat nylon-like substrate, optimised to minimise the colour shift between 0 and 15–45° incidence while keeping chroma C* ≥ 40 and hue near a quarter-wave target. At an equal budget of 3000 evaluations (10 seeds), Nelder–Mead with restarts cuts the median mean ΔE76 shift from 12.4 to 1.4 (red target) and from 25.9 to 5.6 (blue), beating random search and differential evolution, but chroma falls toward the floor and oxide mass rises about 1.8–2.5×. Stylised: flat substrate, three sample angles, recalled indices, no fabrication tolerance; no LLM involved.

garment-stackrobust5 tests

Does an angle-stable structural-colour stack survive layer-thickness error?

Thickness-error robustness of the garment-stackopt angle-stable stacks: the nominal optimum (J 1.4) degrades to 24.9 at 3% layer error and loses to the quarter-wave stack; a sampled robust objective at equal cost recovers part of it (red, 3%: 11.7 vs 13.2 quarter-wave) but not colour drift. Stylised; independent Gaussian errors, 10 seeds.

Abstract Code →

The 8-layer stacks optimised in garment-stackopt are fabricated virtually with independent Gaussian thickness error (3 and 5%) and scored on 200 held-out draws. The nominal optimum (angle shift 1.4 ΔE76) degrades to a mean cost of 24.9 at 3% error, worse than the plain quarter-wave stack (13.2), and only about half of draws keep an acceptable colour. A robust objective averaged over six error draws, at equal total cost, recovers part of this (red target, 3%: 11.7 against 13.2) but not the colour drift, and at 5% error or the blue target the quarter-wave stack is hard to beat. Stylised: flat substrate, no dispersion, uncorrelated errors, 10 seeds, no significance tests, two optimisers.

garment-stackcvar5 tests

Does a tail-risk objective, or a correlated-error model, rescue the angle-stable structural-colour stack?

Negative follow-up to garment-stackrobust: a CVaR (worst-quarter) training objective and a correlated rate-drift error model do not rescue the optimised angle-stable stacks; none beats the quarter-wave stack (red, iid error: mean J 14.1 vs best optimised 16.5). CVaR trims Nelder-Mead's 90th-percentile cost (47.1 to 43.1) at the price of the mean. Stylised; no coating measured.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to garment-stackrobust. The 8-layer stacks are trained on a CVaR objective (mean of the worst quarter of 8 sampled thickness errors) or on errors with a shared rate-drift component (ρ = 0.5), then cross-evaluated on 200 held-out draws under both error models (5% error, 8 seeds, 3000 evaluations). Negative result: no optimised design beats the plain quarter-wave stack (red, independent error: mean cost 14.1 against 16.5 for the best optimised one). CVaR trims Nelder–Mead's 90th-percentile cost (47.1 to 43.1) while raising its mean, and correlated-error training did worse. Stylised thin-film model; nothing was coated or measured.

garment-stackpareto4 tests

How much angle shift can a structural-colour coating shed at a given chroma and oxide mass?

Shift against chroma and oxide mass for the garment-stackopt 8-layer coating: on a grid of chroma floors and mass caps, the best red-target shift is 0.68 at a 4.0 g/m² cap but 2.71 at 3.0 and no feasible run at 2.0 or below (floor C* 40); mass binds before chroma. Stylised; 5 seeds per cell, one optimiser.

Abstract Code →

The 8-layer stacks of garment-stackopt re-optimised on a grid of chroma floors and oxide-mass caps (Nelder–Mead restarts, 3000 calls, 5 seeds per cell). For the red target at a chroma floor of C* 40 the best mean angle shift is 0.68 ΔE76 at a 4.0 g/m2 cap, 2.71 at 3.0, and no run is feasible at 2.0 or below; raising the floor to 60 costs more (2.84 at a 4.0 cap). Mass binds before chroma. Stylised: flat substrate, three sample angles, untuned penalties, a coarse grid and a single optimiser, so cell values are noisy and the front is not smooth.

garment-stacklayers4 tests

Does adding layers cut the angle shift of a structural-colour coating at fixed chroma and oxide mass?

Layer-count sweep (2 to 12) of the constrained structural-colour coating: six to ten layers reach best angle shifts under 1 dE at C* 40 and 4 g/m2 where 2 and 4 layers stay near 3.4, but 12 layers did not search well at the same budget (stylised, 8 seeds).

Abstract Code →

The constrained problem of garment-stackpareto with the layer count varied from 2 to 12 (Nelder–Mead restarts, 3000 calls, 8 seeds per cell). For the red target at C* ≥ 40 and 4 g/m2, 2 and 4 layers reach a best mean ΔE of about 3.4, while 6, 8 and 10 layers reach 0.5–0.8; medians are several times higher, so the ranking among 6–10 is within noise. At 12 layers few runs were feasible, probably a search limit at equal budget rather than a property of the stack. Stylised: flat substrate, three angles, no thickness tolerance; no coating was made.

garment-assist7 tests

Does an assistive garment pay for its own mass?

One-joint ankle exosuit model: active assist cuts modelled whole-body cost 3–14% (gain 0.1–0.5) but a few kg of garment mass erases it; break-even mass ∝ 1/(mass sensitivity). Stylised; assumed constants, no OpenSim/MyoSuite.

Abstract Code →

A one-joint ankle model of an exosuit-style garment: a suit adding a fraction of the biological push-off torque cuts modelled whole-body metabolic cost by 3.1, 8.8 and 14.1% at gains 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5, but a delay of 0.25 of the gait cycle removes the benefit and a stiff passive spring raises ankle cost 17%. Added mass erases the saving at 8.9 kg if each kg costs 1% of whole-body power and at 1.8 kg if it costs 5%; the break-even scales as 1/sensitivity, a number the project does not supply. Stylised: lumped muscle, prescribed gait, assumed constants; not OpenSim or MyoSuite.

garment-assistpower5 tests

Is it the motor or the battery that decides whether an exosuit pays for its own mass?

Adds a motor and battery mass model to the ankle exosuit: at an assumed 8 N m/kg the motor (about 8 kg) makes a gain-0.3 suit raise cost 0.2–1.9%; the sign flips between 8 and 20 N m/kg, battery hours matter little. Stylised; assumed constants.

Abstract Code →

Extends the ankle exosuit model with a power train: motor mass from peak torque and a torque density, battery mass from electrical energy and hours of use, and the resulting mass fed back into metabolic cost. With an assumed 8 N m/kg motor the gain-0.3 suit weighs about 9 kg, 8.4 of it motor, and raises whole-body cost 0.2–1.9%; the sign flips between 8 and 20 N m/kg, while eight hours of battery add under 2 kg. Stylised: every power-train constant is assumed, not sourced.

garment-assistloc5 tests

Does it pay to move an exosuit's motor and battery from the shank to the waist?

Moves the exosuit's motor and battery from shank to waist: the waist layout wins once a shank kg costs more than 1.03–1.39× a waist kg (assumed ratio, swept); at ratio 3 and 8 N m/kg shank +20.7% vs waist +3.3%. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Extends the exosuit power-train model with where the mass sits: a kg at the shank costs an assumed multiple of a kg at the waist, and a waist layout pays a Bowden-cable loss (efficiency 0.6–1.0) and keeps 0.3 kg of cable at the ankle. At gain 0.3 with a 4 h battery the waist layout wins once the shank penalty exceeds 1.03–1.39× the waist one; at ratio 3 and 8 N m/kg the shank suit is +20.7% against +3.3% for the waist suit. The ratio is assumed, not sourced, so the result is the break-even, not a prediction. Stylised.

garment-bowdenbend5 tests

How much cable bend can a waist-mounted exosuit power train tolerate before the shank layout wins?

Replaces the assumed Bowden efficiency with the capstan law exp(-mu*theta): at ratio 3 and mu 0.1 the waist layout beats the shank layout until the cable bends through about 31 rad, so friction loss alone does not decide the layout (hysteresis not modelled). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Replaces the assumed Bowden-cable efficiency in the shank-versus-waist model with the capstan law exp(−μθ) for friction μ and total bend θ. At gain 0.3, a 4 h battery, 8 N m/kg and an assumed penalty ratio of 3, the waist layout stays ahead until about 31 rad of bend at μ = 0.1 (about 15 rad at 0.2), far beyond a hip-to-ankle route, so energy lost to friction does not decide the layout. Hysteresis, backlash and pretension are not modelled, and μ and the ratio are assumed. Stylised.

garment-protective8 tests

What would a suit-like protective garment weigh and cost, and what limits it?
