With a 0.05 s forward lead the push on a blocked tip is 20 N·s/m × speed, so peak lip force tracks approach speed (1.0 N at 0.05 m/s, 4.0 N at 0.20). A camera lowers the share of trials that touch the lips (0.40 against 0.72 at 30 mm sway) without lowering the peak, and its advantage fades with latency (touch share 0.07 at no delay, 0.71 at 0.4 s). A 1 N force cap trims the worst peak but not the share of comfortable feeds. Stylised: all constants are assumed, the peak-force result is largely an identity of the chosen controller, and no human model or Assistive Gym was used.

osrobot-dof7 tests

Does a spoon-feeding arm need more than two joints? Tip mass, lip force and servo cost of 2 to 6 joint arms

Does a spoon-feeding arm need more than two joints? From 2 to 6 joints the tip mass moves only 0.63 to 0.50 kg and lip force not clearly at all, while servo cost triples (stylised; extends osrobot-assist).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib planar model gives 2 to 6 joint feeding arms an operational-space tip mass (servo, link and spoon masses plus each servo's rotor inertia reflected through a 345:1 gearbox) and feeds it to osrobot-assist's lip-contact trials (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, camera arm). The tip mass falls only from 0.63 to 0.50 kg from 2 to 6 joints; the worst peak lip force is identical (2.0 N at 0.10 m/s, 4.0 N at 0.20) and the safe share at 0.20 m/s is 0.60 to 0.65, within sampling error. Servo cost alone triples, from $52–98 to $156–295 (two retailers' listings, 2026-10-19). Most of the mass is the geared-up rotor. Stylised: planar, one pose, position-only task, assumed constants, so the real reasons for more joints (spoon orientation, 3-D motion) are not tested.

osrobot-mjfeed6 tests

Does the stylised feeding-arm lip-force result survive real contact physics? osrobot-assist re-run in MuJoCo

Does the stylised feeding-arm lip-force result survive MuJoCo contact physics? The steady push matches KP × LEAD × speed, but the impact peak is 1.84 × higher and the share fed at most 2 N falls from 1.00 to 0.45 at 0.10 m/s (stylised; extends osrobot-assist).

Abstract Code →

The osrobot-assist spoon-feeding trial rebuilt in MuJoCo (a sphere on two slide joints, two box lips that follow the mouth's sway, MuJoCo soft contact), with the same controller and 200 paired seeds per row. With the arm blocked, the steady contact force equals the controller identity KP×LEAD×speed (2.00 N at 0.10 m/s) but the impact peak is 1.84× higher at every speed (3.68 N), and falls with more contact damping. With a swaying mouth the share fed at most 2 N drops from the stylised 1.00 to 0.45 at 0.10 m/s (30 mm sway, camera arm), with peaks of 11 to 23 N because the kinematic lips sweep into the tip, a contact the stylised model leaves out. Feeding time agrees within 4 % in all but one row. Stylised and preliminary: rigid lips that cannot yield, assumed contact damping, no human model.

osrobot-lipsweep5 tests

Is the peak force of a feeding arm on the lips set by the lips' stiffness, the arm's force loop, or its approach lead?

Is the peak force of a feeding arm on the lips set by lip stiffness, the force loop or the approach lead? Lip stiffness moves the mean peak from 0.32 to 2.02 N at 0.20 m/s (stylised; extends osrobot-assist).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib sweep of osrobot-assist's feeding-arm twin over lip stiffness, loop stiffness and forward lead (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, camera arm at 0.20 m/s). Mean peak lip force rises from 0.32 N at 100 N/m to 1.15 N at 800 and 2.02 N at 6400; the worst trial reaches 6.7 N, above the controller's 4.0 N stall push, so that push is a ceiling only for soft and medium lips. At 0.05 m/s every stiffness stays under 2 N. Stylised: assumed constants, a point mass and a passive user.

osrobot-leanshrink4 tests

If the person being fed judges the spoon better as it nears the mouth, how much of a camera's value does a blind feeding arm get back?

If the person being fed judges the spoon better as it nears the mouth, how much of a camera's value does a blind arm get back? A misjudgement shrinking to zero at the lips lifts the blind arm's safe share at 40 mm from 0.47 to 0.84 and restores every feed; stylised, extends osrobot-leannoise.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-leannoise's planar feeding-arm twin in which the user's misjudgement of the spoon position shrinks, linearly over the last 40 mm, by a swept fraction (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, 0.20 m/s, 100 mm/s lean). A blind arm's share of feeds with peak lip force at most 2 N is 0.83, 0.60, 0.47 and 0.41 for a constant misjudgement of 10, 20, 40 and 80 mm, and 0.99, 0.95, 0.84 and 0.70 when the error falls to zero at the lips; feeds that never reach the mouth (0.50 fed at 40 mm) disappear. With the error shrinking, the blind arm is within 0.02 of the camera arm up to 20 mm; the camera keeps its lead at 40 and 80 mm. Stylised: an assumed linear shrink law, assumed constants, a point mass and no real person.

osrobot-leannoise4 tests

If the person being fed misjudges the spoon, or sees it late, can a blind feeding arm still do without a camera?

If the person being fed misjudges the spoon or sees it late, can a blind feeding arm still do without a camera? A 20 mm misjudgement drops the blind arm's safe share from 1.00 to 0.60 (camera arm 0.78); stylised, extends osrobot-lean.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-lean's planar feeding-arm twin in which the user leans toward a perceived spoon position that is delayed and offset by a per-feed misjudgement (200 paired trials per row, 30 mm sway, 0.20 m/s, 100 mm/s lean). A blind arm's share of feeds with peak lip force at most 2 N falls from 1.00 with a perfect leaner to 0.83, 0.60 and 0.47 at 10, 20 and 40 mm of misjudgement, and only 0.50 of feeds reach the mouth at 40 mm; the camera arm falls from 0.97 to 0.69 and always feeds. A perception delay of up to 0.2 s changes little; 1.0 s drops the blind arm to 0.46. Stylised: constant offset, assumed constants, no safety case.

osrobot-lean4 tests

If the person being fed leans toward the spoon, can a blind feeding arm do without a camera?

If the person being fed leans toward the spoon, can a blind feeding arm do without a camera? At 30 mm sway and 0.20 m/s the blind arm's safe share rises from 0.21 to 1.00 as the lean reaches 100 mm/s (stylised; extends osrobot-assist).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-assist's planar feeding-arm twin in which the user shifts the mouth toward the spoon tip at a swept lean speed (200 paired trials per row). At 30 mm sway and 0.20 m/s the blind arm's share of feeds with peak lip force at most 2 N rises from 0.21 (passive user) to 0.69 at 50 mm/s and 1.00 at 100 mm/s, against 0.71 to 0.97 for the camera arm; at 50 mm sway even 100 mm/s gives only 0.62 for the blind arm. Leaning removes contacts but not the peak force of the ones that remain (4.0 N at 0.20 m/s). Stylised: every constant, including the lean speed, is assumed; no person was modelled or tested.

osrobot-deadline8 tests

When a pest window sets a deadline, is a scout-and-treater fleet or a fleet of inline weeding robots cheaper?

When a pest window sets a deadline, is a scout-and-treater fleet or inline weeding robots cheaper? One scout cannot finish 16 fields faster than 5.3 to 32.5 h; pipeline/inline cost is 1.06 to 1.12 at 0.72 ha, 1.49 at 0.18 ha, and 0.87 to 0.93 at 1.62 ha where it can meet the deadline.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib extension of osrobot-pipeline that adds a hard finish deadline for 16 equal fields and searches up to four scouts, up to 16 treaters and up to 32 inline robots (no new simulation; every price an assumed round number). One scout cannot finish 16 fields faster than 5.3, 15.9 and 32.5 h (0.18, 0.72, 1.62 ha fields) however many treaters it feeds, against 0.7, 2.8 and 6.2 h for 32 inline robots. Cheapest pipeline over cheapest inline: 1.06 to 1.12 at 0.72 ha, rising as the deadline tightens, and 1.49 at 0.18 ha; at 1.62 ha the pipeline is cheaper (0.87 to 0.93) at every deadline it can meet but cannot meet 8 h, where only inline robots can. Stylised: equal fields, hard cut-off, no late-yield curve.

osrobot-pipeline9 tests

If one scout drone feeds ground treaters in a pipeline, can a held fleet beat inline weeding robots?

If one scout drone feeds ground treaters in a pipeline, can a held fleet beat inline weeding robots? One scout keeps only 1.0 to 1.3 treaters busy; overlapping the stages cuts the held-pair penalty to 1.04 at 0.72 ha fields and 0.86 at 1.62 ha, still losing on small fields. Assumed prices; scheduling over osrobot-pairprice's fits.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib scheduling follow-up to osrobot-pairprice using its fitted per-field minutes (no new simulation; every price an assumed round number). Set-up and battery swaps make the scout nearly as slow as the treater, so one scout keeps only 0.99 to 1.33 treaters busy and the cheapest pipeline is always one scout with one treater. Overlapping the stages cuts the held-pair penalty to 1.04 times the inline fleet at 0.72 ha fields (32 fields) and 0.86 at 1.62 ha, from 1.34 and 1.16; at 0.18 ha it stays 1.48 to 1.81 times. Extra treaters finish sooner but raise cost per hectare (13.92 to 24.56 USD for 1 to 5). Stylised: deterministic, equal fields, no weather or failures.

osrobot-pairprice13 tests

Is a scout drone plus a camera-less ground treater cheaper per hectare than one weeding robot, and from what field size?

Is a scout drone plus a camera-less ground treater cheaper per hectare than one weeding robot? With assumed prices and each machine charged for its own minutes, break-even is near 0.5 ha and the pair is about 0.7 times the cost per hectare at 5 ha; held for the whole job it never wins; flips with utilisation, labour and battery life. Stylised, nothing built.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib follow-up to osrobot-scoutpair that prices its matched-kill pair (scout at 1 m/s, 3 m swath, 0.343 killed) against one inline robot, with every price an assumed round number. Simulated time is linear in area (R² ≥ 0.9999 over 0.045 to 1.62 ha), so cost per field is a fixed set-up part plus a per-hectare part. Charging each machine only for the minutes it works, the pair costs about 2.5 times the inline robot on a 0.045 ha field, breaks even near 0.5 ha (0.8 ha at a 4,000 USD scout, 1.3 at 6,000) and is about 0.7 times as much per hectare at 5 ha (extrapolated). If the two machines are held for the whole job, as one dedicated pair would be, it never wins at the reference prices (1.08 times at 20 ha). The verdict flips with utilisation (2,000 occupied hours a year gives 2.09 times at 0.72 ha) and with labour and battery life. Stylised: assumed prices and constants, a straight-line extrapolation beyond 1.62 ha, no registration error or wind; nothing was built or flown.

osrobot-scoutpair6 tests

Does a fast scout platform plus a ground treater beat one weeding robot, and does a mud-aware tour matter?

Does a fast scout platform plus a ground treater beat one weeding robot? At matched kill (0.343) a 3 m scout swath finishes in 26.6 min against about 42 min for one inline robot, but a 1 m swath takes 47.3 min; a mud-aware tour changes nothing (stylised, simulation only).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib follow-up to osrobot-fieldtour that makes the scout a second platform with its own swath and detector, then compares at matched kill because both platforms lose detections as they speed up. With a 3 m scout swath at 1 m/s the pair kills 0.343 in 26.6 min against about 42 min for one inline robot interpolated to the same kill; with the scout's swath cut to the ground robot's 1 m the same kill takes 47.3 min and the pair loses by about 13%. The saving is the swath ratio, not the second vehicle. A mud-aware tour changes the total by 0.1 min or less at 0 to 80% mud. Assumed constants, no registration error and no pipelining or capital cost: stylised, simulation only.

osrobot-fieldtour6 tests

Does a better tour rescue scout-then-treat weeding?

Does a better tour rescue scout-then-treat weeding? 2-opt cuts the tour from 539 m to 468 m but a field still takes 56.1 min against 51.7 min treating inline; scouting loses at every weed density tried (stylised, simulation only).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib follow-up to osrobot-field that swaps nearest neighbour for 2-opt as the second stage of scout-then-treat. 2-opt cuts the straight-line tour over about 232 detections from 539 m to 468 m (random order: 5,403 m), but a field still takes 56.1 min against 51.7 min treating inline (nearest neighbour: 57.0), and scouting is slower at every weed density from 0.05 to 1.2 per m². Stylised: assumed constants, a mud-blind planner, 30 fields per row; no robot was built.

osrobot-field7 tests

For a weeding robot with a cheap camera, is it better to treat weeds as it drives or to scout first and come back, and what does a weak sensor cost?

For a weeding robot with a cheap camera, is it better to treat weeds as it drives or to scout first? Scouting then touring killed the same share (0.399 against 0.401 at 1 m/s) and was slower in all 23 paired rows; lane overlap repays a weak sensor (0.40 to 0.86 killed) at 3.5 times the time. Stylised, constants assumed.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib simulation of a lane-following weeding robot on a 60×30 m field with clustered weeds, a motion-blurred noisy detector and muddy squares. Scouting then touring the targets kills the same share of weeds as treating inline (0.399 against 0.401 at 1 m/s) and is slower in all 23 paired rows, by 2.8 to 7.8 min. Lane overlap repays a weak sensor at a steep price: 0 to 0.75 overlap raises the kill share from 0.40 to 0.86 and the time from 52 to 178 min; no grid configuration reaches a 0.9 kill share at a 0.5 hit rate. Stylised: every constant is assumed, the speed results move with the blur assumption, and the planner comparison is a statement about this cost model.

osrobot-lint13 tests

Can a stdlib static linter catch the lab-protocol faults the Opentrons simulator accepts?

Can a stdlib static linter catch the lab-protocol faults the Opentrons simulator accepts? It flags 362 of the 522 seeded faults to the simulator's 270, adding reused tips, tips left on, sub-minimum volumes and carry-over; stylised, partly circular.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib linter for Opentrons Python API scripts follows tip state, used tip wells, declared well volumes and the liquid in the tip without running the script. On the 522 seeded faults of osrobot-lab it flags 362, against 270 raised by the real simulator and 366 flagged by the twin, adding reused tips, tips left on, sub-minimum volumes and carry-over; it cannot see the travel-height collisions. Agreement with the twin is partly circular (same author, same fault set), and every limit is an assumed value. Stylised.

osrobot-plate7 tests

How fast can a purpose-built robot fill a 96-well plate, and does the robot or the number of channels matter more?

How fast can a purpose-built robot fill a 96-well plate, and does the robot or the number of channels matter more? Eight channels cut the time by 86 to 88 % (9.5 s against 69.7 s for a gantry at 10 µL) while gantry against arm moves it 4 to 14 %, since about 76 % is fixed pipetting actions (stylised; every speed, price and accuracy figure assumed).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib model times a 96-well plate fill on an XY gantry and a two-link arm with 1 or 8 channels. At 10 µL per well one channel takes 69.7 s (gantry) or 66.7 s (arm); eight channels take 9.5 and 9.0 s. Channel count cuts the time by 86–88%; robot type moves it by 4–14%, because 76–79% of the time is fixed aspirate and dispense actions, so well order saves only about 2%. Which robot is faster flips with the assumed speeds; the 8-channel gantry is cheapest per plate-hour by a small margin. With assumed joint noise the arm misses the 1.5 mm well radius often enough to hit all 96 wells with probability 0.005. Stylised: every speed, price and accuracy figure is assumed.

19

The software-engineering loop

Measuring and optimising the agent loop that builds this portfolio: what the run log records, what a run costs, and which work is worth the budget. Topic page →

swe-friction5 tests

Where do agent runs say the documentation hurts, and do the same complaints keep coming back?

Where do agent runs say the documentation hurts? 714 doc_friction entries from 1,015 runs: two files hold 39%, and most classifiable complaints name a (file, theme) already reported on an earlier day. Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib analysis of the doc_friction field in 1,015 dated run records (1 to 18 October 2026): 575 runs (57%) report at least one problem, 714 entries in all. They concentrate: CLAUDE.md and research/PROJECTS.md hold 39% of entries and the top ten files 70% (Gini 0.75 over 115 files). Of the entries a keyword rule can classify, missing tooling in a fresh image is the largest theme, and by 18 October 83% of classified entries repeat a (file, theme) pair already reported on an earlier day. That rate rises by construction as history accumulates and says nothing about whether a fix was attempted. Keyword themes, self-reported field, 18 days. Preliminary.

free-frictionnull8 tests

Do documentation complaints in agent run records repeat more than chance?

Do documentation complaints repeat more than chance? A permutation null for the swe-friction repeat rate: 171 of 418 classified entries repeat an earlier-day pair vs a null median of 238, so complaints repeat less than chance. Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A permutation null for the repeat rate in swe-friction. Of 418 classified doc_friction entries (1 to 18 October 2026), 171 name a (file, theme) pair reported on an earlier day, against a null median of 238 (95% interval 224 to 250; none of 2,000 shuffles reached 171). Complaints repeat less than chance on 16 and 17 October and match it on the 18th, so the rising repeat rate is mostly arithmetic of a growing history. Consistent with fixes landing, but the commits are not linked. Keyword themes, self-reported, 18 days. Preliminary.

free-excitation8 tests

Which test input should you use to calibrate a mass-spring-damper twin?

Which test input should you use to calibrate a mass-spring-damper twin? A resonant sine gives the lowest held-out prediction error (3.1e-4 vs 1.1e-3 for a step) yet the worst Fisher condition number (527 vs 56 to 114); fitted spreads sit within 0.83 to 1.09 of the Cramér-Rao bounds. Stylised, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Fitting mass, damping and stiffness of a lightly damped oscillator (ζ = 0.1) from one 10 s noisy trace under four equal-energy inputs, with Cramér-Rao bounds and 100 Gauss-Newton fits each. A sine at the natural frequency gives the lowest held-out prediction error (mean RMSE 3.1×10−4 against 1.1×10−3 for a step and 2.8×10−3 for an off-resonance sine) although it has the worst Fisher condition number (527 against 56 to 114), so conditioning ranks the inputs backwards. The step estimates damping 4.5× less precisely. Fitted spreads are within 0.83 to 1.09 of the bounds. Stylised: one plant, one noise level, truth inside the model class. Preliminary.

swe-ledger8 tests

What can the run log measure about the agent loop today?

What can the run log measure about the agent loop today? Cost fields are present in at most 1% of 189 runs, a third of listed projects are follow-up families, and every recorded CI-failure count is zero. Preliminary first step of track 10.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib reader of a snapshot of prompts/runs.jsonl (189 runs, 184 listed projects) reports coverage and throughput proxies. Token, cost and tool-call fields are present in at most 1% of runs and wall time is derivable for only 15, so no cost-per-project figure is possible yet. About a third of listed projects sit in follow-up families of three or more, and 24 slugs appear in more than one run. All 143 recorded CI-failure counts are zero, which looks like a success-only field, not a clean record. Preliminary: first step of the ledger milestone; no git-history backfill, no value or correctness scoring.

swe-runcost5 tests

What does an agent run cost, and which runs cost the most?

What does an agent run cost, and which cost the most? 355 priced runs (14 to 18 October): median $0.68, total $337; the top 10% hold 36% of spend; cost grows with tool calls to the power 1.18 (preliminary; API-equivalent estimates).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib analysis of the 355 run records (14 to 18 October 2026) that carry an API-equivalent cost_usd. The median run costs $0.68 (95% bootstrap $0.64 to $0.72) and the 355 together $337; the top 10% of runs hold 36% of spend. Research runs are 47% of spend with the highest median ($0.82), process runs 24% on 14% of runs because of a long tail. Cost scales with tool calls with exponent 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25) and input tokens with 1.37, consistent with context re-read at each step. Preliminary: five days, one model, estimates not invoices, and cost is not scored against value.

swe-errors5 tests

What do agent runs record going wrong, and does it relate to partial outcomes or cost?

What do agent runs record going wrong? 17% of 1,027 runs record an error (24.5% of research runs); environment 28%, own mistakes 21%, collisions 17%; runs with an error end partial twice as often (12.6% vs 6.0%) and cost about twice as much. Preliminary: keyword classifier, self-reported.

Abstract Code →

Reads the free-text errors field of 1,027 run records: 175 runs (17.0%, Wilson 14.9–19.5%) record at least one, 24.5% of research runs against 12.4% of ventures runs. Keyword rules put 28% of the 222 entries in environment and tooling, 21% in the run's own mistake, 17% in collisions with a parallel run and 7% in timeouts; 24% match no rule. Runs with an error end partial 12.6% of the time against 6.0%, and the 30 priced ones cost a median $1.29 against $0.64. An association, not a cause. Preliminary: unvalidated classifier, self-reported errors.

swe-errlabel5 tests

Do the swe-errors keyword rules sort run-record errors correctly?

Do the swe-errors keyword rules sort run-record errors correctly? On a 60-entry blind hand-labelled sample they agree on 40 (66.7%, Wilson 54.1% to 77.3%; kappa 0.59); the ci-or-tooling rule never wins and own-mistake recall is 55%, so the earlier shares are a lower bound for those two. Preliminary: one labeller.

Abstract Code →

A 60-entry blind sample of the run records’ reported errors, hand-labelled once and compared with swe-errors’ keyword rules: they agree on 40 of 60 entries (66.7%, Wilson 95% 54.1–77.3%; Cohen’s κ 0.59). The ci-or-tooling rule never wins (9 hand-labelled, 0 assigned), the run’s-own-mistake class is found with recall 55%, and environment, timeout and collision hold up (recall 92–100%). So the earlier error shares are a lower bound for tooling and own mistakes. Preliminary: one labeller, the same kind of model that wrote the records, and 60 entries.

swe-errfix6 tests

Can the swe-errors keyword rules be improved on 30 hand labels and still help on the other 30?

Can the swe-errors keyword rules be improved on 30 hand labels and still help on the other 30? A two-fold held-out refit (rule order plus greedy keywords) averages 68.5% agreement with the hand labels against 66.7% for the shipped rules (+1.1 entries over 200 splits, range -4 to +7), while the same procedure scores 85% on its own 60 training entries: mostly memorisation. Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

A two-fold held-out check of a mechanical refit (best rule order, then up to six greedily added keywords) of the swe-errors rules against swe-errlabel’s 60 hand labels. Averaged over 200 random run-level splits the refit agrees with the hand label on 68.5% of entries against 66.7% for the shipped rules (+1.1 entries, range −4 to +7), while fitted and scored on all 60 it reaches 85%: most of an in-sample improvement is memorisation. Preliminary: one labeller, 60 entries.

Did research brief v1 change how runs go?

Did research brief v1 change how runs go? Same-days comparison of v0 (342 runs) and v1 (67) on 15 to 18 October: no detectable difference in cost, time or success; the lower v1 error rate (7.5% vs 17.0%) vanishes within unlabelled-task runs (8.3% vs 9.6%); v1 records more doc-friction entries (1.24 vs 0.72 per run, p = 0.0001). Observational.

Abstract Code →

Research runs on prompt v0 (342) and v1 (67) from the same four days, 15–18 October 2026. Cost, wall time and output tokens do not differ detectably (median cost $0.835 vs $0.820, p = 0.72). v1 records fewer errors (7.5% vs 17.0%, p = 0.058), but v0 drew far more extend and new-project tasks, and among runs with no task label the rates are 8.3% vs 9.6%. v1 runs list more documentation friction (1.24 vs 0.72 entries per run, p = 0.0001; 1.28 vs 1.02 among unlabelled runs). Does Opus pay for itself on this portfolio's runs? An Opus run costs about 8 to 9 times a Sonnet run in the same track; with 12 priced Opus runs the ledger cannot compare value per dollar, and a 50% difference in projects per run needs about 129 runs per arm (preliminary; cost only).

Abstract Code →

An Opus run costs about 8–9× a Sonnet run in the same track (process 7.9×, bootstrap 6.7–11.7; research 9.1×, 3.7–12.1 on only 3 Opus runs). The ledger holds 12 priced Opus runs against 342 Sonnet runs, confounded with date and task, so value per dollar cannot be compared yet: detecting a 50% difference in projects per run needs about 129 runs per arm. Preliminary; cost only.

swe-deviations8 tests

Do agent runs that record a deviation from the brief cost more or end worse?

Do agent runs that record a deviation from the brief cost more or end worse? Of 1,564 run records 203 list one; within track they take ~1.6x as long and cost ~1.2x as much, but the cost gap rests mainly on the process track, and they end partial 5 points more often. Observational, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Of 1,564 run records, 203 (13%) list a deviation from the brief, mostly review (59%) and ventures (27%) runs. Within track, deviating runs take about 1.6× as long and cost about 1.2× as much (stratified permutation p < 0.001), but the cost gap rests mainly on the long process track (1.07×, p = 0.052 without it), and deviating runs end partial 5 points more often. Observational and self-reported: preliminary.

swe-callcost8 tests

How well does a run's tool-call count predict what it costs?

How well does a run's tool-call count predict its cost? On 882 priced run records cost is about $0.03 per call, a log-log fit has R² 0.91 and a held-out median error of 9%; the pooled slope 1.22 is partly group mixing (1.10 within Sonnet). Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Of 1,638 run records, 882 carry both a cost and a tool-call count. Cost per call is almost constant (median $0.031, 10th to 90th percentile $0.026 to $0.038); a log-log fit has R2 0.91 and misses held-out runs by a median of 9% (90th percentile 25%), no better than a flat cost-per-call multiplier. The pooled slope of 1.22 (1.18 to 1.26) is partly group mixing: it is 1.10 within Sonnet runs and 0.96 within Opus runs (wide interval). Cost is API-equivalent and derived from the same transcript as the call count, so the fit checks the measurement, not agent behaviour. Preliminary.

swe-cachecost5 tests

Where does an agent run's cost go, and why does it grow faster than its tool calls?

Where does a run's cost go? On 893 run records with per-token-kind usage, cache reads are a median 45% of the API-equivalent cost and 1-hour cache writes 41%, output only 13%; the starting context (about 60,000 tokens) is re-read on every request, which makes cost grow faster than linearly in tool calls (preliminary).

Abstract Code →

Of 1,659 run records, 893 carry per-token-kind usage as well as cost and tool calls. At API-equivalent list prices, cache reads are a median 45% of a run's cost, 1-hour cache writes 41% and output 13%; fresh input is about zero. A linear context model fits the cache-read tokens per request as about 60,000 tokens at the start plus about 1,900 tokens more per request (bootstrap 95% interval 1,500 to 2,200), so at the median run (20 requests) the starting context is 76% of what each request re-reads. That fixed part, written once and re-read throughout, is why cost rises with a log-log slope of 1.16 against requests and 1.22 against tool calls rather than 2. Limitations: API-equivalent dollars from list prices, not a bill; the context model explains only 31% of the per-request variance; descriptive, from one repository's runs.

swe-notests7 tests

Do agent runs that add no tests end worse?

Do agent runs that add no tests end worse? 84 of 621 counted run records add none; within track they end partial 4/84 against 16/537 (+2.6 points, p = 0.23, no detectable effect) and cost less, probably because they do less. Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Of 621 run records that count tests added, 84 (13.5%) add none, mostly research runs. Within track and recording regime they end partial 4 of 84 times against 16 of 537 for runs that add tests: a +2.6 point difference, permutation p = 0.23, so no detectable effect (only 20 partial outcomes exist, so power is low). They cost less (median $0.56 against $0.99 in research), most likely because they do less. Observational and self-reported; preliminary.

swe-devkinds6 tests

Which kind of recorded deviation from the brief predicts a partial outcome?

Which kind of recorded deviation predicts a partial outcome? Of 213 run records with a deviation, tooling failures end partial 22.6 points more often than runs with none (track-stratified p=0.001); skipped steps (+1.3) and switched tasks (+1.3) do not. Keyword classes, observational, preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Of 1,606 run records, 213 list a deviation. Classifying each by fixed keyword rules, runs whose deviation is a tooling failure end partial 22.6 points more often than runs with no deviation within track (permutation p = 0.001, 24 runs in usable strata); skipped steps (+1.3 points, p = 0.67) and switched tasks (+1.3 points, p = 0.63) show no difference. Keyword classes are crude and the data observational: preliminary.

swe-fieldfill5 tests

How complete are the agent run records, field by field?

How complete are the agent run records, field by field? Of 1,362 records, cost, tokens and wall time are present on 47% (0-7% on 13 to 15 October, 61-82% since), merged on 4.6%, and 18.5% of success runs name no pull request (preliminary; presence, not correctness).

Abstract Code →

Counts which fields are present on each of the 1,362 run records in prompts/runs/ (1 to 19 October 2026). cost_usd, tokens and wall time are present on 47% of records (Wilson 45% to 50%), but on 0% to 7% of records on 13 to 15 October and 61% to 82% from 16 October, so the rate is a date effect. merged is filled on 4.6%, a pull request is named on 81.2%, and 237 of 1,279 records with outcome success (18.5%, 16% to 21%) name none. Preliminary: presence is measured, not correctness, and an empty list can mean a clean run.

swe-spendoutput8 tests

Does a bigger agent run buy more output?

Does a bigger run buy more output? Across 157 priced run records that report adding tests, cost and tests added rank together pooled (Spearman 0.57) but weakly within research runs (0.19), and the dearest third yields the fewest tests per dollar; preliminary, tests added is a crude self-reported proxy.

Abstract Code →

Joins cost to tests added across the 157 priced run records that report adding tests (14 to 20 October 2026). Pooled, the two rank together (Spearman ρ +0.57, bootstrap 95% interval +0.44 to +0.68), but inside a track the link is weak for research runs (ρ +0.19, −0.02 to +0.39; log-log slope +0.33, so doubling cost adds about 26% more tests) and imprecise for ventures (ρ +0.39; slope +1.19, interval +0.48 to +1.88). The dearest third of runs yields the fewest tests per dollar (3.7, against 5.4 and 6.0). Preliminary: tests added is a crude, self-reported output proxy that only 21% of priced records fill in, and the pooled figure partly reflects the track mix.

swe-costpermerge6 tests

What does an agent run cost per merged pull request?

What does a run cost per merged pull request? 366 priced runs joined to main's merge history: 75% name a merged PR, $1.26 per merged run against $0.94 per run, process runs about 2.4 times research's; red team never links its PR (preliminary; API-equivalent estimates).

Abstract Code →

Joins the 366 run records (14 to 18 October 2026) that carry an API-equivalent cost_usd to the pull-request numbers in the subject lines of main's first-parent history. 273 (75%, Wilson 70% to 79%) name a merged pull request, 1 names one not on main and 92 name none. A merged run costs $1.26 on average (bootstrap 1.08 to 1.49) against $0.94 per priced run, because 19% of spend sits on runs with no merged PR on record; process runs cost about 2.4 times a research run per merged run. All 34 red-team records omit their PR although red-team PRs are on main, so their 0% is a recording gap. Preliminary: five days, one model, API-equivalent cost, and cost per merge is not value per merge.

swe-backfill9 tests

What does git history say about the agent loop that the run log cannot?

What does git history say about the agent loop that the run log cannot? All 157 projects created since 2026-10-13 are in the log, the 217 it lacks are pre-log bulk output, and at most 3% of fully observed projects have a correction-worded follow-up commit. Preliminary second step of track 10.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib reader of 517 commits touching research/<slug>/ (396 projects, 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-15) fills in what the run log lacks. All 157 projects created since 2026-10-13 are in the log; the 217 it never lists were made in two bulk days (09-29 and 09-30) before the log began. Half of all projects (49%) sit in follow-up families, creations arrive in bursts (median gap 4 minutes), and only 6 of 234 fully observed projects (2.6%, 95% interval 1% to 5%) have a later commit whose subject says it corrects something, a lower bound on defects, not an estimate. No tokens, cost, pull request or CI data; preliminary.

swe-value8 tests

Can two independent passes agree on what a portfolio project is worth?

Can two passes agree on what a project is worth? A three-level value rubric scored two automated ways over 408 projects agrees at chance (kappa 0.07, 95% 0.01 to 0.13), partly from a name-family flaw fixed after the fact (0.25); a blind 30-project hand sample agrees better (0.45 to 0.57, wide intervals). Preliminary, track 10 milestone 3; no correctness term.

Abstract Code →

A three-level value rubric (follow-up, new question, listed milestone) scored over all 408 research/ projects by two automated passes, one from names and order and one from README text, plus a blind 30-project hand sample. The two automated passes agree at chance level (linear Cohen’s kappa 0.07, 95% bootstrap 0.01 to 0.13); a flaw in the name pass (108 *-twin projects counted as one follow-up chain) explains part, and fixing it after the fact lifts kappa to 0.25. Against the hand sample the text pass reaches 0.45 (0.24 to 0.65) and the fixed name pass 0.57 (0.24 to 0.81), n = 30, scored by the rubric’s author. Follow-ups add about as many lines as new projects (median 318 vs 328), so by the rubric they return less per line, a ratio that is largely built in. Preliminary and negative on the automated passes; no correctness term.

swe-prompt7 tests

How many runs does a prompt experiment need, and is it safe to peek at it?

When can a prompt experiment stop? Fixed-n, peek-every-pair and a mixture SPRT simulated on ledger-shaped outcomes: peeking declares an identical brief different in 21% (success rate) to 40% (value) of experiments, the mixture test stays under 5% but needs far more runs than a 97% success rate allows. Stylised, no candidate brief run; track 10 milestone 6, partial.

Abstract Code →

Three stopping rules for a champion-versus-candidate brief experiment were simulated on outcome distributions drawn from the run ledger (success rate 237/244) and from swe-value’s project values: one look at the end, a look after every pair, and a mixture sequential probability ratio test. Looking after every pair declared an identical brief different in 21% of 2,000 experiments on success rate and 40% on value (nominal 5%); the mixture test stayed at 0.4% and 3.9%, at the price of power (92% against 99% at a +0.2 shift in value, stopping after 181 of 400 pairs on average). At a 97% success rate a fixed test needs about 2,200 runs to see a 0.971 to 0.991 change, so success rate is a poor primary metric. Stylised and preliminary: all 244 ledger rows are the same prompt, effects are hypothetical, and the value scores are weak; no candidate brief has been run.

swe-allocate6 tests

Which track should the next run work on, and does a smarter pick beat a uniform one?

Which track should the next run work on? Four allocation policies (uniform, greedy, bootstrap Thompson, knapsack-UCB) replayed offline on 7 tracks' scored projects: greedy and Thompson reach about 80% of the best-arm oracle against 60% for the current uniform pick, but value per line falls with order in 4 of 7 tracks, so the stationary replay overstates the gain. Stylised, offline only, no live trial; track 10 milestone 4, partial.

Abstract Code →

Four track-allocation policies (uniform, greedy value per line, bootstrap Thompson sampling, and a knapsack-style UCB) were replayed offline on 7 tracks, using the 408-project scores from swe-value (value 1 to 3, cost in lines added) under a 20,000-line budget and 300 seeds. Greedy and Thompson reach about 79–83% (pass A) and 75–79% (pass B) of the best-single-track oracle, against 58–60% for the current uniform pick; the UCB variant explores too much to help (62–66%). This is a stylised, preliminary result: arms are assumed stationary, yet value per line falls with order in 4 of 7 tracks (Spearman −0.36 to −0.57), the value scores themselves agree only weakly, lines are a poor proxy for tokens, and no live trial was run, so no policy is adopted.

swe-bootstrap6 tests

How much of the track-allocation gain is luck of the project history?

How much of the track-allocation gain is luck of the history? Block bootstrap of the sequential replay: at 20,000 lines greedy and Thompson beat uniform in 98–100% of 200 histories (intervals exclude zero), knapsack-UCB's does not; the small-budget loss does not reproduce. Stylised, offline only; follow-up to swe-decay.

Abstract Code →

swe-decay replayed track-picking policies on one history, so its intervals ignored history uncertainty. Here each track’s sequence is block-bootstrapped (200 histories). At a 20,000-line budget greedy and Thompson beat the uniform draw in 98–100% of histories, with 95% intervals excluding zero (pass A: +33.4 and +30.8 value points; pass B: +26.7 and +23.5); knapsack-UCB’s interval includes zero. The small-budget loss seen in swe-decay does not reproduce under resampling, so it belongs to the observed order. Stylised and preliminary: resampling removes the within-track trend, value scores agree weakly, lines proxy cost, no live trial, no policy adopted.

swe-decay7 tests

Do the gains from smarter track allocation survive when tracks run out of projects?

Do track-allocation gains survive when tracks run out of projects? Sequential, no-replacement replay: at 20,000 lines greedy and Thompson keep most of their lead over uniform (pass A 134 and 130 against 114), but at 5,000 lines they lose to it (24 against 30). Stylised, offline only; track 10 follow-up to swe-allocate.

Abstract Code →

swe-allocate replayed four track-picking policies with projects drawn with replacement. Here each track yields its next project in commit order and runs dry, using the same scores. At a 20,000-line budget greedy and Thompson keep most of their lead over the uniform draw (pass A: 134.0 and 129.9 against 114.0; pass B: 107.0 and 112.5 against 101.3), reaching 82–97% of a hindsight-greedy reference. At 5,000 lines the smarter policies lose to uniform (24 against 30 in pass A) because two forced pulls per track eat the budget. Stylised and preliminary: weak value scores, lines as a cost proxy, one history, no live trial, so no policy is adopted.

swe-audit6 tests

Do the portfolio's committed results reproduce when the code is re-run?

Do committed results reproduce? A seeded sample of 40 projects with a runnable experiment was re-run: 36 (90%, 95% Wilson 77% to 96%) matched their committed results.txt, 3 timed out under load and 1 needed a missing voice model. Preliminary first pass of track 10, milestone 2; it checks reproduction only, not citations. Second sample of 60 (92 distinct projects pooled): 81 reproduced (88%), no finished run differed; re-running the 5 timeouts serially reproduced all, giving 86 of 92 (93%).

Abstract Code →

A seeded sample of 40 research/ projects with a runnable experiment was re-run on a clean copy and diffed against the committed results.txt. 36 of 40 (90%, 95% Wilson interval 77% to 96%) reproduced: 34 byte-identical and 2 differing only in a timing line. Three timed out at 300 s (four jobs in parallel) and one needs a voice model that is not in the repository, so those four are inconclusive, not failures. Of 713 decimal numbers in the sampled READMEs, 85% appear verbatim in committed result files (the rest are derived or in prose). A second sample of 60 (8 overlapping) brought the pooled total to 92 distinct projects: 81 reproduced (88%, Wilson 80% to 93%), none of the 81 finished runs gave different numbers, and the 11 others are missing tools (Yosys, MuJoCo, a voice model) or timeouts. Re-running the five timeouts one at a time (no parallel load) reproduced all five (two differing only in timing lines), lifting the pooled figure to 86 of 92 (93%, Wilson 86% to 97%); the 6 left are missing tools or the voice model. A mechanical reproduction check on a small sample, with no citation audit, so the correctness term is only partly estimated. Preliminary.

swe-cleanbroken6 tests

When research merges collide cleanly, is the result still right?

When research merges collide cleanly, is the result still right? None of 92 clean replays was broken (28.7% of pairs within 60 min conflict); found and removed two duplicate README bullets the build missed.

Abstract Code →

Replays pairs of research merges that touched the shared index files within 10, 30 and 60 minutes of each other (67 merges, 2026-10-14 to 10-16) and checks the merged tree against the homepage build’s rules. Of 129 pairs within 60 min, 37 (28.7%) conflicted textually and the other 92 merged with no new inconsistency; none was clean but broken. The same checker found two projects with duplicate README.md bullets since the repository fold-in, which build.py missed; they are removed and the build now fails on duplicates. Preliminary: three days, an approximate replay, and consistency rules rather than the full build.

swe-prlifetime9 tests

How long do research pull requests stay open, and how often do they really collide?

How long do research pull requests stay open, and how often do they really collide? Median 0.9 min open (95% merged within 30 min); replayed from real creation times, 2 of 58 shared-file PRs (3.4%) conflict.

Abstract Code →

Joins 122 merged pull requests that touched research/ (2026-10-16 to 10-17) to their real creation times from the GitHub API. The median pull request was open 0.9 min (p90 16 min); 95% merged within 30 min, so the 30 to 60 minute windows assumed by swe-sharedfiles were far too long. Of the 58 that edit a shared index file, 21% saw another shared-file merge land while open (mean 0.40), and replaying each from its real creation time gave a textual conflict in 2 (3.4%, 95% Wilson 1.0% to 11.7%). Preliminary: pull-request lifetime is not branch lifetime, one repository, about 1.5 days.

swe-branchlife6 tests

Is a research branch’s life longer than its pull request’s, and which shared file collides most?

Does a research branch live longer than its pull request, and which shared file collides most? Median 1.1 min from first commit to merge (vs 0.9 for the PR); research/PROJECTS.md conflicts in 5 of 44 PRs that edit it, more than the index files (3 of 58).

Abstract Code →

Adds each of the 122 research pull requests’ first-commit time (GitHub API) to the swe-prlifetime data. Branch lifetime is almost the same as pull-request lifetime (median 1.1 vs 0.9 min, p90 16.1 vs 16.0), because sessions commit at the end of their work; commit dates cannot see the earlier working time. Replayed from the branch start, 3 of 58 shared-index-file PRs (5.2%, 95% Wilson 1.8–14.1%) conflict, versus 2 from pull-request creation. The larger finding: research/PROJECTS.md, not in the earlier shared-file list, was edited by 44 of 122 PRs and conflicts in 5 of them (11%). Preliminary: 1.5 days, one repository.

Do sibling research projects ask different questions?

Do sibling research projects ask different questions? Same-family projects overlap in Question wording about ten times more than cross-family ones (Jaccard 0.078 vs 0.008); preliminary, a crude proxy.

Abstract Code →

Scores the title and Question section of each project’s README by word overlap (Jaccard index). Pairs in the same slug family overlap about ten times more than pairs across families: mean 0.078 over 7,552 within-family pairs in 14 families of five or more projects, against 0.008 over 213,181 cross-family pairs. The closest pairs, such as mimic-mmd and mimic-mmdmujoco (0.917), are mostly deliberate one-condition follow-ups. Preliminary: word overlap is not result overlap, and shared vocabulary is partly legitimate.

swe-sharedfiles7 tests

How often do research merges collide on the shared index files?

How often do research merges collide on the shared index files? 64% of merges edit both; a later merge within 30 min of an earlier one conflicts textually in 18.6% of 59 replayed pairs (assumed branch times, preliminary).

Abstract Code →

Measured from git history (101 research merges, 2026-10-14 to 10-16): 64.4% edit both README.md and projects.json, the median gap between such merges is 30.6 min, and replaying a later merge against an earlier one within 30 min gives a textual conflict in 18.6% of 59 pairs (15.3% in a shared file). Branch times are assumed, not measured; textual conflicts only; preliminary.

swe-schedule6 tests

How many parallel agent runs duplicate each other when they start in the same minute, and what removes the waste?

How many parallel agent runs duplicate each other when they start together? 12.8% of runs at four blind starts; a start gap past the claim latency or scheduler slots remove it (stylised, assumed timings).

Abstract Code →

A stdlib Monte Carlo of start-time collisions among runs that pick from a pool of 11 tracks. Four blind simultaneous starts leave 12.8% of runs redundant (closed form agrees), claim-checking alone barely helps because all runs read before any claim is pushed, a start gap longer than the claim latency drives waste to about 1–2%, and scheduler-assigned slots remove it entirely up to the pool size. Every timing constant is assumed, the pool is uniform, and queueing against usage limits is not yet modelled. Stylised; first step of milestone 5 of track 10.

swe-pickmix10 tests

Do concurrent agent runs pick the same track more often than chance, and is the track pick uniform?

Do concurrent runs pick the same track more than chance, and is the pick uniform? Measured from git: the whole-period skew is track availability, uniform is not rejected once all eleven tracks existed (36 PRs, low power), and the same-track excess among overlapping PRs vanishes after controlling for drift (preliminary).

Abstract Code →

Measured from git history rather than simulated: 218 merged projects since the tracks were set. Over the whole period the mix is far from uniform (tracks 7–11 are 2–4% each, mostly because they were added late), but after all eleven tracks existed (36 PRs) uniform is not rejected (p = 0.25, low power). Same-track pairs among overlapping PRs are 17.9% against 12.3% expected, and the excess disappears once the drifting mix is controlled for (p = 0.115 within merge days). Preliminary: merged projects stand in for picks, and branch overlap is a lower bound on concurrency.

swe-prflow6 tests

What do 526 closed pull requests say about how the agent loop lands work?

What do 526 closed pull requests say about how the agent loop lands work? 87.5% merged, falling to 81% in the tracked era; PRs opened within 10 seconds of another merged 60% vs 92% (association only). Preliminary third step of track 10.

Abstract Code →

A stdlib analysis of the creation and merge times of every closed PR here (#1 to #526). 87.5% merged (Wilson 84.3–90.0%), falling from 93.8% for PRs opened by 10-01 to 81.2% from 10-05 on. Median time to merge is 0.6 minutes, 4.3% of merges happen in four same-second batches after long waits, and PRs opened within 10 seconds of another merged only 60% of the time against 92% for the rest. The last is an association, not a cause. No CI, review or closure-reason data, and the timestamps were hand-transcribed. Preliminary third step of track 10.

swe-orgs10 tests

Which practices of engineering organisations that ship could help an agent loop, and what is there to fix?

Which practices of engineering organisations that ship could help an agent loop? A cited catalogue of 59 practices from 58 sources (batch 19 adds Sentry's LOGAF-marked code review; batch 18 adds Mercari's tiered production-readiness checklist and Apollo's priority-ordered load shedding; batch 17 adds Kohavi, Tang and Xu on controlled experiments and Strathern on measures that become targets; batch 14 adds Reason and Vaughan on organisational accidents; batch 13 adds Rigby and Bird on lightweight review, Humble and Farley's deployment pipeline and Beck's Extreme Programming), scored against the 1,261-run ledger: no new proposal clears a 5% ceiling (negative, preliminary). Ongoing, with a research log; track 10, milestone 7.

Abstract Code →

A cited, growing catalogue of 59 practices from 58 sources (Sentry(Mercari’s production-readiness checklistrsquo;s LOGAF-marked code review, Mercari’s production-readiness checklist, Apollo’s priority displays, Kohavi, Tang and Xu on controlled experiments, Strathern on audit, Perrow on normal accidents, the DevOps Handbook, Reason on layered defences, Vaughan on normalization of deviance, Rigby and Bird, Humble and Farley, Beck, Allspaw and Hammond on Flickr, Parnas, Nygard, Conway, Nagappan et al., Skelton and Pais, Brooks, Fowler, Reinertsen, Toyota, the Rogers Commission, 37signals, Instagram, Google, Microsoft, Facebook, Netflix, Amazon, Etsy, Basecamp, Spotify, Stripe (twice, including its online-migrations post), Shopify, Linear, and postmortems from GitLab and Cloudflare, the SEC’s order on Knight Capital and others), each tagged with company stage, evidence type (four measured, the rest case studies, postmortems, accounts or opinion), the loop element it maps to, how far it transfers to a fleet of agent sessions, and the assumption that does not carry over. The failure reports agree: a safety mechanism or a cost nobody measured before it shipped. Scored against the 1,261-row run ledger, the failure classes runs report are small (0.6–1.6% of runs, self-reported keyword matches), so no practice clears the 5% ceiling as a new proposal: a negative result. Sources were checked by web search only. Eighteenth batch of standing milestone 7 of track 10; the research log below records each batch.

swe-startslot5 tests

Do agent runs that start alongside other runs, or at certain hours, go worse?

Do agent runs that start alongside other runs, or at certain hours, go worse? Raw, crowded starts look better (error recorded 9.8% vs 21.0%) but that is a day effect; shuffled within days there is no detectable difference over 660 timed records, and hour of day shows nothing (negative, preliminary, low power).

Abstract Code →

Joins 660 run records that have a start time (1 to 19 October 2026) to how many other runs started within 5, 10 or 30 minutes. Raw, crowded starts look better (error recorded in 9.8% against 21.0%), but that is a day effect: 13 to 15 October had 47–50% error records and few concurrent starts, 16 October on 6–9% and many. Shuffling the crowded label within calendar days finds no detectable difference (12 tests, one p = 0.018 on a 50-run group, not counted), and six-hour blocks of the day show nothing. Reads the 35 review-track pull requests merged on main from 14 to 19 October 2026 and groups those merged within 10 minutes of each other. Splits the 515 ventures sessions that landed commits from 13 October by prompt version, scope, size, subject and day. 79.6% have a run record against 92.2% for research, and no feature of what the session built separates the unrecorded ones (one venture 80.2%, 1–5 files 78.9%, single commit 80.3%). A reference graph of 723 research READMEs, from slug mentions and git creation times: 61.7% of projects (Wilson 95% 58–65%) are named by at least one later project, but inbound counts are very uneven (Gini 0.69; the most-named is named by 50) and 71% of references stay within a track. Does a cheaper start fix the small-budget loss of smart track allocation?
