swe-decay found greedy and Thompson track allocation losing to uniform at a 5,000-line budget (24 against 30 value points) because two forced pulls per track ate it. Here each track is pulled once, or a shrinkage rule uses no forced pulls. On the observed history one pull each removes the loss (pass A: 33.0 and 33.3 against uniform 30.0) but costs a few points at 20,000 lines in pass B; shrinkage greedy is no better than uniform on the observed order, matches the others on resampled histories, and is insensitive to its prior size. On 200 block-bootstrapped histories every start rule’s 5,000-line interval over uniform still includes zero. Stylised: lines of code stand in for cost, the value scores agree weakly, and no live trial was run.

20

Adversarial human imitation

Can a frozen language model be prompted to write like people, against a detector that is also only prompted? The context suite, the reference detectors and the game loop. Topic page →

mimic-contexts10 tests

How well do prompt-free detectors tell people from a plainly prompted LLM, and do they carry over to unseen kinds of text?

How well do prompt-free detectors tell people from a plainly prompted LLM, and do they carry over to unseen kinds of text? Eight RAID families split by family: n-gram detector AUROC 0.93 and Binoculars-style 0.80 on held-out families, length at chance. Preliminary first step of track 11.

Abstract Code →

Eight text families from RAID (300 human and 300 plain-prompt chat-LLM texts each), split by family: train on five, hold out poetry, reviews and wiki. Prompt-free detectors on the held-out families: character/word n-gram logistic regression AUROC 0.93 (95% interval 0.91–0.94), a Binoculars-style zero-shot score from Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.80 (0.77–0.83), perplexity alone 0.76; a length-only detector is at chance (0.52). Zero-shot scores are weak on mpt-chat text (0.65) while n-grams are not (0.95). Limits: the ‘imitator’ is RAID’s own chat generations, not a prompted or optimised one; three chat models; no author-group labels for fairness checks. Preliminary: first step of track 11, no game yet.

benford-repo5 tests

Do the file sizes and line counts of this repository follow Benford’s law?

Do this repository's file sizes follow Benford's law? Not as a whole (byte MAD 0.018, nonconforming) because templated files repeat the same size thousands of times; counting each distinct size once gives acceptable conformity (MAD 0.0068).

Abstract Code →

First-digit frequencies of the byte sizes and line counts of the 35,648 git-tracked files at one commit, scored against Benford’s law by chi-square and Nigrini’s mean absolute deviation (MAD). All files together are nonconforming (byte MAD 0.0183, line MAD 0.0278), because a few sizes repeat thousands of times (1,071 bytes 1,297 times, 47 bytes 993 times, 4 lines 1,822 times). Counting each distinct size once, byte sizes conform acceptably (MAD 0.0068, n = 12,429). By extension, .json and .html stay nonconforming even deduplicated, and distinct Python line counts are acceptable (MAD 0.0103, n = 476). Descriptive: one commit of one generated, templated repository; an illustration of when the law fails, not a test of the law.

mimic-loop17 tests

Can prompt search alone move a frozen 0.5B imitator past a prompted 0.5B detector, and which proposer does it best at equal budget?

Can prompt search alone move a frozen 0.5B imitator past a prompted 0.5B detector? A stylised first run of the imitation game, four proposers at equal budget on two families: the starting detector is below chance, proposers cannot be ranked at this size, and length is a major confound.

Abstract Code →

A first, stylised run of the imitation game: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as imitator and detector, only prompts change, alternating rounds on two families (reddit, reviews) with four proposers (random, GA, GrIPS-style, local-LLM) at 4 evaluations per side per round. The plain detector starts below chance (paired accuracy 0.12), the final detectors reach 0.12–0.58 on 24 test pairs with intervals of about ±0.2, and the proposers cannot be ranked. Length is a major confound: imitators that wrote longer texts fooled the detector more. One seed; a harness and a first look, not a detection result.

mimic-crossplay12 tests

Does the prompt-only imitation game settle or cycle, and does beating the latest detector mean beating the others?

Does the prompt-only imitation game settle or cycle? Every imitator prompt from mimic-loop against every detector prompt (0.5B on both sides): pure equilibria below chance (reddit 0.396, reviews 0.292), no cycles at a noise margin, and text length tracks detector accuracy. Stylised, one loop seed; model-size question open.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-loop. Every imitator prompt any of its eight runs produced is scored against every detector prompt (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on both sides, 48 titles per cell, detector paired accuracy, 0.50 = chance), giving a 10×7 matrix on reddit and 9×10 on reviews. Both zero-sum games have a pure equilibrium with value below chance (reddit 0.396, 95% title-bootstrap 0.28 to 0.47; reviews 0.292, 0.17 to 0.34): no detector prompt guarantees chance, and no cell exceeds 0.56. On reviews the unadapted plain imitator prompt is the equilibrium imitator. Mean text length correlates with detector accuracy (Spearman 0.76 on reddit, 0.30 on reviews). No cycles at a 0.15 noise margin; overfitting to the latest opponent is small and not established. Stylised: one loop seed, a 0.5B detector that starts below chance. The model-size question is left open.

mimic-anycontext-detect5 tests

Does a prompt-free human-vs-machine detector hold up on context families it never saw?

Does a prompt-free n-gram human-vs-machine detector hold up on context families it never saw? Detector side of mimic-anycontext with no LLM (model download was blocked): AUROC 0.934 on unseen families against 0.985 in-family, and 40 target items close most of the gap on recipes. Stylised: plain-prompt RAID text only.

Abstract Code →

Detector side of mimic-anycontext, run without an LLM because the model download was blocked. A TF-IDF n-gram logistic-regression detector is fitted on seven of eight RAID-derived families and scored on the eighth: mean AUROC 0.934 against 0.985 when fitted inside the family, worst on recipes (0.843), abstracts and wiki. Forty labelled target items close most of the gap on recipes. Held-out generators cost little (AUROC 0.90–1.00) and length does not explain it. Stylised: plain-prompt machine text only, one detector type; the prompt-optimising imitator is not tested.

mimic-anycontext-prompt7 tests

Can a prompt make a 0.5B model detect machine text, and does the prompt carry to families it never saw?

Can a prompt make a 0.5B model detect machine text, and does it carry to unseen families? Negative: the prompted Qwen2.5-0.5B detector is inverted (mean AUROC 0.278 plain, 0.293 universal on held-out families, none above 0.5 on any family) while the n-gram detector gets 0.93. Stylised: one small model, 16 prompts, plain-prompt RAID text.

Abstract Code →

Prompted-detector half of mimic-anycontext. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct answers Yes/No to “was this written by a person?” for RAID human and LLM texts in eight families, with 16 candidate prompts (the plain instruction plus random subsets of a ten-fragment bank). Negative result: the detector is inverted, with mean AUROC 0.278 for the plain prompt and 0.293 for a universal prompt picked on six families and scored on the other two (0.5 is chance; no prompt reaches 0.5 on any family, best 0.424). Picking prompts on selection texts adds +0.015 to +0.033, within selection noise, so the seen/held-out gap (about 0.01) says nothing about transfer. The prompt-free n-gram detector in mimic-anycontext-detect gets 0.93 on the same kind of text. Stylised: one small model, shallow random search, plain-prompt machine text, 30+30 test texts per family.

mimic-mauve4 tests

Does MAUVE, a distribution-level score, rank human-vs-machine gaps the way a text detector does?

Does MAUVE rank human-vs-machine gaps the way a text detector does? Across 20 RAID family × model cells MAUVE (lexical embedding) and a cross-fit n-gram detector agree loosely (Spearman −0.60) and disagree on recipes and news; every cell is far below the human-vs-human null (0.92 to 0.99). Preliminary, no GPT-2 features.

Abstract Code →

MAUVE between human and RAID chat-model text in 20 family × model cells (TF-IDF/SVD embedding, 5 draws of 48–100 texts), against a cross-fit n-gram detector on the same texts. Human-vs-human MAUVE is 0.92–0.99; every human-vs-model cell is at most 0.83. MAUVE and AUROC rank cells loosely alike (Spearman −0.60, p = 0.005; wiki/mistral-chat is hardest for both), but disagree on recipes (AUROC 0.999, MAUVE 0.32) and news (0.97, 0.75), and MAUVE does not track the distinct-2 ratio (ρ = 0.24, n.s.). Preliminary: the embedding is lexical, not MAUVE’s usual GPT-2 features, so values are not comparable with the literature; plain-prompt text only, no LLM run.

mimic-evade5 tests

Can an imitator fool a prompt-free human-vs-machine text detector with cheap surface edits, such as typos, contractions or dropping the chat preamble?

Can cheap surface edits (typos, contractions, no chat preamble) fool the n-gram human-vs-machine detector? Most move held-out AUROC under 0.005; 2% typos cost 0.012 and keeping half the text 0.051 (from 0.927), and a refit detector wins it back.

Abstract Code →

The mimic-contexts n-gram detector (held-out AUROC 0.927) is scored on poetry, reviews and wiki after scripted edits to the machine texts only. Markdown stripping, preamble removal and contractions move it by at most 0.005; 2% typos cost 0.012 (interval −0.014 to −0.010); keeping the first half costs 0.051, the largest drop, and no edit approaches chance. A detector refit on edited training text recovers and exceeds the baseline (0.956 to 0.969), partly by learning text length. Lowercasing and whitespace edits are null by construction. Preliminary: scripted rules, not LLM-chosen edits; one seed.

mimic-whitebox5 tests

How many words must an imitator change to evade a word n-gram human-vs-machine detector that it can read?

How many words must an imitator change to evade a word n-gram human-vs-machine detector it can read? Deleting the 20 most machine-ward word types per text takes held-out AUROC from 0.948 to chance (0.487); a refit detector recovers to 0.94-1.00.

Abstract Code →

A word 1-2 gram logistic-regression detector (held-out AUROC 0.948 on poetry, reviews and wiki) is attacked by an imitator that knows its weights and deletes or swaps the k most machine-ward word types in each of its own texts. Deleting 10 word types drops AUROC to 0.738, 20 to 0.487 (chance) and 40 to 0.150; swapping 20 gives 0.317. A detector refit on text attacked the same way recovers to 0.94–1.00. Stylised: scripted edits with no fluency check, one seed, one detector family, no LLM run.

mimic-blackbox5 tests

How many detector queries does an imitator need to evade a human-vs-machine text detector it cannot read?

How many detector queries does an imitator need to evade a word n-gram human-vs-machine detector it cannot read? About 100 score queries per text, deleting the 20 best word types, take held-out AUROC from 0.948 to 0.520 (white-box 0.487); blind deletion does nothing. Stylised, no fluency check.

Abstract Code →

The word 1-2 gram detector of mimic-whitebox (held-out AUROC 0.948) is attacked by an imitator that sees only the score of each text it submits. It deletes each of Q candidate word types in turn, reads the score drop and removes the k largest. With k=20, 25 queries per text give AUROC 0.873, 50 give 0.722 and about 95 give 0.520, against 0.487 for the white-box attack that reads the weights; blind deletion (0 queries) changes nothing. Stylised and preliminary: a linear detector, one seed, no fluency check on the edited text, and no retraining of the detector against the attack.

mimic-retrain4 tests

Does refitting a human-vs-machine text detector on attacked text stop a black-box evader?

Does refitting a text detector on attacked text stop a black-box evader? It settles after one refit: fresh-attack AUROC stays near 0.81 (from 0.719) while clean AUROC falls from 0.948 to about 0.90. Stylised, no fluency check.

Abstract Code →

A black-box attacker with 50 score queries per text takes the mimic-whitebox word 1-2 gram detector from held-out AUROC 0.948 to 0.719. Refitting the detector on attacked training texts and letting the attacker re-attack settles after one round: AUROC on freshly attacked text stays near 0.81 over four rounds, while clean-text AUROC falls to about 0.90. Edits made against the original detector transfer to the refit ones at 0.85. Stylised: linear detector, one seed, no fluency check, no LLM run.

mimic-genshift5 tests

Does a prompt-free human-vs-machine detector carry over to a generator or decoding it never saw?

Does a prompt-free detector carry over to a generator or decoding it never saw? The mimic-contexts n-gram detector loses 0.01 to 0.02 AUROC on a chat model left out of the fit (0.96 to 0.98 left out) and 0.025 to 0.05 on a left-out decoding (sampling 0.936); averaging over four same-source texts lifts AUROC to 0.999. Preliminary, plain-prompt RAID text only.

Abstract Code →

The mimic-contexts n-gram detector fit on all eight RAID families, scored on text from a chat model or decoding left out of the fit (items split in two halves by source_id, halves swapped). AUROC falls from 0.991 to 0.978 (llama-chat), 0.983 to 0.971 (mistral-chat) and 0.981 to 0.959 (mpt-chat); leaving out sampling decoding costs 0.984 → 0.936 and greedy 0.989 → 0.964, with held-out wiki the weak spot (0.83 on sampling). Averaging the score over k same-source texts lifts AUROC from 0.971 (k=1) to 0.999 (k=4). Human batches are more varied than model batches (recipes distinct-2 0.589 against 0.373 for llama and 0.399 for mistral), but mpt-chat matches or exceeds human variety on poetry and reddit. Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text, three chat models each present in only some families (generator and family partly confounded), one detector type, no LLM run.

mimic-stack4 tests

Does adding a zero-shot perplexity score to the n-gram detector help it catch machine text in families it never saw?

Does adding a zero-shot perplexity score to the n-gram detector help on unseen families? The two scores are uncorrelated within class, but averaging them lifts held-out AUROC only from 0.926 to 0.935 (paired gain +0.009, interval −0.010 to +0.026); fitted stacks do no better. Preliminary, 720 held-out texts, small scorer, no LLM run.

Abstract Code →

The mimic-contexts n-gram detector and its Binoculars-style score (Qwen2.5-0.5B) are uncorrelated within each class (−0.02 human, 0.02 machine), yet combining them barely helps on the held-out families poetry, reviews and wiki: n-gram AUROC 0.926, mean of z-scores 0.935 (paired gain +0.009, 95% interval −0.010 to +0.026), fitted logistic stacks −0.003 and −0.019. It helps on wiki (0.892 to 0.935) and hurts on poetry and mpt-chat, where the zero-shot score is weak. Preliminary: 720 held-out texts, three chat models, a small scorer, one split; no LLM was run.

mimic-surface4 tests

How much text does a prompt-free human-vs-machine detector need, and what does it key on?

How much text does a prompt-free detector need, and what does it key on? The mimic-contexts n-gram detector on held-out families: AUROC 0.65 at 50 characters, 0.84 at 400, 0.93 at 1500; stripping punctuation or shuffling words costs at most 0.014. Preliminary, plain-prompt RAID text only.

Abstract Code →

The mimic-contexts n-gram detector (TF-IDF character and word n-grams, fitted on five families) is scored on poetry, reviews and wiki after cutting each text to its first N characters: AUROC 0.65 at 50, 0.75 at 100, 0.84 at 400 (the length the imitation-game loop shows its detector) and 0.93 at 1,500; refitting on the short text recovers only 0.02–0.07. Stripping punctuation changes AUROC by +0.003 and shuffling words by −0.014, so the detector reads vocabulary, not syntax or formatting (lowercasing and whitespace views are no-ops for this vectoriser). Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text only, one detector, one split, no LLM involved.

mimic-threshold5 tests

If a human-vs-machine detector's threshold is set for a 5% false-positive rate, does that rate hold on a kind of text it never saw?

If a detector's threshold is set for a 5% false-positive rate, does it hold on an unseen text type? Leave-one-family-out with the mimic-contexts n-gram detector: realised rate 0.00 to 0.54 (abstracts 0.54, books 0.18), and recipes catch 1.7% of machine text. Preliminary, plain-prompt RAID text only.

Abstract Code →

The mimic-contexts n-gram detector is fit on seven RAID families and its threshold set so 5% of human text is flagged (out-of-fold), then applied to the eighth. Realised false-positive rates run from 0.00 to 0.54: abstracts 0.54, books 0.18, while news, poetry, recipes, reddit, reviews and wiki sit at 0.00–0.06. On recipes the cut-off is too strict instead: it catches 1.7% of machine text where a threshold set on recipes would catch 46%. AUROC does not show this (books has the best, 0.993, and the second-worst rate). Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text, one detector type, one split, no LLM run.

mimic-recalib5 tests

How many human texts does it take to re-set a detector's threshold for a 5% false-positive rate on a new kind of text?

How many human texts does it take to re-set a detector's threshold for a 5% false-positive rate on a new kind of text? About 80: with the plain 95th percentile k = 20 gives a mean false-positive rate of 9% (36% chance above 10%), k = 80 gives 6.1%; a conformal rule holds 4.9% but costs recall and needs 19+ texts. Stylised, RAID text, one n-gram detector.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-threshold. The n-gram detector is fit on seven RAID families; k human texts of the eighth set its cut-off, 500 random draws per cell. Taking the empirical 95th percentile, k = 20 gives a mean false-positive rate of 9% and a 36% chance of exceeding 10%; k = 80 gives 6.1% and 10%; k = 160 gives 5.5%. A conformal rank rule holds the mean at 4.7–4.9% from k = 20 but gives up recall (0.66 against 0.79 at k = 20) and cannot flag anything below 19 calibration texts. Even at k = 80 one draw lands anywhere from 1.7% to 8.8% (10th–90th percentile). Recalibration fixes the false-accusation rate, not the detector: recipes still catches under half of machine text. Preliminary: plain-prompt RAID text, one detector, calibration from the same population as the test, no LLM run.

mimic-batch7 tests

How many texts from one source does a weak human-vs-machine text detector need before a batch verdict is reliable?

How many texts from one source does a weak human-vs-machine detector need before a batch verdict is reliable? Four all-machine texts give AUROC 0.997 (one text: 0.935); a quarter-machine source needs about 32; but a threshold set on 150 human texts drifts from 7% to 15% false flags at k = 32. Preliminary, RAID text, one n-gram detector.

Abstract Code →

The mimic-contexts n-gram detector scores a held-out RAID family; a batch is k independent texts and its statistic is their mean score. One text separates people from a plainly prompted LLM at AUROC 0.935 (mean of 8 families); four all-machine texts reach 0.997 and eight reach 1.00. If only half the batch is machine, k = 8 gives 0.98; a quarter needs about 32 (0.985); at 10% machine 32 texts give only 0.82. The catch is calibration: with a threshold set on 150 human texts, the share of human batches flagged drifts from 7.4% at k = 1 to 15% on average at k = 32 (books 60%), because the batch mean's spread shrinks while the calibration error does not. Preliminary: plain-prompt text, i.i.d. batches, one detector, no LLM run.

mimic-twinc2st8 tests

Does a classifier two-sample test catch digital-twin errors that a paired trajectory error misses?

Does a classifier two-sample test catch digital-twin errors that a paired trajectory error misses? Stylised pendulum: boosted-tree AUROC 0.72 for a friction error whose RMSE is a quarter of the sensor noise, 0.92 for Gaussian-vs-Student-t noise at zero paired error. Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

A stylised pendulum with Coulomb friction and heavy-tailed (Student-t) sensor noise is the ‘real’ system; twins differ in friction, noise shape or noise level. A classifier two-sample test (5-fold CV AUROC, 800 vs 800 trajectories, 3 seeds) separates real from twin trajectories with boosted trees: a friction error of 0.03 (10%) that moves the noise-free trajectory by only 0.006 rad RMSE — a quarter of the 0.02 rad noise sd — gives AUROC 0.72, and 0.91 at 20%. A twin with the right dynamics but Gaussian instead of Student-t noise of the same sd has paired error exactly 0 yet AUROC 0.92 once second-difference features are added (0.59 on raw angles). A logistic regression on raw angles stays at chance (0.51) throughout, because the start angles are symmetric. Limits: one toy system, two noise models, three seeds, a handful of classifier settings; simulated only, nothing about real hardware. Preliminary, no LLM involved: a side piece of track 11.

mimic-mmd8 tests

Does a kernel MMD test catch the same wrong digital twins as a classifier two-sample test?

Does a kernel MMD test catch the same wrong digital twins as a classifier two-sample test? Stylised pendulum: raw-trajectory MMD is blind to a Coulomb-friction error (power 0.05 to 0.06) that boosted trees catch from n = 200, but MMD on second differences detects a +25% noise-level error at 0.97 from n = 100.

Abstract Code →

A kernel two-sample test (unbiased RBF MMD, median-heuristic bandwidth) is compared with a gradient-boosted classifier two-sample test on the stylised pendulum of mimic-twinc2st. Rejection uses the 95th percentile of the exact twin’s own statistic. Raw-trajectory MMD has essentially no power against a Coulomb-friction error at n = 100–400 per class (0.05–0.06 at the median bandwidth, 0.37 at 0.03× for −20% friction), where the classifier reaches 1.00 at −20% from n = 200. MMD on second differences detects a +25% noise-level error at 0.97 from n = 100, where the raw-feature classifier is at 0.08–0.25. Stylised; 24 classifier replicates per cell, so those intervals are wide.

mimic-mujocotwin6 tests

Does a classifier two-sample test see the integrator, timestep and friction gaps of a MuJoCo digital twin?

Does a classifier two-sample test see the integrator, timestep and friction gaps of a MuJoCo digital twin? Stylised pendulum: AUROC 0.98 for Euler at 0.02 s, 0.53 (null) for a paired error of 0.003 rad, 0.92 for Gaussian-vs-Student-t noise at zero paired error. Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

A MuJoCo hinge pendulum (RK4, 0.002 s, dry friction, Student-t sensor noise) is the ‘real’ system; twins change the integrator, timestep or friction. A boosted-tree classifier two-sample test (800 trajectories per class, 3 seeds) has AUROC 0.98 for semi-implicit Euler at 0.02 s (paired RMSE 0.028 rad), 0.90 at 0.01 s, 0.67 at 0.005 s (0.007 rad) and 0.53 at 0.002 s (0.003 rad), which is not separable from the null 0.51. A friction error of 10% gives 0.52 and 20% gives 0.61. Gaussian instead of Student-t noise of the same sd has zero paired error but AUROC 0.92. Limits: one toy system, one classifier, 3 seeds; the ‘real’ system is itself simulated. Stylised, preliminary.

mimic-mmdmujoco8 tests

Does a kernel MMD test catch the same wrong MuJoCo digital twins as a classifier two-sample test?

Does a kernel MMD test catch the same wrong MuJoCo digital twins as a classifier two-sample test? Stylised MuJoCo pendulum: boosted-tree C2ST power 1.00 at n = 200 for Euler at 0.02 s and a noise-shape error where MMD stays near 0.05; MMD on second differences catches a +25% noise-level error; friction errors undetected by all at n <= 200.

Abstract Code →

A MuJoCo hinge pendulum with Student-t sensor noise is the ‘real’ system; twins change the integrator, friction or noise. Rejection uses the 95th percentile of the exact twin’s own statistic. Boosted-tree C2ST power is 1.00 at n = 200 for semi-implicit Euler at 0.02 s and 0.90 at 0.01 s, and 1.00 for a Gaussian-vs-Student-t noise-shape error, where MMD (raw or on second differences) stays at 0.00–0.07. MMD on second differences does catch a +25% noise-level error (0.95 at n = 100). A 10–20% friction error is invisible to all three at n ≤ 200. Limitations: one toy system, 20 C2ST replicates, two sample sizes. Stylised.

mimic-twinregret9 tests

Does a digital twin that a classifier can tell apart from the real system also make a worse controller?

Does a digital twin that a classifier can tell apart from the real system also make a worse controller? Stylised pendulum: 6 of 15 wrong twins have zero controller regret at C2ST AUROC 0.58 to 0.999; the worst regret (3.8%) comes from a twin with no sensor noise and zero paired error. Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

In the stylised pendulum of mimic-twinc2st with a torque input, a PD controller on noisy feedback is tuned on each wrong twin (48-point gain grid, 200 twin start angles) and scored on 2,000 held-out start angles on the ‘real’ system. Regret is its real cost minus the best grid point’s (0.259). Six of 15 wrong twins have regret exactly 0 in all 12 tuning seeds although the classifier two-sample test separates them from the real system with AUROC 0.58–0.999, among them g/L −20%, whose paired error is the largest (0.25 rad). The largest regret, 0.0099 (3.8%), comes from a twin with no sensor noise at all, whose paired error is 0. Across the 15 twins AUROC and regret correlate only loosely (Spearman 0.46, p = 0.08) and paired RMSE not at all (−0.28). Detecting a twin is not the same as the twin mattering for the task. Limits: one system, one task, a coarse grid that quantises regret, 12 tuning seeds. Stylised, simulated, no LLM: a side piece of track 11.

mimic-twinswing9 tests

On a swing-up task where friction matters, does a digital twin's detectability predict what tuning on it costs?

On a swing-up task where friction matters, does a twin's detectability predict what tuning on it costs? Stylised pendulum: only the two gravity-error twins cost much (3.7% and 8.3% extra real cost); 13 others cost under 0.3% at C2ST AUROC 0.51 to 1.0. Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-twinregret on the same stylised pendulum, now with a torque limit below gravity so the controller must pump energy against friction, then catch the top with PD. Controllers are tuned on 15 wrong twins (60-point grid, 12 seeds) and scored on held-out real starts. Only the two gravity-error twins cost much: g/L +20% adds 8.3% to the best real cost and g/L −20% 3.7%; every other twin is under 0.3%, including no sensor noise, no Coulomb friction and doubled viscous friction, at C2ST AUROC up to 1.0. Spearman AUROC vs regret ρ = 0.16 (p = 0.57), paired RMSE vs regret 0.43 (p = 0.11). Stylised, one task, coarse grid; best gain on the grid edge for several twins.

mimic-twinswinggrid9 tests

Does a finer controller grid change which wrong digital twins cost something on a swing-up task?

Does a finer controller grid change which wrong pendulum twins cost something on the swing-up task? No: the same two gravity-error twins cost 3.8% and 6.1%, the rest under 0.3%; detectability vs regret ρ = 0.38 (p = 0.16). Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

Robustness check of mimic-twinswing with a 144-point gain grid instead of 60 (same pendulum, 15 wrong twins, 12 seeds). The same two gravity-error twins cost much: g/L +20% adds 6.1% to the best real cost and g/L −20% 3.8%; every other twin is at or below 0.3%. Coarse and fine regret rank the twins alike (Spearman ρ = 0.79, p = 0.001). AUROC vs regret ρ = 0.38 (p = 0.16), paired RMSE vs regret 0.25 (p = 0.38): still no reliable link, but 15 twins give little power. Stylised, one task; AUROC borrowed from the earlier run.

mimic-twingrid8 tests

Does a wider gain grid, or a controller that uses the twin's gravity, change which wrong digital twins are costly?

Does a wider gain grid, or a controller that uses the twin's gravity, change which wrong pendulum twins are costly? Gravity errors stay the costly ones; giving the controller the twin's g/L made g/L −20% regret 13 times larger (0.013 to 0.177). Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-twinswing on the same stylised swing-up pendulum, removing two confounds: the best pump gain sat at the edge of the grid, and the controller's gravity constant was fixed. With ke up to 32 (126 controllers, 14 twins, 8 seeds) gravity errors remain the costly twins and sensor-noise errors stay under 0.0010. Letting the controller use the twin's own g/L made gravity errors worse: g/L −20% regret rises from 0.013 to 0.177 and g/L +20% falls from 0.036 to 0.017. Spearman AUROC vs regret is ρ = 0.63 (p = 0.021) but is driven by four gravity twins, and is not comparable with the earlier twin set. Preliminary: one toy system, simulated only.

mimic-twinrand5 tests

Does domain randomization over a wrong digital twin cut the controller regret of tuning on one wrong twin?

Does tuning a controller on a spread of randomized twins cut the regret of tuning on one wrong twin? Stylised pendulum: it brings the no-noise twin's regret from 0.0098 to 0.00006, but a very wide range raises a doubled-noise twin's worst-seed regret 7.5-fold. Preliminary, no LLM.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-twinregret on the same stylised pendulum and noisy-feedback PD task. Gains are tuned on 200 start angles spread over 8 randomized twins (noise level, Coulomb and viscous friction, g/L each uniform on nominal ± w× the real value) and scored on 2,000 held-out real start angles, over 24 tuning seeds. For the no-noise twin, whose single-twin regret is 0.0098, randomization with w = 0.5 brings it to 0.00006, the same as the exact twin. No-Coulomb and g/L +20% twins fall from 0.0014 to 0.00012 at w = 1–2. It does not always help: for a doubled-noise twin regret stays about 0.003 for w ≤ 1 and at w = 2 the mean rises to 0.0057 with a worst seed 7.5× the single-twin worst. Limits: one system and task, a 48-point grid that quantises regret, one randomization family with a shared width. Stylised, simulated, no LLM.

mimic-twinnoiserand4 tests

Does randomizing only the sensor-noise level of a wrong digital twin keep domain randomization's rescue without its blow-up?

Does randomizing only the noise level of a wrong twin keep domain randomization's rescue without its blow-up? Stylised pendulum: the no-noise twin's regret goes 0.0098 to 0 and stays small at a wide range (worst seed 0.0015 vs 0.042 for all-four), but friction and gravity errors are not helped. Preliminary, no LLM.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-twinrand on the same stylised pendulum PD task. Only the twin's noise sd is spread (uniform on nominal ± w×0.02); friction and g/L stay nominal. A no-noise twin's regret falls from 0.0098 to 0 at w=2 and stays at 0.00035 (worst seed 0.0015) at w=4, where randomizing all four parameters has a worst seed of 0.042. A doubled-noise twin improves monotonically (0.0038 to 0.0012), which all-four did not. Friction and gravity errors are untouched (0.00138 at every width). 24 seeds, 48-point grid; preliminary, one toy system, no LLM.

mimic-twinpower5 tests

How many real trajectories does a classifier test need to flag a wrong digital twin, and are the twins it flags the ones that cost a controller?

How many real trajectories does a classifier test need to flag a wrong digital twin, and are the twins it flags the ones that cost a controller? Stylised pendulum: all six twins with controller regret of at least 0.001 are flagged by 80 real trajectories, and so are three that cost nothing. Preliminary, simulated only.

Abstract Code →

On the stylised pendulum of mimic-twinregret, a boosted-tree C2ST with n real and n twin trajectories flags a twin when its AUROC beats the 95th percentile of the exact-twin null at the same n (20 replicates per cell, n = 10 to 160). The six twins whose controller regret is at least 0.001 are all flagged in at least 80% of replicates by n = 80 (by 40 for the four noise-level and noise-shape twins), so the test does not miss costly twins at that size. It also flags three twins that cost nothing (g/L −20%, noise ×0.5, noise ×0.75) by n = 40–80, while Coulomb −10% and −20% stay unflagged at 160. Spearman correlation of power at 80 with regret is 0.52 (p = 0.048, 15 twins). A flag is a cheap alarm, not a verdict on usefulness. Limits: one system, one task, 20 replicates, a null threshold that is degenerate at n ≤ 20. Stylised, simulated, no LLM.

mimic-dialogue7 tests

Does a second turn make a plainly prompted LLM easier to spot in dialogue?

Does a second turn make a plainly prompted LLM easier to spot in dialogue? A prompt-free n-gram detector gets AUROC 0.93 on one imitated user turn and 0.98 on two, on 400 OpenAssistant threads with a 0.5B imitator. Stylised baseline, no prompt optimised.

Abstract Code →

Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, given only a plain prompt, writes a user's second and third message in 400 real OpenAssistant threads. A prompt-free character and word n-gram detector (5-fold cross-validation grouped by thread) gets AUROC 0.93 on a single turn and 0.98 on the two turns together (paired accuracy 0.98); length alone gets 0.65 and 0.71. A quarter of the imitations read like assistant replies; dropping those threads leaves 0.95 for the thread. Limits: volunteer prompter turns, one 0.5B imitator and prompt, one seed, teacher-forced turns, no group-level false-positive rates. Stylised baseline; no prompt is optimised.

mimic-cursor9 tests

Can an imitator that changes its own code fool a human-vs-bot cursor detector, and does shared feedback help either side?

Can an imitator that changes its own code fool a human-vs-bot cursor detector, and does shared feedback help? On DUX cursor strokes of 46 people, a held-out reference detector catches every final imitator at AUROC 0.99 to 1.00 in all four feedback conditions; two-way sharing gave the strongest detectors in cross-play (0.81 vs 0.70 blind, interval includes 0), and an 8x larger search stops at 0.88, the level of replaying real strokes. Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Browser use, the first subject of the adversarial-imitation track beyond writing. Cursor strokes of 46 people from DUX (CC-BY-4.0) against an imitator built from code components and a detector that picks 3 of 11 feature functions, 4 feedback conditions × 8 seeds × 30 rounds at equal budget. A reference detector the loop never saw catches every final imitator at AUROC 0.99 to 1.00; detector explanations and shared imitator code did not make a better imitator. Detectors trained with two-way sharing did best against other runs’ imitators (cross-play AUROC 0.81 vs 0.70 blind), but the paired interval includes zero. An 8× larger search ends at 0.88, no better than replaying a real stroke, so the component library is the limit. Preliminary: one web form, 8 seeds, no model-written code.

mimic-webcam8 tests

Can a generator imitate a person's webcam emotion signals well enough to fool a detector?

Can a generator imitate a person's webcam emotion signals well enough to fool a detector? On DUX Affectiva scores of 46 people, every fixed generator and every loop-tuned imitator is caught at AUROC 0.997 or higher by a detector the loop never saw; only replaying real windows gets close to chance (0.61). Preliminary.

Abstract Code →

Webcam, the third subject of the adversarial-imitation track, signals first: no pixels or faces. Ten-second windows of 12 facial-coding channels (Affectiva scores logged by DUX, CC-BY-4.0) from 46 people, split by person. Six fixed generators from constant to AR(1) with channel correlation, holds and spikes, and an imitator that tunes its own generator code against a 3-feature-group detector for 30 rounds (8 seeds; 4 seeds at 8× the budget), are all separated from held-out people by a boosted-tree reference detector the loop never saw at AUROC 0.997 or higher. Only replaying whole windows of other people gets near chance (0.61, which is the gap between people). Preliminary and stylised: one context, a fixed component library, and windows biased toward moments when the person was using the mouse or keyboard.

mimic-webcam-tails5 tests

Does giving a webcam-signal generator real heavy tails and bursts fool a detector?

Does giving a webcam-signal generator real heavy tails and bursts fool a detector? No: copula and quiet/burst generators still separate from held-out people at AUROC 1.000 (8 seeds); restoring per-window level and spread brings level and spread to near chance, but extremes (0.995) still give it away; copying a real window's value set (G6) puts those at chance too, yet all-groups AUROC stays 0.998 on temporal structure.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to mimic-webcam on DUX facial-coding scores of 46 people. Generators that take each channel's marginal from the training people (Gaussian copula through empirical quantiles; quiet/burst regimes) still separate from 14 held-out people at reference AUROC 1.000 (8 seeds). Matching marginals alone made level and spread easier to catch (0.99–1.00 vs 0.91 and 0.94 for the Gaussian baseline); restoring per-window level and spread brings them to 0.54 and 0.57, but extremes (0.995), holds (0.995) and autocorrelation (0.94) still give it away. A sixth generator that copies a real window’s whole value set puts level, spread, extremes and floor at chance (0.44–0.46), yet all-groups AUROC stays 0.998: holds, autocorrelation, roughness and cross-channel structure carry it. Stylised: hand-built generators, one context, post-hoc final variants.

mimic-webcam-stitch4 tests

Why is block-stitched real webcam signal still caught: the joins, or mixing people?

Why is block-stitched real webcam signal still caught? With 50-frame blocks random stitching gives AUROC 0.887, one person's windows only 0.687, join-matched 0.796, both 0.588 (= whole-window replay 0.597); at 5 frames all are caught (8 seeds).

Abstract Code →

Ceiling study on the DUX webcam expression signals: 100-frame windows stitched from real blocks of 5 to 50 frames, scored by a boosted-tree detector on 14 held-out people (8 seeds). With 50-frame blocks random stitching is caught at AUROC 0.887; blocks from one person only give 0.687; join-matched blocks 0.796; both together 0.588, equal to replaying whole windows (0.597). At 5 frames everything is caught (≥0.989). Mixing people is the larger giveaway, join mismatch smaller, and removing both only reaches the replay ceiling. Every frame is real, so this is not a generator. Stylised: one form-filling context, 46 people.

21

Open-source residential construction

Cutting what it costs to design and build a home, with the engineering done as open, testable code and the designs published. Topic page →

house-framing12 tests

How much lumber, labour and heat does advanced framing save in a house's exterior walls, and does it still carry the roof?

How much does advanced (OVE) framing save in a house's exterior walls? Stylised 28 × 40 ft house: 42% less wall lumber and 27% fewer pieces than conventional 2x6, whole-wall R 16.2 to 18.6, studs at 39% of capacity under 30 psf snow; the lumber is worth only $450–900 a house, so labour carries the case. Not a code check. First project of track 12.

Abstract Code →

An open takeoff of a stylised 28 × 40 ft one-storey house: every stud, plate, header, cripple and block under conventional and advanced (OVE) framing, with the NDS stud and header checks and a parallel-path whole-wall R-value. Advanced 2x6 framing at 24 in used 42% less exterior-wall lumber than conventional 2x6 and 27% fewer pieces, and raised the whole-wall R-value from 16.2 to 18.6. It still used 16% less lumber than conventional 2x4. At 30 psf of roof snow its studs work at 39% of capacity. The biggest single savings were 24 in spacing, the single top plate and header hangers. At assumed lumber prices the wall saving is only $450 to $900 a house, so the case for advanced framing rests on labour, which the model counts as pieces but does not price. Stylised: one house, exterior walls only, no lateral design, no labour rates, and not a code check or a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

house-spans13 tests

How far can a 2x joist, rafter, header or beam span, and which check limits it?

How far can a 2x joist, rafter, header or beam span? Open NDS sizing tool, no table copied: 2x10 SPF floor joists at 16 in span 15 ft 3 in, bending governs most floors and snow rafters, deflection most ceilings; deepest joist at 24 in uses 20–50% less lumber (vibration unchecked). Not validated against published tables. Milestone 2 of track 12.

Abstract Code →

An open sizing tool for simple-span sawn-lumber members, derived from beam formulas and NDS base design values with no span table copied: bending, shear, deflection and bearing checks, a command line, and the governing check named for every result. For SPF No. 2 floor joists at 16 in the longest clear spans are 9 ft 2 in (2x6), 12 ft 1 in (2x8), 15 ft 3 in (2x10) and 17 ft 8 in (2x12). Bending governs 22 of 32 floor cells and live-load deflection the other 10; total-load deflection governs 31 of 32 ceiling cells; bending governs snow-loaded rafters in 29 of 32. The lightest passing floor joist is the deepest at 24 in, which uses 20–50% less lumber than 2x10 at 16 in, but floor vibration is not checked. A cross-check with house-framing found its header bearing area too generous for a single jack under a 2-ply header. Not validated against published span tables, no engineered lumber, no continuous spans, and not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

house-vibration6 tests

Does a floor-vibration frequency limit erase the lumber saved by deep, widely spaced joists?

Does a floor-vibration frequency limit erase the lumber saved by deep, widely spaced joists? Beam-theory first-mode frequency on the house-spans checks: limits up to 10 Hz change nothing, 12 Hz shortens a 2x10 at 16 in from 15 ft 3 in to 13 ft 11 in, 15 Hz moves the least-lumber 12 ft joist from 2x10 to 2x12. Joist alone, limit is a policy knob. Stylised. Track 12.

Abstract Code →

A first-mode natural-frequency check (f1 = (π/2L2)√(EIg/w), derived and tested against the static-deflection form) added to the NDS strength and deflection checks of house-spans, for SPF No. 2 floor joists under 10 + 40 psf. The joist alone is modelled, with no subfloor composite action. Any limit up to 10 Hz changes nothing: the longest strength-passing 2x10 at 16 in (15 ft 3 in) already vibrates at 10.1 Hz. At 12 Hz it shortens to 13 ft 11 in, and at 15 Hz the least-lumber joist at a 12 ft span moves from 2x10 at 24 in (0.83 board feet per sq ft) to 2x12 at 24 in (1.00), while at 14 ft the 2x12 at 24 in no longer passes and 2x12 at 16 in (1.50) is needed. The limit in Hz is a policy choice swept here, not a code-book criterion, and the model is conservative by ignoring the subfloor and optimistic by ignoring live-load mass. Stylised.

house-composite6 tests

How much of a floor-vibration penalty does the subfloor's T-beam action recover?

How much of a floor-vibration penalty does the subfloor's T-beam action recover? Gamma-method partial-composite stiffness on house-vibration: at a 15 Hz limit a 2x10 at 16 in grows from 12 ft 6 in to 13 ft 2 in–14 ft 6 in, depending on two assumed inputs (connection efficiency and panel modulus). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The subfloor modelled as a partial flange of a T-beam by the gamma method (rederived from the parallel-axis theorem and tested against an independent transformed-section calculation), added to the frequency check of house-vibration for a 2x10 SPF No. 2 joist at 16 in. The result depends on two assumed, unsourced inputs, the connection efficiency γ and the panel modulus. At a panel modulus of 0.5 million psi the 15 ft first-mode frequency rises from 10.5 Hz to 12.6 Hz at γ 0.5 and 14.0 Hz at γ 1, and under a 15 Hz limit the span grows from 12 ft 6 in to 13 ft 2 in–14 ft 6 in. Strength checks stay joist-alone; live-load mass is left out, so gains are optimistic. Stylised, not validated against a measured floor, not a design.

house-continuous11 tests

Does a joist lapped over a middle support span farther than a simple-span joist?

Does a joist lapped over a middle support span farther than a simple span? FE beam with pattern loading and NDS checks: two-span peak moment equals a simple span's, so bending-governed floors and snow rafters gain nothing; deflection-governed ceiling joists gain up to 18.5%; 1.5 in bearing on the middle support cuts a 2x10 floor joist to 11 ft 4 in. Not validated against published tables. Follow-up to house-spans.

Abstract Code →

A pure-Python finite-element beam with pattern loading and the NDS bending, shear, bearing and deflection checks of house-spans, for two- and three-span continuous sawn-lumber joists (SPF No. 2). Under full uniform load a two-span joist's peak moment, wL2/8 at the middle support, equals a simple span's, so members whose simple span is governed by bending (most floor joists, all snow rafters) gain nothing from two spans (0.0% in 16 floor cells; three spans add about 5%), while deflection-governed ceiling joists gain 0.6% to 18.5%. With only 1.5 in of bearing on the middle support, the 1.25wL reaction limits a 2x10 floor joist at 16 in to 11 ft 4 in, against 15 ft 3 in with 3.5 in. Stylised: equal spans, no vibration, not compared with published span tables. Not a structural design.

house-unequal9 tests

How far can the beam under a two-span joist sit from the middle of the house?

How far can the beam under a two-span joist sit from the middle of the house? Bending-governed floor joists lose 0.4% of total width at a short/long span ratio of 0.9 and 13% at 0.5 (the short span relieves the long one); deflection-governed ceiling joists lose about 5% per 0.1 of ratio. A 2x10 floor can have its beam 3.5 ft off the middle of a 28 ft house. Stylised; not a design.

Abstract Code →

Two-span sawn-lumber joists (SPF No. 2) with unequal spans, reusing the finite-element beam of house-continuous and the NDS checks of house-spans with pattern loading and per-span deflection. For a 2x10 floor joist at 16 in, moving the beam off-centre costs 0.4% of total clear width at a short/long span ratio of 0.9, 4.3% at 0.7 and 13.3% at 0.5, because the short span relieves the long one (the long span grows from 15 ft 3 in to 17 ft 7 in); a 2x8 ceiling joist, which deflection governs, loses 5.1% at 0.9 and 24.1% at 0.5. A 28 ft wide house tolerates a beam 3.5 ft off the middle. Stylised. Not validated against published span tables, two spans only, no vibration, and not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review. The short span's end lifts off its support whenever live load is on the long span only (−103 lb per joist at a 10 ft short span, −271 lb at 6 ft; 2x10 floor).

house-plan14 tests

Can a house plan be data, and which plan needs the least framing lumber per square foot?

Can a house plan be data, and which plan needs the least lumber per sq ft? Parametric one-storey plan to framing takeoff, bill of materials, room-rule checks and IFC4; best plans use 4.8 to 5.2 bf/sq ft at 640 to 1,024 sq ft with none feasible by stick framing at 1,400; local search hits the exhaustive optimum in 36 of 40 runs where random search hits none. Stylised, not a design.

Abstract Code →

A single-storey house plan as a few parameters: rooms, walls and openings, a framing takeoff with members sized by the open NDS tools of house-spans and house-framing, a bill of materials, IRC-style room-size, light and egress checks, and an IFC4 export through IfcOpenShell. A search over 182,520 plans finds the least lumber per square foot: with two or more bedrooms the best plans use 4.8–5.2 board feet per sq ft at 640–1,024 sq ft and 5.9 at 1,216, and no stick-framed plan in the grid reaches 1,400 sq ft because joists and rafters run out of 2x12. Only 1.3% of the grid passes every check at 1,000–1,150 sq ft. At equal budgets a (1+1) local search found the exact optimum in 36 of 40 runs at 2,000 evaluations and random search in none. Stylised: one rectangular layout, stick framing only, board feet rather than prices, room rules paraphrased from memory, and not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

house-cost8 tests

Where does a new home's price go, and which levers move it most?

Where does a new home's price go, and which levers move it most? Share-anchored model (NAHB 2024): size moves the price most (87.8 to 112.0 for 1,600 to 2,400 sq ft), then storeys, finish level and lot; a 14% framing-lumber cut is worth 0.85% of price (2.4% with labour). Index not dollars, assumed driver splits. Milestone 4 of track 12.

Abstract Code →

A driver-based price model anchored on NAHB's 2024 cost shares (construction 64.4% of the price, framing 16.6% of construction, lot 13.7%, profit 11.0%). Each construction stage scales with floor area, footprint or wall area, and the model reproduces every NAHB share at its 2,000 sq ft reference house. In a sweep, size moves the price most (index 87.8 to 112.0 for 1,600 to 2,400 sq ft), then one against three storeys (111.6 to 97.6), finish level, lot price and foundation type. A 14% cut in framing lumber, the gap between house-plan's default and best plans, is worth only 0.85% of the price, or 2.4% if it also cuts framing labour by 20%. Stylised: a price index, not dollars; the stage-driver splits and lever ranges are my assumptions; the Census reconciliation and a priced takeoff are not done.

house-costsens7 tests

Does the house-cost lever ranking survive its assumed driver splits?

Does the house-cost lever ranking survive its assumed driver splits? Monte Carlo over the splits: floor area stays the largest lever in 96–100% of draws; storeys is the soft claim (swing 9.0–19.9 vs 14.0 baseline); the lumber result does not move. Index not dollars.

Abstract Code →

A Monte Carlo over house-cost's assumed splits of each construction stage over floor area, footprint and wall area (Dirichlet, concentration 5, 20 and 80; 2,000 draws each). Floor area stays the largest lever in 96–100% of draws. Storeys is the soft claim: one versus three storeys swings the price index 9.0–19.9 points at concentration 20 (baseline 14.0), 5.1–24.1 at 5. The framing-lumber result does not move. Seven of ten levers cannot move under this test by construction. Stylised: tests only the splits, not the lever ranges or the NAHB shares.

house-sobol6 tests

Which uncertain input of the house-cost model drives the uncertainty in a house's price?

Which uncertain input of the house-cost model drives a house's price uncertainty? Sobol indices over every lever range, the framing share and the driver splits at once: floor area 53% of variance, storeys 19%, all framing inputs together under 1%. Index not dollars.

Abstract Code →

A variance-based (Sobol) global sensitivity analysis of house-cost, treating the ten lever ranges, the framing materials share and the assumed driver splits as random at once (4,096 base samples, bootstrap intervals). Floor area explains 53% of the price-index variance and storeys 19%; finish level, lot price and foundation type 6–9% each. The three framing inputs together explain under 1%, so the lumber saving optimised in house-plan barely moves the price of a whole house, and the assumed splits explain none alone and 1.7% through interactions. Per square foot, storeys matters more (25–27%). Stylised: the answer is relative to the assumed uniform ranges and ignores correlations.

house-energy9 tests

Which envelope upgrades pay for themselves over 30 years, by climate, and does advanced framing belong in the answer?

Which envelope upgrades pay back over 30 years, by climate? A degree-day net-present-cost search of 640 packages in eight climates: advanced 2x6 framing is in every optimum (13–15% lower cost than a 2x4 baseline); better windows and R-49 attics do not pay at assumed prices. Stylised, assumed prices, not EnergyPlus.

Abstract Code →

A degree-day net-present-cost search (not EnergyPlus) over 640 envelope packages of the house-framing house in eight US climates and two heating systems. The advanced 2x6 wall builds for $42 less than a conventional 2x4 and loses 40% less heat through the opaque wall, and is in every cost-optimal package: 13–15% lower 30-year cost than the baseline ($2,100–4,600). Past the wall the optimum is modest (attic R-30–38, 3 ACH50 air sealing, slab-edge insulation from about 3,000 degree-days); R-49 attics and better windows pay back in 23–190 years. At the assumed window prices the optimum picks U 0.50 windows, which a code floor of U 0.35 costs $440–1,270 to avoid; that result does not survive 4× energy prices. Stylised: every price is an assumption, climates are rounded from memory, and there is no solar gain.

house-wallsystems10 tests

Does any alternative to a wood-framed wall beat it on cost, carbon or heat loss for a small house?

Does any alternative to a wood-framed wall beat it on cost, carbon or heat loss for a small house? In a stylised model wood 2x6 is cheapest in 97% of random draws and lowest-carbon in 100%; SIP, CLT and printed walls win only on labour. Inputs are ranges from memory.

Abstract Code →

Prices six exterior wall systems (wood 2x6, steel stud, ICF, SIPs, CLT, 3D-printed concrete) on the 927 sq ft of net wall of the house-framing house, then runs 20,000 Monte Carlo draws over stylised cost, carbon and R-value ranges. Wood is cheapest in 96.8% of draws, lowest in product-stage carbon in 100% and lowest in first cost plus 30-year heat-loss cost in 99.9%; ICF and SIP save only about $500 of heat-loss present value against $5,500–8,300 more first cost, and SIP would need a 39% price cut to tie. SIPs and CLT take about half the crew hours. Stylised: every input is a range from memory, the result largely follows from them, biogenic carbon, avoided trades and strength are not credited or compared.

house-structure14 tests

Does a small wood-frame house have enough shear wall for wind and earthquakes once the windows and doors are cut out?

Does a small wood-frame house have enough shear wall for wind and earthquakes once the openings are cut out? At 115 mph and SDS 0.50 the 28 x 40 ft house uses 19% of a gable-wall line's capacity at 6 in nailing; the openings, not the load, are what shrink it. Stylised, capacities from memory.

Abstract Code →

Wind and seismic base shear on the house-framing house (28 × 40 ft, one storey) against the segmented shear-wall length its openings leave. At 115 mph and SDS 0.50 the worst case uses 19% of a gable-wall line's capacity at the loosest (6 in) nailing; wind must reach 264 mph before that nailing runs out. Lateral load does not govern this plan, but glazing does: four windows per gable wall cut the usable wall from 24 ft to 11 ft, six leave none. A 16 ft garage door in the gable wall raises the load share to 41% at 6 in nailing, and a centred 22 ft door needs tighter nailing. Advanced and conventional framing carry the same shear. Stylised: the nailing table and load coefficients are from memory and unchecked, and diaphragms, uplift and overturning are not modelled.

house-torsion6 tests

How much does accidental torsion add to the garage-front wall's demand in a rigid-diaphragm wind split?

How much does accidental torsion add to the garage-front wall's demand in a rigid-diaphragm wind split? Offsetting the load up to 15% of the length in house-nailedwall's split raises a 22 ft-door wall from 0.36–0.59 to 0.44–0.71 demand over capacity, still under the flexible 1.05. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Offsets the wind load by up to 15% of the house length in house-nailedwall's rigid roof-diaphragm split. The relief survives but shrinks: for a centred 22 ft garage door, demand over capacity at 6 in nailing rises from 0.36–0.59 (load at the centre) to 0.44–0.71 at a 15% offset, still below the flexible split's 1.05, while the partner wall moves only from 0.27–0.31 to 0.29–0.33. Stylised: placeholder offset, unverified stiffness constants, along-ridge wind only, not a code check.

house-nailedwall8 tests

Does the rigid-diaphragm relief for a garage-front wall survive a nailed-wall stiffness model?

Does the rigid-diaphragm relief for a garage-front wall survive a nailed-wall stiffness model? Four-term pier deflection (bending, shear, nail slip, hold-down) in house-diaphragm's rigid split: yes; a centred 22 ft door falls from 1.05 (flexible) to 0.36–0.59 demand over capacity. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Replaces the toy pier stiffness of house-diaphragm with a four-term deflection (chord bending, panel shear, nail slip, hold-down slip) and reruns the rigid roof-diaphragm split. The sign holds: a centred 22 ft garage door leaves the wall at 0.05–0.19 of its partner's stiffness, and its demand over capacity at 6 in nailing falls from 1.05 (flexible split) to 0.36, 0.48 and 0.59 at 100, 250 and 500 plf. Stylised: every constant is from memory and unchecked, stiffness is a secant at a fixed shear, and the flexible split still governs.

house-diaphragm7 tests

Does the half-and-half load split understate the demand on a garage-front wall?

Does the half-and-half load split understate the demand on a garage-front wall? In a toy stiffness model a rigid roof diaphragm gives the garage line less than half, so the flexible split governs; stylised, torsion not modelled.

Abstract Code →

Re-asks house-structure experiment G with a rigid roof diaphragm: a four-spring sway-and-twist model splits the 115 mph gable load by wall stiffness. In a toy stiffness model the garage line carries less than half (at a centred 22 ft door, demand over capacity at 6 in nailing falls from 1.05 to 0.18–0.63) and the partner wall stays under 0.35, so the flexible split is the governing case. Stylised: the stiffness is an assumption, and torsion, collectors and seismic are not modelled.

house-open-design15 tests

What does an open plan set for a 480 sq ft backyard cottage look like when generated from code? A 24 x 20 ft ADU composed from the track's models: drawings, bill of materials, IFC, lateral check, envelope energy (a tight envelope cuts modelled heating and cooling cost 36-37%) and a cost index. A worked example, not a buildable design; every input assumed.

Composes the track's six earlier models on one concrete design, a 24 × 20 ft one-bedroom accessory dwelling unit, and writes a floor plan and south elevation (SVG), a framing bill of materials (CSV), an IFC4 model and a report. The plan passes every layout rule and member check and needs 2,614 board feet of framing (5.45 per sq ft). A truss roof option (from house-truss) uses 38% less roof lumber than the stick roof (667 against 1,070 board feet, lumber only). Under house-structure's assumed coefficients the short walls carry 1,164 lb of wind per line at 6 in nailing; a tighter envelope cuts modelled heating and cooling cost 36–37% in every climate tested ($72–158 a year at assumed prices). The composition exposed rough edges (the lateral and energy models were built around a different house), the cost index is extrapolated far below its data, and nothing here is a buildable design: it needs a licensed review and a permit.

At what climate does each envelope upgrade start to pay, when climate is a continuous axis?

At what climate does each envelope upgrade start to pay? Climate as a continuous axis over house-energy's model: slab-edge R-10 from 3,271 heating degree-days with gas (2,386 with a heat pump), 3 ACH50 from 5,769, and cooling alone switches on only the attic and air sealing above ~3,000 cooling degree-days. Stylised: unsourced prices, no solar gain.

Abstract Code →

Makes heating and cooling degree-days the axis of house-energy’s 640-package net-present-cost search and finds each upgrade’s exact switch-on point. With a gas furnace and 500 cooling degree-days, slab-edge R-10 pays from 3,271 heating degree-days, an R-30 attic from 4,029, 5 ACH50 from 4,485, 3 ACH50 from 5,769 and an R-38 attic from 8,368; a heat pump lowers each of the first four by about 27% (2,386 to 4,209). Cooling switches on only the attic and air sealing, above about 3,000 cooling degree-days; windows never leave U 0.50. The slab-edge threshold falls exactly in proportion to the energy price. Stylised: house-energy’s unsourced prices, degree-day loads and no solar gain.

house-breakeven10 tests

How much extra can a tight envelope cost before it stops paying back on a 480 sq ft backyard cottage?

How much extra can a tight envelope cost before it stops paying back on a 480 sq ft backyard cottage? The ADU's whole upgrade package can carry $1,409 to $3,104 of extra first cost (3% real rate, heat pump); at assumed prices only the wall switch clearly pays. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Inverts the question house-energy asks: instead of the lowest-cost package, the largest extra first cost each upgrade can carry before its 30-year energy saving no longer covers it, on the house-open-design ADU (24 × 20 ft). The whole tight package (advanced 2x6 wall with R-5 foam, R-49 attic, U-0.27 windows, 3 ACH50, R-30 floor) saves $72 to $158 a year with a heat pump, so at a 3% real rate it can carry $1,409 (Houston) to $3,104 (Minneapolis) of extra cost, and $892 to $1,965 at 7%. Energy is linear in heat loss, so the one-at-a-time savings add up exactly to the package. At house-energy's unsourced unit prices the attic ($319 extra) only breaks even in Minneapolis, air sealing ($500) needs energy 1.3 to 2.6 times as dear, and the windows ($1,392) 2.7 to 5.5 times; the wall switch is the best of the five upgrades. Stylised: degree-day climates from memory, every price assumed, no first-cost data for the wall or floor, not a design anyone should build from without a licensed review.

Does a tighter envelope let a 480 sq ft backyard cottage use a smaller heat pump? The tight package cuts the design heating load about 36.5%, worth a $450 to $1,800 equipment step credit (assumed catalogue and prices) that nearly closes the payback gap of the costed upgrades in three colder climates. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Adds the term house-breakeven left out: the equipment downsizing credit. The design heating load (UA × design temperature difference) of the house-open-design ADU falls about 36.5% with the tight envelope in every climate, but equipment comes in discrete sizes, so the credit is a step: with an assumed catalogue and prices it is $450 (Houston), $1,350 (Baltimore), $900 (Chicago) and $1,800 (Minneapolis) for the whole package, and it is mostly the wall switch that moves the size. Added to the energy break-even, the three costed upgrades (assumed extra cost $2,211) come within $98 to $463 of paying back in the three colder cities but not in Houston ($1,607 short). The size is sensitive to the assumed design temperature and sizing margin, which are unchecked memory, so the credit is a range of one or two catalogue steps, not a number. Stylised: no EnergyPlus, no Manual J, no sourced prices.

When does cooling, not heating, set the heat pump size for a 480 sq ft backyard cottage? Houston’s downsizing credit ($450 at the headline inputs) swings between $0 and $900 across window SHGC and the latent allowance. Stylised: summer design temperatures, solar factors and gains are unchecked assumptions; not Manual J.

A pin-jointed W-type truss solved by a small stiffness solver, with NDS chord and web checks and a search for the lightest passing 2x4 to 2x8 truss at 24 in o.c., against stick-built 16 in rafters and ceiling joists from house-spans. When does building a house's wall shell in a factory beat building it on site? Panel layout, sheathing nesting (1 sheet in 33 saved) and a Monte Carlo of the shell: panelised takes 2.17 d against 1.96 d on site and costs 38% more at assumed rates; it is faster only from about 58 ft long. Closed panels (insulation, wiring, windows built in) cut the gap: cost parity at a factory labour ratio of about 0.45 and a day saved. Stylised, every rate assumed.

Abstract Code →

Splits the exterior walls of the house-framing house into panels, nests the sheathing, loads the trailers and runs a Monte Carlo of the shell crew's days with weather. Panelised took 2.17 calendar days against 1.96 on site and cost 38% more at assumed rates; factory productivity does not change the days because the factory runs behind the foundation, and panelised is faster only from about 58 ft long (78 with no weather, 44 at 30% loss). Factory nesting saved 1 sheet in 33 (bound 26): a 97 in wall on a 108 in sheet wastes the same strip either way. A closed-panel variant (wrap, insulation, wiring and window setting built in the factory) flips the cost result: at a factory labour ratio of 0.45 or better panelising is within 1% of site cost and 0.3 beats it by 10%, and it saves about a day (2.16 against 3.18 d with weather); at 0.6 it still costs 12% more. Joins house-offsite's extra cost of panelising the walls ($1,373 at assumed rates) to house-schedule's interest on working days saved, comparing a factory shell with a site-built house ordered on the same day. How much do fewer handoffs, parallel trades, early ordering and a factory shell cut the time to build a house?

How much do fewer handoffs, parallel trades, early ordering and a factory shell cut a house's build time? Discrete-event Monte Carlo: critical path 100 working days, baseline 214; early ordering -63 d, fewer handoffs -21, a factory shell only -6 unless ordered at day 0 (-78). Stylised, uncalibrated.

Abstract Code →

A Monte Carlo discrete-event model of one house build (20 tasks, a crew per trade, failing inspections, weather, material lead times; 4,000 builds per scenario with common random numbers). The zero-noise critical path is 100 working days but the baseline takes 214: the schedule is driven by waiting. Ordering long-lead materials at day 0 saves 63 days, fewer handoffs 21, parallel rough-in 12.5, faster inspections 11. A factory wall-and-roof shell saves only 6 days if ordered when the foundation starts and 78 if ordered at day 0. All levers together: 96 days, about 1.7% of the price in interest at 8%. Stylised: every duration and rate is my assumption and nothing is calibrated; the 63-day figure rests on a late-ordering baseline.

A second, separately built Monte Carlo schedule (13 tasks, one crew per trade, weather, inspections, long-lead items; 4,000 builds per scenario). A sourced, dated market report. On NAHB’s 2024 breakdown, construction is 64.4% of price and foundations, framing and exterior 26%, so a 20% cheaper structural system moves the price only 5.2%; HUD-code manufactured homes cost about 52% of site-built per sq ft by building the whole house in a factory. In Denver, itemised fees and a 209-day plan review are about 12% of a modelled $462,000 home before land, against 3.5% nationally. 22

Autonomous multi-angle capture

Filming a travel creator from every angle with open, packable hardware and an automated edit: the pixel, perspective, battery and weight limits first, in simulation. Topic page →

capture-crop10 tests

How long a lens can a 360 camera fake by cropping into a reel, and what perspective can no crop fake?

How long a lens can a 360 camera fake by cropping into a reel? An 8K equirect is native only to ~24 mm-equivalent at 1080x1920 (85 mm is a 3.5x upscale), and perspective is set by distance: a stick at 0.8 m enlarges a 10 cm-nearer feature 14% vs 7.6% at an 85 mm framing distance, so portrait looks need a camera standing back. Pixel-count upper bound. First project of track 13.

Abstract Code →

Pixel and perspective geometry for the simplest multi-angle rig, a 360 camera on a pole reframed in software. An 8K (7,680 px) equirect cropped into a 1080×1920 vertical reel is native only up to about 24 mm full-frame-equivalent; 50 mm is upscaled 2.1× and 85 mm 3.5×, and a native 85 mm crop would need a ~27,000 px equirect. Perspective is set by distance: from a stick at 0.8 m a feature 10 cm nearer the lens images 14% larger, against 7.6% from the 1.4 m an 85 mm head-and-shoulders shot is taken at, with the background 1.7× larger. So portrait and compressed-background shots need a camera standing back, whatever the resolution. Upper bounds from pixel counts (real cameras resolve less); framing distances and depths are stated assumptions.

capture-kit10 tests

What should a travel creator pack to film from many angles under a weight budget and the 100 Wh battery limit?

What should a travel creator pack to film from many angles within a weight budget and the 100 Wh battery limit? Exact search over 17,280 kits reaches all 18 band x viewpoint shots at 5 kg; a greedy packer stalls at 12 because lenses need their body (assumed device figures).

Abstract Code →

Exact search over 17,280 kits of cameras, lenses, mounts and battery packs (11,520 legal), scoring distinct focal-band × viewpoint shots (18 at most) and recording hours against carried weight. With a 4 h recording floor, exact search reaches 15 shots at 4 kg and all 18 at 5 kg, while a greedy best-gain-per-gram packer stalls at 12 from 3 kg because a lens is worthless without its body. Without a floor, variety-first search returns kits that record only ~2.2 h. Every device figure is assumed (round class-typical numbers, not datasheets); only the 100 Wh limit is sourced.

capture-rig8 tests

How many cameras, and where, to film a person from every angle?

How many cameras, and where, to film a person from every angle? A 30° gap between neighbours needs 13 cameras on a ring (15° needs 25), but depth error is set by convergence angle, not count: a pair's error falls 11× from 5° to 90° (7.3 to 0.64 mm) while 3 vs 16 ring cameras only halves it. Idealised 2-D lower bounds.

Abstract Code →

A 2-D geometric model of N cameras on a ring or a 90° front arc 3 m from a subject, scored on angle coverage and triangulation error. Cameras buy coverage, angle buys depth accuracy: a 30° gap between neighbours needs 13 cameras (15° needs 25), while centre depth error barely moves with count (0.52 mm for 3 on a ring, 0.23 mm for 16) but falls 11× as a pair’s convergence angle goes from 5° to 90° (7.3 mm to 0.64 mm). Four cameras on a front arc are within 11% of four on a ring. Idealised lower bounds with assumed noise (0.5 px) and no occlusion; novel-view quality is not modelled.

capture-novelview7 tests

How far apart can cameras be before a reel editor can no longer synthesise the angle between them?

How far apart can cameras be before a reel editor can no longer synthesise the angle between them? With exact depth a two-view warp beats cutting to the nearest camera only up to about 30° (24.8 vs 23.6 dB); beyond that holes dominate, and a bystander pulls the limit in to about 15° (ray-traced toy scene; ordering, not decibels).

Abstract Code →

A ray-traced toy scene, two ring cameras, a depth-based warp to the midpoint, scored against the ray-traced truth. With exact depth, synthesis beats cutting to the nearest camera only up to a gap of about 30° (24.8 against 23.6 dB); at 45° it is worse (19.3 against 23.1 dB) because 8% of the target is a hole neither camera saw, though pixels it does fill stay near 29–30 dB. A bystander pulls the crossover in to about 15°, and depth error on the sources costs about 1.4 dB per percent at first (27.5 dB exact, 22.0 dB at 10%). Toy scene with smooth textures and oracle depth: read the ordering, not the decibels.

capture-stereodepth7 tests

Is the depth a camera rig can actually measure good enough for the in-between angle?

Is the depth a camera rig can actually measure good enough for the in-between angle? Block-matching stereo on rendered pairs feeds the two-view warp: mean depth error 14.9% at 3 cm baseline to 2.7% at 50 cm, coverage peaks at 91%, and the result never beats cutting to the nearest camera (22.3 vs 24.8 dB at a 15° gap; exact depth 27.3 dB).

Abstract Code →

capture-novelview assumed independent depth noise of 2–5%. Here depth is measured instead: block-matching stereo on a rendered rectified pair, fed into the same two-view warp and scored against ray-traced truth at a 15° gap. Mean depth error falls from 14.9% at a 3 cm baseline to 2.7% at 50 cm, but coverage peaks at 91% near 20 cm (stereo cannot match occluded or flat pixels), and the synthesised view never beats cutting to the nearest camera: best 22.3 dB at 20 cm against 24.8 dB, with exact depth at 27.3 dB. Independent noise with the same mean error is optimistic by 1optimistic by 1–5 dBndash;7 dB, because real errors are correlated and missing depth leaves holes. Sensor noise of 3% already costs 3 dB. Toy scene, smooth textures, a classic matcher with no learned prior or hole filler.

capture-hybrid6 tests

Can the holes and correlated errors of measured stereo depth be repaired so the in-between view beats cutting to the nearest camera?

Can the holes and correlated errors of measured stereo depth be repaired so in-between synthesis beats cutting to the nearest camera? A hole filler and a no-ground-truth disagreement gate that falls back to the raw nearest camera lift a 15° gap from 22.3 dB to 29.2 dB against 24.8 dB for cutting (held-out seeds 29.2); with a bystander the gate loses its edge (26.1 vs 26.3 for plain filling). Toy scene.

Abstract Code →

capture-stereodepth found that synthesis from block-matching stereo depth never beat cutting to the nearest camera (22.3 against 24.8 dB at a 15° gap). Here the same holey, correlated depth is repaired two ways: filling holes with the farther of the nearest valid row neighbours (27.4 dB), and a gate that needs no ground truth, where the two warped sources disagree or a hole remains, falls back to the raw nearest camera (29.2 dB, 4.4 dB above cutting; the same on three held-out noise seeds). Gains hold from 8° to 30° gaps and at 6–50 cm baselines, shrink to nothing at 6% sensor noise, and with a bystander the gate loses to plain hole filling (26.1 against 26.3 dB). A per-pixel oracle at 32.0 dB bounds what any confidence rule could reach. Stylised toy scene; read the ordering, not the decibels.

capture-follow10 tests

Which platform can follow a travel creator through a crowd and keep the shot?

Which platform can follow a creator through a crowd and keep the shot? A drone that ignores pedestrians frames 99.9% of the time but falls to 39% at 0.3 people/m² once it avoids them; a wheeled robot is stopped by step lines 42–47% of the walk, and a flat-floor one that ignores people passes within 0.5 m ~500 times an hour. 2-D simulation, assumed platform figures.

Abstract Code →

A 2-D crowd simulation of a tripod, a wheeled robot, a wheel-legged robot and a drone holding a camera 2.5 m behind a walking creator among pedestrians who do not react to it. A drone that ignores pedestrians frames the creator 99.9% of the time at any density, but steering around people drops it to 69% at 0.1 people/m2 and 39% at 0.3; a ground robot on a plaza with curbs and one ramp is stopped 42–47% of the walk, and wheel-legs hold the frame 70% of the time in a thin crowd but 4.5% in a dense one. Avoidance and framing trade off: a flat-floor wheeled robot that ignores people frames 98% of the time while passing within 0.5 m of a pedestrian about 500 times an hour. All platform speeds, powers and masses are assumed; pedestrians do not avoid the platforms, and the drone is not limited by altitude, wind or regulation.

capture-edit9 tests

How much of a multi-camera shoot can an automatic edit recover, and what stops it?

How much of a multi-camera shoot can an automatic edit recover? At detector noise 0.3 a fixed 3 s rotation shows mean true quality 0.546, a cut-cost (Viterbi) edit 0.802 vs 0.815 on true scores, and best-score-every-frame 0.723 at 345 cuts a minute; clock sync fails first on short clips (5 s at noise 0.25: 25% over 40 ms). Synthetic quality model, no real footage.

Abstract Code →

A synthetic model of four cameras whose true angle quality changes every 2–8 s, seen through a noisy detector. At noise 0.3 a fixed 3 s rotation shows mean true quality 0.546; an offline Viterbi edit that maximises detected quality minus a cost per cut reaches 0.802 against 0.815 for the same search on true scores, while picking the best score every frame gives 0.723 with 345 cuts a minute and every shot under 1.5 s. The cut cost matters more than detector accuracy (best near 1.0, about 14 cuts a minute). Clock sync from a shared loudness envelope fails first on short clips: a 5 s clip at noise 0.25 is off by over 40 ms in 25% of trials, 15 s in 5%. No real footage, reframing or film-look grade; quality is a made-up random process.

capture-bystander11 tests

When does automatic blurring miss a bystander's face, and which filming platform is conspicuous?

When does automatic blurring miss a bystander's face? On an assumed size-recall model a face detector leaves 5% of identifiable faces unblurred per frame, blurring the head of any detected body under 0.1%, and independent per-frame misses show a face in some frame of a 5 s shot 100% of the time; an offline whole-track blur leaves 0 to 5%. No real footage or detector.

Abstract Code →

An assumed size-to-recall model of blurring strangers' faces while filming in public. A face detector that is 50% reliable at 20 px leaves a face-on face of at least 32 px unblurred 5% of the time per frame (8% at 5 m on an 8K 360 camera); blurring the head region of any detected body instead drops it under 0.1%, because a body is 11× taller than a face. A telephoto frame resolves about 10 identifiable people at once against 2.5 for an 8K 360 view. Per-frame blur is worse than it looks: with independent misses a person filmed for 5 s at the edge of range shows unblurred in some frame 100% of the time, 25% if misses last the whole shot, and an offline edit that blurs a whole track after one detection is left with 0–5%. Size alone does not separate the tall platforms. All detector curves, sizes and angles are assumptions; no real detector or footage; blurring is not legal compliance.

capture-trigger7 tests

Does recording only when something happens save a travel creator's battery, and what does it cost in missed moments?

Does recording only on a trigger save battery, and what does it miss? With 6 thirty-second moments an hour, standby with a 10 s pre-roll uses 19.4 Wh of an 80 Wh continuous day (76% less) and captures 90% of interesting seconds; deep sleep uses 7.7 Wh but captures 69%. Misses and wake latency, not the battery, set coverage. Assumed device figures, synthetic day.

Abstract Code →

A synthetic 16 h day with assumed device figures. With 6 interesting 30 s moments an hour and a trigger that misses 10% and raises 2 false alarms an hour, a standby camera with a 10 s pre-roll buffer uses 19.4 Wh against 80 Wh continuous (76% less) and captures 90% of the interesting seconds; a deep-sleep camera uses 7.7 Wh but captures 69%, because it wakes too slowly to catch the start. Coverage is set by the trigger's miss rate and the wake latency, not the battery; energy decides only for a rig (four cameras: 320 Wh continuous, 78 Wh triggered). Stylised: every device figure is assumed and the trigger is a probability, not a detector.

capture-wake9 tests
