When a camera rig records only on a trigger, should every camera have its own, or should one wake the rest?

When a camera rig records only on a trigger, should every camera have its own, or should one wake the rest? Four standby cameras with their own triggers use 80 Wh of 320 Wh continuous but get all four angles on only 68% of interesting seconds; one sentinel waking the others costs the same and gives 90.5%, and any-camera wake gives 100% for 92 Wh but its false-alarm energy grows with detector count. Assumed device figures.

Abstract Code →

A synthetic 16 h day with assumed device figures and four standby cameras. With 6 thirty-second moments an hour and a 10% miss per detector, a trigger per camera uses 80 Wh (of 320 Wh continuous) but puts all four angles on only 68% of the interesting seconds, since independent misses differ by camera (≈0.94). One sentinel waking the rest costs the same 80 Wh and gives 90.5%; waking all on any camera's trigger gives 100% for 92 Wh but its false-alarm energy grows with the number of detectors (281 against 126 Wh at 40 false alarms an hour). Sleeping the other cameras halves the rig to 41.5 Wh at the cost of the first 7 s of each moment. If the misses are shared, extra detectors buy nothing. Stylised: every figure assumed, not measured.

capture-sentinel10 tests

Where in a camera ring should the sentinel go when the subject faces a favourite direction?

Where in a camera ring should the sentinel go when the subject faces a favourite direction? A sentinel facing the favourite direction misses 8.6% of moments against 34.4% for the one behind; spread cameras' misses are anti-correlated, so capture-wake's independence assumption overstates the all-miss rate by 2x on a ring of 4 and understates it 12x for a tight cluster. Assumed detector figures.

Abstract Code →

A model with assumed detector figures (a miss rate of 3% when the subject faces the camera, 40% when facing away) and a subject whose facing at each moment is von Mises distributed around a favourite direction. In a four-camera ring with concentration κ = 2, the sentinel at the favourite direction misses 8.6% of moments, the one behind the subject 34.4%, and a rotating sentinel 21.5%; the closed form matches a 40,000-moment simulation to within 0.4 points. Misses across a spread ring are negatively correlated (a subject turned from one camera faces another), so assuming independent misses, as capture-wake did, overstates the chance that every detector misses by about 2× on a ring of four; for a tight cluster of cameras the correlation is positive and the independent figure understates it about 12×. Stylised: detector figures are assumed, not measured.

capture-softgate7 tests

Does a soft confidence weight beat a hard switch for repairing stereo-depth view synthesis, and does matching cost help?

Does a soft confidence weight beat a hard switch for repairing stereo-depth view synthesis, and does the matcher's cost help? A ramped weight on warp disagreement beats the hard gate by 0.1 to 0.5 dB in every condition (29.5 vs 29.3 dB held out at 15°) and leaves a quarter fewer seams, closing only a tenth of the oracle gap; matching cost is a worse signal than disagreement (level with hole filling, worse with a bystander). Toy scene.

Abstract Code →

A ramped weight on how much the nearest raw camera replaces a stereo-depth synthesis, driven by disagreement between the two warps, beats the hard switch in every condition tried by 0.1–0.5 dB (29.5 against 29.3 dB at a 15° gap on held-out seeds) and leaves about a quarter fewer false edges, but closes only about a tenth of the 2.6 dB gap to a per-pixel oracle. The stereo matching cost is a worse confidence signal than warp disagreement: gating on it is level with plain hole filling and worse under a bystander or sensor noise. Stylised toy scene, parameters tuned on development seeds.

capture-storage9 tests

How much footage does a multi-camera travel kit produce, and what limits carrying and backing it up?

How much footage does a multi-camera travel kit produce, and what limits carrying and backing it up? Four cameras make ~860 GB a day; cards weigh ~8 g but the evening copy takes 2.7 h on one reader, so a safe plan needs 6 readers and ~450 g (assumed device figures).

Abstract Code →

Data volume, card and SSD weight, nightly offload time and unbacked footage for a rig of 1 to 8 cameras filming 4 h a day for a week, at assumed 60 to 200 Mbit/s bitrates. Four cameras make about 860 GB a day (6 TB a week), yet their cards weigh about 8 g and a camera's battery is 440 to 980 times heavier per recording hour than its card. The binding limit is the evening: one reader copying one day to one SSD takes 2.7 h, so two SSD copies inside 1 h need 6 readers and about 450 g, half an hour is infeasible, and halving the bitrate halves the weight. All device figures are assumed, not datasheets.

23

Sensing, imaging and 3D

Getting more from cheap sensors: fusing cheap IMUs and cameras, computational imaging, and 3D models from real captures, with the error floors that correlated errors set. Topic page →

sensing-imuarray8 tests

How many cheap gyros, fused, match one better gyro at the same cost?

How many cheap gyros, fused, match one better gyro at equal cost? With independent errors the price ratio must beat k² (100 for a 10× quieter unit); shared error above 1/k² means no array size ties; unequal white/bias improvement makes the answer depend on integration time. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Single-axis gyro model with angle random walk and rate random walk (Allan-variance terms) and a fraction ρ of each shared between units. With independent errors an array of n cheap units ties a unit k times quieter only when the price ratio exceeds k2 (9 for k = 3, 100 for k = 10); shared error above 1/k2 means no array size ties (k = 10, ρ ≥ 0.01). If the better unit improves white noise 10× but bias walk only 3×, the number of units needed falls from 100 at 1 s to 10 beyond 300 s, so the answer depends on integration time. Monte Carlo matches the closed form within 0.03. Stylised: illustrative grades, not datasheets; no real IMU data; no prices claimed.

sensing-imutemp9 tests

Does a shared temperature coefficient put a floor under an array of cheap gyros?

Does a shared temperature coefficient put a floor under an array of cheap gyros? The shared part of the tempco does not average out: in the illustrative case a 3× better gyro can no longer be matched at any array size above a 0.2 °C/min ramp over 100 s; compensation quality, not array size, decides.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to sensing-imuarray. Each gyro has a temperature coefficient ci = μ + s·ei; under a temperature ramp the shared mean μ leaves an angle-error floor μrT2/2 that no array size removes. In the illustrative case (100 s) a 3× better unit can be matched at 10–15 units up to 0.1 °C/min but at no size from 0.3 °C/min; a 10× better one at none from 0.1 °C/min. Compensating both grades equally brings the array size back near k2 only at about 2% residual tempco. Monte Carlo matches the closed form within 1%. Stylised: assumed tempcos, no real IMU data, no prices claimed.

sensing-burst12 tests

How many frames from a small sensor, merged, match one frame from a bigger one?

How many frames from a small sensor, merged, match one frame from a sensor with A× the pixel area? A shot-noise-limited burst needs A frames, a read-noise-limited one up to A² (formula and simulation agree); splitting the same total exposure never ties; registration blur and bracketed HDR are measured. Synthetic scenes only.

Abstract Code →

Synthetic scenes with Poisson shot noise, Gaussian read noise and a full-well clip. A burst of N small-sensor frames (each at the large frame's exposure time) ties a sensor with A× the pixel area at N* = A²(sx+r²)/(Asx+r²): A frames when shot noise dominates, up to A² in the dark or at high read noise (simulation, A=4: 4.0 frames in bright light, 14.4 in dim light with 8 e− read noise). Splitting the same total exposure into frames never ties: the burst has more variance than the large frame at every N. With hand shake and Fourier-shift registration, shifts are recovered to 0.09–0.8 px RMS in good light but fail in the dimmest case tested (3.1 px), and the registration blur means A=4 needs about 21 frames in bright light. A bracketed burst recovers clipped highlights (42 dB against 22 dB for one frame). Stylised: synthetic images, global translation only, no real raw files.

sensing-ghost7 tests

What does a moving subject do to a burst merge, and what does robust merging cost?

What does a moving subject do to a burst merge? A plain mean ghosts at every speed and gets worse as frames are added (30.5 dB at 8 frames, 25.0 at 48), median and sigma-clip do no better for a slow subject, and a reference-guided merge keeps improving and ties a 4×-area frame at about 6 frames at 0.1 dB cost when nothing moves. Synthetic scenes only.

Abstract Code →

Still camera, one disc moving across a synthetic burst (Poisson shot noise, Gaussian read noise, a large sensor with 4× the pixel area). A plain mean merge ghosts at every speed tested and gets worse as frames are added (30.5 dB at 8 frames, 25.0 dB at 48 for 0.25 px per frame, against 30.8 dB for one large-sensor frame); median and sigma-clip merges do no better because a slow subject covers each pixel in most frames. A reference-guided merge (add a frame only where it agrees with frame 0) keeps improving, to 37.6 dB at 48 frames, and ties the large frame at about 6 frames; with nothing moving it costs 0.1 dB against the mean, the median 1.3 dB. Stylised: synthetic images, one translating disc, a still camera, untuned thresholds, no real raw files.

sensing-ghostalign7 tests

Can aligning a moving subject, instead of rejecting it, rescue a burst merge?

Can aligning a moving subject rescue a burst merge instead of rejecting it? Inside the subject, yes (37.0 dB against 31.5 for reject-only and 32.8 for a 4×-area frame at 8 frames), but over the whole image rejecting is as good or better (31.7 against 31.8 dB), the aligner moves 10–31% of static pixels on noise, and the revealed-background ring stays 4 dB short of the large frame. Synthetic scenes only.

Abstract Code →

Still camera, one disc moving across a synthetic burst (Poisson shot noise, Gaussian read noise, a large sensor with 4× the pixel area). A per-pixel sub-pixel alignment to the reference frame, followed by a rejection test, reaches 37.0 dB inside the disc at 8 frames and 1 px per frame, against 31.5 dB for reject-only merging and 32.8 dB for the large frame. Over the whole image it is no better than rejecting (31.7 against 31.8 dB at 8 frames, 34.4 against 35.6 at 24) because the aligner moves 10–31% of static pixels on noise, and in the ring where the background is covered and revealed no variant gets within 4 dB of the large frame. Stylised: synthetic scenes, one flat rigid disc, translation only.

sensing-superres10 tests

Can a burst of hand-shaken low-resolution frames recover detail that merging and upsampling cannot?

Can a burst of hand-shaken low-resolution frames recover detail that merging and upsampling cannot? At 2× in bright light a least-squares reconstruction reaches 29.5 dB at 16 frames against 24.0 for merge-and-upsample and 26.6 for merge-and-deblur, so 2.9 dB is sub-pixel information; it nearly vanishes in dim light and falls to nothing at about 0.27 px of shift error. Synthetic scenes only.

Abstract Code →

Synthetic 32×32 frames from a box-averaging sensor (Poisson shot noise, 3 e− read noise), shifted by up to two pixels, reconstructed on a 2× grid by regularised least squares. In bright light it reaches 29.5 dB at 16 frames and 30.7 dB at 32, against 24.0 dB for register, average and bilinear upsample and 26.6 dB for register, average and deconvolve: 2.6 dB of the gain is deblurring the pixel box and 2.9 dB (4.0 at 32 frames) is sub-pixel information. In dim light that part is within ±0.3 dB; registration error of 0.27 LR pixel erases it. Against a sensor with 2× the linear resolution and the same total light the burst wins at 2 frames and loses from about 4; at 3× it ties at 16 frames and at 4× it wins. Synthetic scenes, translation only, no mosaic or lens blur; the reconstruction is plain Tikhonov, not a published method.

sensing-timesync7 tests

How many milliseconds of camera-to-gyro time offset double a fused attitude error, and can online calibration recover it?

How many milliseconds of camera-to-gyro time offset double a fused attitude error, and can an alignment fit recover it? About 12–14 ms at 30 deg/s motion; the fit recovers it to ~1 ms with motion and fails on a still platform. Synthetic, single axis.

Abstract Code →

Single-axis simulation: a 200 Hz biased gyro and a 30 Hz camera whose timestamps are late by td, fused by a complementary filter. At 30 deg/s motion the error doubles at 12–14 ms; the doubling offset is 32–34 ms at 10 deg/s and 8–10 ms at 90 deg/s, and grows with camera noise. A gyro-integral alignment fit recovers the offset to about 1 ms rms and restores the zero-offset error, but fails on a nearly still platform. Stylised: one axis, constant offset, angle measurements only, synthetic noise.

sensing-syncskew6 tests

How much motion does a camera-to-gyro offset fit need, and what does clock skew do to a one-off calibration?

How much motion does a camera-to-gyro offset fit need, and what does clock skew do to a one-off calibration? A 20 ms offset needs about 16 deg/s rms motion to fit reliably; 1000 ppm skew leaves 0.254 deg error after a fixed-offset fit against 0.155 deg when skew is fitted too. Stylised, synthetic.

Abstract Code →

Same single-axis gyro and camera world as sensing-timesync, with the camera stamp error growing as td = td0 + skew·t. An alignment fit recovers a 20 ms offset within 5 ms in 8 of 8 runs at 16 deg/s or more, but only 2 of 8 at 1 deg/s and 0 of 8 at 0.3 deg/s. A camera clock 1000 ppm fast raises attitude error from 0.152 to 0.514 deg uncorrected and 0.254 deg after a fixed-offset fit, while fitting offset and skew together gives 0.155 deg up to 2000 ppm; skew recovery needs a window of about 40 s. Stylised: one axis, linear skew, synthetic noise, skews exaggerated to show an effect in 40 s.

sensing-scan2cad12 tests

How accurate must a scan be to rebuild a part as parametric CAD?

How accurate must a scan be to rebuild a part as parametric CAD? On synthetic plate scans, RANSAC plane and circle fits give all five dimensions within 0.2 mm for noise up to 0.2 mm, but at 0.5 mm noise the error is a bias (thickness −0.20 mm) that more points do not remove, and a 0.5% scale error alone moves an 80 mm length by 0.40 mm. Synthetic, one shape.

Abstract Code →

Synthetic point-cloud scans of an 80×40×10 mm plate with two 8 mm holes, fitted by RANSAC planes and circle fits. With scan noise of 0.2 mm or less every scan gives all five dimensions within 0.2 mm at 2 000 points or more (worst RMS 0.09 mm). At 0.5 mm noise only 0–50% of scans are usable at any point count because the error is a bias: thickness reads 0.20 mm low and the bias grows with the inlier band (−0.07 to −0.38 mm for 1.5σ to 4σ). A scale error of 0.5% from a reconstruction with no scale reference already moves an 80 mm length by 0.40 mm. Stylised: one shape, assumed Gaussian noise, pre-registered scan, generated CadQuery script not run.

sensing-recon11 tests

How many photos does a usable 3-D reconstruction need?

How many photos does a usable 3-D reconstruction need? On a synthetic object with known cameras, 12 views on a full orbit triangulate every feature, 8 views 89% and 4 or fewer at most 13%; per-point error then depends on pixel noise and pose error, not view count. Triangulation stage only (synthetic).

Abstract Code →

Synthetic bumpy-ellipsoid object, 800 features, pinhole cameras on an orbit with known poses and linear (DLT) triangulation. On a full orbit 12 views reconstruct every feature, 8 views 89%, 6 views 59% and 4 or fewer at most 13%, because a point must be seen by two cameras. Once triangulated, error is about 0.0028 object radii per pixel of image noise, a 1° pose error does the damage of about 2 px, and a narrow baseline (5° span) raises error about 7× against a 40° span. Triangulation stage only: matches and poses are given, there is no occlusion, mesh or splat, and no real images.

sensing-thermalfuse10 tests

Does a low-resolution thermal camera find people in darkness and smoke, and what does misalignment cost?

Does a low-resolution thermal camera find people in darkness and smoke, and what does misalignment cost? On synthetic scenes RGB finds 36% in bright light and none in the dark or dense smoke, thermal alone 65% everywhere (capped by warm decoys), fusion 94% in bright light and the thermal level otherwise; a 4 px (one thermal pixel) displacement costs the fused detector 19 points and 6 px erases the gain. Synthetic only.

Abstract Code →

Synthetic 64×64 scenes with people, cold clutter and warm non-person decoys, seen by a grey RGB camera (shot and read noise, smoke airlight) and a 16×16 thermal camera (0.3 K noise, 10% of the visible smoke extinction assumed). At 10% false alarms per image, RGB alone finds 36% of people in bright clear light, 13% at smoke transmittance 0.4 and none in the dark or dense smoke; thermal alone finds 65% in every condition, capped by the decoys; fusing them gives 94% in bright light and falls back to the thermal level otherwise. A thermal camera displaced by 2 px costs the fused detector 7 points, 4 px (one thermal pixel) 19, and 6 px leaves it below RGB alone (0.12 vs 0.37); training with displacement jitter keeps 0.54 at 6 px but loses 9 points when aligned. Stylised: synthetic scenes, logistic-regression detectors on local contrast, sideways shift only, no real data.

sensing-vio8 tests

Which upgrade buys the most visual-inertial accuracy: a sharper camera or a better IMU?

Which upgrade buys the most visual-inertial accuracy, a sharper camera or a better IMU? On a planar synthetic smoother only camera resolution moved drift (1280 px 1.2 % vs 1.7 % at 640 px); a 0.25–4× change in IMU noise did not, on 12 s paths. Stylised, not EuRoC.

Abstract Code →

A planar synthetic visual-inertial smoother (bearing landmarks, 100 Hz gyro and accelerometer) on 12 s paths, 8 paired seeds. Camera resolution moved drift: 1.18 % of path rms at 1280 px against 1.65 % at 640 px and 8.9 % at 320 px. Scaling IMU noise 0.25× to 4× changed it by under 10 %, inside the noise. Limitations: the smoother has no marginalisation and diverged on 30 s paths, so the IMU result is for short runs only; planar, synthetic, not EuRoC.

sensing-ghostedge6 tests

Does modelling the sub-pixel coverage of a moving subject fix the edge ring that burst merging leaves behind?

Does modelling the sub-pixel coverage of a moving subject fix the edge ring? Yes, on a known shape: a layered disc-over-background model fitted from the burst lifts the ring from 27.1 to 33.1 dB at 8 frames and 2 px per frame (4×-area frame: 31.7 dB), less at slow speeds, and it is sensitive to a 0.5 px centre error. Synthetic flat disc only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to sensing-ghostring, where no merge or mask fixed the edge ring. Here each frame is a layered mix, a·disc + (1−a)·background, with sub-pixel coverage a from a fitted disc, and the background solved by least squares over the frames. On the same synthetic bursts at 8 frames and 2 px per frame the ring goes from 27.1 dB (aligned plus reject) to 33.1 dB with the disc fitted from the burst itself (large sensor, 4× area: 31.7 dB); at 0.5–1 px per frame it gains 0.4–2.2 dB and stays below the large frame. It is sensitive to geometry: a 0.5 px centre error drops the ring to 25 dB. Stylised: the model assumes the exact shape of the synthetic subject (a flat disc), so this is an upper-bound-style result, not a general deghosting method.

sensing-ghostring6 tests

Can a background estimate or a subject mask fix the edge ring that burst alignment leaves behind?

Can a temporal-median background or a subject mask fix the edge ring that burst alignment leaves behind? No: four ring treatments leave it at 21.6–27.2 dB at 8 frames against 31.6–32.0 for a 4×-area frame, none beats plain aligned-plus-reject (27.0 dB), and the mask misses most of a slow subject. Synthetic scenes only.

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to sensing-ghostalign, on the same synthetic bursts (one disc moving across a still scene, Poisson shot noise, Gaussian read noise, a large sensor with 4× the pixel area). Four explicit treatments of the edge ring — frame 0 alone, a per-pixel temporal median, the aligned merge, the reject-only merge, each gated by a subject mask estimated against the temporal median — all leave the ring at 21.6–27.2 dB at 8 frames against 31.6–32.0 dB for the large frame. None beats plain aligned-plus-reject (27.0 dB at 1 px per frame); the median is the worst (22.3 dB) unless the subject moves 4 px per frame, and the mask recalls only 44–64% of a slow subject. A negative result. Stylised: synthetic scenes, one flat rigid disc, translation only.

24

Energy supply and dense energy storage

How densely, cheaply and durably energy can be stored, and what mix of supply and storage meets demand at least cost: the physical limits first, then devices, costs and grids, in open code. Topic page →

energy-home10 tests

How big should a home's solar array and battery be, and at what installed price does the battery pay?

How big should a home's solar array and battery be, and at what price does the battery pay? Hourly model on synthetic weather (assumed inputs): a 6 kW array meets 35% of an 8,000 kWh/yr load, a 10 kWh battery lifts it to 59%, and the battery pays only below about $451/kWh installed at $0.05 export (assumed price $800).

Abstract Code →

An hourly simulation of rooftop solar plus a battery on an 8,000 kWh/yr home, over 20 seeded synthetic weather years (Haurwitz clear sky, a three-state cloud chain, an invented load) with assumed round-number prices. A 6 kW array alone meets 35% of the load; 5, 10 and 15 kWh of battery lift that to 49%, 59% and 62%, then returns diminish fast. With import at $0.30 and export at $0.05 per kWh a 10 kWh battery pays only below about $451/kWh installed (assumed $800), $143 at $0.20 export, and never when export is paid at the import price. Stylised: synthetic weather, flat tariff, no incentives or degradation; not installation advice.

energy-tou8 tests

Does time-of-use pricing make a home battery pay, and which size?

Does time-of-use pricing make a home battery pay, and which size? On an assumed tariff with the flat tariff's average, a 10 kWh battery behind 6 kW PV breaks even at $641/kWh installed against $444 flat (assumed price $800); only 2.5 to 5 kWh clears $800, and the peak price steers the answer (energy-home with hourly prices).

Abstract Code →

Adds an hourly time-of-use import price to energy-home's solar-plus-battery model (10 seeded synthetic weather years, assumed three-band tariff with the same $0.296 average as a flat $0.30). A 10 kWh battery behind 6 kW of PV breaks even at $641/kWh installed with peak-only discharge and off-peak grid charging, against $444 on the flat tariff, still under the assumed $800. Only small batteries clear $800 ($856 at 2.5 kWh, $847 at 5 kWh); 15 and 20 kWh fall to $427 and $320. Half-filling from the grid ($674) beats a full fill ($641). Break-even tracks the peak price ($307, $641, $1,208 at $0.28, $0.45, $0.70). Stylised: assumed tariff, synthetic weather, fixed dispatch rule, no degradation.

energy-mix6 tests

What is the cheapest mix of solar, wind, gas and storage that cuts a power system's emissions, and what does the last 5% cost?

What is the cheapest mix of solar, wind, gas and storage that cuts emissions, and what does the last 5% cost? PyPSA on 2019 German hourly demand (assumed costs): $79/MWh all-gas, $113 at an 80% cut, $177 at zero emissions with 10.6 TWh of hydrogen storage; abatement cost $30/t to $1,765/t for the last 5%. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A single-node PyPSA model of Germany's 2019 hourly demand (ENTSO-E data via Open Power System Data) with solar, wind, gas, a battery and hydrogen storage sized together under an emissions cap. Gas alone costs $79/MWh; a 50% cut adds $5.6 using wind only; 80%, 90%, 95% and 100% cuts cost $113, $131, $144 and $177/MWh, the last needing 10.6 TWh of hydrogen storage. Implied abatement cost rises from $30/t to $1,765/t for the last 5%. At zero emissions the hydrogen tank price moves the answer from $152 to $254/MWh; without hydrogen, batteries alone give $287. Stylised: assumed costs, one weather year, one node, no grid.

energy-density10 tests

How much energy can each storage technology hold per kilogram, at the most?

How much energy can each storage technology hold per kilogram, at the most? First-principles ceilings that reproduce five published values within 0.3% (Li-S 2,567, Li-O2 3,458 Wh/kg). No battery couple exceeds 1.65 eV per reactant atom, so light atoms set the winners (Wh/kg = 26,801 × eV/atom ÷ g/mol); flywheels top out near 0.3 eV/atom, heat and pumped hydro far lower. Active material only. First project of track 16.

Abstract Code →

Theoretical ceilings from first principles for batteries, hydrogen, flywheels, pumped hydro and heat, reproducing five published values to within 0.3% (lead-acid 170, Zn-air 1,086, Li-S 2,567, Li-O2 3,458 Wh/kg; Al-air 8,100 on Al). No battery couple releases more than 1.65 eV per reactant atom, so the spread comes from atomic mass: Wh/kg = 26,801 × eV per atom / mean g/mol. A carbon-fibre flywheel holds at most 756 Wh/kg (0.34 eV per atom), sand at 500 °C 107 Wh/kg of heat (41% recoverable as electricity) and water lifted 300 m 0.82 Wh/kg. Ceilings for the active material only, with some voltages and material properties assumed.

energy-volumetric7 tests

How much energy can each storage chemistry hold per litre, and does the ranking by weight survive?

How much energy can each storage chemistry hold per litre, and does the ranking by weight survive? Volumetric ceilings from reactant densities: zinc-air 9,659 Wh/L with air, Li-ion 1,382, lead-acid 724, hydrogen 1,314 at 700 bar.

Abstract Code →

Volumetric ceilings (Wh/L) for the couples of energy-density, from the sum of reactant mass over assumed handbook density. With oxygen taken from air, zinc-air reaches 9,659 Wh/L, lithium-oxygen 6,104 and aluminium-air 5,887, against 1,382 for graphite/LiCoO2 and 724 for lead-acid. The ranking changes with the basis: lithium-sulfur beats graphite/LiCoO2 by 6.8 times per kg but only 2.1 times per litre (lithium is light and bulky), while zinc-air beats lead-acid by 6.4 times per kg and 13 times per litre. Hydrogen holds 1,314 Wh/L at 700 bar and 2,314 as a 20 K liquid. Sand at 500 °C holds 171 Wh/L as heat. Active material only; densities are assumed, not checked.

energy-practical6 tests

How close do real batteries, flow cells and hydrogen tanks get to their first-principles ceilings?

How close do real batteries, flow cells and hydrogen tanks get to their first-principles ceilings? A Panasonic NCR18650B cell reaches 0.64 of the Li-ion reactant ceiling (243 of 380 Wh/kg), LiFePO4 0.25–0.45, lead-acid 0.21–0.24; DOE's projected 700 bar H2 system is 5.1% hydrogen by mass against 24–41% ideal. Small sourced dataset, primary and secondary rows marked. Second project of track 16.

Abstract Code →

A small sourced dataset set beside the ceilings of energy-density. A Panasonic NCR18650B cell (data sheet) stores 243 Wh/kg, 0.64 of the 380 Wh/kg graphite/LiCoO2 reactants could release; commercial LiFePO4 reaches 0.25–0.45 and lead-acid 0.21–0.24. DOE’s projected 700 bar hydrogen system (1.71 kWh/kg) is 5.1% hydrogen by mass against 23.8–41.3% for an ideal carbon-fibre sphere. Round-trip efficiency runs from 50% (compressed air) to 85% (advanced lead-acid). Limited: five families, five of seven data rows read through secondary pages, gap not split into causes.

energy-thermal9 tests

Can a house-sized sand heat store carry summer heat into winter, and how does its electricity use compare with a heat pump?

Can a house-sized sand heat store carry summer heat into winter? A transient model: 10 MWh after 120 days needs 222 m³ (70 if lossless) and returns 26% of the electricity as heat, so a COP-4 heat pump wins unless its electricity is 15× dearer; a days-scale store at house size. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A transient finite-volume model of a spherical sand store in mineral wool (a hot-water tank run through the same code), checked against analytic cases. A store sized to still give 10 MWh after 120 days needs 222 m3 (against 70 if lossless) and returns only 26% of the electricity put in as heat, so a COP-4 heat pump wins unless its electricity costs 15× more, before capital cost. After a day or a week the same store returns 79% and 73%: a days-scale store at house size, seasonal only near 1,000 m3 (43% left after 180 days). Stylised: assumed properties, a sphere, instant uniform charging, no pipes or ground.

energy-lcos9 tests

Which energy-storage technology is cheapest per MWh delivered at 1 hour, 1 day and 3 weeks?

Which storage technology is cheapest per MWh delivered, by duration? Li-ion wins to about 4 h ($116/MWh), cavern stores beyond ($109 vs Li-ion $337 at 24 h), cavern hydrogen only past ~300 h. All inputs assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Levelised cost of storage for lithium-ion, vanadium flow, pumped hydro, cavern compressed air and cavern hydrogen, from capital cost, round-trip efficiency, life, fade and charging power. With round assumed inputs Li-ion is cheapest to about 4 hours ($116/MWh at 4 h) and costs about 3× a cavern store at 24 hours ($337 vs $109); cavern hydrogen beats Li-ion above 11 hours but cavern compressed air only above 308 hours. Li-ion would need an energy cost of $43/kWh instead of $200 to win at 24 hours. The 8–10 hour winner flips with the discount rate and charging price. Stylised: every input is assumed and unsourced, caverns need geology, one fixed use pattern.

energy-cell6 tests

How much better can a lithium-ion cell get by redesigning its electrodes, and does a smarter search help?

How much better can a Li-ion cell get by redesigning its electrodes, and does a smarter search help? In a PyBaMM model, thicker, more porous electrodes with more negative capacity lift energy after 100 cycles from 109 to ~143 Wh/kg (+30%); random, Bayesian and session-agent proposers end within 3% of each other. One aggressively ageing parameter set. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A PyBaMM single-particle model with electrolyte of an NMC811 / graphite-SiOx cell, scored on discharge energy per kilogram of electrode stack after 100 cycles at a fixed current. Four design numbers (positive thickness, two porosities, negative-to-positive capacity ratio) are searched with 30 evaluations by random search, Gaussian-process Bayesian optimisation (5 seeds each) and the session agent proposing by hand (one run). The reference cell scores 109 Wh/kg; all three reach 141–143 (+30%) with a thicker, more porous positive electrode and about 30% more negative capacity, and their seed ranges overlap, so no proposer is shown to be better. Limits: one aggressively ageing parameter set, constant-current charge only, stack not finished cell, optimum at the search bounds. Stylised and simulated, not a tested cell.

energy-lcos-mc6 tests

How robust is the cheapest energy-storage technology at each duration when costs are uncertain?

How robust is the cheapest storage technology by duration to uncertain costs? Monte Carlo over energy-lcos: Li-ion wins 96% of scenarios at 2 h but 18% at 8 h; no technology wins over 48% between 6 and 12 h; caverns win most from 24 h. Ranges assumed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A Monte Carlo over the energy-lcos model: 4,000 scenarios draw each technology's energy cost, power cost and efficiency from assumed ranges, plus the discount rate (3–10%) and charging price ($10–100/MWh), and count how often each is cheapest. Lithium-ion wins 96% of scenarios at 2 hours, 64% at 4 and 18% at 8; between 6 and 12 hours no technology wins more than 48%, so the point-estimate winner is a coin toss there. Caverns win most scenarios from 24 hours (compressed air 61% at 24 h, 81% at 100 h) and hydrogen 69% at 500 hours. Charging price is the largest single swing in cost. Stylised: every range is assumed, draws are independent and uniform, and the use pattern is fixed.

25

Robot societies among people

Simulated societies of AI-driven robots living among simulated people: the conventions that emerge, who sets them, what they cost people, and watchable episodes made from seeded runs. Topic page →

society-robotnorms14 tests

How many robots does it take to change how a crowd walks?

How many robots does it take to change which side a crowd walks on? Robots that hold a programmed side tip a crowd once they are 16–32% of it, more when people remember more past partners (simulation matches mean field within 0.02); just short of that they make people collide up to 14× as often as adaptive robots, and placement matters more than numbers when people meet only neighbours. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Robots as a committed minority in a passing-side convention. Simulated people take the side most of their last M partners used; robots hold a programmed side. The tipping share grows with memory: 16%, 22%, 28% and 32% of the crowd for M = 5, 9, 17 and 25, within 0.02 of a mean-field prediction. Just below it, robots that hold their side make people collide up to 14× as often as robots that adapt (0.27 vs 0.020 conflicts per meeting). When people meet only neighbours, evenly spread robots tip everyone from 12–14%, while one block of robots converts under 10% of people even at half the crowd. Stylised: one binary choice per meeting, no geometry.

society-plaza13 tests

Do robots that keep to one side make people walk on it, or jam the corridor?

Do robots that keep to one side make people walk on it, or jam the corridor? In a social-force corridor, robots that adapt change nothing, but robots that hold the left cut people's speed from 0.91 to 0.39 of desired by 30% of the crowd and halve lane separation, while people move to their side only gradually (no sharp tipping, unlike the 1D model). Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The 1D society-robotnorms passing-side model rebuilt as a social-force corridor (60 simulated walkers, 30 m × 6 m). Robots that adapt to people change nothing. Robots that hold the left slow people from 0.91 to 0.81 of desired speed at 5% of the crowd and to 0.39 at 30%, halve the lane separation (2.75 m to 1.43 m), and move people to their side only gradually (at most 54% of people at memory 9), with no sharp tipping in 300 s. Includes a seeded browser replay. Stylised: 8 seeds, one parameter set, simulated walkers only.

society-trust10 tests

Can a robot fleet's reputation survive one bad incident?

Can a robot fleet's reputation survive one bad incident? In a model where trust spreads by experience and gossip, a dent always recovers because people keep meeting robots; reputation is lost only through avoidance (at a 0.30 avoid-below threshold, 20/20, 18/20 and 0/20 crowds recover under neutral, 2× and 4× negativity in gossip), and robots that explain failures recovered every time. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Simulated people hold trust in a robot fleet, updated by their own encounters and by gossip in which bad news may travel further than good. Trust that is only dented recovers in every case. What sinks a reputation is avoidance: if people stop using robots below a trust threshold of 0.30, an incident at error rate 0.8 is recovered in 20/20 crowds with neutral gossip, 18/20 when bad news counts 2×, and 0/20 at 4× (final mean trust 0.947, 0.871, 0.282). Robots that explain failures (each costing 0.3× the trust) recovered in every setting. Stylised: 100 simulated people, one shared reputation, a hard avoidance threshold, no fitted parameters.

society-commons11 tests

What does it cost robots to let people go first at a shared lift or narrow pavement?

What does it cost robots to let people go first at a shared lift or narrow pavement? At load 0.9, deference cuts people's wait 6.5× (4.60 to 0.71) and raises robots' by 2.6 units; total waiting cost is conserved, so it pays only if a person's wait costs more than a robot's, and a lone defector waits far less (2.08 vs 7.65). Queueing model within 2.7% of closed forms.

Abstract Code →

People and robots share a one-at-a-time crossing. At load 0.9, robots that always let waiting people go first cut people’s mean wait from 4.60 to 0.71 time units and raise the robots’ from 4.61 to 7.21; the total waiting cost is the same for every share of deferential robots (4.14–4.15), so deference moves waiting rather than removing it, and pays exactly when a person’s wait costs more than a robot’s. A lone selfish robot waits 2.08 against 7.65 for deferential ones (the dilemma). Under overload (load 1.2) half the robots deferring costs them 10.5% of their crossings and gives people 20% more. Simulation within 2.7% of M/G/1 closed forms. Stylised: one server, Poisson arrivals, fixed crossing times.

society-llmtown8 tests

Do robot agents keep the norms they state?

Do robot agents keep the norms they state? A pluggable town harness with a deterministic stub (no language model run): a robot stating "always yield" keeps it in 1 − 0.4×pressure of meetings (1.00 to 0.60), and people's cost per meeting rises from 0.20 to 1.08. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A harness for a small town of robot agents that state a door norm each day and then act among scripted people, scoring how often action matches statement and what it costs people. Any agent with state_norm and act plugs in; a deterministic stub is tested, and an optional model adapter is provided but was not run. With the stub, a robot stating ‘always yield’ keeps it in 1 − 0.4×pressure of meetings (1.00, 0.80, 0.60 at pressure 0, 0.5, 1; 20 seeds) and people’s cost per meeting rises from 0.20 to 1.08. These follow from the stub’s own rule: no language-model result is claimed. Stylised; non-adaptive scripted people.

society-twinfidelity6 tests

Does the robots-in-a-corridor conclusion survive a more humanlike crowd?

Does the robots-in-a-corridor conclusion survive a more humanlike crowd? Adaptive robots stay free and committed robots never flip the crowd in all five simulated crowds, but the size of the slowdown (loss of 0.17–0.49 of desired speed at 30% robots) and of personal-space intrusions (0.03–0.36 of agent time) depends strongly on how humanlike the people are. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The society-plaza corridor rerun with four crowds of simulated people: varied speeds and sideways-push weights, a 0.4 s reaction delay, 30% stubborn walkers, and all three (10 seeds per cell). Adaptive robots stay free and committed robots never flip the crowd (at most 58% prefer their side) in every crowd. The size of the slowdown (a loss of 0.17 to 0.49 of desired speed at 30% robots) and of personal-space intrusions (0.03 to 0.36 of agent time; reaction delay alone gives 0.087 with no robots) depends strongly on the crowd. Hand-chosen perturbations, not fitted to data; simulated walkers only.

society-stubborn9 tests

How many robots does it take to change a crowd's walking side when some people never adapt?

How many robots does it take to change a crowd's walking side when some people never adapt? With 0, 20, 40 and 50% stubborn walkers the mean-field tipping share (memory 9) rises 0.217, 0.240, 0.283, 0.329, simulation agrees within 0.02, and committed-robot conflict costs barely change. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The society-robotnorms committed-robot model with a share s of stubborn people who always walk right. The mean-field tipping share for memory 9 rises from 0.217 (s = 0) to 0.240, 0.283 and 0.329 at s = 0.2, 0.4 and 0.5, and memory 5 and 9 coincide from s = 0.4. Simulation (200 people, 12 seeds) agrees within 0.02 at every s when “tipped” means a majority of adaptive people on the robots' side. Conflict costs of committed and adaptive robots are unchanged by stubborn people. Stylised; simulated walkers only.

society-blocs11 tests

How many robots does it take to change a crowd's walking side when some people always walk on the robots' side?

How many robots does it take to change a crowd's walking side when some people always walk on the robots' side? Each 5% of always-robot-side people cuts the memory-9 mean-field tipping share (0.217) by about 0.04, 25% tip a crowd with no robots, opposing blocs raise the bar, and simulation agrees within 0.01. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

The society-stubborn model with a share sl of people who always walk the robots' side and sr who always walk the status-quo side. For memory 9 the mean-field tipping robot share falls from 0.217 to 0.176, 0.131, 0.080 and 0.023 at sl = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15 and 0.20 (about 0.8 robots saved per ally), and a crowd with 25% allies tips with no robots. Opposing blocs raise the self-tipping share (0.219 to 0.300 as sr goes 0 to 0.3), equal blocs are a knife edge, and simulation (200 people, 12 seeds) agrees with mean field within 0.01 at seven bloc mixes. Opposing blocs alone cost 0.195 conflicts per human meeting. Stylised; simulated walkers only.

society-converts8 tests

Does a stubborn block that slowly converts let a smaller robot minority tip a crowd's walking side?

Does a stubborn block that slowly converts let a smaller robot minority tip a crowd's walking side? With 40% stubborn walkers, 24% robots never tip (0 of 12) but tip all 12 at 0.1% conversion per round (median round 721).

Abstract Code →

The society-stubborn model with 40% stubborn walkers who each convert to an ordinary memory-rule walker with probability c per round. With the block fixed, 24% committed robots never tip the crowd (0 of 12) and 28% tip 5 of 12; with c = 0.001 both tip all 12 (median round 721 and 185), and at c = 0.1 at round 59 and 31. At 20% or fewer robots no crowd tipped at any c. Conversion mostly buys speed and moves the threshold towards the no-stubborn value. Stylised: simulated walkers, spontaneous conversion, 200 people, 12 seeds; the mean-field clock is only a rank-order check.

society-show10 tests

Can a simulation run be turned into a watchable, honest episode?

Can a simulation run be turned into a watchable, honest episode? Five seeded, labelled-fiction episodes of a robot town built on society-trust, with turning points found by code and a narration read from the record: even-handed gossip recovers, 4× negativity locks the town out, explained failures recover, and 2× ends both ways by seed. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Five seeded, clearly labelled fictional episodes of a robot town, built on society-trust: 48 invented townspeople, a trust-coloured grid, turning points found by code from the recorded data and a narration whose numbers all come from that record. Even-handed gossip recovers 46 rounds after the fix; gossip that weighs bad news 4× locks the town out (48 of 48 avoid working robots at round 399); robots that explain failures recover in 29 rounds with nobody avoiding; and at 2× the same settings recover on seed 0 and lock out on seed 1. Episodes are single illustrative runs, not statistics; stylised model, no viewer study.

26

Agentic co-design of low-cost robots

Designing a cheap robot and its controller together in simulation, with an agent, CMA-ES, Bayesian optimisation and random search at equal budget, for civilian domains. Topic page →

codesign-gripper9 tests

Which printable two-finger gripper holds eight different objects for the least plastic, and can an agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation at 40 simulations?

Which printable two-finger gripper holds eight objects for the least plastic, and can an agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation at 40 MuJoCo evaluations? Median best objective 0.991 (Bayesian opt) vs 0.979 (CMA-ES), 0.965 (random) and 0.963 (session agent, one run); the cheapest winners (0.5 g flat fingers) are also the most fragile when object offsets triple. Stylised, no learned policy.

Abstract Code →

A parametric 3D-printable gripper finger (length, thickness, pad width, V angle) scored in MuJoCo on eight objects with a per-design grip force. At 40 evaluations the median best objective is 0.991 for Bayesian optimisation, 0.979 for CMA-ES, 0.965 for random search and 0.963 for a session agent’s hand-written proposals (one run; Bayesian optimisation matched or beat it in 10 of 10 seeds). The best designs are tiny flat fingers (0.5 g), but re-scored with object offsets tripled they hold 5 of 8 objects against 6 of 8 for the agent’s wide V. Rigid, stylised, no learned policy, nothing printed.

codesign-sar8 tests

Which cheap wheel-legged rover covers the most stylised rubble under a 120 USD parts cap, and does a session agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation?

Which cheap wheel-legged rover covers the most stylised rubble under a 120 USD cap, and can an agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation at 40 evaluations? Wheel radius at its bound plus about 0.5 N m torque reaches the ceiling (J 0.783, 69 USD); Bayesian opt and CMA-ES 0.782, session agent 0.783, random 0.716; stylised, falls never occurred.

Abstract Code →

Five design variables (wheel radius, wheelbase, flipper length, drive torque, battery) are scored on twelve held-out random-rubble terrains with Gamma-patchy friction, each design with its own evolution-strategies speed-and-flipper policy (not PPO). Wheel radius at its 90 mm bound with torque of about 0.5 N m reaches the ceiling J = 0.783 (16 of 20 m) at 69 USD. Median best J at 40 evaluations: Bayesian optimisation 0.782, CMA-ES 0.782, session agent 0.783, random search 0.716; the gaps at the top are within policy-search noise. Falls were zero throughout, so the tip-over and recovery path is untested. Stylised statics, assumed unsourced prices, one agent run with a calibration-time prior.

codesign-agri7 tests

Which three-finger pad design picks the most unbruised strawberry-like fruit under a 60 USD cap, and does a session agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation?

Which three-finger pad design picks the most unbruised strawberry-like fruit under a 60 USD cap, and can an agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation at 40 evaluations? Bayesian optimisation did (median J 0.635 against the agent's 0.618); about 20% of fruit are lost to clutter collisions no pad setting changes. Stylised, assumed constants.

Abstract Code →

Five design variables (pad width, pad length, pad modulus, grip force, finger count) are scored on 600 simulated fruit with ripeness-dependent bruise thresholds, wet and dry friction and placement error, using closed-form line-contact pressure, friction hold and a capture-and-clutter law. At 40 evaluations the median best objective is 0.635 for Bayesian optimisation, 0.618 for a session agent’s hand-written proposals (one run, by the model’s own author), 0.611 for CMA-ES and 0.574 for random search; all 20 Bayesian-optimisation seeds matched or beat the agent. The best design (25 mm pads, 0.19 MPa, 8 N, three fingers) picks 74% clean; about 20% of fruit are lost to clutter collisions that no pad setting can change. Stylised, with assumed constants and no learned policy.

codesign-logistics7 tests

Which suction gripper picks the most of a stylised mixed tote under an 80 USD cap, and does a session agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation?

Which suction gripper picks the most of a stylised mixed tote (boxes, polybags, bottles) under an 80 USD cap, and can an agent beat CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation at 40 evaluations? The agent's best J was 0.519 against 0.478 for Bayesian optimisation (median of 20 seeds); the best design is two 18.5 mm cups at 80 kPa and 60 L/min, and a catalogue-default single 30 mm cup scores 0.075. Stylised, assumed constants.

Abstract Code →

Five design variables (cup diameter, cups in a row, pump vacuum, pump flow, cup compliance) are scored on 600 simulated items (boxes, leaky polybags, bottles) with a cup-fit law on each item’s flat patch, vacuum lost to leaks, holding force against 1.5× a 1 g-accelerated load, and a pick-time penalty. At 40 evaluations the median best objective is 0.478 for Bayesian optimisation, 0.361 for CMA-ES and 0.328 for random search; a session agent’s hand-written proposals (one run, by the model’s own author) reached 0.519, and 1 of 20 Bayesian-optimisation seeds matched it. The best design (two 18.5 mm cups, 80 kPa, 60 L/min) holds 77% of items quickly; a catalogue-default single 30 mm cup holds none quickly (J 0.075). Stylised, with assumed constants, no learned policy and no general-purpose arm modelled.

codesign-aero9 tests

Should a quadrotor’s airframe and its learned attitude controller be sized together, or one after the other?

Should a quadrotor's airframe and its learned roll controller be sized together? Yes in this stylised model: joint CMA-ES reaches 5.25° RMS roll error, equal to the grid optimum, against 7.06° for lightest-airframe-first; a controller reused across airframes is worse on 41% of them.

Abstract Code →

A 15-minute inspection quadrotor with two airframe variables (arm length, prop diameter) and a three-gain roll policy found by CMA-ES, scored on held-out gusty step-tracking episodes. At 320 evaluations, joint CMA-ES reaches 5.25° RMS (the brute-force grid optimum is 5.25°), against 5.63° for joint random search, 5.52° for a frozen controller, 5.88° for bilevel search and 7.06° for design-first (lightest airframe, then tune). A controller tuned on one airframe and reused on others is 1° or more worse on 41% of cells. Gust level did not move the optimum. Stylised roll-axis model with assumed constants; the policy is linear, not deep RL; no flight software-in-the-loop.

codesign-aero-robust7 tests

Does the best quadrotor airframe stay best when motor strength, mass and motor lag are randomised?

Does the best quadrotor airframe stay best under widened motor-strength, mass and lag randomisation? Mostly: top five unchanged (Spearman 0.75), but retuning gains helps the median airframe 0.91° (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Robustness follow-up to codesign-aero: 50 feasible airframes, each with roll gains tuned on the nominal, a narrow or a wide randomised plant (torque 0.7–1.0×, inertia 0.9–1.3×, motor lag 1–2×, assumed). With nominal-tuned gains the nominal and wide rankings have Spearman 0.75 and the same top five; the nominal optimum is 2nd of 50 on the wide plant, 0.17° behind the best. Tuning gains on the wide plant helps the median airframe by 0.91°. One tuning run per cell, so neighbouring ranks are within noise. Stylised, roll axis only, simulation only.

codesign-aero-joint5 tests

Should a quadrotor’s airframe and controller gains be searched jointly when the plant is uncertain?

Should airframe and gains be searched jointly under an uncertain plant? Yes in this stylised model: joint CMA-ES at 960 evaluations (5.75° median held-out, 8 seeds) beats random search and a 4800-evaluation grid-then-tune best cell (6.00°).

Abstract Code →

Follow-up to codesign-aero-robust: joint CMA-ES over arm length, prop diameter and three roll gains, trained on the wide randomised plant, against uniform random search at equal budget and against grid-then-tune. On held-out episodes the median CMA-ES winner reaches 5.75° at 960 evaluations (8 seeds, 5.70–5.87°) and 5.74° at 4800, random search 6.17° and 5.96°, and the grid’s best cell (4800 evaluations, picked on the held-out set) 6.00°. Stylised: assumed constants and ranges, roll axis only, five parameters, coarse grid reference.

codesign-aero-seeds6 tests

Is the quadrotor airframe ranking from one tuning run reproducible, or is it tuning noise?

Is the airframe ranking from one tuning run reproducible? With wide-tuned gains yes (Spearman 0.99 over six replicates); with nominal-tuned gains it is noisier (0.84) and the earlier 0.17° regret was within noise (stylised).

Abstract Code →

Seed-repeat follow-up to codesign-aero-robust: the 50-airframe grid is re-tuned and re-scored six times with independent CMA-ES, training and held-out seeds. With gains tuned on the wide randomised plant the ranking is highly reproducible (Spearman 0.99 between replicates, same top five every time); with nominal-tuned gains it is noisier (0.84, winner varies in arm length), so the earlier “rank 2, 0.17° regret” was inside the noise. Retuning for the wide plant helps the median airframe by 0.88° on average. Stylised (assumed constants, roll axis only, six replicates).

codesign-transfer6 tests

Does the ranking of printable soft-fruit gripper designs survive a shift in friction, fruit, placement error and print tolerance?

Does the ranking of soft-fruit gripper designs survive a shift in friction, fruit, placement error and print tolerance? Yes in this model (Spearman 0.993 over 600 designs), but the nominal optimum loses 13% of its J and a robust optimum gains only about 0.015 on average; sim-to-sim, assumed ranges.

Abstract Code →

Takes the codesign-agri contact model unchanged and widens what it holds fixed: per world the fruit size, placement error, wetness, bruise threshold and stem pull are drawn, and the printed gripper differs from the design (pad modulus, force and width tolerance). Over 600 random feasible designs and 30 held-out worlds the Spearman rank correlation with the nominal world is 0.993, so a nominal winner is a good candidate. The level still falls: the nominal CMA-ES optimum loses 13% of its objective (0.653 to 0.567), and a robust optimum trained on 10 other worlds gains only 0.015 on average and 0.034 in the worst world, from single runs. Sim-to-sim in a stylised model with assumed ranges; no gripper was printed.

codesign-ceiling7 tests

Which grasp scenes can no printable two-finger gripper hold, and what limits the ceiling?

Which grasp scenes can no printable two-finger gripper hold? 10 of 140 (7%), all spheres with the hand more than about 2 mm above their centre height; lowering only the hand holds all 10, so the 0.85 plateau in codesign-diagnose is scene geometry, not friction or force (stylised, found after the fact, one intervention).

Abstract Code →

Why every method in codesign-diagnose plateaued near 0.85. A MuJoCo sweep of 150 feasible gripper designs over 140 grasp scenes (cylinders, spheres, boxes of 150–1500 g) finds that 10 scenes (7%) are held by no design at any force, and all 10 are spheres where the simulated hand sits more than about 2 mm above the sphere’s centre height. Lowering only the hand height holds all 10 (hand at table level) or 8 of 10 (hand at sphere-centre height), so the ceiling comes from the scene geometry, not from friction, mass, force or finger strength; relaxing the finger strength limit lifts the best single design from 0.77 to 0.89 on fresh scenes. Stylised simulator; the 10-scene pattern was found after the fact and confirmed by one intervention.

codesign-diagnose10 tests

Does diagnostic feedback (a failure summary, full rollout logs) help a design loop find better printable grippers than the score alone?

Does a failure summary or full rollout logs help a gripper design loop beyond the score alone? No: three scripted readers end at 0.84 to 0.86 best test success, like random search, CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation (stylised, rule-based readers, not an LLM).

Abstract Code →

Three scripted readers of a MuJoCo gripper co-design loop differ only in what they may read about each design: the score, a failure summary, or full rollout logs. At 40 designs and 8 seeds all end at 0.84–0.86 median best held-out grasp success, the same as random search, CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation (standard error about 0.05), and the richest reader proposes the worst designs on average. Negative and stylised: the readers are author-written rules, not an LLM.

codesign-forcefresh10 tests

How much of a best-of-40 gripper design's score is selection noise when every design gets its own trained grasp force?

Do agent-proposed gripper fingers beat random search, CMA-ES and Bayesian optimisation when each design gets its own trained grasp force? On 40 held-out scenes all methods' best seeds reach 0.93 to 0.95 and the ranking is within noise; on 100 fresh scenes the session agent's 0.95 falls to 0.81, level with the baseline median (stylised, preliminary, mostly negative).

Abstract Code →

Companion to codesign-gripper with a different objective and a searched grasp force. Five parameters of a 3D-printable two-finger gripper (width, thickness, length, V-groove depth, TPU pad) are searched under a print-time cap; for each design a grasp force is tuned in MuJoCo and the design is scored on 40 held-out scenes (cylinders, spheres, boxes of 100–900 g). With 40 designs each, the best seeds of all three baselines reach 0.93–0.95 test success (medians 0.875, 0.887, 0.900 over 8 seeds) and one session-agent trajectory (n = 1, hand-written proposals) reaches 0.95 after 20 designs. On 100 fresh scenes every method’s best design drops 0.06–0.07 on average and the agent’s falls to 0.81, level with the baseline median: the task is nearly saturated and the ranking is within noise (standard error about 0.05). Stylised: assumed costs and strengths, rigid fingers, grid-plus-refine policy search rather than deep RL, nothing printed.

27

Laundry-hanging robots

A robot that takes clothes from a dryer or a loader and hangs every item, with hangers designed in a simulation feedback loop: drape models, hanger shapes, hang-or-fold decisions and the robot cell. Topic page →

hanger-fit14 tests

What hanger shape keeps a shirt in shape, and can one hanger fit every size?

What hanger shape keeps a shirt in shape, and can one hanger fit every size for a laundry-hanging robot? In a 2D cloth-drape simulation the best single fixed hanger leaves garments 2.1 cm RMS from their worn shape (5.4 cm for a child's tee), one adjustable-width hanger set per garment 0.18 cm, and a rack of four widths under 1 cm for every size; thin wire ends fold the cloth at the tip. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A 2D cloth-drape model (discrete elastic chain with penalty contact, solved by L-BFGS) scores how far a garment hangs from its worn shape, and CMA-ES designs the hanger. Over seven sizes from a child’s tee to XXL, the best single fixed hanger averages 2.1 cm RMS shape error (5.4 cm worst). One adjustable-width hanger set per garment averages 0.18 cm (0.22 worst), 12× better, and a rack of four widths keeps every size within 1 cm. Wire and plastic hangers fold the cloth at the tip (about 65°/cm against 14° worn); a 2–3 cm round end removes it, but a loop scored on shape alone converges on wire-thin ends. CMA-ES beats random search (0.19 vs 0.44 cm at 150 drapes). Stylised: 2D, no friction, assumed fabric constants.

hanger-fold13 tests

Should a laundry robot hang a garment or fold it, and what can it sense to tell?

Should a laundry robot hang a garment or fold it, and what can it sense to tell? A stretch-set and crease-set model on five fabric archetypes: woven shirts and linen are better hung, tees, fleece and heavy knits better folded; shoulder width, mass and stretch when lifted pick the better action for 89–91% of 600 simulated garments (always fold: 59%). The split depends mostly on the assumed crease model. Stylised, assumed fabric constants.

Abstract Code →

Adds a stretch-set model for hanging (permanent shoulder lengthening from hanger-fit’s drape) and a crease-set model for folding to five fabric archetypes, prices both in cm of departure from the pressed shape, and learns a rule on 600 simulated garments. Woven shirts and linen are better hung, t-shirts, fleece and heavy knits better folded. Shoulder width, mass and stretch when lifted choose the better action for 89–91% of garments in 5-fold cross-validation (always fold: 59%; adding the fabric class: 94%); width alone adds nothing. The split is driven by the assumed crease model: a 6 h stack instead of 48 h moves the share better hung from 41% to 8%, while a hundredfold change in the stretch penalty moves it from 48% to 37%. Stylised: every fabric constant is assumed, the population is synthetic, no motion.

hanger-insert20 tests

How does a laundry robot get a hanger into a garment, and what does it cost the neck?

How does a laundry robot get a hanger into a garment, and what does it cost the neck? A swept-section model of a rigid, telescoping or folding hanger passing a neck or hem loop: rigid hangers need 43–61 cm of loop, a tee's neck stretches up to 33% and a buttoned shirt collar cannot take them at all (shirts go in at the hem, 10 s against 6 s); a hanger that collapses to a 10 cm half width needs 31 cm. The round end hanger-fit wants costs about 3 cm more. Stylised, assumed constants.

Abstract Code →

A swept-section geometry model passes a hanger through a garment’s neck or hem loop: the loop must reach round the hull of the hanger’s cross-section, and a planner finds the path of least stretch. A rigid hanger needs 43–61 cm of loop (a whole arm), which stretches a tee’s neck by up to 33% against an assumed 35% limit, and a buttoned woven collar cannot take it, so every shirt goes in at the hem and has its hook threaded out blind (about 10 s against 6 s). A telescoping hanger collapsed to a 10 cm half width needs 31 cm and passes five of seven shirt sizes; folding the arms down 60° needs 37–40 cm. The 2–3 cm round end that hanger-fit needs adds only about 3 cm of loop, so insertion changes the width design, not the end. Stylised: planar hanger, perimeter bound rather than cloth, assumed stretch limits and robot constants.

hanger-cell12 tests

How many dryers can one laundry-hanging robot serve, and what limits it?

How many dryers can one laundry-hanging robot serve, and what limits it? A discrete-event model of the whole cell (pick, sense, feeder, insertion, rail, fold table) fed by hanger-insert and hanger-fold: with assumed times one arm clears a 25-item load in 8.9 min (about 5 dryers), a second arm adds 22% before the fold table binds, and the five hanger designs differ by at most 3%; pick and fold times dominate. Stylised, assumed station times.

Abstract Code →

A discrete-event model of the whole cell (pick, sense, hanger feeder, insertion, rail and fold table) fed with hanger-insert’s insertion times and hanger-fold’s hang-or-fold shares. With assumed pick and fold times, one arm clears a 25-item dryer load in 8.9 min (169 items/h, about 5 dryers on a 45 min cycle); a second arm adds 22% and then the fold table is the bottleneck. The five hanger designs differ by at most 3% in time per load. Doubling the fold time adds 5.9 min and doubling the pick time 3.4, against under 1 min for insertion, though a threefold slower insertion costs a one-arm cell 22%. A poor picker (0.60 success) costs 13% throughput but leaves 7 of every 100 items for a person. Stylised: every station time except insertion is an assumed placeholder, no layout or collisions.

hanger-print11 tests

Can the hanger a cloth simulation designed be 3D-printed, and does it hold a garment?

Can the hanger a cloth simulation designed be 3D-printed, and does it hold a garment? hanger-fit's adjustable shape and four-width rack as parametric STL and OpenSCAD with a beam check: the round-ended arm has a safety factor of 40–70 in assumed PLA, a wire-like arm 0.13, and no useful width fits a 220 mm bed whole (one arm with its hub does). Stylised, assumed material constants.

Abstract Code →

Exports hanger-fit’s adjustable shape and four-width rack as parametric STL and OpenSCAD, with a cantilever strength, deflection and print-bed check. Printed flat in PLA under assumed constants (1.5 kg garment, 2× motion factor), the round-ended arm (end radius 2.86 cm) has a safety factor of 40–70 at 12 mm depth and bends under 0.04 mm, so strength never limits it; a wire-like arm (end radius 1.5 mm) has a safety factor of 0.13 and fails. No hanger of useful width fits a 220 mm bed whole, but one arm with its hub does up to 24.8 cm. Stylised: assumed material constants, flat extrusion, OpenSCAD files not rendered, no two-piece joint.

hanger-pick11 tests

How should a laundry robot pick one garment out of a tangled dryer load?

How should a laundry robot pick one garment out of a tangled dryer load? In a stylised disc-pile model aiming at a visible opening takes 13.4 assumed seconds per garment against 22.7 for pinching the top and regrasping, and pushing garments aside first is slower (17.7 s); one arm then serves 151, 110 and 127 items an hour. Assumed times, not a robot.

Abstract Code →

A stylised 2D pile of overlapping disc garments, 40% with the opening hidden by the garment itself, emptied by three scripted policies with assumed times. Aiming at a visible neck or waistband takes 13.4 s per garment against 22.7 s for pinching the top and regrasping; pushing garments aside first is slower (17.7 s) because neighbours rarely hide every opening, the garments themselves do. In hanger-cell the policies give 151, 110 and 127 items an hour for one arm, against 169 for its placeholder pick. Stylised: assumed times, disc cloth, not a measurement of a robot.

hanger-pickbreak5 tests

How long may a laundry robot spend finding a garment's opening before blind pinching is faster?

How long may a laundry robot spend finding a garment's opening before blind pinching is faster? On paired piles of the stylised pick model, aiming wins only if the detector costs under about 9 s per pick (95% interval 8.9 to 9.6, assumed times); the limit falls as regrasps get likelier to succeed or more openings are hidden. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

On paired piles in the stylised hanger-pick model, aiming at a visible opening beats a blind pinch only if finding the opening costs under 9.2 s per pick (95% interval 8.9 to 9.6, assumed times). The threshold grows with the time of a regrasp (2.9 s to 18.7 s for 2 to 12 s), shrinks as regrasps succeed more often (14.7 s to 3.9 s) and as more openings are hidden (15.3 s to 0), and does not depend on pile size. Sweeping garments aside first beats aiming only when a sweep costs under half a second. Stylised: every time is an assumed placeholder.

hanger-misaim5 tests

How often may a laundry robot's opening detector aim wrong before blind pinching is faster?

How often may a laundry robot's opening detector aim wrong before blind pinching is faster? In the stylised hanger-pick model each 10 points of detector error cost about 1 s of look-time budget: 9.2 s per pick when perfect, 4.5 s at 50% wrong, none when always wrong. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

In the stylised hanger-pick model a wrong aim costs one wasted grasp and then the same regrasp hunt as a blind pinch. The look-time budget of the detector falls almost linearly with its error: 9.2 s per pick when perfect, 6.3 s at 30% wrong, 4.5 s at 50%, about 0 when always wrong (300 paired piles, assumed times). At a 1 s look aiming still wins until about 88% of aims are wrong; at 5 s the limit is 43%, at 9 s 3%, and an 11 s look loses even when perfect. Stylised: every time and probability is an assumed placeholder; error is independent per pick.

hanger-3d4 tests

Does the 2D hanger result survive in 3D, with front and back panels and a hanger arm of finite depth?

Does the 2D hanger result survive in 3D? With an arm as deep as the garment a 3D cloth sheet matches the 2D drape (within 0.05 cm for round-ended hangers) and the best width is again 1 cm over the half shoulder; a shallow arm lets the front and back panels fall 5–8 cm and raises a wooden hanger's error from 0.4 to 2.0 cm. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

A 3D cloth sheet (stretch, shear and bending in both directions, penalty contact with a swept arm) reproduces the 2D hanger-fit drape when the arm is as deep as the garment: shape error within 0.05 cm for the round-ended and wooden hangers and within 0.6 cm for thin wire (which is resolution-sensitive). The width finding holds: the best arm is 1 cm wider than the half shoulder for child, M and XXL tees, in 2D and 3D. What 2D cannot show is depth: on a 3 cm half-depth arm the wooden hanger's whole-sheet error rises from 0.4 to 2.0 cm, and on a rod to 3.8 cm, as the front and back panels fall 5–8 cm below the arm. Stylised: assumed fabric constants, one 20 cm strip, coarse grid (0.5 cm by 2.2 cm), no collar, sleeve seam or friction.

hanger-cellpick6 tests

How many dryers can one laundry-hanging arm serve once the pick is simulated, not assumed?

How many dryers can one laundry-hanging arm serve once the pick is simulated, not assumed? A one-arm cell drops from 169 to 147 garments an hour (5.1 to 4.4 dryers) with look-then-aim picking and to 104 with blind pinching; with two arms the fold table is the limit. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

Replacing the assumed 8 s, 0.85 pick of the hanger-cell discrete-event model with the hanger-pick pile model cuts a one-arm cell from 169 to 147 garments hung or folded per hour (5.1 to 4.4 dryers) with look-then-aim picking, and to 104 with blind pinching. With two arms the fold table is the limit and the policy matters little (206 assumed, 201 aiming, 179 pinching); quartering all pick times still leaves about 6.2 dryers. Aiming leaves 2.8 garments per 100 for a person, pinching 7.2. Stylised: every station time is an assumed placeholder.

hanger-split13 tests

Can a laundry hanger be printed in two halves on a 220 mm bed, and is the bolted joint strong enough?

Can a laundry hanger be printed in two halves on a 220 mm bed, and is the bolted joint strong enough? A half-lap hub joint with two M4 bolts lets every width up to XXL print on a 220 mm bed; the joint (safety factor 3.7–13) is then weaker than the arm (40–70), and printed pegs fail. Stylised, assumed material constants; nothing printed.

Abstract Code →

A half-lap hub joint with two M4 bolts lets every hanger-fit width up to the 25.8 cm XXL print on a 220 mm bed as one part printed twice. In a beam model with assumed PLA constants, the joint, not the arm, is then the weak point: safety factor 3.7–13 against 40–70 for the arm, set by bolt bearing on the half-depth boss, and the joint needs 4–9 mm of depth against the arm’s 0.8 mm. Printed pegs instead of bolts fail (safety factor 0.9–1.8 for 4 mm pegs). Stylised; nothing was printed or tested.

hanger-wrap5 tests

Does a second 3D cloth model, wrapped over the hanger arm, agree with the 2D hanger drape?

Does a second 3D cloth model, wrapped over the arm, agree with the 2D hanger drape? On the cases both run, it picks the same best arm width (22.8 cm for a size M tee; error correlation 0.994) and adds the bend across the arm (119 deg/cm over a 0.5 cm arm, 34 over a 2 cm one), but disagrees for a heavy knit on a thin arm and is not grid-converged. Stylised.

Abstract Code →

An independent 3D mass-spring sheet that wraps over a round-ended arm (cross-check of hanger-3d), draped on the hangers of hanger-fit with the same fabric constants and mass. It picks the same best arm width as the 2D chain (22.8 cm for a size M tee; error correlation 0.994 over a width sweep), with error 0.1–0.4 cm higher near the optimum, and adds the bend across the arm: 119 deg/cm over a 0.5 cm arm against 34 over a 2 cm one. It disagrees for a heavy knit on a thin arm (17.8 cm against 5.6 cm error) and is not grid-converged (1.19 against 0.62 cm at 1 and 0.5 cm spacing). Stylised, assumed fabric constants.

Machine learning on qualitative data

What LLMs make possible with interviews, open-ended survey answers, reviews and tickets, and when counts built from an LLM's codes can be trusted. Topic page →

qual-correction13 tests

Can you do machine learning on qualitative data with an LLM, and when can you trust the numbers?

Can you do machine learning on qualitative data with an LLM, and when can you trust the numbers? Simulated LLM coders with known error: an 89%-accurate coder (κ = 0.72) understates a 30% code at 26% with 0% interval coverage, and when it reads one group's answers less accurately the naive group gap has the wrong sign (+3.6 against −4 points, "significant" 80% of the time). Prediction-powered inference with 200 hand-coded answers per group removes the bias and narrows intervals 23–26% against hand-coding alone, but is wider below ~80% coder accuracy. Stdlib tool (κ, Krippendorff's α, PPI). Simulated, no real model.

Abstract Code →

An LLM can code free text (“does this answer mention cost?”) so that it can be counted and modelled like numbers, but its codes need a correction first. In a seeded simulation, an 89%-accurate LLM coder (Cohen’s κ = 0.72) understates a 30% code at 26%, and its naive 95% interval covers the truth in 0 of 1,000 studies. When the LLM reads one group’s answers less accurately, the naive group gap comes out at +3.6 points against a true −4, the wrong sign, and is “significant” 80% of the time. Prediction-powered inference with 200 random hand-coded answers per group removes the bias, covers the truth 95–98% of the time and gives intervals 23–26% narrower than hand-coding alone. Below about 80% coder accuracy, though, its interval is wider. Includes a stdlib tool (κ, Krippendorff’s α, PPI) and a survey of five ways LLMs bring qualitative data into ML. Simulated coders, not a real model.

qual-regression5 tests

What happens to a regression coefficient when the regressor is an LLM's code?

What happens to a regression coefficient when the regressor is an LLM's code? Naive OLS gives 0.74 for a true 1.00 (0% coverage) and biases a perfectly measured covariate when coder error depends on it; DSL with ~210 hand-coded items fixes both (coverage 94–97%) but narrows the coded coefficient's interval only 14%; per-class PPI fixes 3-class shares. Simulated coders.

Abstract Code →

Regressing an outcome on an LLM's codes attenuates the coded variable's coefficient (0.74 for a true 1.00, interval coverage 0% in 300 simulated studies) and, when the coder's error depends on another covariate, biases that perfectly measured covariate too (0.467 against 0.50, coverage 60%). Design-based supervised learning (DSL) with about 210 hand-coded items drawn at a known 7% rate recovers both (1.01 and 0.50, coverage 94–97%) but narrows the coded coefficient’s interval by only 14%. For a 3-class code, naive class shares are off by up to 8.5 points with 0% coverage; per-class PPI covers 95.5–97%. Simulated coders only; no real LLM was run.

qual-real6 tests

Does the prediction-powered correction work on real hand-coded text?

Does the prediction-powered correction work on real hand-coded text? On 3,188 GoEmotions comments a naive-Bayes coder (kappa 0.14) is wrong on prevalence (13% against 25%, 0% coverage) and overstates a length gap six-fold; PPI repairs both but is wider than hand-coding alone. Not an LLM (no key).

Abstract Code →

On 3,188 real Reddit comments with human emotion labels (GoEmotions), a naive-Bayes coder (kappa 0.14) reports 13.3% negative emotion against a human 25.3% (coverage 0 of 500 draws) and a short-versus-long gap of −0.170 against a true −0.028, because it misses 94% of negative emotion in short comments but 70% in long ones. PPI with 200 hand-coded items recovers both (coverage 0.94–0.97) but is 6–19% wider than using the hand-coded items alone, since the coders are weak. The coders are a trained classifier and a word list, not an LLM (no API key).

qual-hypothesis7 tests

Do hypotheses about what separates two sets of documents survive a held-out check?

Do hypotheses about what separates two sets of documents survive a held-out check? On 5,313 GoEmotions comments a word-counting proposer's effects are 7.6× too large at 100 discovery comments (1.5× at 2,000); a BH check on 3,000 held-out comments confirms almost nothing with shuffled labels, but 36–59% of confirmed hypotheses are the label's own vocabulary. Not an LLM proposer.

Abstract Code →

On 5,313 real GoEmotions comments, a word-counting proposer that picks the 20 words most associated with negative emotion in a small discovery sample overstates their effects 7.6× at 100 discovery comments (0.095 against 0.013 held-out) and 1.5× at 2,000. A Benjamini–Hochberg check on 3,000 held-out comments confirms 0.8 of the 20 at 100 comments and 14.7 at 2,000, and with shuffled labels confirms almost none (at most 5.5% of splits any), but 36–59% of confirmed hypotheses are the label's own vocabulary (“sorry”, “hate”), so replication is not explanation. The proposer is not an LLM, and the restatement flag is a crude word list.

qual-register4 tests

Does a coder's error depend on writing register, and can a hand-coded sample tell?

Does a coder's error depend on writing register, and can a hand-coded sample tell? On 3,188 GoEmotions comments, error differs by 1.9 points (naive-Bayes) or none (lexicon) between formal and informal text, yet the naive register gap is three times too large; an audit with up to 800 hand-coded items flags it no more often than chance. Not an LLM (no key); register is a proxy, not a dialect.

Abstract Code →

On 3,188 real GoEmotions comments split by writing register (formal: capitalised and ends in punctuation), a naive-Bayes coder's error rate differs by only 1.9 points (0.282 formal, 0.263 informal) and a lexicon coder's by none, yet the naive register gap is three times too large (−0.043 against −0.0145, coverage 0%). A z test for differential error on a random hand-coded sample of 50 to 800 items flagged 3–6.5% of samples, the false-positive rate, so an ordinary audit cannot see a difference of this size (a rough calculation puts it near 8,000 items per group); prediction-powered inference covers the gap (95.6–96.8%). Register is a typography proxy, not a dialect label, and the coders are not LLMs.
